<header>LETTERS</header>
<meta>catchword: my</meta>

I am overcome with embarrassment by the disparity between Your style and mine, which betrays my lack of skill in the public light—a lack that ought rather to remain hidden in the shadows. Indeed, it would be better to keep it concealed, were it not in the interest of our current age for the learned world to know upon what pillars the <term>August House of Guelph</term><note>original: "Domus Augusta Guelphica." The ancient and powerful European dynasty ruling Brunswick-Lüneburg. The term "August" refers both to their venerable status and to their father, Duke August the Younger.</note> now rests, and for a promise to be made, by some clear sign, of what all good people may expect from You. 

For since you began this exercise of literary exchange with me—through the kindness of your Most Serene Lord Father—I have come to know, with both amazement and great joy, the perfect standard of your **Education** and **Instruction**, the nobility of your **Character**, the brilliance of your **Talent**, the sweetness and courtesy of your **Manners**, and the faithfulness and skill of those **Governing** <note>original: "Administrantium." This refers to the tutors and court officials responsible for the princes' upbringing.</note> your affairs. Yet this would be of little value unless, through my efforts, this "example without equal" <note>original: "sine Exemplo Exemplum." A rhetorical flourish suggesting the princes' progress is unprecedented.</note> were made known to others and set forth as a model to be imitated by the **Youth** of more noble standing. Although this may do little for my own reputation...

<summary>Johann Valentin Andreae expresses his humility regarding his own writing style compared to that of the young princes, arguing that publishing their correspondence serves as a public testament to the excellence of their education and the future of the House of Guelph.</summary>

...is joined with mine, the dullness of which your sharpness, the squalor of which your brilliance, the roughness of which your refinement, the sluggishness of which your eagerness, and the decay of which your radiating light exposes. This one thing I most earnestly ask of You: that just as you already represent your Father—that incomparable example of our age—in *Piety, Virtue, Learning, and Courtesy* <note>original: "Pietate, Virtute, Eruditione, & Comitate." To me, nothing among earthly things has shone more favorably or more majestically than this; indeed, it encompasses the very sum of my happiness. And so that...

Three hundred fifty-three Letters from Your hand, in this eight-year period and more since you received me into Your favor, I have received with deep reverence. Whether I received them with greater pleasure, or admiration, or indeed amazement, I could not easily say. had produced; But when one after another [of these letters] bore witness to the wonderful inclination of Your noble mind toward me—or more truly, Your condescension—and a kindness <note>original: "facilitatem", meaning ease of access or affability</note> hardly ever heard of, I truly had to admire this generosity; nor shall I ever cease to admire it as long as I live, because I can find no example of it anywhere else.

But now, after I have also been drenched by the rain of Your Munificence, which never fails to flow from Your most merciful letters and waters my entire household <term>Oeconomia: here referring to the management of his domestic and financial affairs, which the Duke’s patronage supported</term>, I am completely stunned that, throughout all this time, no weariness <note>original: "nauseam", literally a sense of sea-sickness or disgust</note> toward me has crept over You, so that Your Patience has grown to such a number and accumulation [of letters], and that I need not fear any exhaustion or silence on Your part toward me in the future. while I freely profess myself unworthy of the name of Your Client and Servant. Therefore, I present myself to You, Most Indulgent Prince, and for three hundred letters, I give three thousand—nay, tens of thousands—of thanks, most humbly; and since I find no other example in the Holy Scripture <note>original: "Sacro Codice"</note> that fits You so well as that of the Angel Raphael <term>Alexicacus: a Greek epithet meaning "averter of evil." # LETTERS #

->DEDICATION<-

<meta>catchword: las (completing "Epistolas")</meta>

I am at a loss; you have *withdrawn* <note>original: "subduxisti"</note> me from many injuries and *exalted* <note>original: "sublimâsti"</note> me among Your Clients. What shall I repay? **NOTHING**. For just as all things came from nothing, so that which is Everything leaves nothing but nothingness behind it; or indeed, if there remains any residue within me, let it be this one tiny point of my heart—or let it be the heart itself—upon which is inscribed **WEIGH OUT** <note>original: "EXPENDE"</note>. This is, of course, the eternal memory of Your Great Deeds <note>original: "Magnaliorum"</note>, and the arrows of my sighs, sent upward to God for Your well-being and that of Your family. If these should satisfy You (and they will indeed satisfy Your Greatness), oh, what a blessed Debtor I am, to whom so easy a payment is entrusted! 

I pray to **GOD** from my soul that after one and then another Century <term>Centuriam: A collection of one hundred items; here referring to the groups of letters being published.</term> of letters, I may owe new thanks to You while You are safe and vigorous, and that I may pay them again with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength, for I am indebted to You with a devotion second only to that which I owe **GOD**. For the present, please receive the interest <term>interusuriam: literally "inter-interest," referring to a payment made for the interim use of capital; here used metaphorically for the gratitude offered before the full debt can be repaid.</term> on this debt: the letters of Your most Noble Sons—

<summary>Andreae expresses his profound gratitude to Duke Augustus, claiming he can offer "nothing" in return for the Duke's protection other than his heart's devotion. He presents the letters of the Duke's own sons as a form of metaphorical interest on his massive debt of gratitude.</summary>

# Explanation
## of the
## Frontispiece.

Bodies placed beneath the Sun, from which they receive splendor, return it to that same source in turn—especially the Moon, which Astronomers teach is not seen when in conjunction with the Sun, because having turned away, she directs back all the light she has drawn to the place from which she received it. From this comes the precept and example given to the ministers of Great Men by **Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa** <note>A powerful Roman general and architect (c. 63–12 BC) who famously attributed his successes to Emperor Augustus rather than himself.</note>, that they should reserve the Name of their achievements for their Masters; so that however much they might excel among others, they would voluntarily grant that same credit to them. With this same caution, **Joab** announced to **King David** that he himself should come to capture **Rabbah** <note>referring to the biblical siege of Rabbah in 2 Samuel 12:26-28; Joab stopped his victory so the King could take the final credit.</note>, now constricted by the cutting off of its water, lest the victory be seen as his own. And **Julius Agricola** <note>The Roman general who conquered much of Britain; his biography was written by his son-in-law Tacitus.</note> never exulted in his deeds for his own fame, but as a minister, he attributed his fortune to his Author and Leader. **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), the Roman historian.</note> also testifies that among the ancient Germans, it was a primary Oath of loyalty to assign their own deeds to the glory of the Prince. How much more rightly then did **David**, the King who was once a shepherd, mindful of his former lot when he had contributed a great sum of Gold, Silver, and Bronze for the construction of the Temple, declare thus:
> To You, **Jehovah**, it is in Your hand both to make great, and to con- <note>original: "con-"; this is a partial word completed on the following page as "confirmare," meaning to strengthen or confirm. The quote is from 1 Chronicles 29:12.</note>

# THE STAIRCASE OF DESTINY
# OF AUGUSTUS,
## Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg.
->On his 70th Birthday.<-
->In the Year of Christ 1648.<-

---

*It was night, and sleep, pitying the hard labors of men,*
*poured calm rest through weary limbs;*
*and now it gradually gave way to the whitening East,*
*at that time when true dreams are said to come to sleepers,*
<note>In classical literature, dreams occurring at dawn were believed to be prophetic or "true."</note>
*a time you could call neither quite morning, nor yet night;*
*I seemed, carried away in sleep, to see the Court of Lüneburg.*
*There, the Welf heights <note>original: *Guelphyta*; referring to the Welf/Guelph dynasty and their residence in Wolfenbüttel.</note> rise with their lofty roofs;*
*the bright palace shines, a seat most worthy of the gods;*
*it is enclosed by walls and solid structures on every side,*
*while moats with standing waters surround it.*
*Within, everything glitters with royal luxury.*
*The great gate of the house, columns of solid rock,*
*bronze beams, and posts with iron hinges,*
*stand above the bridge held up by strong chains.*
*The roof shines on both sides, raised high with many chambers*
*and dense halls beneath the gables.*
*Here the Duke’s Archive and the records of Clio <note>original: *Clejus*; likely referring to Clio, the Muse of history, signifying the palace's role as a center of learning and record-keeping.</note> shine.*
*The Court stands nearby, opposite the royal roof,*
*inhabited by the talents of the Fathers and the Holy Senate,*
*where nourishing Themis <note>The Greek goddess of divine law and order.</note> claims her seat, and*
*the Virgin Astraea <note>The goddess of Justice, who was the last of the immortals to leave the earth at the end of the Golden Age.</note> keeps her tribunal; they stand facing the long*
*porticos of the hall, furnished with firm columns.*
*Attached nearby is the Church, hallowed by piety,*
*above which the halls and many dining rooms shine,*
*looking down from above into the clear moats.*
*Near these appear the inner sanctuaries of the Great Gods,*

There, the works of craftsmen and floors of painted marble 
shine, and <term>mosaic floors<note>original: *asarota*; refers to a specific type of Greco-Roman mosaic floor that depicts "unswept" scraps from a banquet.</note></term> lie beneath their figures,

I cannot fill my mind enough, and I burn with looking 
at these things with my eyes, while I turn them over in my eager mind; 
while I am amazed, and remain fixed in a single gaze, 
even daring to touch a Book closer with these fingers. 
Suddenly **Augustus** stood there; the doors having been opened, 
he enters, dressed in fur, the **Venerable Hero**; 
his robe sweeps the ground, and a <term>small cap<note>original: *pileolus*; a skullcap often worn by scholars or clergy.</note></term> 
brushed the white hair on the top of his head; then by chance turning 
a paper in his hands, he seeks out the lecterns of books with thirsty eyes.

## The Fatal Staircase of AUGUSTUS, consisting of seven steps, described with its two ends.

The steps of the staircase stood at the end of the archive-room,
*The Staircase was marked by seven triple-cleft steps,*
*This signifies the turns of fate and the Master's fortune,*
*[So the Spirit, who perhaps guided me, advised]*
*By which it is granted to Augustus to escape to the upper airs,*
*Each step marks two <term>lustra<note>A *lustrum* is a period of five years; therefore, two lustra equal ten years.</note></term>, and a ten-year course.*
*And already he towers above by as many steps of age,*
*Since burning Virtue carried Him to the highest peaks,*
*Standing now at the honored peak of old age.*
**[a]** <margin>1. The happiness of the lineage.</margin> *The first portion of the staircase gives entry to life,*
*And represents the first five-year periods of a blossoming age,*
*And the Brunswick Line, from a happy birth of blood,*
*Once led from the great lineage of <term>Torquatus<note>A reference to the Roman family of the Manlii Torquati, whom the House of Welf/Brunswick claimed as ancestors to assert ancient Roman nobility.</note></term>;*
*A long series of Fathers, a long line of time; who could recount*
*So many Heroes, a race from the high stock of the Gods?*
**[b]** <margin>Albert the Great, ninth ancestor of Augustus.</margin> *Shall I speak of the battles of Albert, and the fights of Mars,*
*From which he earned for himself the name "the Great" through the ages?*
*Or* **[c]** <margin>Magnus the Pious, the seventh [ancestor].</margin> *shall I recall the Great one warming with solid piety?*
*From whom the paternal race comes, to whom victory later brought praise,*
*And carried the Name to the heavens for* **[d]** <margin>Otto the Victorious, the third [ancestor].</margin> *Otto.*
*And it is enough for the great-great-grandfather of Augustus, if I touch on the nearest,*
*Lest we go back through ten centuries, from one [man]*
**[e]** <margin>1579.</margin> *the illustrious Mother Ursula gave Augustus to his father Henry;*
*She was born to Francis, Duke of Saxony and <term>Angaria<note>Angria or Angaria was a historical region of the medieval Duchy of Saxony.</note></term>,*
*And likewise born from a mother of the Elbe, Sibylla,*
*(Each lineage connected in royal preparation)*
*After whom she impressed the name from her sword-bearing brother* **[f]** <margin>Augustus, Elector of Saxony.</margin> *[Augustus],*
*Whom he set for himself as the <term>rule<note>original: *amussim*; a carpenter's tool used to ensure a surface is perfectly flat, here used metaphorically for a standard of conduct or a perfect model.</note></term> of his life's reign,*
*By whose examples he well established this threshold of his age,*

**[a]** 1. The happiness of the lineage. **[b]** Albert the Great, ninth of Augustus's ancestors. **[c]** Magnus the Pious, the seventh. **[d]** Otto the Victorious, the third.
**[e]** 1579 <note>The year of Duke Augustus's birth.</note>. **[f]** Augustus, Elector of Saxony <note>The Duke's godfather and namesake; "sword-bearing" refers to his office as Imperial Arch-Marshal.</note>.

[g] <margin>Capacity of nature.</margin> From here, he applied his mind to the noble arts,
And his capable intellect, he softened just like wax,

Becoming an Augustus no less in greatness than his name sounded.
[h] <margin>II. Teachability of Intellect.</margin> Under these auspices, he pursued his course even more keenly,
Now that the golden <term>bulla<note>A golden amulet worn by Roman children to ward off evil; here, it signifies the Duke's transition from childhood to formal education.</note></term> was removed from his simple heart,
He shaped his mind with letters, and with various sweet sounds
He formed his speech, and forged his tongue with the thunder of eloquence,
Following the precepts of both worldly things and moral conduct.
[i] <margin>Skillfulness of Judgment.</margin> And now, with skillful effort, he tires out his very tutors,
Being his own model, he now surpasses both himself and them;
Thus his father Henry and his great uncle <note>Likely referring to Duke Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, a major figure in the family's intellectual history.</note> spurred him on;
He received these stimuli of virtue and seeds of praise
Just as tinder receives fire from sharp strikes;
He nurtured them within himself and exercised his young strength with character;
Hence came his fiery vigor and his heavenly image,
Conquering all things through a diligent and teachable investigation.
[k] <margin>III. Diligence in Studies.</margin> Later, when mature age arrived in years,
And the strength of his character stood firm in his noble breast,
He rose higher to compose a lofty mind
For the great work of Virtue and the glory of the Ancients;
Now encouraged by his own praise, he lightened his labor,
Firing his mind with the love of coming fame.
He pursued his work diligently, and in reading books
He spent his leisure, meditating upon the learned arts;
From which he gained wisdom greater than his fate, even before his first beard.
[l] <margin>1594.</margin> **Rostock** <note>original: *Rostochium*</note> knew this, and the Academy of the **Neckar** <note>original: *Academia Nicri*, referring to the University of Tübingen located on the Neckar river.</note>
[m] <margin>1596.</margin> was amazed; **Strasbourg** <note>original: *Argentina Trebocum*</note>
[n] <margin>1598.</margin> marveled at the Duke's sharp wisdom.
There he bore himself famously, though hardly more than a youth,
Leaving the learned of both places with a longing for him;
[o] <margin>Agility in Equestrian Exercises.</margin> To these arts of Peace, he also joined the reins of Mars <note>A metaphor for military and physical training, referring to the Roman god of war.</note>.

<meta>This page concludes the poetic panegyric for Duke Augustus the Younger, celebrating the restoration of his ancestral seat at Wolfenbüttel and his 70th birthday in 1648. It compares his patronage of the arts to that of the Roman Emperor Augustus and the legendary patron Maecenas.</meta>

For a long time, the castle and the royal seat of the Guelph were missing from these lands;
For an eight-year delay, this piece was missing from the royal robe, [o] <margin>[o] 1636.</margin>
But at last, by a great miracle, it was restored to our Duke, [p] <margin>[p] 1643.</margin>
So that it is equaled by few, and surpasses many in the abundance of its wealth.
Add to this the ancient loyalty and the steadfast spirit of the Brunswick—
->the same,<-
Let a river of fortune gild Augustus and the Fatherland!
[q] <margin>[q] The Liberty of Munificence.</margin> From this, the grace of his munificent right hand commends him,
So that scarcely anyone ever departs from this modern-day Titus <note>Reference to the Roman Emperor Titus, famously known for his generosity.</note>
In grief or with empty hands. Instead, as if to a sacred
->altar,<-
A long line of artisans flows together, where everyone finds not only a Master
But a Maecenas <note>Gaius Maecenas, the famous Roman patron of poets like Virgil and Horace.</note> and a true companion of their craft.
Who would not bring all their hopes and efforts here?
Here, where one does not see a Chimera <note>A mythological monster; here representing a deceptive or worthless pursuit.</note> preferred over a learned man,
Nor a foolish Choraebus <note>A figure in Greek myth known for stupidity, contrasted here with Thales, the wise philosopher.</note> favored over a Thales with a more frenzied mind.
Here one hears not of wine, nor of Venus <note>Used here to mean lust or excess.</note>, nor of empty spectacles and
->pomp,<-
But that the Arts are nourished and refined monuments are brought to completion.
And while others in this stormy time despise the Muses <note>The Camoenae, Roman goddesses of song and poetry.</note>,
Just as the Jew Apella <note>A stereotypical name for a Jew in Roman satire (specifically Horace), here referring to the religious avoidance of pork.</note> avoids the pig, or that Old Man of Samos <note>Pythagoras, who famously forbade his followers from eating beans.</note> avoids the bean: the Brunswick Hero alone
Cherishes them, and holds the skillful in great honor—
Just as that first Augustus once did in the City of Rome,
Who alone held the peaceful reins of the Empire,
A patron of the learned alongside his kind Maecenas.
Proceed, Augustus, Glory of the World! Protect the Clarian Sisters <note>The Muses, named after the Clarian oracle of Apollo.</note>,
Champion them, so that you may live forever in song!
And the Julia of Helmstedt <note>The University of Helmstedt (Academia Julia), which Duke Augustus significantly supported.</note>, now truly your own daughter,
Reassuring her father, shall raise your name to the stars by your merits!
[r] <margin>[r] VII. Longevity of life.</margin> The summit has been reached, and the final goal
->remains,<-
To be stepped upon by an August foot—may the Heavens grant it!
[s] <margin>[s] Augustus’s 70th Birthday, April 10, 1648.</margin> For now he reaches twice-seven periods of five years <note>2 x 7 x 5 = 70 years.</note>,

<meta>This page concludes the celebratory poem for Duke Augustus the Younger's 70th birthday. While the previous page focused on the Duke's physical vitality and the wonders of his court, this section shifts toward a prayer for the preservation of his achievements—specifically his library and collections—against the ravages of war and fire, eventually wishing him a peaceful transition to eternal glory after a long life.</meta>

*An inexhaustible Horn of Plenty, and a fitting display,*
*A harmonic choir, and the various ornaments of these*
->*places,*<-
*The honor of Justice, of Art, and of Religion,*
*And may it be allowed to celebrate these sights in light poetic verse:* <note>The original "cothurno" (buskin) refers to the high-soled boot worn by Greek tragic actors, signifying an elevated or formal poetic style.</note>
*We have eyes, ears, and the whispers of fame.*
*No face was seen, except for what the painting spoke,*
*Submitted by a majestic hand, a living Image,*
*Meanwhile, I shall feed my eyes with this sight, and with these*
*Small letters, which come to me in such numbers from Bruno's court,* <note>original: "Brunonis ab aulâ." This refers to the court of the Duke of Brunswick (Braunschweig).</note>
*But may I be consoled by these sleepless visions in my dreams,*
*And may these nighttime encounters happen to me often!*
*[u] Now we seek the Divine Power with an elevated prayer of the*
->*mind,*<-
*May he preserve this Palladium* <note>In antiquity, a "Palladium" was a statue of Pallas Athena that protected a city; here, Andreae uses it to refer to the Duke's library and collections as the spiritual safeguard of the state.</note> *for us for many years,*

*Nor Bellona* <note>The Roman goddess of war.</note> *dare to violate with her grasping right hand;*
*Keep these far away, O Father, and make all these things firm,*

*His better part* <note>The soul.</note> *shall fly eternal above the stars,*
*His body, purified with Ambrosia and a divine scent,*
*Shall strip off its mortal limbs among the deified Heroes:*
*Clothed in the perpetual flower of winged Youth,*
*May they crown him at last with a halo and the brightness of Heaven!*
*[x] But let that day be slow to arrive, later than our own years,*
*And not until, as an Elder, he has equaled a perfect age,*
*When that Majestic Head, leaving the world which he governs,*
*May approach Heaven, and favor those who pray from afar,*
*From where he may see the good deeds of his own sons*
*To be greater than his own, and rejoice to be surpassed by them!*

## LETTER II.
### Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial letter 'A' with a background depicting a pastoral landscape with foliage.</image-desc>As a pledge of your leaning benevolence and your most ready zeal, I have received and now hold the early performance of your duty, by which you deigned to congratulate me on my seventeenth birthday by praying for every good fortune. Because this gesture proceeded especially from you—whose true piety and integrity of life I have perceived from my own family, and whose distinguished learning I know well from your books—it offered me, as it were, a handle <note>original: "ansam"; a classical idiom meaning an opportunity or starting point.</note> for writing, which I have all but kissed with joy. But I would wish you to be clearly persuaded of this: that I, as I do for few like you, so I venerate, love, and value you most highly for your excellent gifts and virtues:

## LETTER IV.
### To the Very Reverend and Most 
### Distinguished Lord Doctor,

You judged that the prayer recently sent was not a sufficiently certain pledge of your future devotion toward me, unless you further adorned and enriched me with a most welcome and truly precious gift, which was finally delivered just in the past few days. But having long been more than certain of that devotion, and having received the mathematical books of the most celebrated Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, famous for his role in the Gregorian calendar reform and his widely-used textbooks.</note>, I have now gladly fallen into your debt <note>original: "in æs tuum incidi"; a Latin idiom meaning to owe someone money or, metaphorically, a great favor.</note>. If I could now repay it with interest—as much as one can give thanks in words—I would not allow myself to be surpassed in kindnesses even by that Alexander the Great, whose character I am accustomed to admire and some of whose traits I set before myself to imitate. I know, however, that you will grant me a truce <note>original: "inducias"; here meaning a delay or extension of time to fulfill a promise.</note> if, as you suggest and most lovingly urge, I promise to devote my efforts to these studies hereafter. I understand the utility of these subjects both from your own writings, where [I have acquired] a moderate [knowledge] of Politics and

In political and historical matters, I will not speak of mere prudence, but of sagacity—which I judge to be entirely necessary for those in my position. For I am well aware of the brilliant and wise things written by Aristotle in the third book of his *Politics* <note>Aristotle's *Politics*, Book 3, Chapter 3, discusses the nature of the state and the identity of the citizen, topics essential for a future ruler.</note> and by his commentators. With God’s gracious help, I shall acquire this sagacity; I will taste of these subjects and learn to apply them to the practical uses of this life. 

As for what you were pleased to write—expressing how immensely you feel honored by my letters—the saying of the comic poet seems to apply to you here: *“You do so, yet you forbid me,”* <note>original: "Ita facis, me vetas"; a common Latin reference to a character who performs a favor or honor while modestly telling the other person not to mention it.</note> since nothing has been said, or could be said by me, that could ever equal your merits toward the Church, the State, and all good men. My own harvest, however, still lies hidden in the blade <note>original: "messis adhuc in herbâ"; a classical metaphor (from Ovid) meaning that one's potential is still in the early stages of growth and has not yet reached fruition.</note>, which, as God grants grace and strength (for I do not resist a good omen), will finally be able to ripen in its own time. 

Finally, so that I may not be troublesome with too many words: if the mutual exchange of letters pleases you—since you asked jokingly (as if this were something that had to be won from me through prayers) that I might more often bless you with my "elegant writings"—I seize the opportunity with both hands. I do this not because I have persuaded myself that, in this infancy of my writing, my pen could produce anything particularly elegant, but so that, like your spiritual son, through the repeated reading of your letters, I may appear and become more learned and better in the eyes of my **Most Clement Lord Father** <note>Referring to Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, a famously learned ruler and the Prince's father.</note> and my most beloved teachers. 

Farewell to you and them, most excellent Sir, and may you thrive well and long with all your people in our most afflicted Fatherland <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War, which was still ravaging Germany in 1643.</note>.

Given at Brunswick,
August 1st, Year 1643. <note>original: "Cal. Sext." or the Kalends of the Sixth Month, which in the Roman style used by scholars refers to August 1st.</note>

Of Your Reverend
Dignity,
Most observant,
*RUDOLPHUS AUGUSTUS.*

# LETTER V.

## To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,

Indeed, I could use this saying of Terence <note>original: "Tute facis, me vetas"; a quote from the Roman playwright Terence meaning "You do it yourself, yet you forbid me." The Prince is playfully pointing out that Andreae is being overly modest while praising him.</note> against you: *“You do so yourself, yet you forbid me,”* since you deem me worthy of such and so great a title, of which I think myself plainly unworthy. No one is ignorant of those things which I wrote to you, Most Distinguished Man, and yet I can understand nothing else from your letters than that you wish me to bless you—or rather, enrich you—when I myself instead need to seek my "elegancies" (as you call them) from you. Doubtless you praise me in this way not because I am already worthy, but as one who, in time and with increasing age, might make myself not unworthy of that praise.

Political and historical works are now being read by me, but Mathematics (God willing) I shall learn at some point in the universities. There, I will use this work by Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, famous for his role in the Gregorian calendar reform. His textbooks were standard across Europe.</note>, which your generosity has shared with me. For this gift, I give you my greatest thanks, which I shall repay with my utmost effort whenever I am able. Farewell then, Most Distinguished Lord Doctor, and teach me with your wisdom whenever you have the time.

Given at Brunswick                          Your most affectionate
on the Nones of August <note>August 5th.</note>                       friend,
in the year 1643.

->RUDOLPH AUGUSTUS.<-

*...might entice [me] to profess openly before a fifteen-year-old Prince of flourishing talent how little progress I have made in writing letters, now that I have recently entered my fifty-eighth year of age. Yet I bear this "disgrace" of mine patiently, as long as it is joined with Your glory, which I favor so heartily that I do not fear to hope or even wish for it to be greater than that of Your Father—who until now has been known as the greatest among men of letters.* <note>The Prince's father was Duke August the Younger of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, a famed scholar who founded one of the largest libraries in Europe.</note> *Furthermore, as to your conviction that the basics of Mathematics <term>Matheseos: the mathematical sciences, including geometry and astronomy</term>—which are most suited to your current very capable age—should be deferred until your university studies, I would wish to be further informed by your tutors. If they think it ill-advised to entangle and distract your mind with the abstruse technicalities of Mathematics while you are steeping your talent in Politics and History, they agree with me entirely. But if they should hear that I wish to offer the principles of Arithmetic and Geometry, as well as Chronology and Cosmography—without which History and Statecraft <term>Politia: the art of government and social order</term> are nothing—and to introduce the use of the ruler, the compass (especially that most ingenious Proportional <note>original: "Proportionalis"; likely referring to the Proportional Compass or Sector, a sophisticated calculating instrument used by engineers and nobles at the time.</note>), and the understanding of instruments, machines, and structures through play and relaxation, then I think they will be less difficult with me. Especially if they consider that arduous exercises of mind and body await your older years, leaving little time for these more pleasant studies. But your most wise Father will see to these things more rightly. For me, it is enough to have witnessed your mind's progress in every noble thing, with the prayer that as you are a rising sun, the Sun [your father]—when he sets after many years by the necessity of nature—might be less missed for the welfare of the Fatherland <term>Salute Patriæ: the safety and well-being of the state</term>. I beseech you, continue to testify to the inclination of your mind through your elegant letters in your leisure, and count me among your most humble clients, who*

->*keeps watch with constant prayers.*<-

<header>THE YEAR 1643. LETTER VII.</header>

### To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,

A constant awareness of the promise by which I recently bound myself compelled me to satisfy your most delightful letter by responding as quickly as possible. I acknowledge my fault in this matter, and I am not entirely certain whether I can use this meager excuse: that because of the daily occupations of my studies, it has not been possible until now to fulfill this duty toward You. Yet in excusing myself, I now accuse myself more heavily; for I shall never regret spending even a great part of my study time in writing letters to You. It is all the more proper for me to do this so that I do not seem to want to frustrate Your expectation, nor to be seen wishing to be freed from the requirement of rendering to You an account of my progress and leisure, as commanded by my *Most Illustrious Father* <note>original: "Illustriss. Genitoris"; the Prince is referring to Duke August the Younger of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel</note>.

For why should I fear to write to You—a beginner <term>tyro: a novice or recruit</term> to such a practiced Master—lest perhaps you think that I, constrained until now by fear and shame, have decided that delays must be woven? On the contrary, Your fair-mindedness cannot fail to interpret my every effort skillfully. And if, while doing this, I should stumble—as the necessity of making mistakes is almost imposed on a man of my age—the fault will be all the more tolerable because these hurried letters I direct to You do not arise from youthful heat or ill-considered impulse, but from the respect with which I rightly follow the commands of my *Most Clement Lord Parent*. I do this so that by this kind of obedience I might bind his merciful mind to me, and daily deserve and obtain from You more effective vows and prayers by which you may favor my beginnings.

As for our little dispute regarding *Mathematical studies* <term>studiis Mathematicis: the branch of learning including geometry, arithmetic, and astronomy</term>, if it should be called that, the Tutors <term>Informatores: the private instructors responsible for the Prince's daily education</term> agree entirely with You and Your excellent advice...

of mine: since this is also the opinion of my **Most Merciful Lord Parent** <note>original: "Clementiß. Dn. For the rest, be certain that I will always be a friend to you, as you do not cease to offer vows and prayers for...

## LETTER VIII.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### Most Merciful Lord,

I accept your omen, proceeding as it does from your filial piety toward your **Most Renowned Father** and from the devotion of my own innermost feelings; I send in return a "Fixed Sun," expressed in a certain emblem according to the dullness of my wit <note>A common gesture of scholarly humility</note>. For who among good men would not wish for your **Most Praised Father** either "Platonic years" <term>The Platonic Year (Annus Magnus) is the period of approximately 25,800 years it takes for the constellations to complete a full cycle; here it implies extreme longevity</term>, or even more years added from their own lives? Surely, by a new miracle, one would wish the **Sun** to be either stationary or retrograde <note>A reference to the biblical miracles of Joshua and Hezekiah mentioned on the previous page</note>, if one compares this "Prince without Example" <note>Meaning a Prince who is unparalleled</note> with the Heroes of both our own and the ancient age. You are indeed blessed now, and shall be even more so in the future, the longer **Hesperus** <note>The Evening Star, signaling the end of the day</note> looks back upon your **Sun** before its setting. Let us truly join our vows and prayers, perhaps with upheld hands; certainly, as long as he is safe, we need not doubt that the public safety will remain secure.

Regarding your **Studies**—piety being the ruler of all studies—your **Most Merciful Father**, the best judge of all, will decide most correctly. For at the age which you are now approaching, he produced such examples of perfect erudition throughout **Germany** that I know not whether any the like have been seen or heard, before or after him, in this high rank of the social order. Truly, our **Tübingen** <note>The University of Tübingen, where both the Duke and Andreae studied</note> shall never cease to remember this one Example and to boast of him. 

Oh, that God would truly grant me this: that with peace restored to **Germany** (for which we pray as suppliants) and with the **Academies** rising again, I might behold you as the **Most Magnificent Head** of our **Tübingen** and the **Prince of Letters**. May I admire the **Son** after the **Father**, so that just as the father's fame once kindled me as a young man with unquenchable fire, the son's fame may bathe me as an old man with incredible pleasure. That the **Merciful Father** <note>God</note> may grant this to us, and that your **Guides** <term>Conductores: the Prince's tutors and governors</term> may promote it with all faith, industry, and skill, I most humbly and dutifully pray with all the exertion of my soul,

# LETTER IX.

->*Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,*<-

I was delighted in no small measure by that most clever **Emblem**, to which my own unpolished letters seem to have provided the occasion; I was no less captured by the happy coincidence through which, while I was occupied with other matters, I was able to engage my Teacher. I cannot return a gift of equal value; let it suffice to confess that by your invention, you have excellently expressed the sentiment of my mind and the sum of my prayers, and at the same time, you have offered a fresh and most welcome example of sincere devotion toward the **Most Merciful Parent** <note>Refers to Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg, a famed scholar and book collector</note>.

As for what you write—that my **Most Merciful Parent** was once honored by you at **Tübingen**—I now learn this for the first time from your letters. I would gladly satisfy my desire to travel there if the decision were mine to make; I would go not because I presume myself to possess such goodness of talent that I could equal my father’s footsteps or ever merit your admiration, but because I personally long to behold his physical presence and to more deeply embrace that spirit on whose flourishing fame we have thus far relied. However, if what is said regarding the devastation of the **Duchy of Württemberg** is true—as I almost do not doubt it to be <note>A reference to the catastrophic effects of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) on the region</note>—I hardly think my **Most Illustrious Lord Parent** will choose that seat and mistress of **Studies** for me. Unless perhaps, as sometimes happens in the human body, where the heart can endure even when the outer limbs are badly affected and weakened, so it might be that among so many evils, and under those sprouting...

## LETTER XI.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-

That my little gift was not unpleasing to You, most flourishing Prince, I believe happened chiefly because of Your affection for Him whose image it represents. ### LETTER XII.
->**Very Reverend and Most**<-
->**Renowned Sir,**<-

To your letters sent to me not so long ago, I return a brief response this time, though certainly more extensive than duty requires. I do this not so much in obedience to the command of my **Most Gracious Lord Parent** <note>Referring to Duke August the Younger (1579–1666), a famous scholar-prince and bibliophile</note>, but rather with a most willing mind and a most joyful hand, guiding the pen to the best of my modest strength. It is truly lovely for the affections of those who love to be joined; but what could happen more lovely to me, a boy, than to be held and cherished by Your Reverence with such pious and sincere affection? Your love for me penetrates my mind with such delight that I imagine I feel as if I were being cherished in the very bosom of Piety and Virtue themselves.

I pray for your venerable gray hairs <note>Original: *venerandis Tuis canis*; a respectful reference to the recipient's old age and wisdom</note>, for long and undisturbed paths of prosperity, and that your prayers, hands, and voices may be granted to the **afflicted Church** <note>A reference to the Lutheran Church during the devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)</note> for a very long time yet; for she herself looks far and wide upon your virtues. ### LETTER XVIII.
#### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
#### Most Clement Lord,

I can never say how much delight I take in your little letters, sweetest Prince—letters that are perhaps too learned for your age. For in them I smell the fragrance of the Lily of the Valley, and I taste the Hyblaean <note>Mount Hybla in Sicily was famous in classical poetry for the sweetness of its honey; here, Andreae uses it to compliment the Prince's "sweet" and affectionate writing style.</note> nectar of your love with which you embrace me; nothing could be sweeter to me in this exhausted old age. ## LETTER XXI.

### Most Illustrious and High Princes,
### Brothers, my most merciful Lords,

That I see my efforts do not displease you has made me truly happy. Since I owe everything I have to your Lord Father—my most merciful Prince and Hero—I shall never repay that debt more happily than if I can count out some small portion of it to you. Indeed, whenever anything comes to hand that might delight your eyes or stir your intellects, I shall by no means think the opportunity should be neglected. 

But now, concerning the 66th birthday of your Father, which is so greatly desired by us all, it is especially for you to rejoice and for me to congratulate you from the heart. God graciously extends his years, not only for the good of his Church and the State, but for your benefit and the honor of the House of Guelph <term>Guelph: The House of Welf (Welfen), one of the oldest and most distinguished royal dynasties in Europe, to which the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg belonged.</term>. He does this so that He may fortify your youth—still tender in this iron and stormy age <note>A reference to the hardships of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which was still raging at the time of this letter.</note>—with both the precepts and the living examples of Virtue. As long as his living and healthy archetype <note>original: *archetypum*; here meaning the original "pattern" or "model" of a perfect ruler.</note> remains for you, you are safe. We, for our part, shall celebrate with his image, which you will receive from me shortly under the title *The Model Prince* <note>original: *Principis Exempli*; likely a commemorative essay or emblem Andreae composed for the Duke's birthday.</note>, marked for this joyful birthday. I send this with the prayer that it may be of use and bring lasting public joy. Farewell, and be joyful with your illustrious Mother and Sisters.

...fortunate and happy [archetype] you might possess. Therefore, I present to you his Image—and indeed one not even expressed skillfully enough, but rather like a shadow of the image <note>original: "imaginis veluti umbram"; Andreae humbly suggests his written or artistic depiction is only a pale reflection of the Duke's actual greatness.</note>—so that by looking upon it, you may conceive with a noble spirit what and how much lies before you to be imitated, and reach it with a happy progress. 

Truly blessed are you, for whom the summit of virtue must be sought not through winding paths or detours, but by a straight and unimpeded way; you need only follow in the footsteps of your Father. His example is rare among Princes—indeed, it is almost without precedent—and this binds you all the more strongly to ensure that those things which you hear and see in his presence, and observe to be praised publicly (and even evidently crowned by God Himself), you yourselves might also successfully express. You must do this for the benefit of the Church and the State <note>original: "Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ"; the dual pillars of 17th-century social order.</note>, as well as for the growth and adornment of your own House. May **CHRIST** wish this to be a most auspicious beginning; I humbly pray to Him for the health of your Father, Mother, and your renowned family.

# LETTER XXIII.

->Most Illustrious and High Princes,<-
->brothers, my most merciful Lords,<-

Indeed, my little gifts <term>munuscula: a Latin term for small, humble tokens or gifts, often used by scholars to downplay the value of their work when presenting it to patrons.</term> are not so great that they deserve any thanks from you. On the contrary, they serve this purpose: if God has granted any measure of grace to me—who am the greatest of debtors—I may humbly offer and present it all to you in good faith as a testament of my submissive spirit. 

For what remains to me of earthly comforts and resources in this calamitous time <note>A reference to the ongoing devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).</note> that I do not owe entirely, after God, to your Parent, my Lord and Hero? I am indebted to him on such an immense account that the servant in the Gospel (Matthew 18) <note>Refers to the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant, who owed his king ten thousand talents—an astronomical sum.</note> was hardly bound by a greater one. Since you accept such an easy payment of this debt—namely, some small delight for the eyes or assistance in your studies...

### LETTER XXVI.

->To the Most Illustrious and Highborn Princes,<-
->Most Merciful Lords,<-

I see I have to do with a Geryon <note>In Greek mythology, Geryon was a giant with three bodies, three heads, and one set of limbs; Andreae uses this as a clever metaphor for the three brothers—Rudolf August, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albrecht—working in perfect unity</note>, by which you have eluded either my folly or my sluggishness with an ingenious retribution. But come, I accept your Geryon as a good omen, and I offer another of my own in return, marked with hieroglyphic signs—namely, of the kind I expect from you and desire for your lands. What I intend, you will understand yourselves through your own sagacity; however, let others recognize it from these marks. 

One Head belongs to you, which is **AUGUST** <note>original: "AVGVSTVM"; a play on words referring both to the princes' father, Duke August the Younger, and the Roman imperial title implying majesty and divinity</note>, shining for the three brothers with the light of piety; the mind and spirit are the same, the heart in harmony. May this be eternal for you, for the sake of the public welfare <note>original: "publica salute"</note>, to which a disagreement between brothers is a plague. Let the steward <note>original: "Promus condus"; a Roman term for the household official who managed both the storage (condus) and the distribution (promus) of goods</note> of illustrious generosity receive and return in kind. 

Let the duties of hands and feet be distinct, yet let all things administered by each of you be guided by one mind, namely the prime mover <note>original: "primo mobili"; in the science of the time, this was the outermost sphere of the heavens that gave motion to all others; here, it refers to a central governing principle</note>, as the directress. Hence, on the right is the torch of religion, lit from the Sun above; on the left is the law of the Land <note>original: "lex Regionis"</note>, inscribed on the tablets of justice. From there comes the honor of the arts or of learning <note>original: "eruditio"</note>, and from here the just defense of Mars or of arms <note>original: "Martis defensio"</note>, which may temper the times of peace and upheaval. To this is added fortune from commerce and trade, and a portion or income from agriculture, without which this vast animal <note>The state or the "body politic"</note> cannot live. ...namely, the reward and prize for the good, and the punishment and warding off of evil. Added on both sides are, on the right, the love of the clergy and the esteem of the nobility; on the left, the support of laborers and care for the poor. It is through their incense, shield, machines <note>original: *machinis*; likely referring to the industrious tools or "engines" of the working class</note>, and prayers that public safety is established. You have here, most illustrious trio of Princes, a Geryon <term>Geryon: A giant from Greek mythology with three bodies, here reinterpreted as a symbol of three brothers or powers acting as one</term> whom I compare with yours. If you exercise your most noble wits in further explaining and gutting this figure—for I have only displayed the outer parts—and if you strive to express it in your very work, you will one day bless your lands. Then, with God's favor, your father's applause, your mother's rejoicing, and your House exulting, you will make all of Germany indebted to you. This is the heartfelt wish of one who constantly keeps watch before God for the growth of the Guelph line <note>The House of Guelph (or Welf) was the ancestral dynasty of the Dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg</note>.

To your most Illustrious Excellencies,
Stuttgart: September 10, 1644. Your most humble client.

...not a monster, or a Tyrant, breathing destruction upon the human race, but rather three brothers who were extremely powerful in the three islands facing Spain. They lived in such great harmony that they seemed to be ruled by a single mind. Nor did Hercules, that "averter of evils," come to Spain because of their crimes; rather, he was drawn by a desire for plunder, because they abounded in herds, which at that time were the only form of wealth. And so, having moved past the triple Geryon <term>Geryon: A giant from Greek myth with three heads or three bodies, usually depicted as a monster slain by Hercules. Here, the brothers interpret him as a positive symbol of fraternal unity.</term>, you persuade the three brothers toward **HARMONY**. You promise them wealth and happiness—things that cannot exist without the Divine Will and Piety, without Literature and arms, or without the love and protection of the honorable arts and the methods of earning a living. For it is likely that these brothers worshipped the **GODS** with great care according to their custom, were very powerful in arms by land and sea, and zealously fostered and increased all the arts that the necessity of that recent age had invented. These are the external parts of your "Hieroglyphic Geryon"; this is what those most elegant anatomical letters indicate. However, so that we may "eviscerate" it and examine its inner workings—that is, as we explain it ourselves, expanding for our own use what you have set forth in brief—you provide counsel where you might have given a command. We obey quite willingly, for if we should dissect <note>original: *secuerimus*; the brothers are using a metaphor of "anatomizing" or "dissecting" the symbolic drawing to understand its hidden meanings</note> any part with less skill than required, we look forward to your instruction.

We begin from the fulcrum <note>original: *fulcro*; the base or support of the symbolic figure or emblem</note>, and from its left side—namely, the joined hands by which you signify the **PRAYERS AND VOWS OF THE POOR**. While the Cyclopes <term>Cyclopes: One-eyed giants, used here as a metaphor for powerful, lawless, and cruel men who lack moral "vision."</term> of our own time not only mock these prayers but also seize the goods of the poor and shed their blood, treating these unfortunates not as human beings but as four-legged beasts, we must take all the more care. We must ensure that we are not swept away by the torrent of such detestable examples, and that we do not believe the Divine Power is unmoved by tears or prayers—simply because the [punishment] for such great crimes...

### THE YEAR 1644.

...[lest] we persuade ourselves that because punishment is deferred, they will go unpunished. Therefore, you may be confident that what seems a great paradox to many is certain and established among us: that the prayers of the poor and the charity bestowed upon them are not a weakness, but among the strongest supports of a Commonwealth. Nor should we consider as poor only those who, lacking everything for life, are forced to beg for alms from door to door, but also those whom the atrocious calamities of this long war <note>This refers to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which was in its final years when this was written and had devastated the German lands.</note> have drained—the remnants of humanity, half-naked, starving, and constantly exposed to new injuries day and night.

He who despises their groans and prayers—whether they be against him or for him—we believe has stripped off his humanity and lost all sense of the divine. Just as the histories of the Christian centuries testify, those of illustrious families who were generous toward them have flourished in wealth and power at home, in fame abroad, and in good health and a long line of descendants. There survive as examples from Greek legislation the terms for *Xenodochia* <note>original: "Xenodochiorum"; guest-houses or hospitals for strangers.</note>, *Ptochotrophia* <note>original: "Ptochotrophiorum"; almshouses for the poor.</note>, *Brephotrophia* <note>original: "Brephotrophiorum"; nurseries for abandoned infants.</note>, *Orphanotrophia* <note>original: "Orphanotrophiorum"; orphanages.</note>, and *Gerontocomia* <note>original: "Gerontocomiorum"; homes for the elderly.</note>. We recall Charles the Great <note>Charlemagne.</note>, the Capetians <note>The royal dynasty of France.</note>, Robert and Saint Louis; and we often hear what Daniel once advised Nebuchadnezzar (Chapter 4:27) <note>"Break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by showing mercy to the poor."</note>, and whom David proclaims blessed in Psalm 41:1 and following. 

Finally, from Leviticus 25:35, we examine the meanings wrapped in the "hieroglyphic" sign of joined hands <note>The "joined hands" likely refers to a specific part of the Geryon emblem or a symbol of fraternal and charitable unity.</note>; whether we have attained them will be for your judgment. If this specimen of "evisceration" <note>The brothers continue the metaphor of "dissecting" the symbol to find its inner truth.</note> is approved by you, we will shortly gird ourselves for the rest, with God’s help; if not, you will not find it a burden to advise us, as we will follow your counsel either way. Farewell, meanwhile, and continue to love us.

Wolfenbüttel,
October 8, 1644.

## LETTER XXVIII.

### Most Illustrious and Highborn Princes,
### Most Merciful Lords,

I am greatly delighted that my *Geryon* <note>In Greek mythology, Geryon was a giant with three bodies, three heads, and one set of legs. Here, Andreae uses it as an emblem for the three prince-brothers acting as one.</note> was in accord with your own mind and feeling; I marveled that it was reconstructed into a most true mythology by your own talent. A good deed indeed! For that triple **HARMONY** <note>original: "CONCORDIAM"</note> which I heartily wish for you three brothers as the height of your happiness, you embrace of your own accord, thus establishing the invincible strength of your Renowned House. How truly excellent this is, that you have thought to dissect <note>original: "evisceranda"; literally "to disembowel," meaning to get to the heart or essence of the matter.</note> first what the worldly mind considers last: namely, the humble and tearful prayers of those whom today’s *Cyclopes* <note>The one-eyed giants of myth, here representing the unfeeling, brutal soldiers and oppressors of the ongoing Thirty Years' War.</note> and monsters of men tear apart and trample. Whether the prayers of the poor are against someone or in their favor, everything fortunate or dire truly depends upon them. 

For who does not see in History that the most powerful kingdoms are either established or overturned by this—either through piety toward the poor or the injury done to them? We would seek the causes of such falls in vain within *political secrets* <note>original: "Politicis arcanis"</note> or *reasons of state* <note>original: "Status rationibus"; the principle that the interests of the state justify any means, which Andreae contrasts here with Christian morality.</note>. Therefore, I praise not so much your industry—you who have *hit the nail on the head* <note>original: "acu rem tetigeritis"; literally "touched the matter with a needle."</note>—as your inclination toward the wretched. While the poor call down destruction by cursing their whips, their skinners, and their *executioners* <note>original: "lanistas"; literally those who trained gladiators for slaughter, used here for military oppressors.</note>, they will win for you, through their pious prayers and vows, bloom, life, peace, abundance, and glory—behold the wealth of poverty!—and they will make you truly Blessed. 

It remains that what you have successfully accomplished in this one pillar, you might not find it burdensome to do successively in unraveling others equally; I will consider it truly honorable to me, and not foreign to your studies. It will suffice if, in each letter, one foot of this harmonious stature is explained, lest I wish to be a burden to you, or an obstacle to more serious studies, or [seem]...

## LETTER XXIX.
### To the Very Reverend and Most
### Distinguished Lord Doctor,

We are delighted that the first specimen of our Anatomy <note>Andreae uses "Anatomy" metaphorically to mean a detailed structural analysis of the state or the "Geryon" emblem.</note> was pleasing to you. For by that, we are encouraged to dissect the rest. On the Left Side of your Geryon, joined to the prayers of the poor, is the **PRESERVATION OF THE CRAFTS**, which you also place as the foundation of Republics. Geryon teaches that this is so. For if Geryon had not determined the same, how could he have been powerful by land and sea? 

Anyone who sees a ship which we commit to the raging Sea will imagine to himself that it was neither fathered by the earth nor dropped from heaven, but will understand it to be a human work; a machine that can no more be built without craftsmen than a man can wander the sea without a ship. To build such a massive structure, the hands of carpenters, blacksmiths, weavers, rope-makers, and those who handle pitch are necessary. Geryon held all these crafts in the highest esteem, increased them, and made the best use of them. 

Indeed, who can accomplish anything in war without the use of arms? Where would you get your blades, swords, missiles, and spears unless the art of mining iron were known? Therefore, Geryon did not despise the utility of the iron-miners in the Republic, and he also supported the blacksmiths who forged his military weapons. With flocks, herds, horses, and others...

<summary>Andreae transitions from the spiritual to the practical, arguing that the "Preservation of the Crafts" (labor and industry) is the essential foundation for a state’s naval and military power. He uses the metaphor of shipbuilding to demonstrate how a great kingdom relies on the coordinated labor of many specific manual trades.</summary>

...abounded. Therefore, we also bring to mind that he <note>Referring to Geryon, the mythical giant Andreae uses as a symbol for the State.</note> must have had with him tanners, shoemakers, wool-workers, and tailors—unless it seems truer that they used the skins of wild beasts (after the manner of the Germans), which can also be admitted. And so Geryon teaches that a Republic <note>original: "Remp.," abbreviation of "Respublica," meaning the state or commonweal.</note> cannot exist without Crafts; reason teaches the same, and the *Examples* of many most flourishing Republics also prove it—which are so much happier the more ingenious their craftsmen are.

For when men first founded *Cities*, their intention and their prayer was that they might be secure from storms, wild beasts, and robbers. Then *Industry* began to exert itself among those joined together, and one person thought of this, another of that, so that they might not only *live*, but also *live well*. The ancient Germans, and among them especially the *Fenni* <note>A reference to the "Fenni" described by the Roman historian Tacitus; a people he depicted as living in extreme, though contented, poverty without houses or metal.</note>, also lived, but miserably indeed, since they fed on grass, used the skins of wild beasts for clothing, and the ground for a bed. Who, indeed, would not far prefer our present splendor and convenience to that barbarism? We rightly acknowledge that we are more refined than they because of our craftsmen. 

Therefore, those who attempt to remove craftsmen from the Republic could easily render the human race fierce and prone to war; but those who urge that craftsmen be retained in the Republic desire to nourish *peace and concord* among men. Leaving aside many things pertaining to this, *Most Distinguished Sir*, we conclude this letter thus: that the crafts ought to be dear to the guardians of Republics. It is even permissible for the rulers themselves to learn some of them, not to gain a profit from them, but for pleasure, and sometimes even for necessity. For we read concerning *Demetrius Poliorcetes* <note>Demetrius I of Macedon (337–283 BCE), known as "The Besieger" for his innovative engineering and massive siege engines.</note> that he was a most excellent Mechanic, who built machines so that he could capture fortified cities. I therefore give you the greatest thanks for this monument of your love toward me. As often as I take it into my hands (which shall be very often), the memory of this most welcome gift will be renewed in my mind. My *tutors* <note>original: "Informatores," the private instructors responsible for the Prince's education.</note> also admit they owe you no small debt, because you chose to praise *their names and their cares* in the dedicatory letter and to make them publicly known.

I would stop here, were it not that I felt I must not omit a matter that has troubled me until now. I worry that in my most recent correspondence, when I asked you to greet Duke ULRICH of Württemberg <note>Ulrich of Württemberg (1617–1671), a contemporary and kinsman of the Prince.</note>, my most beloved kinsman, and to remind him of the brotherhood we entered into at Brunswick, I might have overstepped the bounds of modesty befitting my age. Certainly your long silence, which seems almost like forgetfulness, nearly persuades me that I have. I shall be freed from this worry if, when you have the time, I am informed that the offering of service to my kinsman—which I repeat now with a friendly greeting—was well received.

*It is not within my modesty to interrupt your more elegant studies too often with empty letters.*

### LETTER XXXVI.

->*Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,*<-

Since such is your happiness, most flourishing Prince, that you were born as a sprout of the **August House of Guelph** <note>The Welf or Guelph family is one of the oldest and most powerful dynasties in European history.</note>, from **Augustus** himself—the **Sun** <note>original: "Phœbo," referring to Apollo/Phoebus as the sun-god</note> of your house—and since you were formed **according to the Example of Augustus** <note>A wordplay on both the Duke’s name and the Roman Emperor Augustus, implying a model of perfect leadership.</note>, and will one day succeed as **heir to those August Virtues and the realm**, bringing light to **all of Germany**, it is only right that **you recognize these gifts of heaven and be stirred in your spirit toward all high things. This refers to the three sons of Duke Augustus: Rudolph Augustus, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albert.</note>. ->To the Very Reverend Lord<-

# LETTER XXXVIII.
## Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
## Most Gracious Lord,

Although I value everything regarding Your Highness most highly, I prize this above all with great applause: that I openly observe you *happily advancing on the path of Virtue, and striving for the palm <note>original: "palmam"; the palm branch was a classical symbol of victory and excellence</note> belonging to your renowned Father*. And although your piety toward your Father in his old age, and your devotion to the instructions of your advisors, easily achieves this, nevertheless, I do not doubt in the slightest that you are carried there by the spontaneous nobility and teachability of your own Character, so that you may one day emerge as MORE EXCELLENT than the ELDERS (according to the Spartan song and chorus) <note>original: "ad Spartanam cantilenam & chorum"; this refers to an ancient Spartan tradition where three choirs (boys, men, and old men) sang. The boys sang "We shall be better than you," promising to surpass the generations before them.</note>—namely, that you might surpass your Grandfathers and Great-grandfathers. For you understand through your own insight how extraordinary a debt you owe to the expectations—not only of your own lands and peoples—but to all of Germany and the Church of Christ, owing to your excellent cultivation and the precise example set within your own home. 

Shine forth, therefore, most flourishing Prince, toward where the happy stars lead you—not so much those stars above, as those that are around you—and exceed our hopes as much as divine favor may grant beyond the lot of mortals, according to our prayer. I, the least among your dependents, do not hesitate to echo the words of John the Baptist: *“You must increase, but I must decrease.”* <note>original: "Te crescere oportet, me vero minui"; a quote from the Gospel of John 3:30, used here to express the mentor's joy in his student's rising status as he himself grows old.</note> Therefore, may GOD add whatever remains of my old years to your years and your growth, and may He render YOU an INSTRUMENT OF PUBLIC WELFARE as most...

### LETTER XXXIX.

->**To the Right Reverend**<-
->**Lord Doctor,**<-

I am pestering you with my letters, while you overwhelm me with your gifts. I had barely finished writing my previous letter to you when some paintings, executed by an elegant hand, were sent to me as a gift from my Lord Father, along with a book in which the festivities and equestrian games celebrated on the birthday of your best and my most dear Prince Ulrich <note>original: "Huldarici"; Prince Ulrich of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1613–1667), the younger brother of the writer</note> are excellently displayed. This is a great sign of your great and never-failing love; and just as that moves me deeply, so this—that I lack the means to show my gratitude to you—grieves me most of all. However, as I leave everything at this time to the care and concern of my Lord Father, I easily promise myself that He will by no means fail me in this regard. In the meantime, I wish for you to be certain that I will finally show my gratitude in deed, when circumstances, age, and strength permit. Farewell, and continue to favor

Year 1644.

### LETTER XL.

->**To the Very Reverend and Most**<-
->**Distinguished Lord Doctor,**<-

Everyone knows well that there are various types of histories and various uses for them. Of these, if one excludes sacred history, I am fully persuaded—according to my current judgment—that none brings us greater pleasure or more utility than *patriotic and domestic history*. I can easily see that you are of the same opinion from that *Life* <note>original: "Vitam"; a biography</note> which you present to me and my brothers, written by your elegant hand—the life not just of a *Country*, but of a *Great Parent*. Your ever-burning love for us has overwhelmed me with many gifts, but I admire none of them more than this illustrious *Mirror* <note>original: "Speculum"; referring to the "Mirror for Princes" literary genre, where a biography serves as a moral and behavioral model for a ruler</note>, in which I see the brilliant rays of *my nurturing Sun* <note>original: "Nutrientis mei Solis"; a metaphorical reference to his father, Duke August</note> ever shining. I confess, and indeed with a blush (unless you consider that my unlearned years might yet deserve pardon), that although this *Life* was always before me, I have not until now looked into it with the proper admiration and observant eyes. But now, since you set it out for me, depicted by your learned and successful pen, it will always be that:

> *Which shall give to me the spurs of virtue, the seeds of praise,*
> *And the examples to follow:* (while,

From these things it is easily clear how much I owe to you and your love; my youth, which knows nothing of pretense, will convince you that I acknowledge this with a most well-wishing heart. Nor will you find it difficult to believe that I shall not fail you in the future, if I promise this one thing: *That I will always walk in the footsteps of my father.*

Farewell. ->To Your Reverence.<-

Wolfenbüttel, July 16,
1644. ->Most respectfully.<-

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,*<-

While I respond diligently and seriously to your frequent letters, I might seem to some to be seeking the praises with which your kindness has so far overwhelmed me, and to think myself worthy of them. Although I ought not to suspect this of you; for you know that just as flattery is far from you, so ambition is far from me. You surely intend this: *you praise in order to teach*, and while you proclaim great things about me, you openly advise me on what I must do now, and even more in the future. With this profession of my modesty, I temper the excess of your letters—an excess not of love, but of honor. Nor will there be need hereafter for time spent either in excusing myself or in returning like for like.

As for what you add here from the Gospel, *He must increase, but I must decrease* <note>original: "Me crescere, Te minui oportere"; a reference to John 3:30. Andreae had humbly compared himself to John the Baptist and the Prince to Christ, suggesting his own time was passing as the Prince’s began.</note>, I am bound to reply from another perspective: that you are great among those born of women <note>original: "inter mulierum filios"; an allusion to Matthew 11:11, where Jesus praises John the Baptist</note>, indeed the *Greatest* of the scholars of our age, and it is of the highest importance to the Church and the Republic of Letters <term>Republic of Letters: The "Respublica literaria," the international community of intellectuals and scholars who shared ideas during the 17th century</term> that you feel perhaps some old age of the *body*, but none of the *mind*. 

For your merits are certain and present, while those things you proclaim about me are uncertain, although I trust that your prayers will obtain this from God: that I may be able to satisfy, to some extent, the expectations of my Lord Father, of yourself, and finally of the public. Fare well with your family, and continue your work.

Wolfenbüttel,
August 13, 
Year 1644.

->Yours,<-

->RUDOLF AUGUST<-

### LETTER XLII.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**Most Clement Lord,**<-

I am greatly indebted to Your Highness for interpreting my affection for You so kindly. For you may easily understand how far I am from flattery by the tribute I wrote for your Father <note>Johann Valentin Andreae had written a biography/eulogy for Duke August of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, Rudolf August's father</note>, whom I praised far below his actual merits. I did this so I would not seem to be praising him to his face, acting more as a Historian than an Orator, presenting a bare image of Virtue. I wish for you to feel the same regarding my services toward You: specifically, that I am not so much congratulating You on the immense benefit of your proper education and upbringing (than which nothing greater could happen at your age), as I am approving of your obedience and docility. Through these qualities, you bring delight to your Father (may he live as long as possible!) and raise the hopes of all your people for the most praiseworthy progress and growth of your House. Truly, I praise in you this "pliable wax" <note>original: "ductilem ceram"; a common 17th-century metaphor suggesting a young person's mind is soft and ready to be molded by virtuous teaching</note>, upon which your Father’s character is happily impressed, and I follow you with my pious prayers. The greatest of these prayers is for the **LONG LIFE OF YOUR FATHER**, which may perfect, solidify, and strengthen all our expectations regarding You—the one thing upon which your own safety and the public welfare depend.

For you are not unaware of the saying of a certain Wise man: that those who do not act badly are happy, and those who act well are happier, but those for whom it is a necessity that they *cannot* act badly are the happiest of all. It is as if the condition of Youth, when joined with great fortune, can scarcely keep a straight course without the "bit and spurs" <note>original: "frænum & calcaria"; a classical metaphor for the discipline and encouragement needed to keep a soul on the path of virtue</note>, and the very necessity of acting well might serve as a total rule of life. While such a rule may seem a bit harsh to others, I understand that for you it is very easy: namely, that you compose your whole self according to the sight and nod of your illustrious Father and the warnings of your Teachers. For this reason, I congratulate You from my heart and prophesy all the best for you.

### III.
# Correspondence with Prince Anton Ulrich.
## LETTER XLIII.

*Reverend and Most Illustrious Man,* <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714), the younger brother of Rudolf August and a future Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, is writing here as a young student of Andreae.</note>

When I received your letter a month or two ago—as welcome as it was full of every elegant charm—the desire to respond immediately entered my mind. That memory was still fresh when you forestalled my response with yet another gift, both artistic and most delightful to me. This gift is that **Daniel**, most beautiful in his horrific cave, safest among cruel wild beasts, surrounded by heavenly company in a solitary prison. Though held in a dreadful kind of servitude, he is nevertheless most free; and in the dark opening of the earth, he is nonetheless closest to God, shining with the brilliance of holy confidence. 

Meditating on this more than once, I examined that picture with fixed attention, and I had already decided to give thanks along with my reply. However, for a third time, I have now received from you—who deserve so well—both the testimony of your public voice and the rare love you show toward me as well as toward my Lords and Brothers, together with a *beautiful little book*. Indeed, this book is one that we must handle "with a nocturnal and a diurnal hand" <note>original: "nocturnâ & diurnâ manu"; a classical idiom meaning to study a text night and day, or constantly</note>, serving as an undying sign of your affection for us...

### LETTER XLII.

->Most Illustrious and Serene Prince,<-
->Most Gracious Lord,<-

*I owe much to Your Highness for interpreting my affection toward you so kindly. ### LETTER XLIV.
## Most Illustrious and Most High Prince, Most Gracious Lord,

Since you value my various services—of whatever kind they may be—so highly that you even count them worthy of mention, my affection for you grows. It was already **most intense** <note>original: *intensissimus*</note> through a certain silent movement and impulse, so that I hold both your writing style and your **brush** <note>original: *penicillum*; this refers to the Prince's artistic and literary talents, as he was a noted patron and practitioner of the arts.</note> in total delight; I gladly admit that I owe you more and more encouragement for these talents. Indeed, I greatly rejoice that the image of **Daniel** among the **Lions** <note>A reference to the biblical story often used by Andreae as a metaphor for the pious person surviving the "lions" of the Thirty Years' War.</note> reflects back to you something of my own likeness. For it is truly so: in the dreadful cave of this filthy age, unless God held back the bloody teeth, one's life would never be safe.

I owe immense thanks to your Serene Father <note>Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note>, and I shall pay a portion of them through the *Example of a Prince* <note>original: *Principis Exemplo*; this refers to the "Mirror for Princes" literary genre, which provided moral and political instruction to rulers.</note>, which shortly—if your Father permits—I will present to you brothers. It is a mirror, so to speak, into which you may gaze to see what kind of men the **Public Welfare** <note>original: *Salus Publica*</note> demands and expects of you, so that you may express those qualities through a happy reflection. For in your father, you possess the sum of the Christian religion, the very Body of Law, an entire Encyclopedia, a living Library, and a compendium of illustrious virtues. I humbly pray to God that He might preserve this priceless treasure, lively and peaceful, for as long as possible.

Since my humble efforts find some place of delight with you, I do not cease to respond to your letters, which are both polished with every kind of elegance and filled with the most loving affection toward me. ### LETTER XLVIII.

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord,<-

Among the genuine disciples of Matthaeus Hafenreffer <note>Matthaeus Hafenreffer (1561–1619) was a prominent Lutheran theologian at Tübingen and a mentor to Andreae</note>, there was one Michael Schäfer, a *man notable for his profound learning and the uprightness of his life*. By his reputation, he was called to the Court of FREDERICK, Duke of Württemberg, our Great leader <note>Frederick I (1557–1608), Duke of Württemberg, who sought to make his court a center of learning</note>, but his life was shorter than the interests of the Christian cause required <note>original: *pro re Christiana*, meaning his early death was a loss to the church</note>. Departing this life in the year of Christ 1608, he left behind more works begun by his exceptional talent and outstanding will than were actually completed. 

Among these works is this *Isagoge* <term>isagoge|a scholarly introduction or primer to a subject</term>, written once for the private use of myself and other beginners in Theology. Although it has already been made public once or twice through my efforts, it seemed most fitting to me that it should now be combined with Hafenreffer’s *Loci* <term>Loci Communes|a standard systematic collection of theological topics used in Lutheran education</term> (from which it originated), now condensed into a core. This is done by a certain right of my own and out of the trust of a former close friendship. However, it will be all the more distinguished if you, *Most Reverend and Flourishing Prince*, would adorn its frontispiece...
