### LETTER L.

->Very Reverend and Most<-
->Distinguished Sir,<-

*The beautiful little book, which you sent to me as a gift,* you call a "precious gift"; and that it is rightly called so, my own feelings, the excellence of your style, and my filial affection [for your father] gladly concede. In no way can one venerate the memory of a Parent and Lord more holily or more enduringly than by reflecting upon all his deeds and words, and by embracing the reputation and the character of his mind even more than that of his body. It is most true that just as the faces of men are frail and mortal, so too are the images of the face; but the form of the mind is eternal. One cannot preserve or express that form as successfully through the art and materials of others as one can through one's own character—as the exalted Roman writer <note>The Roman historian Tacitus, writing about his father-in-law, the general Gnaeus Julius Agricola</note> says of his father-in-law *Agricola*: *For he, having been narrated and handed down to posterity by that son-in-law of his, has remained, remains, and shall remain in the minds of men, in the eternity of time, and in the fame of his deeds.* <note>original Latin: "Qui quidem per illum Generum suum posteritati narratus & traditus mansit, manet, mansuruſque eſt in animis hominum, in æternitate temporum, famâ rerum." From Tacitus, *Agricola*, 46.</note> I return to you, *Reverend Sir*, these tokens of deeper affection according to my small measure, and I kiss your elegant hand which guides me. Greetings and farewell, *shining ornament of the Republic of Letters* <note>The "Republic of Letters" (Respublica Literaria) was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars and writers in the 17th century</note>, and continue hereafter to love, advise, and teach

### LETTER LII.

->*To the very Reverend and most Distinguished Sir,*<-

I do not deny that it is among my chief desires that your love and expectation of me might be satisfied in some part. Even though you return the obligation of debt <note>original: *æris alieni*, literally "another's copper," a common Roman idiom for financial debt</note> with an application that is both pleasant and eloquent, I nonetheless stand as your more closely bound Debtor. Through this literary breath, I return the thanks I owe and a mutual love; do not doubt that, if it were ever granted through the turmoils of these times, I would indeed show you the very dwelling in which my soul is enclosed, which is earnestly devoted to your Reverence’s virtues. Meanwhile, I shall daily owe a greater benefit to Fortune, because I am permitted to become a Debtor more deeply encumbered by your love. To pay the debts of obedience, you shall compel me by a free decree of your admonitions; nor will the opportunity be lacking for me to proceed from there with a more joyful step, and to strive with all my strength toward the goal which a bright Genius <note>In the 17th century, a "Genius" referred to a guardian spirit or a person's natural talent and guiding intellect</note> might perhaps have set before me. One who lives bound to you in a faithful bond of love ardently asks the Heavenly Divinity to grant you, who are so deserving, a long life still and years of unhindered prosperity.

->*Your Reverence’s,*<-

Wolfenbüttel,

### LETTER LXI.

->*Truly Reverend and Most Renowned Sir,*<-

There is no reason for you to fear that the *bitterness of your letters might cause me boredom*, as you write; for although my hand is tender, it will always be found prompt and ready for yours. ### LETTER LXII.

->Truly Reverend and<-
->Most Renowned Sir,<-

Behold, I take up my pen again while it is still warm from my recent writing, prompted by Your Reverend Dignity by a new kind of kindness. For you arranged through my **Most Serene Father** <note>original: Serenissimum Parentem; likely referring to Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note> to have the **French-German New Testament** delivered to me. This gift is all the more pleasing to me because the French language is learned more holily from a Sacred author than from a secular one. I, however, mindful of my duty, return the greatest thanks possible to Your Reverend Dignity. For what else can be expected of me at this tender age? Great, I confess, are your merits toward me; nevertheless, I hope, by God’s favor, that it will one day come to pass that I may show a sign of my grateful heart, even if I cannot repay you as fully as I wish. In the meantime, I ask that you be content with my goodwill toward you; just as I owe you my most submissive service, so I shall never cease to acknowledge that debt. Farewell, **man born to serve others** <note>original: Vir demerendis hominibus nate</note>, and love the one who loves you most.

Given at Wolfenbüttel, July 8, 1644.

The most devoted to
Your Reverend Dignity.

May [God] grant... <note>original: Faxit...; the text cuts off here and continues on the next page</note>

## LETTER LXIV.

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord,<-

*As for your dealing with me through an eloquent intermediary <note>The Prince had evidently been using a tutor or secretary to compose his letters</note>, although even this is most honorable to me, nevertheless, if it is not a burden, I beg you to stop. For I do not demand a master of rhetoric from you at this tender age, but a boyish exercise; I shall value your own erasures and grammatical slips <note>original: Solæcos; "solecisms" or errors in the rules of grammar</note> more than some polished letter written by another. Give me, therefore, sweetest Prince, your own hand, your own attempts, and your own insults against **Priscian** <note>Priscian (fl. 500 CE) was the author of the standard Latin grammar textbook; "to break Priscian's head" or "insult Priscian" meant to make a grammatical mistake</note>, which he will easily forgive you for here, being mindful of the one who never wrote poorly only because he never wrote at all. We, truly, shall measure your progress by these and shall accompany them with pious prayers. I believe this will not be unwelcome to your most praised Father, and to me it will truly be sweeter than all honey and more delightful than sugar. Farewell, sweetest Prince, and return your hand <note>Meaning: write to me in your own hand</note> to me, which I humbly kiss with affection. 17 July 1644.*

You disapprove of the fact that I have dealt with you through an *Interpreter* <note>original: Interpretem; here referring to a secretary or tutor who assisted with the Latin composition</note> until now, desiring my own hand and my own attempts. # LETTERS OF THE YEAR 1645.

## I. With three Princes.

### LETTER LXVIII.

->*Salutations, Peace, and Christ, and happiness for the present year.*<-

->**Most Illustrious and Most Serene Princes,**<-
->**Most Merciful Lords,**<-

Even though both your sagacity and the diligence with which you have explained <note>or "unraveled"</note> a single right foot of Geryon <note>original: Gerionis; Geryon was a three-bodied giant in Greek mythology. Andreae uses this as a clever metaphor for the three princes to whom he is writing</note> is most pleasing to me, nevertheless, I shudder entirely at the very name of Bellona <note>the Roman goddess of war</note>, by whose "friendly" companionship we are again miserably tormented. Indeed, what is being waged today is by no means "war" <note>The author likely plays on the Latin word "bellum," which means "war" but is identical in form to the word for "beautiful" or "fine"</note>, but rather public robbery. I do not deny that war was, and can sometimes be, honorable, necessary, and even pious; but what I should say about the Beast of this time <note>a reference to the ongoing Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which devastated Germany</note>, which seems to compete with the gates of hell <note>original: tartari porta</note> and swallows whole fortresses through the impiety of its cause, I simply cannot find the words. Therefore, I most highly approve of this in your letters: that you favor defensive measures more than offensive ones. I pray from my heart to God, the Protector of your lands, that the necessity of defending them may never fall upon you, except fortunately and with growth for the Christian cause. Truly, may nourishing Peace and the Prince of Peace, CHRIST, look upon us, and may He keep you safe and flourishing. Farewell again, and look kindly [upon me].

->**To Your Most Illustrious and Serene Highnesses,**<-

January 1, 1645.
From your most humble client.

### Very Reverend and Most Distin-
### guished Lord Doctor,

The anatomical continuation of your Geryon <note>original: Gerionis; a mythological three-bodied giant, here used as a metaphor for the three princes Rudolf August, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albrecht</note> will be delayed eight days from now, though not without cause. For because we were recently inspecting weapons and discussing wars—the end of which all who bear the name of Christian in Europe hope for with prayers and tears, or are certainly bound to hope for—we thought it not unfitting to join our own prayers with yours. Nor did we think it would be unwelcome to you to do so under the auspices of the New Year <note>original: Novi Anni</note>, which people everywhere are accustomed to celebrate with favorable omens and to treat as sacred. Indeed, the greatest and first concern ought to be for the Commonwealth <note>original: Reip., an abbreviation of Respublica</note>, upon which our own welfare and that of our people depends.

We pray therefore from the bottom of our hearts: first, that this year which we are now entering may be as far removed from the events of those years just passed as happiness is from misery, or calm from the storm; and that it may be marked by a notable example of miraculous help sent down from heaven for us and for our descendants. Secondly, we pray that you and your family may obtain no small portion of heavenly kindness during this time of transition. But if it should seem otherwise to God—his anger, by which Europe now burns, not yet having been atoned for—we nevertheless pray that He may be willing to keep you and yours safe amidst the waves and tempests, and to deign to grant you those blessings which, in the midst of so many evils, might serve as an antidote <note>original: alexipharmaci; a term for a medicine that protects against poison or infection</note>. This is the same sentiment of our Instructors <note>original: Informatorum; the tutors responsible for the princes' education</note>, in whose name we also add a respectful greeting to you. Meanwhile, we remain as we have always been, namely:

->*Your Reverence's*<-
Wolfenbüttel <note>original: Guelpherbyti; the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note>, 13
January, the Year 1645.

### LETTER LXX.

->*Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,*<-

The obligation by which we have bound ourselves to you—and those who continually urge us on your behalf as a creditor—does not allow us to delay the payment of our debt any longer. We wrote recently that empires are sustained by arms and war as if by pillars, with your Geryon <note>original: Gerione; a mythological three-bodied giant, here used as a metaphor for the three princes mentioned on the previous page</note> leading the way; and you approved our opinion concerning defensive wars, adding a prayer which we pray with all our heart that God <note>original: DEVS</note> may see fit to fulfill. We confess that the mention of war is unwelcome in these times, in which it has degenerated so greatly. Indeed, if anyone were to measure the "rights of war" by the actual deeds committed, they would find no rights at all. Instead, lamenting a violence more ferocious than any barbarity, one would doubt what could possibly be "legitimate," or if there can be any alliance between laws and an ordeal that we experience as the worst of all things.

If you listen to those who are in charge of this war when they speak, they seem to hold views on the laws of war that are not entirely absurd. They seem to admit to the horrors we marvel at more through fate and the "necessity of sinning" than by deliberate counsel or fixed purpose. They know the laws of war, we say, but while they conduct their affairs, they violate and bypass them. They are either carried away by ill-advised zeal, or captured by the deceptive name of "liberty," or conversely, they are eager to diminish that liberty—as if the Commonwealth <note>original: Resp., abbreviation for Respublica</note> would be more stable if the citizens were accustomed to a stricter state of servitude. Consequently, they care for neither the lands nor their inhabitants, provided that religion and liberty remain intact—believing that inhabitants will not be lacking for the lands, nor lands for the inhabitants. 

But let us return to Geryon, having contemplated the Censer <note>original: Thuribulum; a vessel for burning incense, symbolizing prayer and religious duty</note>, by which he is indeed secure through arms, but safer through RELIGION—

<meta>catchword: rem (the start of the word 'tutiorem' or 'safer' continued on the next page)</meta>

<summary>In this letter, the author reflects on the grim disparity between the theoretical "laws of war" and the brutal reality of the mid-17th century conflicts, emphasizing that true security for the state (and the three princes) lies in religion rather than just military force.</summary>
<keywords>Thirty Years' War, Geryon metaphor, laws of war, defensive war, religious devotion, political liberty, the Commonwealth</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Letter LXX, which began on page 75. The previous page discussed the "rights of war" and how leaders often violate them despite knowing them. This page shifts focus to the role of religion as the essential foundation of the State (Republic) and social order.</meta>

<page-num>77</page-num>
<header>THE YEAR 1645.</header>
<sig>D 3</sig>

...you mean the Republic <note>original: Remp. (Respublica); the state or commonwealth</note>. Even the ancient Nations felt this regarding their own Superstitions—most of which were absurd, false, and empty. How then could we Christians doubt the necessity of affirming the worship by which we venerate the Divine Power <note>original: Numen</note>? Yet those pagans held Religion as a mere instrument of Rule. The Politicians among them, who were themselves mockers of religions, judged it a wise and necessary *tactic* <note>original: technâ; a Greek-derived term for a clever device or trick</note> to restrain the impulses and spirits of the unruly multitude. For us, however, it is the bond between God and man, which we confidently assert regarding our own faith as having been given and revealed to man by God Himself. He who cherishes and follows this also obeys the *Laws* and the Magistrates; he is a *good Man and a good Citizen.*

We know that most flourishing kingdoms existed in the past, and still exist today, without the practice of the Christian religion. Yet, beyond the fact that they were never entirely without *some* Religion, those kingdoms endured so long so that they might finally embrace God’s greatest mercy; this occurs so that our own happiness may shine more brightly in comparison to the darkness in which they are wrapped. If you take away Religion, what will follow but universal wars, slaughter, and rebellions? Truly, unless a person living in a Republic—perhaps one who is a bit too bold—persuades himself that there is a GOD who both sees and cares for what we do, he will be restrained by no barriers of the Laws and by no fear. Indeed, if an opportunity seems to favor him, he will cast off the yoke and, if he can, turn everything upside down <note>original: misceat quadrata rotundis; literally "mix squares with circles," a classical idiom for creating total chaos</note>.

But the breadth and dignity of this subject requires several letters, so let it be permitted to break this thread until the next time. Meanwhile, your most devoted servants wish from their hearts that you may fare well.

-> *To Your Reverend Dignity* <-

*Wolfenbüttel, January 21,*
*In the Year 1645.*

-> *Your most observant [servants].* <-

## LETTER 71.

->Very Reverend and Most<-
->Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

Recently, because of the shortness of time and so that my letters might remain within a reasonable length, it was necessary to suddenly break off the dissertation I had begun concerning RELIGION. We have written, however—and I do not regret repeating it—that Religion is certainly among the strongest supports of the Republics <note>original: Rerumpubl. (Respublicae); the state or commonwealth</note> above all, without which no Empires or Princedoms <note>original: Principatus; sovereign states or territories ruled by a prince</note> can exist. 

Indeed, no one will be able to deny this at first glance; yet if you consider the uprisings and wars that are stirred up because of religion, you might not give assent immediately, but rather hesitate as if at a crossroads. But we think of it this way: just as there can be many causes for a single thing, so the true causes must be accurately distinguished from the false ones by wise men. For there is no one who would allow their mind to be stained by such thoughts as if the Christians of old—while they were opposing pagan <note>original: Ethnicæ (Ethnicus); used here to refer to non-Christian or "heathen" religions</note> idolatry—brought about the devastation of regions, the overthrow of Republics, and other crimes of which they were accused by their enemies. 

Nor will anyone be so impious as to believe that the Eastern Christians could have defected to *Muhammadan* <note>original: Mahumetanum; referring to the expansion of Islam</note> fury, setting aside the Christian faith, for the sake of avoiding the calamities they suffered for so many centuries. For as it is known that pagan and Muhammadan abomination is from the Devil, so no one should doubt that all those evils and miseries are from the same author, and are by no means to be attributed to Religion. This is because the opinions that prevailed among those peoples regarding the worship of the Deity <note>original: Numinis (Numen); a term for divine power or a god</note> (if it can even be called worship) do not deserve the name of Religion. But what of those things to us, which for a hundred and...

...that have happened for more years in Europe, will it not seem? Must it not be confessed that almost all wars have arisen on account of Religion, as well as changes of Empires, seditions, and the defections of subjects from their Princes? This might perhaps seem to be the case to those who see nothing except what is before their feet, and do not penetrate into the hidden depths of human affairs. The causes of war in this century are the same as in previous ones: namely, *Ambition* and *Greed*, which are covered by the beautiful veil of Religion. Therefore, moved by no [just] cause, we complain about Religion or accuse it; we encrust *our own vices* with the *pretext of the holiest thing*, careless of God and men. It were to be wished that all those who were part of or the authors of these deadly calamities had known, or still knew, what Religion is, or how one must live according to it, and had proved—and would prove—their knowledge by their deeds; then not even the name of discord would be heard among us, Mars <note>The Roman god of war; here used to personify war itself.</note> would roar while bound in chains, kingdoms and nations would flourish, everyone would enjoy an abundance of divine gifts, and finally, what we strive to prove would be revealed: *namely, that Religion is the firmest foundation of Republics* <note>original: Rerumpubl. (Respublicae); used here in the classical sense to mean the state, commonwealth, or public affairs</note>. So much for the time being. Live well with your family, and continue to exercise [your duties].

With the approach of the French toward us and the encounter with the Bavarians, everything here resounds with the noise of arms; because of this, I received all the more eagerly your pious prayers for the safety of my homeland and myself, which is currently in no small danger. I have prayed to GOD that, since these prayers proceeded from such a good mind and sincere affection, He may allow them to be fulfilled and most generously repay you for this piety shown toward us. I also read with pleasure, and with the applause of a precise judgment and right sense, the "anatomy of the censer in Geryon" <note>original: thuribuli in Gerione anatomen. Indeed (if we speak only of the truer and unique kind), Religion is to some a matter of conscience, to others a game; to some a form of worship, to others an instrument; to some a faith, to others an *opinion*. Would that this last thing [mere opinion] did not today obscure that light kindled in Germany and make the clarity of the **Israelite fountain** <note>A biblical metaphor for the pure word of God or divine truth.</note> muddy once again. For it is easier to deplore than to correct how much damage that "Faith"—I might almost call it *faithless*, being lawless, shameless, senseless, sapless, and soulless—brings to the cause of Christ; and to rebuke or reproach it is not at all safe.

Therefore, you Most Illustrious Princes must take all the more care and apply yourselves—if you wish the affairs over which GOD has willed you to be placed to be safe, flourishing, and growing—to continue your true zeal and effort for religion, looking upon the most praiseworthy and almost unique **Example** of your Father. He conducts the affairs of religion with both **scepter** <note>representing his royal authority and power</note> and **pen** <note>representing his scholarship or legislative work</note>, but most especially with the intimate movement and feeling of his heart; he is as conspicuous for his upright faith in the **Church of GOD** as he is crowned by the most happy success of his counsels. For whatever the Holy Scriptures promise to religious Princes by both word and example, you see that clearly performed and renewed in your most religious Father, and you enjoy the fruits of it. I humbly pray to the eternal deity that this may be continuous and perpetual for you and your renowned House, and that He may protect you and your instructors (to whom I send a most dutiful greeting... <note>original: salutem; the word is cut off by the catchword "lutem" at the bottom of the page.</note>)

...to examine the MARKS of *True Religion*: which we do, not so much to further confirm the Truth of the Christian Religion, as to make the falsehood and impiety of other Ceremonies more clearly evident. Therefore, let this be the *First* foundation of True Religion; that it turns and directs us and our worship toward GOD, the Best and Greatest, <note>original: "DEVM Opt. Max." (Deum Optimum Maximum), a title originally used for Jupiter but here reclaimed for the Christian God.</note> the Creator of all things; for through Religion, man is reconciled to GOD for salvation. However, the salvation of men is to be joined to GOD; for neither the World, nor the things that belong to it, can make man blessed: but He alone who created him makes man blessed. All PAGANS <note>original: "ETHNICI," referring to Gentiles or non-Christians.</note> have therefore fallen away from hope, they who adored either Creatures lower than themselves, or Demons, from whom no hearing and no help was to be hoped for, but rather destruction was to be expected. But indeed, so that you may grant *True* worship to GOD, it is necessary that you first know Him rightly; yet no one attains the knowledge of what GOD is through reason alone: for which reason, just as a Peasant, who has never seen the Court, could hardly assign the honor which is due to a Prince; much less could a man, as a man, know how GOD is to be rightly worshipped. Let us, poor wretches, confess that we cannot approach GOD, unless He deigns to descend to us; our ascent is the descent of GOD. This, therefore, is the *second mark* of True Religion: that it teaches us a worship relying upon the Word of GOD, and revealed by Him. By this argument, the ancient JEWISH <note>original: "IVDAICÆ."</note> Ceremonies fall away, by which GOD did not wish to be worshipped forever, but only for a time, until He should come whom they had foreshadowed. <note>The author refers to the Christian belief that Old Testament laws were "shadows" or types that were fulfilled by the arrival of Jesus Christ.</note> Furthermore, because Nature understands its own corruption in some way, and at the same time recognizes that a cleansing is supremely necessary for itself—which is not found among the Philosophers, much less among the Politicians—that *third* <term>Distinguishing Mark</term> <note>original: "Gnorisma," a Greek word for a characteristic or identifying feature.</note> of True Religion...

I had written the most recent letters on the day before the Ides of February [February 12th] of this year, and the earlier ones on the Kalends of January [January 1st], since I was unable to do more because of poor health, which still holds me. How excellently you have touched upon the marks of the truer religion and, as it were, hit the nail on the head <note>original: "acu rem tetigistis," literally "touched the thing with a needle," a Latin idiom for being exactly right</note>, so that it might be distinguished from any false ones! You have also distinguished it against the religion of the Jews, which was limited by time and covered by a veil <note>A common 17th-century theological metaphor suggesting that the Old Testament laws were a "veil" that was lifted by the coming of Christ</note>; and by the expiation due for our sins through Christ, which is unknown to Philosophers, inaccessible to Politicians <note>In this context, "politicians" likely refers to those focused solely on secular statecraft or worldly power</note>, but by the Saracens (or rather Hagarenes <note>original: "Hagarenis." These indeed are the marks which both establish the True religion and prefer it above all others that the World holds. I will add, however, if you allow it, a finishing touch <note>original: "coronidem," a Greek-derived word for a flourish or finishing stroke at the end of a book</note>, or ornament: namely, the gifts <note>original: "charismata"</note> of the Holy Spirit. Through these He bestows heroic impulses and a life far more perfect than any "Idea" of Philosophy might attain, so that the Christian Religion, flashing with divine light and miracles, excels all others and alone commands by its practical effects. 

Whence it is especially incumbent upon us that we practice <note>original: "profiteamur"</note> this religion more than we merely profess <note>original: "confiteamur"</note> it, and express it in deed rather than boast of it with the mouth; indeed, that we experience it in the heart rather than display it outwardly, and that we lean solidly upon this rather than be ruled by mere opinions. If you persevere in this study, illustrious Princes, you will reach GOD himself, the aim of religion; you will grasp CHRIST, the center of religion; and you will fix His merit as the foundation of religion and the anchor of your salvation. Indeed, by your Life...

### LETTER LXXVI.

->To the Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,<-
->Most Merciful Lords,<-

*Because you are not at all weary of reciprocating letters with me, I both owe much to you and congratulate myself greatly; indeed, I take no small relief from my grief regarding our public misfortunes from that source.* Those things which you have argued so excellently and elegantly regarding rewards please me exceedingly. If you are rightly imbued with the zeal for conferring such rewards, I would affirm that you will have attained a great part of the duty of a Prince, into whose hands God will one day deliver this glorious office. For while it is our part to deserve well through faith, diligence, labor, and daring; so indeed it is yours to acknowledge, value, repay, and crown those efforts, since otherwise a Court might bear the mark of ingratitude. 

In my lifetime, I saw a most rare example of this virtue—which I like to call *compensatory virtue*—in Philip Louis, Count Palatine of Neuburg <note>Philip Louis (1547–1614) was known for his effective administration of the Palatinate-Neuburg</note>, an incomparable Prince. He maintained ministers, but only the most select and highly trained, with modest salaries <term>salaries: "stipendiis," referring to regular base pay</term> indeed, but with perpetual rewards, to such an extent that he honored nearly every outstanding act with some gift or honor. To this he added the charms of conversation and, frequently, small gifts or tokens <term>tokens: "missilia," literally things thrown or distributed as favors</term>. By this means, he ensured that they could not be drawn away elsewhere even by the offer of lavish salaries, for they considered it a matter of conscience to desert so easy and generous a Master—

->To the Most Reverend and Distinguished<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

We have received your letters, dearer than gold, which are to be stored among our most precious treasures. Your Geryon <note>original: "Gerion". In classical mythology, Geryon was a giant with three bodies; here, it likely refers to a specific literary work or a metaphorical figure representing a complex legal or political system being discussed by the correspondents.</note> has added PUNISHMENTS to rewards, concerning which something must also be set forth. And since there are many types of these, we shall treat only those which are Capital <term>Capital punishments: from the Latin *caput* (head), referring to punishments involving the loss of life or legal standing</term>, through which human blood is shed. *Indeed, it seems absurd to some that a sinful man, who is himself subject to God’s judgment, should condemn one like himself—and an image of God—to death, when God nonetheless spares him and invites him to repentance.* By this opinion, the wickedness of men is greatly strengthened, and the bond of human society is dissolved. Nor can this be accepted or approved under the appearance of *Mercy* <note>original: "Clementiæ"</note>. For examples are not lacking of divine *Vengeance* <note>original: "Vindictæ"</note>, both sudden and slow, upon the wicked. God Himself commands in many places that evil must be removed from the City, by which it is rendered unclean. Paul <note>The Apostle Paul; the author is referencing Romans 13:4, which discusses the authority of the state.</note> himself warns that the Magistrate is to be feared and obeyed, for he does not gird on the sword in vain. Indeed, those whose salvation is despaired of, whose actions are detestable, and whose memory and recollection cannot occur without loathing, ought to be afflicted with such punishments; for them, it is beneficial to depart, as if never to return to their former selves. And this is done not so that past deeds may be undone—which is impossible—but so that the same acts may not be committed in the future. For man is joined to man by such kinship that he cannot take away a life unless driven by the weightiest cause. Even if such a cause exists, those who mitigate capital punishments and turn them into others—such as condemna-

</meta>

condemnation to the galleys <note>original: "triremes"</note> or to labor in the mines <term>Mining labor: known as *opus metallicum*, this was a Roman form of penal servitude often used as an alternative to execution</term>, following the example of the Romans and other nations. However, there are two *rocks* <note>meaning pitfalls or dangers</note> to be avoided by the Magistrate in inflicting Capital punishments:

The *first* is that he should not exercise his ingenuity in seeking out new forms of torture. Far be the monstrous cruelty of *Mezentius* <note>An Etruscan king in myth who tied living men to corpses</note>; the bull of *Phalaris* <note>A hollow bronze statue in which victims were slowly roasted alive</note>; the "wife" of *Nabis* <note>An iron-maiden-like machine fashioned after the tyrant's wife</note>; the torches and lights of *Nero* <note>Who famously used Christians as human lamps</note>; the prisons of *Sulla*; the horses of *Diomedes* <note>Who fed his guests to his man-eating horses</note>; or the cages of King *Louis* of France <note>Louis XI, who was notorious for keeping prisoners in cramped iron cages</note>. For he who wishes to seem clever and a master in these matters pours out human blood with the greatest joy, as if it were of no value.

The *other* is that he should not be present himself for the punishments while the accused are being interrogated. Our Tacitus writes in his *Agricola* (chapter 45, note 4): *Nero withdrew his eyes and indeed ordered crimes, but did not watch them; whereas under Domitian, the chief part of our miseries was to see and to be seen.* The words of *Vitellius* are especially detestable, for when he had ordered men to be killed in his presence, he said *that he had wished to feed his eyes.* Finally, the Magistrate must take care not to mock those condemned or speak harshly to them, but should follow the example of *Joshua*, who considered even the sacrilegious *Achan* worthy of the name "*son*" <note>A reference to Joshua 7:19, where Joshua speaks compassionately to Achan before his execution to encourage a confession</note>. By this reasoning, he will avoid the hatred that accompanies this office, maintain his own innocence safe amidst the guilty <note>original: "fontes," likely a printer's error for "sontes," meaning the guilty or criminal</note>, and stabilize this human society as much as he is able.

For the rest, we grieve that your illness persists, which is perhaps increased by the common calamity. Remember that you and those like you, upon whose counsel and prayers the Republic rests, must seize hope even where none appears, and must not abandon your post, however trembling or stumbling you may be. May GOD give you those things which lead to your benefit and that of the Fatherland. Farewell, from

->Your Reverend Dignity's<-
->Most Devoted [Servants].<-

->OF THE SACROSANCT TRINITY<-

We celebrated the Feast yesterday <note>The Feast of the Holy Trinity.</note>, and on the preceding day in Hafenreffer’s Compendium <note>Matthias Hafenreffer (1561–1619) was a Lutheran theologian. His *Loci Theologici* was a standard textbook used to teach doctrine in the 17th century.</note> we came upon the passage concerning GOD, where you write briefly but forcefully: *The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity cannot indeed be compared to any human thing, but it can nevertheless be shadowed forth in some way through the faculties of the soul.* Indeed, we are not unaware that those who attempt to scrutinize it beyond what is permitted are overwhelmed by the majesty of its glory, like those who, while they fix their eyes on the brilliance of the *Sun*, blunt the sharpness of their sight; just as our Master Hafenreffer explains these things, in whose teachings we can safely rest. However, just as we behold all things under the Sun by its benefit, so with God’s help, we perceive the things that are of God, namely when those things which reason cannot find are revealed to us, and then the soul sees, weighs, and approves them. An example of this matter will, as we hope, shine forth from what is to be said. *The rational soul has two faculties, namely the intellect and the will; the Soul is not entirely intellect, nor entirely will: this is not the Intellect, nor is that the Will.* For often we do not want what we understand, and we want what we do not understand: So the Divine Es-

...essence is not the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit: Neither is the Father the Son, nor is the Son the Holy Spirit. *However, the very letters we write prove that the human soul possesses understanding;* moreover, not only living creatures but even inanimate ones cry out that GOD is endowed with the highest intellect—for their exceptional and utterly marvelous order could only exist from an intellect. *These letters are the external operations of the human intellect; the whole world is the external operation of the Divine.* But the first and foremost operation of the Intellect remains within the Intellect; and because there is nothing except the infinite in the infinite GOD, in and through this operation He begets the SON from eternity, who is also GOD, and whom we call the WORD OF THE FATHER <note>original: "VERBVM PATRIS." Truly, the soul loves what it wills, whether it is good or believed to be so; even that which lacks reason and soul has its own inclinations and its own desires:* Thus GOD wills from eternity what He understands from eternity; *But what does He will? Himself, surely—that is, goodness itself.* Nor does the Father only will Himself, but the Son does as well, and therefore the HOLY SPIRIT proceeds from both: For this reason He is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, and is also the *Love of the Father and the Son; now, in GOD, to understand is to exist, as is to will:* Thus the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one Essence <term>Essentia: the fundamental "stuff" or being of God, shared by all three persons</term> and power with the Father. *Here we rest the pen, and we ask that you respond as to whether this contemplation seems analogous to the faith—unless perhaps (heaven forbid) ill health causes a delay. For the rest, we maintain our old ways. Farewell.*

Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelph." The Latin name for the city of Wolfenbüttel, seat of the House of Guelph.</note>, June 3, 1645.

# LETTER LXXXI.
## Most Illustrious and Highborn Princes,
## Most Merciful Lords,

Although *everything is a hindrance to my writing, as I am preparing for my return home and have not yet fully recovered my health, nevertheless, fired by the ease and elegance of your letters, I considered it a matter of shame, let alone a fault, if I did not offer at least something unpolished in return for such great favor toward me.* And indeed, let Geryon <note>Geryon was a triple-bodied giant from Greek mythology. In the 17th century, the name was sometimes used as a derogatory nickname for opponents or to mock the concept of a three-part being; here, the author likely dismisses a specific critic or a particular complication.</note> now keep his own affairs to himself. Truly, that you have, on this occasion, turned your attention to the contemplation of the Most Holy Trinity <note>original: "SS. Triadis"</note>—as much as is permitted to us through shadows—this is both pious and praiseworthy, for which I congratulate you from my heart. This mystery, otherwise incomprehensible to reason, shone even upon the more wise among the Pagans <note>original: "Gentilibus"</note>, whether by interaction with the Church (which is more likely) or by a deeper investigation of the remnants of light <note>The "remnants of light" refers to the idea that some knowledge of God remains in human reason even after the Fall of Man.</note>. But oh, the unhappy Antitrinitarians <note>A group, such as the Socinians, who rejected the traditional doctrine of the Trinity, arguing it was irrational or unscriptural.</note> of our time, who babble with shameless and blasphemous mouths that all this is placed as if in mere conjectures, and that madmen persuade themselves of it—though nothing could be more absurd or impossible, and it becomes a coarse fabrication. You act more rightly, who both grasp this holy mystery with simple faith and also admit the granted supports of reason, like rays of the inaccessible Sun through shade; in which matter Philippe de Mornay <note>A prominent French Protestant diplomat and theologian (1549–1623) whose work *De la vérité de la religion chrétienne* sought to prove Christian doctrines through reason.</note>, in his book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, proved himself an excellent man. May the Most Holy Trinity and Unity <note>original: "SS. Trias & Monas"</note> preserve this right understanding for you forever, and make it greater day by day, as I pray with my whole soul.

->To your Most Illustrious, Highborn, and Merciful Excellencies<-

Stuttgart, June 18,
1645.

Your most humble servant.

# Most Illustrious and Most Highborn Princes,
## Lords by far most merciful,

*The sweetness of your letters is such that, even if I should think it best to spare your dignity or the intensity of your studies, I nonetheless cannot abstain from inviting them of my own accord, driven by an excessive longing for them; I promise myself your generosity will indulge this boldness of mine. For why should I not seek them out with the greatest zeal? In them I find both a most polished style and thoughts far beyond your age, as well as clear images of Virtue, which promise something great for the service of the Republic <note>original: "Reip." (short for Republicae). Here, it refers to the general "Commonweal" or the public state of the German territories.</note>, for all of Germany, and most especially for your own lands and peoples.* I truly congratulate them all the more because I see so few of your Rank <note>original: "Ordinis Vestri"</note> who are being led toward this most upright way of reasoning—or rather, to put it more accurately, who allow themselves to be so educated. There is no lack of <term>courtly disgraces</term> <note>original: "Aularum dehonestamenta," referring to sycophants or corrupt officials who lack moral or intellectual character.</note> who do not fear to suggest that these studies are unbecoming to your high station, pronouncing in a <term>bovine voice</term> <note>original: "bovina voce." This likely implies a coarse, loud, or unthinking manner of speaking, like the lowing of cattle, contrasting with the "polished" speech of scholars.</note> that nothing is more lowly than a Prince who is pious, humane, and literate—simply so that they might not lack masters under whom they may act like revelers without punishment. But to me, as I turn over the entire history of the world, nothing occurs more certainly or more frequently than that those who were religious, upright, and learned were also the ones who were happy and glorious; whereas the atheists, the fierce, and the barbarians were subject to sorrowful disasters and the ruin of their states. But these matters have been carried out more elegantly in your own Nesselius’s <note>Likely referring to Martin Nessel (1607–1673), a notable German scholar and educator who served as a tutor to young nobles.</note> <term>Panegyrics</term> <note>A formal public speech or written text delivered in high praise of a person or thing.</note>, so there is no need to repeat them. I pray to GOD as a suppliant that you may strive under the most exact <term>Paternal Idea</term> <note>The "Idea" here refers to the Platonic sense of a perfect model or archetype—specifically, the example set by their father as the "Best Prince."</note> of the Best Prince, until you are able to plant firm feet for yourselves to complete the journey of Virtue and highest Praise, and to seize the Crown of your most Illustrious Ancestors in a most happy race.

### LETTER LXXXIII.

->***Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,***<-

We are glad that you take some pleasure from our letters. For us, indeed, nothing is more welcome than this exchange of letters; though it may be troublesome to you and cost you time, it is truly useful and necessary for those of us who are learning. For whether you extol the remarkable Virtue in your own writings, or exhort us to those things which we ought to do, we recognize the duty of a Teacher and a friend—but a wise one, seeking not his own growth, but ours. For this, we not only give thanks, but desire to return the favor. 

We recall the promise regarding the dissection of <term>Geryon</term> <note>original: "Gerione." In Greek mythology, Geryon was a monster with three heads and three bodies. Here, he is used as an anatomical and political allegory.</note>. Indeed, it would be unseemly and quite foolish to have dwelled only on the contemplation of the feet and the base upon which they rest, while neglecting that which gives life, as it were, to the whole mass—without which those Three Heads, and the six feet and hands, would constitute a Monster, breathing toward its own destruction. 

You understand that we are hinting at **CONCORD** <note>original: "CONCORDIAM," meaning harmony or political agreement.</note>, which you place in the heart. For it is she who teaches each member of a great body its own duty. She is the preserver of the arts, of trades, of military discipline, of agriculture, and of religion—the very things for which you laid down the bases and foundations. For just as the world does not bear two Suns, nor the human body multiple Hearts, so it is necessary that a state with "many hearts"—if we may speak thus—must perish. Although, however, for the Republic...

<meta>This page concludes Letter LXXXIII (83), written from Wolfenbüttel on September 9, 1645. It continues the discussion of political and fraternal unity (Concord) begun on the previous page, contrasting the mythological Geryon with historical tyrants who practiced fratricide.</meta>

<page-num>99</page-num>
<header>YEAR 1645.</header>

Although harmony is extremely necessary, it is nevertheless maintained with the greatest difficulty among so many men who seem almost naturally inclined toward disagreement. The armed authority of the Laws sanctions this harmony in whatever way it can. But among Germans—whose blood is common, whose education is joined, and who for the most part share the same customs and similar inclinations—we consider such harmony to be natural and nearly necessary. Therefore, fraternal enmities, quarrels, and those deadly wars that sometimes arise among Illustrious men are abominable and an insult to Nature itself. Those who, for the sake of their own advantage or to avenge private injuries, either incite or nourish and feed such discord among those joined by such a close bond, are to be cursed with every possible devotion.

Many examples of fraternal **Concord** exist in our own House <note>The House of Brunswick-Lüneburg, to which the young Princes belonged.</note>, to which is added *Geryon* <note>original: "Gerion." A giant from Greek myth usually depicted as a monster with three heads or three bodies.</note>, believed to be triple-headed and triple-bodied—not because he was that kind of monster, but because three brothers, sweetly harmonious and of one mind, used the same counsels in the Republic and seemed to be ruled by a single spirit. We remember writing that this was the origin of the fable. 

We detest the *Cains, Esaus, Abimelechs, the younger Cyrus, the Jugurthas, Neros, Caracallas, Atahualpas* <note>original: "Attabalipas." A reference to the Inca emperor Atahualpa, whose civil war against his brother Huáscar was frequently cited by 17th-century European writers as a contemporary example of tragic fraternal strife.</note>, and others who, by inflicting violence upon Nature herself, thirsted for their brothers' blood. On this occasion, it was helpful to reread the speech of *Micipsa* <note>A King of Numidia (in modern Algeria) whose deathbed speech is recorded by the Roman historian Sallust.</note> which he gave to his sons as he was dying, from which we have gathered these words:

> *Who is a closer friend than a brother to a brother? Or what stranger will you find faithful if you have been an enemy to your own kin? For my part, I hand over a kingdom to you; it will be firm if you are good, but weak if you are bad. For* **BY CONCORD** *small things grow;* **BY DISCORD** *the greatest things fall apart.* <note>original: "nam CONCORDIA parvæ res crescunt: DISCORDIA maximæ dilabuntur." This is one of the most famous political maxims of the Renaissance, taken from Sallust's "The Jugurthine War."</note>

But perhaps we wander too far afield. Farewell, and please respond. We bid your son greetings. Wolfenbüttel, September 9, 1645.

->To Your Most Observant Dignity.<-

## LETTER LXXXIV.

### Most Illustrious and Serene Princes, most merciful Lords,

How pleasant to me, and of what great value, the exchange of your letters is, I do not wish to repeat so often, lest you suspect in me any bit of flattery, which I entirely abhor. Let me only be permitted to pray that no weariness of this task ever steals upon you; to avoid which, I will easily allow less frequent writing, especially if it should interfere with your studies. Furthermore, I owe you great thanks for returning to the finishing of **Geryon** <note>original: "Gerionem." Referencing the myth discussed on the previous page where three bodies represent three harmonious brothers.</note>; it seemed indeed—as you yourselves ingeniously observed—that **Concord**, who was the Mother of this three-bodied fiction, rightfully demanded that your wisdom and diligence pay her some tribute, as if you were to establish yourselves, harmonious brothers, as a "Geryon" of this current age. 

To achieve such happiness and to provide so illustrious an example, although History will gladly come to your aid, those things born "at home" <note>Referring to the Princes' own family history and domestic examples.</note>, as you write, will both affect you more and bind you more tightly. For this reason, I congratulate you from my heart and command you to continue in this consensus. Truly, how the sense of fraternal blood seethes in the midst of those discords which Satan is accustomed to sow, a memorable example from the **Electoral House of Saxony** <note>The ruling family of the Electorate of Saxony, a powerful state within the Holy Roman Empire.</note> has taught. Though you cannot be ignorant of this story, I will not be reluctant to recount it.

**Frederick** and **William**, brothers and Dukes of Saxony, were set against one another by the schemes of courtiers over the division of their inheritance. This was done with such bitterness that neither the Emperor’s authority nor the counsel and prayers of the **Estates of the Empire** <note>The *Reichsstände*, the various princes and authorities who held a seat in the Imperial Diet.</note> had any power to pacify them; instead, they believed the matter had to be decided by arms and mutual slaughter. And now, each army stood facing the other, [threatening] a great slaughter of Christian blood...

## Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,
### Most gracious Lord,

*Your letters, which are full of elegance and favor toward me, are nothing if not most precious and pleasant; indeed, nothing could be more opportune for relieving the distress of my mind and body. For although the fierce storm hanging over my Fatherland <term>Patria</term> <note>Referring to the ongoing devastation and political instability in the German territories during the final years of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).</note> shakes me deeply, and my illness, recurring at intervals, trials me harshly, I nonetheless seem to be soothed by the breeze and West Wind <term>Zephyro</term> <note>The Zephyr was the personification of the gentle west wind in Greek mythology, symbolizing a calming or restorative influence.</note> of Your Highness’s kindness, which promises a harbor of safety even after a shipwreck. Therefore, best of Princes, do not grow weary of writing those letters, in which such excellent consolation for both public and private misfortunes is placed before me. Added to this is the affection of your Tutors <term>Informatorum</term> toward me, which I perceive in your letters; if I did not value this highly, I would rightly be called unjust and ungrateful. Indeed, regarding the explanation of Geryon <note>original: "In Gerione." Geryon was a mythological giant with three bodies joined at the waist. In this correspondence, it serves as a metaphor for the three princely brothers acting with a single will.</note>, I beg you to continue—unless it be a burden—so that no subject for writing may be lacking. For since you not only grasp my meaning exactly but also, through your shrewd character, uncover even more than I intended, this industry of yours, as well as your pious and wise study, cannot but be vehemently approved by me. It promises us, in time, a perfect Prince and a rival to your father. I pray to a merciful God that this may happen for a happier and more peaceful Germany after its disaster is overcome, through your Threefold Cord <term>Triplici Vestro funiculo</term> <note>A likely reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12: "A threefold cord is not quickly broken," symbolizing the strength found in the brothers' unity.</note>. May He keep you, distinguished Prince, safe and sound along with your German brothers. Farewell, and look with favor*

->upon your most humble Client,<-

Stuttgart, March 19,
->in the year 1645.<-

# Most Illustrious and High Prince,
### Most gracious Lord,

Nothing is more precious or more pleasant to me than Your letters, filled with elegance and favor toward me; nothing is more timely in relieving my sickness of mind and body. For however much the cruel storm that threatens my Fatherland <note>This refers to the closing years of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which devastated the German territories.</note> shakes me deeply, and my disease—flaring up at intervals—harshly tries me, I yet seem to be soothed by the breeze of your Clemency and by a <term>Zephyr</term> <note>A gentle west wind, often used in classical literature to symbolize a favorable or healing influence.</note> that promises me a harbor of safety even after a shipwreck. Do not, therefore, best Prince, grow weary of writing those letters, in which an excellent solace for both public and private evil is provided for me. 

To this is added the love of your tutors for me, which I perceive in your letters; if I did not value it highly, I would rightly be called unjust and ungrateful. Regarding <term>Geryon</term> <note>original: "Gerione." In Greek mythology, Geryon was a giant with three bodies. Here, as in the previous page, he serves as an allegory for the unity of three princely brothers.</note> indeed—so that matter for writing may not be lacking—please proceed with the explanation, if it is not a burden. For since you not only follow my mind exactly but also draw out even more through your sagacious wit, I cannot but highly approve of this industry of yours, and your pious and wise study; it promises us that you will one day be a perfect Prince and a rival to your father's greatness. 

That this may happen for a happier and pacified Germany, after this disaster has been overcome, through your <term>Triple Cord</term> <note>original: "Triplici Vestro funiculo." A biblical reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12: "A threefold cord is not quickly broken," symbolizing the strength found in the unity of the three brothers.</note>, I pray to a propitious GOD, who may protect, keep, and save you, renowned Prince, along with your German brothers. ->To Your Illustrious Highness,<-

I wished for them to reveal their "Sun" to our world so it would not go unknown, and to make the benefit plain before our Sun sets upon us <note>The writer uses "Sun" metaphorically to refer to the reigning Prince, suggesting he is a source of light and life for the region, and perhaps noting his advanced age.</note>. For it was unworthy that so great a Prince, your incomparable Father—who surpassed the ideal types of the rhetoricians and the examples of the historians—should be ignored by so many of his contemporaries. It would be a shame if the learned offered no other gratitude to his living virtue, which has walked among us and survived so many years, other than to say one day that he has been taken from our sight. Therefore, let us acknowledge that he is among us and (long may it be so!) continues to survive; let us, as private citizens, value him and earnestly pray to God, the merciful preserver of such a great gift. I owe you much for your kindness toward my only son, whose letters written on my behalf <note>original: "vicarias literas." Literally "vicar letters," meaning letters written by a proxy or substitute.</note> you did not disdain. Since I appoint him the heir of my obedience and perpetual respect toward your Serene House, and bind him to you by the bond of <term>homage</term> <note>original: "homagii." A formal acknowledgment of loyalty and service to a feudal lord.</note>, he could never be happier than if he might one day prove himself a useful servant through all his loyalty, labor, and mental effort. May CHRIST guide you, most Illustrious Brothers and great ornaments of a great house, so that you may continue, increase, and even surpass the immense fame of your great Father. Farewell, and look upon me with favor.

->Stuttgart, August 7, 1645. — From your most humble client.<- <note>original date: "VII. Eid. Aug." The writer uses the Roman calendar; the Ides of August was the 13th, and counting seven days back (inclusive) brings us to August 7.</note>

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished<-

I received the greatest joy from your letter, which assured me of your recovery—the proof of which was your own handwriting. For this news, I give thanks to God and implore His Omnipotence that He may wish to keep you safe for many years yet for the benefit of the Church and your family. I clearly recognize your kind spirit toward me, for you grant a sort of "soul" to letters, even when they are sometimes so cold <note>original: "frigidæ." However that may be, I wish you to be persuaded that they come from the heart; you are one who prefers such sincerity to magnificent words.

I remember that I recently preferred your letters to those of your son—not because I am happy to be without his, but because I have sometimes wished to receive them both together. I desire that what I wrote in my previous letters be repeated to him. You added nothing concerning the **Battle of Nördlingen** <note>The Second Battle of Nördlingen (also known as the Battle of Alerheim) took place on August 3, 1645, just weeks before this letter was written. Our **Gerion** <note>Likely a nickname or a reference to a specific mutual acquaintance, student, or perhaps a literary project currently "at rest."</note> is still sleeping; I shall wake him shortly. ## LETTER XCI.

### Most Illustrious and Exalted Prince,
### Lord, by far most Gracious,

*With what pleasure of soul I read Your Highness's letters, and how much I value them, I shall never be able to fully explain. They are surely tokens of your continued favor toward me, which is to be extended even to my son; they are guarantees that no weariness from my own dull letters has yet crept in, since you invite them of your own accord with your most elegant ones. Indeed, you are even willing to receive those of my son, who is unworthy of such great fortune. On this account, I congratulate my son and rejoice from my heart for myself; I give the greatest possible thanks on behalf of us both. I conceive a certain hope that this brightness of your Most Serene House—which began with my grandfather, Dr. Jacob <note>Likely Jacob Chimarrhaeus or a similar family figure who served the court. But even if God denies this to me, contrary to my greatest and only desire (as my health has been greatly afflicted and weakened throughout this entire year), so that I am less able to visit you and testify to my service in person, I would not despair that my son will do so. I have consecrated him to your service by my own vow and the resolve of my soul; he will undoubtedly reap some fruit from your munificence through the services of his great-grandfather Jacob to your Church, which I believe are not yet forgotten. May Christ bless this devotion and gratitude of mine toward you.*

## LETTER XCII.
### *To the Very Reverend and Most Illustrious*
### *Lord Doctor,*

I shall begin from the final part of your letter. You apologize for its length, but I believe you do so without reason, for I read your writings in such a way that I always wish they were even longer. I, however, wish to be briefer now, because I have written so recently. It is truly painful that the **Duchy of Württemberg** has been for some time a refuge for both factions <note>This refers to the alternating occupations by Imperial and Protestant forces during the Thirty Years' War.</note>. The examples of military lawlessness following a **Victory** are well known. For the arrogant **Victors** pursue their **Victory** as long as they are able; but the **Vanquished**, who wander here and there without a leader, are accustomed to vomit out the hatred and anger—which they could not vent against the enemy—upon the wretched villagers <note>original: "paganos," referring here to the rural peasantry who bore the brunt of the war's cruelty</note>. Truly, we provide a great proof of patience; and just as the ancient age saw the extreme limit of liberty, so we see the extreme of servitude.

I have written to my son, whose letter I read with pleasure. Indeed, it seems he was recommended more out of fatherly affection than because he stood in need of it, for his own virtue recommends him sufficiently. There is no doubt, however, that your own extraordinary gifts, and those of his great-grandfather **Jakob Andreae** <note>Jakob Andreae (1528–1590) was a famous Lutheran theologian and primary author of the Formula of Concord; his legacy was a powerful "social capital" for his descendants</note>—who in his time was a man of great benefit to all **Protestants**, but especially to the **Duchy of Brunswick**—will serve as a most ample recommendation among all the godly and the followers of the Gospel Truth. Therefore, I repeat what was in my son's letter: and may the Most Illustrious Lord Parent, being most well-disposed toward you, see to the rest.

From the North there is nothing, except that **Peace** has been ratified there; the **Swedes** are moving from **Holstein** into the Empire. I am reading **Cornelius** <note>Tacitus, the Roman historian known for his analysis of power and tyranny</note> diligently, and from him I learn the manner in ci-

## LETTER XCIII.

Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
My far most merciful Lord,

I believe you have already often noticed *with what a devoted spirit I am drawn toward you, and how I favor your auspices with all my prayers; and now I wish it to be more and more a matter of record. May* GOD *grant that this boy grows for the use and increase of the Christian kingdom, both for Christ his Savior, and for you his sponsor, and for us his parents; and that we may one day be able to return the favor of your greatest kindness. ### LETTER XCIV.

->To the Very Reverend and Most<-
->Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

Your letter of September 24th, along with the mechanical drawings of the Columns and *gateways* <note>original: "Propylæorum," referring to monumental entrance structures in classical architecture</note>, and their notable decoration and beautiful additions, has been delivered: for which I give you great thanks. I wonder, in examining them, that the *Tuscan* order was omitted by the designer *Vredeman de Vries* <note>original: "Frisio," referring to Hans Vredeman de Vries (1527–1604), a Dutch architect whose treatises on the five classical orders were widely influential in Northern Europe</note>, especially since the diligence of that most ingenious man plays so skillfully and artistically with the variation and decoration of the *Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite* columns. At the same time, I am reminded of the genius and luxury of *Ancient Greece*, from which *Italy, France, Spain*, and others who display wondrous buildings have borrowed most things. While our own age strives to surpass their glory, it finds an industry and dexterity not unequal to its passion; it bears witness again by a *new example* that not everything among the *ancients* was better.

For the rest, I judge the praises with which you heap upon my letters to be unnecessary; they are as far from elegance as your own words are from all flattery. For I have long since recognized that you do not flatter by praising (which would be unseemly for a good man and suspicious to me), but rather that you encourage me toward *Virtue*—which such tributes follow—as if by applying spurs. You would experience this in person if you were present. Nor, indeed, can this frequent exchange of letters be unwelcome, because the *Most Illustrious Lord Parent* <note>likely referring to Duke Augustus the Younger, the father/ruler mentioned in the previous correspondence</note>, by allowing this kind of correspondence between us, demands two things of me: namely, that I repeatedly prove my diligence to his *Highness*, and that I appoint you as the *judge* of my daily progress.

## LETTER XCV.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->By far the most gracious Lord,<-

Since I see that you are fatigued neither by reading my letters nor by writing your own to me, I indeed become bolder, so that I may continue to obey you, or, if you prefer, continue this imposition. What we ought to hope for or despair of regarding Peace, based on the changing fortunes of war <note>original: "Martis vicissitudine," literally "the vicissitudes of Mars," the Roman god of war. This refers to the ongoing volatility of the Thirty Years' War</note>, we do not yet clearly see. Therefore, we await from GOD what we think is most difficult to obtain from men; He who has until now held the governance of the world for the benefit of His Church—in a manner clearly different from our own opinion—will thus continue to rightly provide for His people and our affairs, and will prove Himself a Victor even in yielding. I owe much for Your Grace toward my son; if the services rendered by his great-grandfather to Your churches should overflow upon him through Your favor and auspices, he will be blessed, and will easily forget his longing for his own homeland. I humbly offer my greetings to your Most Illustrious Brothers, and commend myself entirely to you all; may Christ keep you safe, increase your prosperity, and distinguish you. Farewell and look upon us with favor.

<margin>October 23, 1645.</margin>
->To Your Most Illustrious Highnesses,<-
->From your most dedicated client,<-
->And most devoted intercessor.<-

## EPISTLE 96.

->*Most Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,*<-

I received with joy from your letter the news that, in choosing a godfather <note>original: "Susceptore," a sponsor or spiritual guardian in the rite of baptism</note> and spiritual father for your grandson—recently born to your daughter Agnes Elisabeth—you have taken special account of me, preferring an absent friend over those closer at hand. From this, indeed, anyone can understand how much you value me, as you wished for me to be the guarantor <note>original: "fidejussorem," a legal term for a surety or bondsman, here referring to the sponsor's role in making vows on behalf of the child</note> for your own blood in that mystery by which he has been initiated into Christianity and even into eternal life. 

Therefore, I rightly offer my thanks for your honorable judgment of me, praying with you that this little son of yours, cleansed by the blood of Christ and adopted as an heir to the heavenly kingdom, may grow in this present age to the glory of God, his Father and Redeemer; to the honor and ornament of his parents; and to be the delight of your old age. As for the other duties which a kind affection toward you commands and custom requires, my Illustrious Father will fulfill my role; His Highness will confirm—perhaps with a more precious token—how pleasing it is that you committed this sacred office to your friend, just as I am now doing through this paper letter. Farewell. *Wolfenbüttel <note>Wolfenbüttel was a significant residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg and a major cultural center in 17th-century Germany.</note>, November 4, 1645.*

->To Your Revered Dignity,<-
->Most devotedly.<-

*Whether it be for writing or for literary exercise—or, to speak frankly, for my own greatest pleasure and ornament—I see that I owe it to you, and that I must seek it out of my own accord; so far am I from needing your encouragement, however kind it may be. I am very glad that the figures by Frisius <note>Likely Hans Vredeman de Vries (1527–1609), a Dutch architect and artist famous for his influential books on perspective and the five orders of architecture.</note> regarding the proportion and ornament of columns according to the rules of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose work "De architectura" was the foundational text for Renaissance and Baroque architecture.</note> were not unpleasing to you, both because you did not disdain my small gifts and because you apply your mind to these matters, which are by no means unbecoming of a Prince. I would certainly have added those which the same author produced no less cleverly regarding the Tuscan column for the use of stonemasons and sculptors, if they had been at hand; I shall see to it that as soon as they are obtained, they shall follow. Now, however, I shall work diligently on preparing for you a traveling case of mathematical instruments <note>original: "theca instrumentorum Mathematicorum peregrinatoria"</note> by the inventor Furtenbach <note>Joseph Furtenbach the Elder (1591–1667), a German architect and engineer from Ulm, renowned for his design of mathematical instruments and theaters.</note> himself, so that nothing may be lacking to foster your most praiseworthy passion. For just as it is fitting for you to strive with your sublime nature and noble mental effort, so it is fitting for us to compete with humble obedience and the readiest services. This is so that we may one day obtain a Prince no lesser than his great Father; one not inferior to the expectation of the Fatherland; one not unequal to bearing the Guelph orb <note>The House of Guelph (Welf) was one of the oldest and most powerful noble dynasties in Europe, ruling the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note>; but one for whom all Ranks may congratulate themselves of their own accord and in rivalry, and give thanks to God. We, your indebted and diligent intercessors, will be present before Him, that He—from whose single propitious hand good Princes come—may bless us abundantly and happily in you. I, that is, and my son who honors you with me, and all of us who, after GOD, owe our salvation solely to your Most Serene House. Farewell and be favorable, together with your most Illustrious Brothers (whom we desire to be safe).*

->To Your Illustrious Highness<-

<margin>Nov 13, 1645.</margin> Your most humble client.

I am greatly pleased that the illustrations by De Vries <note>original: "Frisii"; referring to Hans Vredeman de Vries, a Dutch architect and artist famous for his work on perspective and the five orders of columns</note> regarding the proportions and ornamentation of columns according to the rules of Vitruvius <note>A Roman architect of the 1st century BCE whose "Ten Books on Architecture" was the foundational text for Renaissance and Baroque building</note> were not unwelcome to you. I rejoice both because you do not despise my small gifts and because you apply your mind to these matters, which by no means misbecome a Prince. I would certainly have added those things which the same author produced no less ingeniously for the use of stonemasons and sculptors regarding the Tuscan Column, if they had been at hand; I will see to it that as soon as they appear, they shall follow. 

Now, however, I will work diligently on preparing for you a traveling case of mathematical instruments <term>Theca Instrumentorum Mathematicorum: a luxury kit for a gentleman-scientist, containing tools like compasses, rulers, and surveying devices</term> through the inventor Furtenbach <note>Joseph Furtenbach the Elder (1591–1667), a German engineer and architect famous for his treatises on mechanics and instruments</note> himself, so that nothing may be lacking to foster your most praiseworthy passion. For just as it is fitting for you to strive with a sublime nature and noble exertion of mind, so it is fitting for us to compete in humble obedience and the most ready service. This we do so that we may one day possess a Prince no less great than his distinguished Father; one not inferior to the expectations of the Fatherland; and one not unequal to bearing the weight of the Welf world <term>Guelphicæ: referring to the House of Welf (Guelph), one of the oldest and most powerful European dynasties, to which the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg belonged</term>. Indeed, he should be one for whom all the Estates <note>The "Orders" or social classes of the realm</note> will congratulate themselves of their own accord and in rivalry, and offer thanks to God. In His presence, we shall stand ready as your devoted intercessors, praying that He—from whose favorable hand alone good Princes come—may bless us abundantly and happily in you. I mean myself, and my son who honors you with me, and all of us who, after God, owe our well-being solely to your Most Serene House. Farewell, and look with favor upon us, along with your Illustrious Brothers (whom we pray may remain safe).

->To your Illustrious Highness,<-

November 13, 1645.
Your most humble client.

## LETTER XCVIII.

->To the Very Reverend and Most<-
->Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

If there be any joy or solace in having had companions in misery, I have certainly felt some from your recent letters, in this, the uttermost ruin of our affairs. For if you have suffered your trials <note>original: "manes"; literally "shades" or "spirits of the dead," used here metaphorically to mean the ghosts of past tragedies or personal afflictions</note>, we have suffered ours. On that account, we pity you all the more and, as if to extinguish a common fire, we send forth even more burning prayers to God. One would almost have to despair of Peace, because our hopes have already been frustrated so many times, were it not for the consideration you suggest in your letter: that God always guards His Church amidst these furies of the world and the Devil, which keeps the pious in a state of hope. For what purpose, I ask, would God preserve this "machine of the world" <note>original: "mundi machinam"; a common 17th-century metaphor for the universe as a complex, God-driven mechanism</note>? Perhaps so that, as if in a Theater, great vices might be committed by Illustrious Men, only to be watched by those of lower station? Was not the earth and its goods promised to the pious? If you use these goods rightly and look back toward the Benefactor from whom they proceed, then greater things are brought forth from the most abundant pantry <note>original: "penario"; a storehouse or larder</note> of divine bounty, blooming with new peace. If, however, you forget God and, like beasts who snore and yawn once they are full, you dwell only on earthly things, they will be snatched and dragged away by others—who are indeed no better themselves, but are useful for this purpose: to punish the former and, by this means, lead them back to the right path. But why do I speak of these matters with such a great Theologian? Please return a reply to my son, with my greetings. The brothers bid you greetings and wish you well, as do I.

->To Your Reverend Dignity<-

Wolfenbüttel, November 13, 1645.

### Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
### My far most merciful Lord,

I congratulate my nephew—who shares your name—and I rejoice from my heart that you have most kindly interpreted our confidence in your favor toward us, and that you have not unwillingly undertaken the Christian duty of a Godfather <note>original: "Patrini"; the role of a spiritual sponsor in baptism, which often carried significant social and political weight between a subject and a Prince</note>. Truly, with your incredible sagacity, you correctly divined that I wish to transplant my offshoots <note>original: "palmites meos"; literally "my vine-shoots," a common 17th-century metaphor for children or family members</note> into another land, namely my homeland, and to dedicate them to your auspices. I pray with my whole heart that this may be as fortunate for them as your rule is most happy and long-lasting for you.

I adore Christ, to whom my nephew has sworn his Vow <note>original: "Sacramentum"; in this context, it refers to the baptismal oath, using the language of a Roman soldier's oath of allegiance to his commander</note> with you as his guarantor, and whom he has in turn put on with the pledge of the Holy Spirit. I pray that Christ may render him a worthy and useful citizen of His holy City <note>The "City of God" or the Kingdom of Heaven</note>, one who may venerate, cherish, and follow you as a father with filial devotion, as a Lord with ministerial obedience, and as a Prince with the highest and most deserved honor. And in Heaven, where the distinctions between persons shall be removed, may he have you as a co-heir of eternal Goods.

Meanwhile, Most Illustrious Prince, we strive with the highest prayers for this one thing: that you keep your heart—which you have testified to be so well-wishing toward us through this great benefit—whole and continuous for us. We could never receive or value a more precious pledge than this, neither now nor hereafter. May the propitious Trinity <note>original: "Trias"</note> preserve the illustrious Trio <note>original: "Ternionem"; likely referring to three brothers of the princely house</note> of brothers, to the delight of their most Serene Parents, as the offspring of a most ancient House, the glory of Germany, the benefit of your subjects, and the salvation of the Christian Commonwealth. Thus I pray.

->Of Your Illustrious Highness<-

Stuttgart, Nov. 19, 1645.
on the Day of St. Elizabeth <note>original: "die Elisabethæ"; the feast day of St. Elizabeth of Hungary, November 19</note>.

Your most humble client.
