### LETTER 100.

->Very Reverend and Most Distinguished<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

I hold this reciprocal exchange of letters to be as pleasant to me as it is necessary, serving as a form of recreation, provided that it is not burdensome to you while you are occupied with sacred cares and other business. For my own letters are always of such a character that much ought to be added to them, or taken away, lest they be completely spiritless or tedious; yours, however, are so polished that I never leave off reading them without being more learned, or better, and more kindled toward virtue. You shall therefore continue hereafter—not for your own sake, certainly, but for mine—as you rouse my studies and do not allow them to be covered over with rust. Even these letters of yours, which I recently received, how elegant and adorned they are! I used to think that *Frisius* <note>Hans Vredeman de Vries (1527–1609), a Dutch Renaissance architect and designer famous for his influential books on perspective and the five architectural orders</note> was the inventor of column ornamentation; you teach me, from the rules of *Vitruvius* <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose ten-volume work 'De architectura' was the primary authority on classical architecture for the Renaissance</note>, that they were composed by him according to those ancient standards. Furthermore, I am possessed by a desire to see the *Tuscan* style <note>original: "Thufcam"; referring to the Tuscan Order, the simplest and sturdiest of the five classical orders of architecture</note>, because you give me hope of unearthing it from somewhere. Since you have not disdained to assist me, and have helped in preparing the *traveler's case* <note>original: "Thecâ peregrinatoriâ"; a specialized portable kit or chest designed for a scholar or nobleman to carry writing materials, books, or instruments while traveling</note>—which I think about even in my dreams—you shall make me your debtor; I will strike out this debt only when something can proceed from me that may prove my mindful spirit. For the rest, the better and more religious a man you are, the more I trust that God will hear the prayers you pour out for the health and safety of our family; I pray in turn that He may richly crown you with all the blessings of body and soul.

->To Your Reverend Dignity.<-

Wolfenbüttel, December 1, 1645.

->Your most respectful servant.<-

<header>THE YEAR 1645.</header>

# LETTER 101.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### Lord most gracious by far,

It is just as you write: there is little comfort to be found in the company of misfortunes. Instead, the pain is doubled, and good men are called upon to quench the common conflagration, as it were, with their prayers. For we in these lands have for a long time provided the stage for the tragedy of raging Mars <note>original: "Marti furenti"; a poetic reference to war, as Mars was the Roman god of war</note>. While we might have hoped for relief from poverty, protection from oppression, or finally a home for our exile from You—whom we thought were placed in a safer location—now that we hear that even your walls, altars, and hearths are burning, we are dismayed with all our soul and fear the destruction of Troy <note>original: "Ilii excidium"; a classical allusion to the total ruin of a city, referring to the fall of Troy</note>. 

But since such is the condition of the Church in these lands, that a comfortable and stable home is scarcely ever granted to her for long, but rather only a tent <note>original: "tabernaculum"</note> or a hut, and since the flatteries of this life have been more harmful than any Crosses <note>a reference to suffering or religious persecution</note> or banishments, we must believe that the Peace which the common people desire does not promise the growth of Christ’s kingdom. War by no means hinders the progress of piety, provided that each person looks rightly to the salvation of their own soul and is carried upward toward a longing for heaven by the evils of the earth. 

Indeed, there have sometimes been "Halcyon days" <note>original: "Halcyonia"; a Greek-derived term for a period of peace and calm</note> for the Church, and we experienced them for over a hundred years, which were held as signs of God's favor; nor would I deny that the scourge of such a savage and long-lasting war, by which we are now being tested, is a sign of His anger. But to those considering the matter more closely, it will easily occur that the very harvest and vintage of that long peace supplied the material for this misfortune and the fuel for the fire now burning: namely, profane piety; pagan literature; unjust justice; barbaric customs; and that entire "Christian Hermaphrodite" <note>A metaphor for a person or society attempting to combine incompatible Christian virtues with worldly or pagan vices</note>, whom Christ long ago...

### LETTER 103.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most*<-
->*Renowned Lord Doctor,*<-

Since, by the grace of Almighty God, we are about to bring the old year to an end and begin the new, it is required by gratitude and our duty that we give thanks to divine goodness from our hearts. For in these most wretched times <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648), which was still raging in the German lands at the time of this writing.</note>, in which so many lose their lives and fall from their fortunes, He has nevertheless deemed us worthy of His singular favor and protection. And because this is a clearly singular benefit, bestowed upon us from heaven, it is right to offer Him special thanks and praise. May He furthermore extend His almighty hand over us and, in this new year and many following, grant my dearest *parents* and *paternal relatives* <term>agnates</term> <note>original: "Agnatos." Because this prayer rises from the depths of the heart, *God, the Thrice Best and Greatest* <note>original: "DEVS ter Opt. Max.," a Christian adaptation of the Roman title for Jupiter, *Iuppiter Optimus Maximus*.</note>, will hear this vow and grant these prayers, for they are pious and necessary. Farewell.

->*To Your Reverend Dignity,*<-
**In haste, Wolfenbüttel, 23rd**
**of December, 1645.**
->Most Devotedly,<-

My dearest brothers bid me send you their greetings; they wish for you a happy beginning, success, and end to the new year, and they add their own vows to my own.

### LETTER 104.

*Most Renowned Lord Master,*

Your letter has been delivered to me, filled with many praises (of which you deem me worthy). It stands as a witness and a pledge of your affection and goodwill toward me. ...could not have happened to me in a more pleasing way. For the Greeks, that day was most auspicious on which Socrates and Alexander the Great began to enjoy this light <note>An idiom for being born.</note>; to your Reverend Dignity, gratefully counting the recurring years of my life seems to be a duty of piety. The Cretans used to mark happier days with *white pebbles*, but sadder ones with *black* <note>original: "albis lapillis... nigris," a classical reference to the Roman and Greek custom of marking the quality of a day with stones</note>; I am very easily led to believe that the same is observed by your Reverend Dignity regarding my fortune. *Xerxes* held sacred the day on which he took up the Scepter, and, girt with the Diadem on that day, he bestowed *gifts* <note>original: "strenis," specifically New Year's or celebratory gifts</note> upon the Persians. For the nobles, however, he prepared a dinner so sumptuous and magnificent that the Greeks declared it perfect in every respect. You follow in the footsteps of this hero, *Most Reverend Sir*, for I not only perceive that you hold sacred that day on which I began my life, but you also present me—rather than others—with gifts. Nor is there any doubt that I would experience the third <note>Referring to the "sumptuous dinner" mentioned in the Xerxes anecdote.</note>, if it happened that we were together.

The *gift* <note>original: "Strena"</note> which you send pleases me wonderfully, so much so that daily, or even ten times a day, I feast my eyes upon it; and all the more so because, through the diligent instruction of my teachers, I more sharply condemn and detest the abominable traditions and empty pride of the *Papists* <note>original: "Papicolarum," literally "Pope-worshippers," a derogatory term used by Protestants during the Reformation and Counter-Reformation.</note>. I have fixed that *image* <note>original: "Ideam," likely a satirical print or engraving sent as a gift.</note> to the wall, so that it may provide a source of mockery to all who visit me. With what, indeed, shall I repay you, *Most Reverend Sir*? I have already offered my soul, most devoted to your Piety, so many times that I am ashamed to mention it; for I willingly confess that I am already entirely, entirely *in your debt* <note>original: "in ære Tuo," a Latin idiom meaning "in your debt-book" or "under your obligation."</note>.

Accept therefore with a benevolent hand, *Most Reverend Sir*, that for which I am most bound to you, and which your letters suggest you need: namely, our most ardent prayers for the recovery of your former health. You are now enjoying the *mineral waters* <note>original: "acidulis," referring to tart or carbonated medicinal springs frequented for health; spas were common destinations for the 17th-century elite.</note>; enjoy them most healthfully, return from there most happily, and [live]...

## LETTER 108.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Princes, Lords most gracious by far,

I confess indeed that I owe a separate reply for each of your most pleasant letters; but since a public prayer <note>original: "Supplicatio." A formal day of intercession and fasting decreed by the church or state, in this case for the success of peace negotiations.</note> must be officially announced for our churches to ward off obstacles to that peace so longed for, and so necessary for the weary state of Germany; and since there is a rush of business and letters to be written, I easily hope to receive from your kindness an indulgence for this brevity for now, to be earned back at another time with a more expansive style. This indulgence will perhaps be won by the fact that your letters share one and the same subject: namely, our mutual, pious struggle to seek from heaven the safe and vigorous vitality of your Most Serene Father, my most gracious Lord and Master. The benefit of his health is particular and proper to you, but it overflows abundantly upon me, and is to be desired most greatly by the Christian World. Happy are you indeed, who understand that your Father’s life is your own life, and that all the affairs, hopes, resources, and strength of your entire well-being are situated in it. I refrain from demonstrating this by citing the sad, contrary examples of other illustrious families, lest it seem perhaps hateful or tedious.

Furthermore, regarding what I owe you for your tireless zeal—by which you repeatedly exercise my exhausted pen <note>original: "exuccum meum calamum." Literally "my juice-less pen," a humble trope meaning his writing talent is dried up or weary.</note> and rouse my dry letters—I have neither fully grasped it in my mind, nor easily explained it in words, nor ever performed it in deed. To me, indeed, it is most pleasant to see: now the mature judgment of my Prince **RUDOLPH AUGUSTUS**; now the artistic hands <note>original: "artifices manus." Prince Anthony Ulrich was a noted patron of the arts, a novelist, and a poet; the author here praises his creative talents.</note> of my Prince **ANTHONY ULRICH**; now the [virtues] of my Prince **FERDINAND ALBERT’s** youth...

We do not know if the fame of these springs has reached your ears, and so we have seized this subject for writing so that if you have heard nothing of them, you might learn of it from us, being closer; or if you have heard greater things (as is the custom of rumors), you may understand how much credit should be given to them. *May God, Best and Greatest, keep you safe. Wolfenbüttel, July 14, 1646.*

### II.
# With Prince RUDOLPH AUGUSTUS.
## LETTER 111.

### LETTER 112.

#### To the Very Reverend and Most Famous Lord Doctor,

During the past feast days <note>Likely referring to the Christmas and New Year season.</note>, I received two letters from you. In the first, you reveal your opinion concerning wars, which you judge to be more useful to Christianity than a continuous peace. You are driven primarily by this reasoning: that during a war, Christians become weary of the world, whose delights and deceptive flatteries they otherwise get tangled in, hardly turning their thoughts toward heaven. This is because excessive prosperity and the premature enjoyment of fleeting happiness tend to stifle their spiritual desire. In this matter, I entirely agree with you; nor would I wish what I recently wrote in haste to be understood in any other way than that God willingly grants peace to Christians as a supreme blessing—provided that the means by which peace is prepared and retained are cultivated by them, and preferred above all—

### LETTER CXIV.

## Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
## Most clement Lord,

The greater your eagerness for writing is, the more clearly this duty of responding falls upon me, lest by a rustic bashfulness I should seem to have begrudged myself your elegances. I prefer, therefore, to earn the name of "untimely" rather than "lazy," and to thrust my trifles <note>original: "nænias." Literally "incantations" or "nonsense," here used as a humble term for his own writings.</note> upon you, as long as I understand that you are not at all fatigued by them. That the *Frisiana* <note>Refers to the works of Hans Vredeman de Vries (1527–1609), a Dutch architect and artist famous for his studies on perspective and the classical orders.</note> please you is very gratifying; he was a man whose genius was to be compared with few of his time. ### LETTER CXVI.

->**Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,**<-
->**Most Gracious Lord,**<-

While bodily weakness and weariness of spirit release me from all my official duties, I realize that this one task still remains for me: to devote myself to sending and receiving your letters, than which nothing is more desirable to me. ### LETTER CXVII.

->**Very Reverend and Most Illustrious Lord Doctor,**<-

Although you are not unaware of how pleasing your letters are to me, you nevertheless perpetually excuse the promptness and eagerness which you use in responding, and with which I am especially honored. Moreover, I thank you for the fact that at the end of your letter you so generously and earnestly promise all your services. For nothing is more pleasant than your friendship, and that of those like you...

### LETTER CXVIII.

->*Very Reverend and Most Illustrious*<-
->*Lord Doctor,*<-

I have received the most elegant letter with which you honor me, and in which you extol both *happiness* and the *virtue* by which it is attained. It is surely the offspring of a strong mind, not one languishing in a sick body, although you write that you are dejected in spirit due to the physical contagion <note>The author uses "contagio" to describe how the illness of the body "infects" or weighs down the mind/spirit.</note>. This refers to high social standing, wealth, or political power.</note>, which others deem worthy of the name "happiness." Yet, unless modesty, moderation, a mind in control of itself, and the other virtues you praise are present to eagerly adorn and distinguish it, I consider such fortune to be the height of misery. Nor should this be considered a paradox, since no one is *more miserable than the vicious man*; moreover, wickedness, insolence, and power...

In this way, they imagine Hercules placed at the crossroads <note>A famous classical allegory where the young hero Hercules must choose between the easy path of Pleasure and the difficult path of Virtue</note>, preferring the rough and unpolished speech of Virtue over the musical melodies of Pleasure. How rightly and wisely you do this, Most Illustrious Prince, and clearly according to the spirit of your Most Serene Father <note>likely Duke Eberhard III of Württemberg, or a deceased predecessor if the "rest" implies death</note>. For just as in a life of great fortune nothing is more poisonous and harmful than the honeyed voices of flatterers, so too in the formation of great minds, there is hardly anything more pestilential than a soft and overly indulgent hand. That such indulgence has never corrupted your character is proven to me by your patience with my freer warnings and my unconstrained style of writing. This is evidence to me of a more certain innocence, on account of which very many [owe you...]

## LETTER 121.

### THE YEAR 1646.

I am moved by Tacitus (whom I otherwise often agree with) when he writes in the *Annals* [Book 6, chapter 22]: <margin>][</margin> *“At each person’s birth, their future is destined; but some things turn out otherwise than predicted due to the deceits of those speaking in ignorance, and thus the credibility of the art is corrupted, even though ancient times and his own age produced clear evidence of it.”* <note>original: "Primo cujusque ortu futura destinari; sed quædam secus, quàm dicta sint, cadere fallaciis ignara dicentium..." Tacitus is here discussing the tension between fate and the human failure of astrologers.</note> Yet I am more pleased by what he writes about these men in the books of the *Histories* [Book 1, chapter 22]: *“They are a class of men unfaithful to those in power, and deceptive to those who hope.”* Similarly, Cicero writes in the second book of *On Divination*, where he explicitly refutes their reasoning using both logical foundations and experience.

And whether Tacitus is to be believed regarding what he mentions about Thrasyllus, Tiberius, and Agrippina, I do not know; <note>Thrasyllus of Mendes was the personal astrologer to the Emperor Tiberius. Agrippina the Younger was the mother of Nero and also famously consulted astrologers regarding her son's future.</note> and even if those events had truly occurred, is it not still permitted to say that the Devil is able to command the unbelieving at his own pleasure? I have taken care to transcribe the passage from Cicero here, so that you would not need to search through the volume yourself. He who understands this correctly and meditates upon it will easily guard himself, for he will perceive the source from which those who wrote on this matter after Cicero drew their ideas.

However, you teach that yet another class of men must be avoided (whom we call <margin>((</margin> <term>Statists</term> <note>original: "Statistas." In the 17th century, this referred to political schemers or those who practiced "Reason of State" politics, often viewed as Machiavellian or amoral.</note> or <term>Hyper-politicians</term>), from whom a greater danger is to be feared. This is because they are not mocked in the way those fortune-tellers are, but rather they acquire followers and admirers. They are not even so **impudent**, nor do they seek their food and daily bread through a common craft; rather, they creep in under the pretext of **prudence**. Because they believe that they alone can penetrate the secrets and counsels of those who rule the world, they wish to excel above all others and be held in high regard.

The former group [the astrologers] profess as truth what they themselves hardly believe to be probable, which is a sign of their impudence. The latter [the Statists], in place of that true prudence by which God wishes the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Resp." or "Respublica," referring to the state or organized political community.</note> to be preserved, admit illicit remedies, which is a sign of their malice. The former cling to created things, and [render] men [careless] of the Divine...

### LETTER 134.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My Lord, by far most Clement,

It happened very inconveniently that at almost the same moment, your letters were delivered to me here and mine were requested for return, at a time when there was very little leisure and a great deal of noise. This is bound to happen when one must rely on accidental messengers rather than fixed and hired ones, as the departure time of the couriers remains strictly set. Therefore, so that I might not appear "deaf" <note>i.e., unresponsive</note> to your most elegant letters, I have sent in my place the Jesuit Recupito <note>Giulio Cesare Recupito (1581–1647), a Jesuit scholar known for his work on natural phenomena, including the eruption of Mount Vesuvius.</note>, a vocal enough wanderer here at the mineral springs <note>original: "acidulis erronem." I thought him worthy of your reading, both for the weight of his subject matter and the polish of his style, as well as for his skill in <term>physical investigation</term> <note>original: "Physicæ indaginis," referring to the study of natural philosophy or the natural world.</note>. Admit the man, and at your leisure—unless it is a burden—explain what you think of him. Farewell, and may you be happy along with your **Illustrious** brothers. 

Calw, May 27, 1646.

# Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
## My Lord, by far most Clement,

I wrote to You recently both more briefly and more hurriedly <note>original: "tumultuosius," suggesting a state of confusion or haste</note> than I should have. I have already apologized for this fault through *Recupito* <note>Giulio Cesare Recupito (1581–1647), a Jesuit scholar whose work was discussed in the previous letter.</note>, a man not lacking in eloquence—though, as is the *character* of his Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits). The author often displays a mix of intellectual respect and denominational suspicion toward Jesuit scholars.</note>, he is somewhat lacking in modesty. But You have avenged that haste with Your silence; You could decree no harsher punishment against me, since nothing is as sweet or as desirable to me as Your letters.

However, my grief was mitigated both by the *Distinguished Mr. Gosky* <note>Martin Gosky (c. 1586–1656), a physician and Neo-Latin poet at the Prince’s court.</note> and by that *Wedemann*, whoever he may be. The former, with the skill of his genius, adorned that *Rose* <note>Likely a reference to a poem or a symbolic gift sent to the Prince.</note> which had been sent with a single couplet more than I could have achieved with an entire letter. The latter informed me of the fateful significance of Your most happy birthday falling on the *Preparation Day of Pentecost* <note>original: "Pentecostes Parasceven," referring to the Friday before Pentecost.</note>, and the auspicious occurrence of the *Illustrious Harmony* <note>This may refer to a specific musical work or a philosophical concept of order favored by the Prince.</note>. Both have deserved my highest praise.

But now, which You may perhaps wonder at, I am sending another *Jesuit* to You whom I happened to encounter here. He is better in *Philosophy* than in *Theology*: *Caspar Ruthard, the Cosmologist* <note>Caspar Ruthard (died 1663), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer.</note>. I have copied out the title and summary of his little book, published in quarto, since it was not possible to obtain the physical copy itself. It can easily be obtained in *Frankfurt*, if I am not mistaken. He seemed to me to express not uncleverly in a few words what others push onto us in massive volumes, thus looking out for illustrious minds that do not wish to be overwhelmed. When You have seen it, I think You will approve—or certainly not disapprove—of my plan, which is uniquely intent upon and devoted to Your benefit. I am distressed that the *traveling chest* <note>original: "Capsam itinerariam." These chests often contained books, manuscripts, or scientific instruments being moved between scholars.</note> is being delivered to You so slowly.

Given from the *Baths of Zell* <note>original: "Thermis Cellensibus," referring to Bad Boll, known for its medicinal sulfur springs.</note>, June 3, *Year 1646*.

->Of Your Illustrious Highness<-
->The most humble client.<-

## LETTER CXXXVI.

### *To the Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,*

Between April 29 and May 20, you sent four letters to me. I am grateful that you set aside your more serious business to not only read mine, but also to respond so promptly. Your last letter was sent from Calw, where you traveled for the sake of recreation and to visit friends. I sincerely hope, from my heart, that this journey proves as joyful for them as it is beneficial for the strengthening of your health. 

I also learned from your second-to-last letter that you met with your sons-in-law <note>original: "Generos"</note>, along with their wives and children—among whom is a grandson to whom you gave my name. I do not doubt that this gathering was celebrated with the greatest joy; for nothing can be more welcome to a father than to see those who must one day follow in his footsteps, and in whom his life will be perpetually extended. Likewise, nothing is more welcome to children than to be refreshed by the affection of him from whom they received not only the origin of their life, but also an example of living rightly. I believe, and indeed I predict, that the consideration of this happy occasion has largely removed the illness by which you have been troubled until now.

I thank you for the **ROSE** you sent, as well as for the *Astroscopium* of Wilhelm Schickard <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635) was a famous polymath and inventor of an early mechanical calculator. The *Astroscopium* was his star-charting device.</note>. The former delights the sight and brings to mind the ancient Egyptian way of writing <note>original: "Ægyptiorum antiquum scribendi modum," likely referring to hieroglyphics or symbolic emblems</note>; the latter commends not only its most ingenious author, but especially those women who are said to have added the appendix. 

The case of Furttenbach <note>Joseph Furttenbach (1591–1667), a German engineer and architect famous for his "cabinets of curiosities" and technical publications.</note> has not yet been delivered, but I expect it daily. Its author will excite the greatest joy in me, and it will be quite pleasant to become known to him through correspondence. For the rest, as to what is to be hoped for regarding the *Peace of Germany* <note>A reference to the ongoing negotiations that would eventually lead to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), ending the Thirty Years' War.</note>,

## LETTER CXXXVIII.

->To the Very Reverend and Most<-
->Renowned Lord Doctor,<-

It is most pleasing to me that while at the mineral springs <note>original: "acidulis"; likely referring to the spa at Bad Teinach mentioned on the previous page.</note>—where for the sake of your health you ought to set aside your usual labors—you have remembered not only to keep me occupied but also to communicate what new and unusual things you find there. I received the *Jesuit* by Recupitus <note>original: "Recupitum Iesuitam"; likely referring to the works of the Jesuit author Giulio Cesare Recupito (1581–1647).</note>, as you will understand from my own writings; having begun the reading, I immediately discovered at the very start that he is infected with the common plague of the Papists, namely superstition: which you seem to attribute to the impudence that is the characteristic mark of his Society. Another man by the name of *Ruthard* <note>original: "Ruthardus"; likely Anselm Ruthard, a Cistercian monk and author.</note> (a name which was until now unknown to me) promises many things in the title he sent; I would wish for it to be among my books. While I am writing this, a report comes to mind that we just received from *Paris* <note>original: "Lutetia"</note>: namely that four *Jesuits*, having deserted their Society, have preferred another order. They promise that they will bring to light the secrets of the *Jesuits*, hidden until now—by which they do not cease to deceive the *Christian World* <note>original: "Christiano Orbi"</note> in order to establish their Society—and that they will expose their fallacies. We brothers are indeed well; we hope that you also are well. From Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti"</note>, June 23, 1646.

->The most devoted to<-
->Your Reverend Dignity.<-

# LETTER CXLI.
## Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### Lord by far most gracious,

ALthough in our exchange of letters I willingly acknowledge myself inferior to you in every respect, I would not wish to yield to your diligence; for while it affects and refreshes me beyond belief, it also rouses me and shakes off that lethargy which ill health pours over me. *I have sent Recupito <note>Giulio Cesare Recupito (1581–1647), a Jesuit author known for his vivid description of the 1631 eruption of Mount Vesuvius.</note> to you, not as a Jesuit—than which kind of men nothing is more wicked or more pestilential—but as a not-uneloquent describer of a horrific event. Others with similar defects followed his example and experienced the same power; but the water, applied against other diseases, also benefited many. From this came fame, and then a rush of people; soon this "Pandora" <note>The author likely uses this name to imply a sudden, all-encompassing phenomenon or a "cure-all"</note> was extolled even beyond the powers of Nature. It stirred up not just a crowd, but nearly armies of people, who set up camps in a very thick oak grove (for apart from a small farmhouse and a mill, dwellings are far away) and held their own *scenopegia* <note>original: "scenopegia"; a Greek term for the Feast of Tabernacles, here referring to the temporary booths or tents built by the pilgrims</note>. For I myself went there, marvelling at the gullibility of the people and so that I might explore the spring in person.

It bubbles up from the root of a large oak tree with such a great force of water that it immediately forms a stream. However, it is hardly sufficient for the uses of so many people and for the constant transportation [of the water] to all regions. Because of this, my approach to it was difficult, but the return through the besieging beggars was far more difficult. The water is indeed very clear and very cold; for drinking, it is somewhat sluggish or muddy rather than brisk. *Surgeons* <term>Chirurgis; at this time, surgeons were often distinct from university-trained physicians, focusing on external treatments and wounds</term>, *however, by no means neglect this medicinal water, which our own citizens have found to be most healthy for many ailments. When she was very close to the city on her return, she slipped and spilled the water. Anxious about the situation and weary of the road, she refilled the vessel from the nearest spring and substituted it for her mistress’s medicine. Her mistress was happily cured by it, and the maid’s trick turned into a joke. I recount these things to you not to disparage the reputation of the Hornhausen springs* <note>Hornhausen was the site of a famous "miracle spring" discovered in 1646 in the territory of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg</note>, *which I hear have now gushed forth five in number, each of a different taste; rather, I wish to show that even the highest and most excellent blessings of God can, through the vice of the human mind, be contaminated by superstition; neglected through ignorance; applied inappropriately through error; converted to abuse through imposture; or extolled too highly by gullible rumors—and finally, they can be cast aside out of disgust, lest it ever seem that a mere fable was being acted out.*

*But I shall stop, lest while I strive to be too helpful, I become a burden. We have as guests at our court a most illustrious pair of brothers, the Princes of Württemberg-Montbéliard,* <note>The House of Württemberg-Montbéliard was a cadet branch of the ducal house of Württemberg</note> *who are most highly instructed in letters, languages, and practical experience beyond their age and common lot, from whom I send greetings. May God preserve you, the Renowned and Most Illustrious Brothers, born for the good of Germany and given to your lands, and may He increase His gifts toward you; Him I adore as a suppliant.*

->*To Your Illustrious and Most Noble Excellencies*<-

## LETTER 147.

*To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,*

Although I am uncertain what I should write to you this time, the command of my Illustrious Lord Father and the affection I feel for you compel me to devise something at least in appearance, so that I may complete this page as a small day's task. For it happens to me now as it does to those who have long exchanged conversation; for just as when business is concluded and the reasons for their meeting are explained, they turn to trifles and wandering chats, so when this day destined for letters supplies nothing worthy of you, I did not want to fail in my duty, lest I seem to have delayed our literary exchange <term>literarium commercium; the formal network of correspondence between scholars in the early modern period</term>. # THE YEAR 1646. LETTER 149.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,*<-

I would not demand letters from your Reverend Dignity, unless this mutual exchange and the remarkable benefit I take from it did not affect me so wonderfully; for they abound both with advice very necessary for me and with a variety of matters in which I find no small refreshment and learning. I have heard regarding Furttenbach’s *Neapolis* <note>Joseph Furttenbach (1591–1667) was a German architect and engineer. *Neapolis* (published 1640) was his work on the design and fortification of a "new city."</note>, and I believe that the Author, long ago commended to me and others, will publish nothing unworthy of himself. His labors will serve the utility of the State, especially in our time, in which the fury of Mars <note>Mars was the Roman god of war. This refers to the ongoing Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which devastated Germany.</note> consumes what was built by our ancestors with great expense and praiseworthy industry. May God grant, however, that nourishing Peace return, by which his arts <note>The "parts" or "arts" of peace, such as architecture and engineering mentioned above.</note> may thrive and flourish, and those who cultivate them may receive a reward worthy of their virtues. May He likewise keep you and yours safe. Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherb."</note>, August 11, the year 1646.

[ma]ximas <note>This completes the word "maximas" from the previous page.</note> thanks I give, and I pray from my heart that the Divine Power may be favorable to you in all your desires.

I have read through the Moral Theology of the Jesuits as soon as I received it from you; I had known it previously in parts, but now it is gathered into one short volume. How sweetly indeed do these shameless men <note>original: "perfrictæ frontis homines," a Latin idiom for those who have "rubbed their foreheads" so they can no longer blush from shame.</note> laugh in their sleeves at these papers—men accustomed to provoke the whole world against themselves and to elude it with their tricks and crafts. Other weapons and Herculean torches <note>A reference to the myth of Hercules and the Hydra; Hercules used fire to sear the necks of the many-headed monster to prevent them from regrowing.</note> are needed against this manifold Hydra. For the Pope has no more harmful serpents to fear in his own bosom; nor do the Catholics have more insatiable leeches; nor the Evangelicals <note>In this period, "Evangelical" refers to Protestants, particularly Lutherans.</note> more deep-digging sappers <note>original: "cunicularios," referring to military engineers who dug tunnels (mines) to collapse enemy fortifications.</note>; nor the world more hostile furies. Indeed, from all the accusations I have happened to read against this order—so infested against the human race—I am plainly convinced that its primary movers are Atheists in Theology, Necromancers in Philosophy, Corruptors in Literature, Disturbers in Politics, Imposters in Economy, and the pests of all commerce, to be detested and avoided by all mortals. 

But it happens by our own fault that, while we proscribe nearly all religion along with letters and good character, they impose upon uncultivated minds with a mask of piety, erudition, and modesty. While pretending to do one thing, they do their own—namely, they raise themselves up toward this mass, formidable to all social ranks, like a Trojan Horse destined to overthrow Troy <note>original: "Ilium," another name for the city of Troy.</note> hereafter. # YEAR 1646. LETTER 151.

->Very Reverend and Most Distinguished<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

**I** have received your Reverence's <note>original: "Rev. Dignit. Tuæ," a formal honorific</note> letters, in which you report quite pleasant news regarding the healing spring <note>original: "fonte salutifero"</note> that appeared in the year 1632 in the territory of Württemberg, which is very similar to the one at Hornhausen <note>The spring at Hornhausen in Saxony became a massive sensation in the mid-17th century, drawing thousands of people who believed its waters had miraculous healing properties.</note>. For these I give you thanks, informing you that they earned great applause from our local physicians, who are suspicious of most—indeed, all—things that rumor has spread about these springs thus far. They do not dare to deny that some individuals have indeed been healed, but they also keep a count of the deaths of those who, after using the waters, fall into even more serious illnesses and are suddenly extinguished by them. It is said that the power of these waters is now diminishing somewhat, yet the superstition of the people does not decrease; they flock there from everywhere, not only from the common folk but even the more powerful classes. Moreover, stories not unlike your maidservant’s report are told concerning a certain citizen of Goslar <note>A historic town in Lower Saxony</note>—whether these tales are invented by idle people, or whether the same old play is always being acted out in this world, with only the actors changed. Our Most Illustrious Father <note>Likely referring to a Duke or Prince, given the formal "Illustrissimus" title</note> cannot be swept away by this common persuasion, nor can those of our household who have used the waters confirm that their health has been changed for the better. However, physicians of no ordinary learning and experience affirm that they have seen the mute speaking by the benefit of these waters, the deaf hearing, and the use of limbs restored to the paralyzed. If these things are true, the matter will be closer to a miracle; and if not everyone who uses them experiences the same effects, it will seem that the failure should rather be blamed on the type of disease, the patient's diet, immoderate eating, or other factors. Regarding this matter—as is best with recent events—I suspend ju-

### LETTER 152.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**Lord by far most merciful,**<-

*The more familiar and clearly spontaneous your Highness’s <note>original: "Cels. T.", abbreviation for Celsitudo Tua</note> letters are, the more pleasant they are to me. It is not that I am not greatly delighted by the abundance and elegance of your style, but rather so that this exchange of letters may not be a burden to you, or an obstacle to your better studies, since you are of such diligence that in this passing year alone, you have already sent me your twentieth letter. It will suffice, therefore, if you cast onto paper without care or worry whatever happens to occur to your free mind, provided that you do not grow weary of this literary correspondence. I do not know, in truth, whether you value my letters enough to preserve any of them. I certainly hold all of yours in the highest esteem and have placed them in a treasury <term>cimeliarchio: a repository for precious items or a private archive</term>, intending to bring them to light one day, if I am permitted by the indulgence of your Serene Father and yourself. To this end, I keep a copy of my own sterile and dry letters via a secretary <term>amanuensem: a scribe or personal clerk</term>, both so that the difference between "roses and nettles" <note>A metaphor comparing the Prince’s elegant writing to the author’s plain style</note> may be clear, and so that it remains fixed in my memory with what trifles of mine I elicited your elegances. I have, however, recorded certain things on my sixty-first birthday to share with you—a summary <term>breviarium: a concise record or life-summary</term> of my life—so that you might catch a glimpse <note>original: "per transennam inspiceres", an idiom meaning to see something briefly or through a lattice</note> of its story, lest I should bring you letters entirely empty of substance. These are currently being printed <note>original: "sub prælo sudantes", literally "sweating under the press"</note>; I am sending the first pages now and will send the rest in succession, so that you may delight your noble mind with them. It has been a long time since I have seen anything from the artistic hand of your illustrious brother, Lord Anton Ulrich, though I would not dare to interpret this as any indignation against me from such a lovely spirit. As for the more tender age of your brother Lord Ferdinand Albert, I would not wish to be troublesome. It is enough for me that they flourish and grow for the happiness and honor of your House. But I return to my letters, the first of which I have lost; it was written three years ago [in the year 1643], in which I heartily congratulated you on your seventeenth birthday. If it should happen to be hidden among your discarded papers, I would wish it to return to me, perhaps as a copy, to be placed at the head of the others. But if it has vanished into the darkness it deserved, another will easily be substituted. But I must stay my hand <note>original: "de tabula manum", a classical idiom for stopping work or finishing a task</note>, as there is enough of these trifles already. May GOD increase, adorn, and preserve the most illustrious Guelph Trio <note>original: "Ternionem Guelphicam", referring to the three princely brothers: Rudolph August, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albert</note> with years, gifts, and blessings. ### LETTER CLIV.

->Most Illustrious and High Prince,<-
->Lord most merciful by far,<-

**Y**our two letters written on the 11th and 18th of last month, I finally received on the 30th; they were received all the more eagerly and read with greater pleasure because, while trapped in the prisons of Mars <note>original: "Martis carceribus", a classical metaphor for the confinement and danger caused by wartime</note>, I was held by an intolerable longing for them. I feared that with the trade of our letters hindered, I might have to go without those things for a longer time, which are the most immediate and effective means of refreshing the weariness of my spirit. Now that the roads have been reopened somewhat, I return to my duty and offer the greatest thanks I owe, because you have fulfilled my long expectation with doubled and more extensive letters, which were full of kindness, elegance, and wisdom. Regarding the Hornhausen springs <note>The mineral springs at Hornhausen became a sensation in 1646, with reports of miraculous healings attracting thousands of people during the war.</note>, I would not rashly detract anything from them, nor would I minimize the notable benefits of Nature or even the Miracles of God found there; nevertheless, time will eventually reveal the errors, credulity, and even the deceptions of many people.

*...happens, I still doubt whether it can be without a sense of impiety, having been taught by the example of my own spring at Capfenhardt* <note>original: "Capfenetensis"; the author likely refers to a local mineral spring he frequented or wrote about, perhaps near Göppingen</note>. *But should we wonder, or should we rather pity—amidst such a sudden gathering of people—the most wretched condition of our arrogant and untamed bodies? How much more rightly would they act if, in the offices they hold by God's command and favor, they were always mindful of the human lot and referred all their actions to the accounts of conscience, rather than preferring to feign that they are immortal gods, subject to no diseases.*

There is no limit to the extortions, plundering, and pillaging. But these are things you must expect from those who follow the path of arms. Let us instead pursue a peaceful service, and so...*

### LETTER 155.

->To the Right Reverend and Most<-
->Famous Lord Doctor,<-

Not without cause do I accuse my own letters of excessive familiarity, as I am usually accustomed to hasten them along; not that I might return any equal to **yours**, which are certainly always most elegant, but so that I may attest, in even a few words, how pleasing this exchange of letters is to me nearly every week. And so that you may recognize this in these lines as well, I am replying crudely and briefly to three letters, the first written on the 5th, the second on the 12th, and finally the third on the 19th of the month of August. I do this not because each individual letter is not most worthy of a singular response, but so that I do not now act contrary to the custom which I have maintained until now and which you approve. First, however, I heartily congratulate you both on the long duration of a **happy marriage**, as you declare, and on your **61st Birthday**. ### LETTER CLVI.

## Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
## My most merciful Lord,

**I**t is incredible to say how much pain the eclipse of our literary correspondence <note>original: "literarii nostri commercii eclipsis"; a scholarly way of describing a long gap in their exchange of letters</note> causes me. For besides the fact that nothing is more delightful to me than Your letters, the most inclined affection for me that shines through them surpasses all other pleasures. Therefore, I am trying every possible path to reach You once again, however much the detour of those routes may be lengthened and the delay of a response made more lasting. Indeed, I have seen nothing from You since the 18th of August, which feels like an entire year to me. I do not doubt that one or another of Your letters has either been intercepted or is closely besieged at **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustæ"; the city of Augsburg was a major hub of communication and trade, frequently affected by the movements of the Thirty Years' War</note> along with our excellent **Hainhofer**; <note>Matthias Hainhofer (1571–1647), a prominent diplomat, art agent, and correspondent of the author</note> I wish we might soon hear that the city has been liberated without the slaughter <note>original: "lanienam"</note> of the innocent common folk, for whom we deservedly pour out burning prayers. What the face of things will be there, and what hope will remain for our affairs when writing is not at all safe, You will guess for Your own part from Your excellent wisdom; namely, to put it in one word, that a most certain servitude is prepared for us. To this, not even a restored **Peace** would bring any relief—so far is it from the case that, under the **furies of Mars**, <note>original: "Martis furiis"; a mythological reference to the madness and destruction of war</note> any breathing-space can be expected by us, who are exposed to the whims and the plunder of both sides. But whatever may finally happen (which is not at all to be measured by the scale of human reason), we should certainly conclude that it will turn out for our salvation; the examples of past events undoubtedly demonstrate this in abundance, since **GOD** will by no means leave His work unfinished. And since this cause is not a private one, nor does it pertain only to individual men, but is common to the whole **Church of God**, we do not doubt that You also are moved by the sense of our afflictions, so that You truly pity us and direct Your counsels toward...

## LETTER CLVIII.
### *Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,*

I have no doubt that the siege of the city of Augsburg <note>original: "Augustanæ urbis"; Augsburg was a key strategic city during the Thirty Years' War, suffering a brutal siege in 1646 by Swedish and French forces</note> has until now stood in the way of the couriers passing back and forth, through whose service we conduct this literary exchange. Now that the siege has been lifted (as report suggests, and as is certain to me), I am persuaded that the many letters I have written since the 18th of August have finally reached you through the care of Mr. Hainhofer <note>Philipp Hainhofer (1578–1647), a prominent Augsburg merchant, diplomat, and art collector who facilitated high-level correspondence across Europe</note>.

Moreover, since this shorter route was obstructed, you sought and found another, albeit longer one in the meantime, so that nothing should be lost from my weekly task. I understand from this how pleasing this service of yours is to you, just as it is certainly burdensome and heavy; if that journey which you indicated had actually occurred, I would not have looked down upon the glory of a busy man.

However, no one—*O best of men, and most devoted lover of your country*—is untouched by the public calamity that you deplore. I say "public," for not only do we know what we have endured, but I want you to be persuaded that not just the news, but the very feeling of your misfortunes reaches us. Few foresee what fate awaits Germany hereafter; many more dread it; all wait with focused minds. Yet your thoughts are pious, and your hope, which you place in God, knows no falsehood. He never sets aside His care for *His Church on Earth*, but protects her amidst the turmoils of the age and the assaults of the Devil and his instruments through His truly marvelous providence and power. But if we were able to bring a remedy to such great evils, if our plans, if our strength [could avert] the [ruin] <note>original catchword: "pestem", literally "plague" or "destruction"</note> hanging over our fatherland...

### LETTER CLIX.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->My Lord by far most merciful,<-

What a drink of cold water offered to a weary traveler, fainting with thirst, is to him, so were your most flavorful letters to me, which you had sent on September 10th. However, the "tempest of Mars" <note>original: "Martis intemperies"; a poetic way of referring to the storms of war, as Mars is the Roman god of warfare</note> had blocked them from me until the 3rd of this November. This happened all the more harshly to me because no letters of yours accompanied the later ones written by your Serene Lord Father on September 15th and 22nd (which were delivered correctly to me); even now, from that date, nothing from your side has appeared here among us. Now, although you are (it seems) hurrying, yet since you compare yours with the refinement <note>original: "lima"; literally a "file," a common metaphor for the polishing and correcting of literary work</note> of others, you have surely achieved this: that if any other letters are stuck on the road (as I indeed hope), I shall wait for their arrival more patiently, since it is established that you are safe—which is my salvation—and favorable—which is my greatest pleasure. For

## LETTER CLXII.

### Very Reverend and Most
### Distinguished Lord Doctor,

I will deal with you more briefly now, because you have already responded to many of my letters, or are preparing to respond. For you must not be overwhelmed—you who are able to employ your time much better than in writing letters of this kind. One most pleasing chapter, which concerns your **travels** <note>original: "peregrinatio," referring to the scholarly or educational journeys often undertaken by 17th-century intellectuals.</note>, as it has stuck deeply in my mind, so it seemed right to take it up again in these lines. And I easily agree that you neither regret nor are troubled by them now, you who have brought back such fruit from them, and have walked holily and before the Lord in every place. For I believe that the memory of a life once lived innocently is the strongest support of **old age**; whereas, however much you change the face of the landscape, the conscience and image of ill-advised deeds and wrongly admitted errors constantly recurs to a restless soul. As for the fact that you judge the letters, which I have given to you thus far at the command of my Most Illustrious Lord Father, worthy to be printed one day with your own—while I can agree regarding yours, I completely disagree with you concerning mine. For most of them are childish, and

### LETTER CLXIII.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord,<-

*Although everything here is difficult and somber, and my illness, which had eased for a while, has flared up again, nothing is harder for me than your silence. ## LETTER 164.

->Abundant and Constant Greetings<-
->*And happiness for the coming year.*<-

**Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,**
**Most Merciful Lord,**

*I do not wish to overwhelm you with my letters, of which I have already sent three before this one, not yet replied to by you; but I also do not repeat the prayer of good omen for the coming year after this, which I poured out more warmly for you eight days ago,* <note>The author refers to a previous letter containing New Year's blessings.</note> *certain that those things which proceed from an upright and devoted heart are held as valid by God. I am very glad that you received the Furttenbachian design* <note>original: "Furrenbachianam ideam"; this likely refers to a design or architectural plan by Joseph Furttenbach (1591–1667), a German engineer and architect famous for his work on theater design, mechanics, and fortifications.</note> *safely through unsafe roads, lest the work be lost for the author, a noble and industrious man, who deserves well of you and wishes to prove his zeal. I recently sent you the small book by Master Wagner,* <note>likely Tobias Wagner (1598–1680), a prominent Lutheran theologian and chancellor at the University of Tübingen.</note> *intended for you and my Prince Johann Friedrich, complete and bound; I shall shortly send another copy with a more elegant binding, along with the pages that are still missing. I truly understand that it is a joy and of the highest importance to me that you receive eagerly those things which proceed from me to you with zeal and obedience. I ask with all respect that you continue to do so, out of your natural generosity, and that you fulfill this joy more and more. Farewell and cherish*

->Your Illustrious Highness's<-

Stuttgart, December 16, 1645. <note>original: "17. Cal. Ianuarii Anno 1646"; in the Roman calendar, the 17th day before the Calends of January 1646 is December 16, 1645.</note>

most humble client.

### LETTER 166.

I have received the fifth and final volume of the letters of *Melanchthon* <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a primary architect of the Reformation and a collaborator of Martin Luther. This letter acknowledges a new edition of his correspondence.</note>, which you, Reverend and Most Renowned Sir, wished to dedicate to my Most Illustrious Lord Father. Both from the preface and from reading certain letters, I have understood that you are still most well-disposed toward my Most Illustrious Lord Father and me, as you have been until now. For this reason, I thank you, and I am compelled to admit that the history of that era is illuminated in no small measure by this edition. And just as Melanchthon is praised by everyone for his writings, so you also are most worthy of praise—you who not only value his already published books so highly, but have also wished to give life to those which the injustice of time <note>original: "injuria temporis"; a common Latin phrase for the loss of historical records through neglect or war.</note> would have stolen from us. I pray that those who know how to judge such things rightly may reward your labor with honor, love, and material support; I continue to commend myself to your favor. Farewell. *Wolfenbüttel, April 21, 1646.*

->Your friend,<-
->RUDOLPH AUGUSTUS.<- <note>Rudolph Augustus (1627–1704) was the Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. He was a significant scholar-prince and bibliophile.</note>

### III.
### With Prince ANTHONY ULRICH,
### LETTER 167.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Renowned*<-
->*Lord Doctor Johann Valentin Andreae,*<-

I most deeply wish that our year, growing young again <note>original: "repuerascens"; likely a play on words regarding the Prince’s own youth (he was 12 at the time) and the "rebirth" of the new year.</note> with so many good things, may bloom for you with as many little buds of flowers as the meadows are suddenly accustomed to see and be filled with in Spring. Indeed, after a longer silence of letters than I was accustomed to, as I set out to write these words, both the passage of the months and my spirit toward you—most inclined toward you as is only right—have commanded me to begin with a prayer. For what else could I do, than measure back love with love? It is a love, however, which I do not so much measure back as I venerate from the bottom of my heart. You wished for the memory of yourself to grow fresh again—though it has never formed a callus <note>meaning the Prince's memory of his mentor has never grown "hard" or "numb" through neglect</note> with me, nor while I draw breath will it ever—by means of a gift (for which I owe you immense thanks). It is a gift that is, by every more elegant judgment, and for that very reason, more pleasing to me than any other. But while I remain fixed with a single gaze upon the most accurate engraving <note>original: "sculpturâ"; likely a printed portrait of Andreae sent as a gift</note>, I am easily brought to the opinion that the gift speaks as if for its giver, and that I shall obtain nothing dearer, just as I could receive nothing from a dearer hand. Well done, then, in that most tender affection toward me; and may you never regret having striven to be first in your duties. Farewell.

->*To your Reverence*<-

*Given at Wolfenbüttel,*
*January 11, 1646.*

->**Most devotedly yours,**<-

## LETTER 168.

->To the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince, my by far most clement Lord,<-

The infrequency of your pen has been abundantly compensated for by your engraving tool <note>original: "caelum"; referring to a burin or chisel used for engraving. Andreae is making a wordplay between "calamus" (pen) and "caelum" (engraving tool), as the young Prince was practicing the art of printmaking</note>, in which you have successfully applied your study and effort. Your Most Serene Father <note>Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg, a famous book collector and scholar</note> shared some specimens of this work with me, which delighted me greatly. I considered it my duty that, if any works of rare artists—of whom Rubens <note>Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640), the celebrated Flemish Baroque painter whose work was highly sought after by collectors</note> was easily the prince in our age—should fall into my hands, I should send them to you to assist your noble endeavors. I would indeed do this more frequently, were it not that the distance between places and the dangers of the roads <note>A reference to the ongoing hazards of travel during the latter years of the Thirty Years' War</note> made such transport more difficult.

In the meantime, I congratulate myself on that graciousness of your noble soul, by which you do not disdain my slight little gifts <note>original: "levidensia munuscula"</note>. Truly, you understand that through these images <note>original: "simulacra"; likely prints or artist's studies</note> my spirit is revealed to you—as much indebted to the great merits of your father, as it is most dedicated by all my prayers and services to the prosperity of his House. Nothing more fortunate could happen to me on earth than the hereditary continuation of that Virtue and Clementness toward me; I pray Christ may abundantly reward this with a long succession of years, as well as an increase of blessing and happiness. Farewell, Most Illustrious Prince, and unless it be a burden, bless me alternately with your pen and your engraving tool, remaining favorable toward

->Your Reverend and Illustrious Highness’s<-

Stuttgart, January 28,
1646.
most humble client.

### To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished
### Lord Doctor Johann Valentin Andreae,

I read your letter, sweeter to me than any honey, with great pleasure, and I noted your congratulations to me and my brothers on the happy return of the birthday of our most clement and loving Father <note>Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1579–1666), who was a celebrated scholar and patron of Andreae</note>. Truly, the love you cherish for us always provides you with new proofs by which you can show that same affection to us as clearly as possible. Please accept my greatest thanks for that most generous gift of both affection and prayer. I know you are not led to consider me so fallen <note>original: "degenerem"</note> that I would not easily join in this most perfect wish.

For beyond the fact that I am bound by the duty I owe my most clement and loving Father—and also by my own benefit, which will endure as long as my youth is guided by such a great Spirit <note>original: "Numine"; a classical term for a divine power, here used respectfully to refer to the Duke's guiding influence over his children's education</note>—I feel moved by your own example. You even dare to compete with me in honoring His Highness; indeed, you almost snatch the prize from me. However that may be, my small strength <note>original: "viriculæ meæ"</note> will not discourage me from this contest; I would consider it a sin <note>original: "piaculum"</note> to be outdone in affection and will, even if I cannot match the result—provided, of course, that our competition remains friendly. Meanwhile, I ask that you continue to delight me with your writings, as is your custom. Farewell.

->*Your Reverence’s*<-

Written at the castle in Wolfenbüttel, <note>The primary residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note>
April 21, 1646. ->*Most devotedly bound.*<-

### LETTER 170.

->To the Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord,<-
->Doctor Johann Valentin Andreae,<-

May your love for me always be so ardent that I never set myself to the duty of responding unless I am bound by a debt of gratitude <note>original: "Gratiûm," referring to the Graces of mythology, personifications of charm and gratitude</note>, which you command me to return for your most elegant gifts. Indeed, the engravings <note>original: "cælaturæ"; likely copperplate prints or etchings</note> which you recently sent are so elegant that I have already grown accustomed to feeding both my eyes and my mind upon them. Now I am held by the most intricate windings of the *Labyrinths*; now by the most delightful arrangements of the *gardens*; now by the most artistic spouting of the *fountains*.

I am most especially moved, however, by the modern depiction <note>original: "inhabitatio," literally "habitation" or "dwelling"</note> of the Mountain of the Decalogue <note>Mount Sinai, where the Ten Commandments (the Decalogue) were given</note>, once famous for the proclamation of the Law and the presence of the Divine. I have no doubt that if it were possible to behold all these things more closely and in person, they would be by far the most pleasing sights. Be that as it may, may Your Reverence <note>original: "T. Rev."</note> accept my thanks for the display of such things, which move the spectator by their print and image, but would move one even more by the sight of the objects themselves.

Furthermore, I easily perceive that you use "spectacles of love" <note>A metaphor suggesting that Andreae's affection makes him see the Prince's work as better than it is</note> toward me, for in your recent letters you call those hands "artistic" which are accustomed to painting only trivial things on paper with a crude brush. Truly, I respect Your Reverence’s judgment regarding my efforts; however, I will not allow myself to be persuaded by it to think of my own works as highly as you praise them. I also congratulate myself on that *Poetic Attempt* <note>original: "Conamine isto Poëtico"</note>, since it seemed not inelegant to your most learned palate. Indeed, you have encouraged me so that I shall no longer blush to continue such things in the future, especially with my teacher <note>Likely the famous linguist and court tutor Justus Georg Schottelius (1612–1676)</note>—who is quite successful in this—as my guide, by whom you are greeted in return with dutiful respect. Farewell.

Sent from Wolfenbüttel, June 9, 1646.

Your Reverence’s
Most devoted.

->*Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,*<-

Finally, I cease to restrain my pen, as I have done for a long time, and I put a limit to my silence, which perhaps seemed almost Pythagorean <note>original: "Pythagoreum"; referring to the strict vow of silence, often lasting five years, required of the disciples of the philosopher Pythagoras</note> to you. It is customary for those who have a long interval between letters to accumulate a heap of subjects to write about during that leisure, and so they more than compensate for their slowness with long-windedness. 

Since I too have indulged in such leisure for a little while, I think I should wander more freely into this literary field and use the most powerful arguments to persuade you that *my love for you, ever respectful of you, has in no way diminished.* But what need is there for those? You know my mind, and I know yours: namely, that we both know each other’s minds to be unchanging in mutual love. 

What then shall I write? I shall write so that you may write back. But you yourself know that your handwriting is most welcome and instructive to me; you also know that I delight in your letters as your leisure allows. I write this, therefore, that you may be well and mindful of me. 

I hold both in my prayers, well aware that while you are healthy, the many things within you remain healthy—those tireless vigils <note>original: "pervigilia," referring to late-night studies or intellectual labors</note> of an enviable intellect; and that you, by being mindful of me before my God, have not let the memory of me be erased, which your prayers <note>original: "suspiria," literally "sighs" or "pious aspirations"</note> joined with mine will not permit. Farewell and stay safe.

->To Your Reverence,<-

Given at Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti," the Latin name for Wolfenbüttel, the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note>,
September 8, 1646.

->Your most devoted.<-

## LETTER 172.

->**Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,**<-
->**Lord, by far most merciful,**<-

Even if it would never have been part of my modesty to demand a letter from You, nevertheless, because You gave one to me of your own accord without being asked, it was as honorable to me as it was most welcome to receive. I wish You had added something produced by Your own artistic hand and chisel <note>original: "caelo"; a tool used for engraving. The Prince was a talented amateur artist</note>, in which I am accustomed to take wonderful delight, so that I might judge Your progress from it, as far as is permitted for me. I heartily congratulate that distinguished man, Lord Schottelius <note>Justus Georg Schottelius (1612–1676), a famous linguist and the Prince's tutor</note>, the guide of Your studies, on his happy wedding. I strongly approve that You, along with Your most illustrious brother, were a great ornament to the occasion. I wish that this favor and value You have granted to the man's loyalty and skill—and to literature itself—might stand as an example in this century so hostile to the Muses <note>the Muses represent the arts and sciences</note>. For how much more noble is this than in places where good learning does not so much wither as it becomes a source of envy and harm to those who possess it. Clearly, where ignorance rules, the liberal arts serve unworthily. 

But may God preserve this spirit in You, so that in imitation of Your Great Father <note>Duke August the Younger, famous for his massive library</note>, there may remain foster-fathers and guardians for the learned. For among the Germans, a great many have now degenerated into the ferocity of Mars <note>the god of war; a reference to the ongoing Thirty Years' War</note> and a disdain for Minerva <note>the goddess of wisdom</note>. I believe You have received the *Saint Eustace* of Dürer <note>original: "Eustachium Dureri"; a famous copperplate engraving by Albrecht Dürer noted for its intricate detail</note>, recently sent to You as a gift, which stands out among the works of that supreme artist. Now I have other delights prepared for You at my house, which await a suitable carrier. For I feel I owe kindling to Your fiery and versatile genius, as I easily believe such things will redound to the benefit of the Republic <note>original: "Reip."; referring to the common good or the state</note>. I do this not to flatter You or to insinuate myself, but so that I may aid Your progress with whatever little effort of mine I can offer,

## LETTER 173.

->**Fortune looking back!**<- <note>original: "Fortunam respicientem!" A classical expression for a sudden turn of good luck.</note>

From the moment my name first became known to you, very Reverend and most distinguished Sir, no day has passed, I believe, that has not bound me to you in some way. You have blessed me again with a new gift: an engraving—more like a sculpture than a mere bronze—of that famous Nuremberg painter <note>original: "pictoris Norici"; referring to Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528)</note>, which the initials A. D. "imprisoned" at the base indicate <note>original: "initiali incarceratâ"; a clever description of Dürer’s famous monogram, where the letter D is placed inside the legs of the A</note>. I could easily believe it lacks nothing, unless Zeuxis or Parrhasius <note>legendary painters of ancient Greece known for their realism</note>, or someone else equally favored by Minerva <note>the Roman goddess of wisdom and the arts</note>, were to add colors and its natural form. I wish I could declare in words how welcome it was; *you have deserved well of me, and well of my collection of paintings*, to which this has now been added and stored away as a distinguished ornament and a clear testimony of your love for me. Because of this, I profess that I owe you no small debt; but I wish you would show me in turn how you think I might be of use to you. Do not doubt the pleasure I take in doing a favor, for which I burn, but believe me to be most devoted to you. I was writing this with a running pen <note>original: "currente calamo"; meaning written in haste</note> on November 10th, which was the birthday of our blessed *Luther* and the day of Pope *Martin’s* death. <note>Martin Luther was born Nov. 10, 1483. Pope Martin V died in 1431, though Andreae is likely making a symbolic connection between the name Martin and the two opposing religious figures.</note>

*To Your Reverend Dignity,*
Most respectfully.

I add a greeting from the dearest brothers, who expect more frequent news from
*Your Reverend Dignity.*

### LETTER 172.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**My most merciful Lord,**<-

Although it would never have been part of my modesty to demand a letter from You, yet because You gave it to me unasked and of your own accord, it is as honorable to me as it was most deeply welcome in its receipt. And I wish you had added something from your own skilled hand and engraving tool <note>original: "cælo"; the burin or tool used for engraving metal</note>, by which I am accustomed to be wonderfully delighted, and to judge, as far as is permitted to me, your progress from that point. I congratulate from the heart that distinguished man, Master Schottelius <note>Justus Georg Schottelius (1612–1676), a famous German grammarian and tutor to the princes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note>, the guide of your studies, on his happy marriage; and I strongly approve that you, along with your most illustrious brother, were its greatest ornament. I wish that this mark of favor and value, bestowed by You upon the man’s loyalty and skill—and upon literature itself—might serve as an example in this century so hostile to the Muses <note>The "Muses" represent the arts and learning, currently "hostile" because of the ongoing Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)</note>. For how much more noble is this than where good literature does not merely wither, but becomes a source of envy and loss for those who possess it. Truly, where ignorance rules, the liberal arts serve unworthily. But may God preserve this spirit in your family, so that, in imitation of your Great Father <note>Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1579–1666), a famous book collector and scholar</note>, there may remain nurturers and protectors for the learned—those who, for the most part among the Germans, have degenerated into the ferocity of Mars <note>the god of war</note> and a disdain for Minerva <note>the goddess of wisdom and art</note>. I believe you have received the *Saint Eustace* by Dürer <note>referring to Albrecht Dürer’s famous large copperplate engraving of St. Eustace, c. 1501</note> recently sent to You as a gift, which stands out among the works of that supreme artist. Now, other delights are prepared for You at my home, which await a suitable carrier. For I feel I owe some nourishment to your fiery and versatile intellect, because I easily believe these things will redound to the benefit of the Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipublicae"</note>; for I do this not to flatter You or to ingratiate myself, but so that I might aid your progress with whatever small effort I can manage,

# LETTER 173.
->*Fortune looking back [upon us]!*<-

From the time my name first became known to you, most Reverend and Distinguished Sir, I believe no day has passed that has not bound me to you in some way. You have blessed me again with a new gift—an engraving rather than a bronze work—by that famous painter of Nuremberg <note>original: "pictoris Norici"; referring to Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528)</note>, as suggested by the letters A.D. joined in a monogram at the base. I would easily believe that nothing is missing from it, unless Zeuxis or Parrhasius <note>Famous rival painters of ancient Greece known for their realism</note>, or someone else to whom Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and the arts</note> shows equal favor, were to add colors and a life-like form.

I wish I could declare in words how welcome it was; *you have deserved well of me and well of my art collection*, to which this piece has now been added and stored as a distinguished ornament and a bright testimony of your love toward me. Because of this, I profess that I owe you no small debt; but I wish you would in turn reveal your mind as to how you think I might be of use to you. Have no doubt of the pleasure I have in showing gratitude, for which I burn, but believe me to be most devoted to you. Written with a running pen <note>original: "currente calamo"; written in haste</note> on the 10th of November, which was the birthday of our blessed *Luther*, but the day of death for *Martin* the Pope <note>Martin Luther was born Nov. 10, 1483. Andreae notes the coincidence of the name Martin, though the historical Pope Martin V died in February.</note>.

->**Your Reverend Dignity’s**<-
->**Most respectful [servant].**<-

I add greetings from my dearest brothers, who look forward to more frequent letters from your Reverend Dignity.

### LETTER 174.

->Health to You!<-

A mournful message perhaps reached you not long ago, *most Distinguished Sir*, regarding the death of the most blessed *Mr. Saubert* <note>Johann Saubert the Elder (1592–1646), a prominent Lutheran theologian and librarian in Nuremberg</note>, our greatest friend, whom we lament with you deeply and from the heart, as is only right. What shall we foretell? Surely, as the great "Atlases" of literature depart <note>A metaphor for scholars who support the "heavens" of knowledge</note>, those *Gothic* and *Hunnic* ages <note>A reference to the barbarian invasions of Rome, here used to describe a return to an age of ignorance and lack of culture</note> will return—ages which long ago brought upon the world the forgetting of all elegant learning and all noble arts. Yet it is not right that we should trouble the will of *God, the Best and Greatest*, with our many griefs and consternation. He aims his bow; let us lay aside our breastplate and offer a chest open to the wound <note>A Stoic and pious expression of submission to divine will</note>.

You ask that I send you something crafted by my own hand, which I did not long ago; but I greatly fear whether it dares to come before your sight, as the lines are drawn with little grace. I received that *engraving* by the most skillful *Dürer* <note>Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), the famous German Renaissance artist</note>—as I also mentioned in my last letters—with a hand no less ready than joyful (indeed, most joyful!). To tell the truth, at first glance I did not sufficiently recognize *that holy Hunter* <note>Saint Eustace (often confused with Saint Hubert), the subject of a famous engraving by Dürer</note>, who lies prostrate on his knees with folded hands before the *beast*.

What should be decided regarding that honor and submission? Perhaps he marvels that the *crucified Christ* springs forth from the *Stag’s* head, whereas there are many Christians in whose brains Christ never tends to sprout, and even more rarely in their hearts or on their lips. So it entirely seems to me; I wish you would communicate to me what your own mind is on this matter. Meanwhile, fare as well as possible with all your family, and keep me in your favor. Written with a somewhat hurried pen <note>original: "celeriori calamo"</note>, on the 7th day of December, 1646.

->*Your Excellence’s most devoted servant.*<-
