YEAR 1646. / LETTER 175. / [Wishes for] Much Health.

->*And a most auspicious following year.*<-

Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,
my most merciful Lord,

You pray for Fortune to look back upon me; I in turn pray for Janus <note>The Roman god of beginnings, gates, and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking toward the past and the future</note> to look auspiciously upon you. This is what my homeland and these lands need most of all. Would that we might behold him bringing back peace to us, and restoring halcyon days <note>A period of calm and peace; the term comes from a Greek myth about a bird that calmed the sea to lay its eggs</note> to the Church as it faints under its burdens. Without these, death itself might rightly be judged preferable to any life spent in perpetual languor. For you, however, may he happily add growth in mind and body, as well as an increase in talent and skill, in which you already so greatly excel; and, as I entirely foresee you will be, may he promote you in his progress toward the pinnacle of a perfect Prince.

I could easily guess that the *St. Eustace* by Dürer <note>Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528) was the leading artist of the German Renaissance. His "St. Eustace" is his largest copperplate engraving, famous for its detailed landscape and animals</note> would not be unwelcome to you, coming if not from my own hand, then certainly from the hand of a supreme artist. In this man, it is marvelous that, emerging from a crude and barbarian age, he was the first of the Germans to rise to the perfection of his art through the imitation of Nature. Moreover, he left no one second to him, being so absolute in all its branches: engraving, sculpture, statuary, architecture, optics, symmetry, and the like. Indeed, he had no equal except for Michelangelo Buonarroti <note>The famous Italian Renaissance polymath (1475–1564)</note>, the Italian, who was his contemporary and rival. Dürer left behind works (of which I once owned a great part) that easily exceed the span of a single man's life, even while poverty was his constant companion in a frugal life. Today the Italians value him highly, and they are angry with us, because we do not recognize our own domestic treasures and ornaments—

### LETTER 178.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord*<-

## LETTER 179.

->*To the Reverend and Most Renowned*<-

Your *Letters* help me greatly, for by their brilliance they always return me more learned than before; moreover, your *Little Gifts* <note>original: "Munuscula"; likely referring to small books or commemorative tokens</note> delight me much, which are always of such a kind that I am compelled to use and turn them over in both my hands and eyes for a long time. I owe you many thanks besides for the devoted wish which you wished to pour out <note>original: "expectorare"; literally "to take from the heart or breast"</note> for my own *Birthday* as well; for as much as I attribute to your Piety and Devotion, I trust that this wish will also have much weight in the ear of God. In place of repayment, I greatly desire and hope for His favor upon your own wishes and interests. Meanwhile, continue to inform and delight me with *Your Writings*—

### LETTER 180.
->*Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,*<-

Let us return at last to our literary fellowship <note>original: "consortium literarium"; referring to their shared intellectual and spiritual exchange</note>, which I perceive has been interrupted for a long time now. Hitherto, I have not wished to be an intrusion upon your more serious affairs, nor to interrupt them with letters. For I know—and with me no small part of the world knows—how great you are even in your most busy leisure <note>original: "otiis negotiosissimis"; a classic Latin wordplay (oxymoron) suggesting that even his "time off" is spent in productive scholarly work</note>. It is truly a matter of your genius, which, when it grows warm with your natural spirit, prepares such wonderful heavenly delights for the world, mixed with the most abundant salt of the precepts of life <note>original: "sale uberrimo"; "salt" here refers to wit, wisdom, and spiritual preservation</note>. However it may be, I cannot restrain myself from stealing a little bit of time from you to be spent on the reading of this letter <unclear/> your Reverence in my mind <unclear/> to you again, so that if you, as is your custom, <unclear/> from here, the most pleasant Echo of our love will resonate between us. Truly, even when I write nothing to Your Reverence, I am not unmindful of you. Yet, what could I think more fair than to offer you a toast to your memory, and to commend my own memory to you through letters? I add that this confession is like a feast to me; if you add your own to it, I shall be called happy. Farewell, and continue to love me.

Given at Wolfenbüttel, 8 September 1646.
->To Your Reverence,<-
->Your most observant.<-

### LETTER 181.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord most gracious by far.<-

Whenever I write to your Illustrious brother, Rudolf August <note>Prince Rudolf August of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1627–1704)</note>, I feel as though I have written to you at the same time, and have offered up all my affairs along with my pious prayers. Yet, such is your incredible affection toward me that this does not satisfy you, unless you provoke specific letters of my own addressed to you, and entice them with your most elegant writing. You clearly wish for a mutual echo <note>original: "Echo"; a poetic way of describing a back-and-forth correspondence</note> of letters to resonate between us. I accept the condition, but on this one term: that you do not substitute someone else more eloquent <note>original: "vocalem"; literally "vocal" or "expressive," implying he wants the Prince's own words, not a secretary's</note> to write in your place, since nothing is more lovely to me than your own voice—yours, I say. You must remember, however, that old men who have passed their sixtieth year <note>Andreae was 60 years old in 1646</note> are less resonant and lack strength in their lungs <note>original: "lateribus valere"; literally "to be strong in the sides," a classical idiom for the physical stamina required for public speaking or projection</note>; yet I shall respond to your voice with what exertion I can, whenever you wish. For I could never fully explain what delights are produced for me either by the image of your person <note>original: "imago corporis Tui"; likely referring to a portrait of the Prince hanging on his wall</note> displayed upon my wall, or by the character of your soul expressed upon these papers. Therefore, write boldly, sweetest Prince; you will never weary your correspondent, so long as I see that my responses are pleasing to you. How much I truly love and honor you, I shall soon testify with a certain small, humble gift <note>original: "munusculo aliquo levidensi"; a "levidense" gift is one that is slight or of thin texture, a modest offering</note>, which I know will not be unwelcome. Farewell, and unless it is a trouble, greet the conductor of your studies <note>his tutor or governor</note> on my behalf.

->Your Illustrious Highness’s<-

Stuttgart, 8 November
1646. ->Most humble client.<-

### Postscript to Prince Rudolf August <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704) was the eldest son of Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel; he was a student of the author at the time.</note>

Before I had sent these letters off, another of yours arrived, dated the 1st of this month, in which you again approve of my former excursions <note>likely referring to previous scholarly writings or shared academic projects</note>. However, you then seem to forbid the publication of our letters <note>original: "publicationem literarum"</note> which I am planning, for reasons that are by no means to be feared by you—who are flourishing and conspicuous in the arena of public life—but only by me, who am a veteran and faded. Nevertheless, even at the cost of my own ill-repute, I would wish the rays of your noble mind and style to come forth into the public and earn a memory among posterity. I humbly beg, through your incredible humanity and kindness, that you allow this and indulge your client, who is most dedicated to you until his final breath; for the rest, I shall act most obediently according to your command.

Stuttgart, 18 December 1646.

### LETTER CLXXXV.

**Most Illustrious and Most Serene Princes,**
**Lords most gracious by far,**

Even if I lacked all other reason to write to You, this occasion which presents itself of its own accord—the most worthy of all, most pleasant to me, and without doubt most welcome to You—would deserve to be mentioned. It is the tenth day of April, the day upon which these words of mine will present themselves to You. It is a day we must rightly hold as venerable <note>original: *Augustus*; a play on the name of the Princes' father, Duke August</note> and festive, for it has dawned auspiciously as the sixty-ninth birthday of Your Most Serene Father and Lord. While the German and Christian worlds, and the entire choir of men of letters <note>original: *Literatorum*; the scholarly community</note>, rightly applaud and cheer for him, this is nevertheless Your own most immediate and special blessing and joy. You yourselves understand how much You owe to God the Giver for this; for it is entirely unnecessary for me to explain to You how much protection, support, and foundation is placed for You in the longevity of your Lord Father, and in his vigorous and lively old age. For the very face of these sorrowful times cries out for a man most highly equipped with all heavenly gifts—a man whom the upheavals in Germany, the wounds of the Church, the ulcers of the Republic of Letters <term>Republic of Letters: the long-distance intellectual community of scholars and writers in the 17th century</term>, and the vices of the age all demand. Indeed, we have no one whom we might truly compare to Your Renowned Father; therefore, so that we may have him with us for as long as possible, let us all [join] in common... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "prece-" indicates the next page begins with the word *precibus*, meaning "prayers."</note>

Truly, may Christ fulfill the desires of the Lord Father, and Yours, and mine; may He keep you safe and blessed. Farewell and be favorable.*

## LETTER 186.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,
### My most merciful Lords,

**T**he more deeply I remain in Your debt, the more difficult I find it to extricate myself on this solemnity of Christ the Victor Ascending into Heaven. # LETTER 187.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Princes, My far most merciful Lords,

**I**f Your letters brought nothing but elegance, they would be desired by me as a means by which I might be educated; and coming from such a place, which I must truly revere, they are to be sought of my own accord. Furthermore, they are full of a most abundant courtesy, which is most suitable for <term>soothing the bitterness of this time<gloss>A likely reference to the hardships of the Thirty Years' War, which was in its final stages in 1647.</gloss></term>. But because, in this flower of your youth, they give me great hope—and indeed, assurance—of the greatest public utility as the years and your fortunes progress, and they present themselves to me as guarantees of private favor, it is truly a matter of how much I should value...

That You will receive these with a fair mind and a serene countenance, I cannot doubt, given the many proofs of Your easy-going nature and kindness.

For me, indeed, it would be a matter of pride to be in Your hands and before Your eyes—things that may occasionally remind You of me, that is, of Your most devoted Client. I, on the other hand, feed my eyes upon the sight of Your portraits and that of Your Great Father, refreshing my soul and finding material to proclaim Your Virtue, Your gifts of intellect, and Your progress—rare for this age and status—to my visitors. And behold, I have erected a tablet for that purpose in my *Selenianum* <note>original: "Seleniano"; likely referring to the author's study or museum, named after "Selene" (the moon) in honor of Duke Augustus’s pseudonym, Gustavus Selenus.</note>, and another destined for the praise of Your Philosophical Court; I have added a description of these so as not to send an empty letter. Would that these most honorable guests might one day see this *Selenianum* of mine in person; no sight could happen to me that would be more sublime or more memorable. Meanwhile, may You...

# LETTER CLXXXVIII.
## Most Illustrious and High Princes,
## My most merciful Lords,

The late arrival of Your letters and the early departure of the courier <note>original: "veredarii"; a postal messenger or mail carrier.</note> mean that no response worthy of your kindness and elegance is at hand; it must be deferred for a week <note>original: "in octiduum"; literally "into eight days."</note>, if God prolongs my life. the various spans of this life traversed, and especially the investigations of an unwearied mind, the libraries searched everywhere, the monuments left behind, and the exhausted labors; but also the conflicts with envy and slander undertaken in various ways, and the tested shifts of Fortune, and a lifespan extended beyond **twelve lusters** <note>A "lustrum" is a period of five years; twelve lusters indicates the author is over sixty years old.</note>—at last, the ears and eyes of the Schools, the Church, and the Court will one day testify to these things. As I weigh them in my mind, although many things occur to me that I might wish were undone, or done and undertaken differently, yet very many things remain which sweetly affect my soul and soothe my gray hairs with the memory of those events, so that I am not in the least ashamed or regretful to have lived; rather, it inflames me to offer immortal and infinite thanks to **GOD**.

For although neither a splendid **LINEAGE** <note>original: "NATALES"; referring to noble birth or high social standing.</note>, nor an abundance of fortune, nor a greatness of dignities and honors fell to my lot beyond the common condition—things which for many have turned out to be a burden rather than an ornament, and a source of condemnation rather than salvation—nevertheless, in this mediocrity of my lot, very many things were granted by Divine gift. If these gifts are less than the offerings received by others when taken individually, yet when joined together and heaped into one, they deserve esteem, admiration, and the highest praises of a propitious **GOD**.

For what do I not owe to You, **Triune GOD**, most Wise **GOD** the Creator, most Loving **GOD** the Redeemer, most Merciful **GOD** the Sanctifier? You who deigned that I be born a human, be reborn for Heaven <note>A reference to Christian baptism.</note>, be born into Your Church, and be born alongside the best of Your people. You granted such parents who were themselves useful to Your cause (though few in number) and blameless in tending to earthly matters, and who evidently experienced Your blessing in their offspring. Above all, they entrusted to me that Religion which You purged of dross through the ministry of Your **Blessed Luther** <note>original: "B. Lutheri"; referring to Martin Luther. The author, Johann Valentin Andreae, was a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note>, which I have embraced with firm faith...

# LETTERS

*...embraced, shaken by no contradictions of reason, shattered by no hesitations, weakened by no worldly spectacles, and untainted by the false colors of Sects; I myself have confessed this true and sincere faith and have professed it for more than forty years, ready with Your help to bring and prove the same to Your very Tribunal with an undaunted spirit.*

Truly, my father's house was—without boasting—a *School of Piety, a workshop of the Arts, a refuge for the Afflicted, a hospital for the poor, and a legitimate and most praiseworthy expenditure of Wealth;* but my *Mother* was an *Example of all Virtues beyond her sex, and an unconquered Heroine* <note>original: "Virago"; in the 17th century, this term was a high compliment for a woman possessing heroic courage and strength of character.</note> *through all the shifts of fortune. To her, before You my* GOD, *I would easily attribute whatever good has been received, to her mediation and intercession; and I would count it among my highest delights to have returned some gratitude to her while on earth. Having become a widow when I had scarcely left boyhood, she placed me in charge of her household management and admitted me to my father’s writing-desks* <note>Referring to his father's private papers, archives, or professional business.</note>, *employing me as a youth in cares greater than my age.*

My *EDUCATION*, *while indeed not refined in its first beginnings, yet by the judgment and skill of David Mageirus* <note>David Maigret (Mageirus) was a respected 17th-century educator who tutored children of the intellectual elite.</note> *it turned out more polished and more liberal than that which—being freed from slavish obedience and submissive imitation—might introduce one into the variety of things and a truer insight. Since a capable intellect and a tenacious memory supported it, and the use of libraries was added besides, it contributed a massive weight of knowledge rather than a structured form of erudition. However, I gained this benefit from it: that I might look more closely at how much emptiness exists in things, and how much is still unknown. From this, I became free in mind, a sparing admirer of the boasting of others, a slow follower, and a difficult champion, because by Your guidance, my* GOD, *You have happily extricated* <note>original: "expedi-"; the text breaks mid-word at the end of the page.</note> *me from the many errors and entanglements of my path...*

# LETTER CLXXXIX.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,
### My by far most merciful Lords,

Since I currently *have nothing else at hand with which to feed your learned eyes from the great number of pictures of various kinds—intended for your use and honorable pleasure—I have selected these of a smaller size. With these, I might fulfill my duty of writing and simultaneously ensure that my letters do not always convey more words than substance, thus making the task of replying more pleasant and easier for you. If I understand that this is not unpleasing to you, I shall continue with further and further submissions. My household is still under the hands of Aesculapius* <note>The Greek god of medicine; the author means his family is still suffering from illness and under a doctor's care.</note>, *whom I wish were more successful. Hence, everything is hindered for me. But one must rest under the hand* of GOD, *which I pray may be propitious and favoring toward you,* Most Illustrious Princes, *for every kind of growth and glory. Farewell, and continue to favor [me].*

### LETTER CXC.

->Most Illustrious Brothers, Princes and<-
->my by far most merciful Lords,<-

Looking upon this two-faced Janus <note>original: "Iani Bifrontis." Janus was the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking toward the past and the future; he is the namesake of the month of January.</note>, or rather at the boundary between this passing year and the beginning of another, I easily understand how many vows I owe You and pray for; yet I find nothing *new* to pray for You. This may seem strange, but (such is Your good fortune) it is certainly most true. For you so abound in the gifts and goods of heaven and earth alike that an increase in them can scarcely be expected; rather, only their continuation and permanence seem worth wishing for You—which I, as a humble suppliant, pray to God Almighty <note>original: "Deum Opt. Max." (Deo Optimo Maximo), a title meaning "To God, the Best and Greatest."</note> may be confirmed and auspicious for You. 

To explain myself briefly: as long as both your Parents are safe, all things are safe and happy for You—[thanks to] that ruby <note>original: "carbunculo"; a precious red gemstone, here used as a metaphor for spiritual brilliance or a "shining light" of the Church.</note> of the Church, that diamond <note>original: "adamante"; a stone of legendary hardness, symbolizing the unshakable strength of the State.</note> of the Republic, and that union of letters. [And through] that glory of the female sex, the Crown of Your House, and the Example of our age—by which marks (far be it from me to use flattery) I designate your public and private eminence above the rest of mortals. I know indeed that it is a common vice of men not to recognize their present blessings and to judge them unfairly—indeed, even to call those things "bad" which are actually good. This public error was critiqued by the Illustrious Carlo Pasquale <note>original: "Carolus Paschalius" (1547–1625), a French diplomat and scholar known for his work on ethics and statecraft.</note>, a noble Frenchman, in a little book on that subject titled *On Ingratitude* <note>original: "Ingratitudinis."</note>, written with no less eloquence than ingenuity, bringing into the light...

->Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,<-

## LETTER CXCIII.
# To the Princes ANTHONY ULRIC and FERDINAND ALBERT etc. <note>Anthony Ulrich (1633–1714) and Ferdinand Albert I (1636–1687) were the younger sons of Duke August of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Anthony Ulrich would become one of the most significant art patrons and novelists of the Baroque era.</note>
### Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,
### Lords far most clement,

I cannot explain how much pleasure I take from your most delightful letters. For I see both that my services are not unwelcome to you, and that my work—whatever it may be—is most rightly placed. This fills me with incredible joy and raises in me a firm hope that this favor shown to me will not be temporary and wavering, as is often the case, but continuous and eternal. Regarding the paintings, by which I understand you are moved and delighted, I shall send more and more; nor is there any reason you should owe me any thanks, since you receive them through the kindness of your Most Serene Lord Father. <note>Duke August the Younger, who was a close friend and correspondent of the author.</note> This is my sole aim: that since you abound at home in precepts and examples for the cultivation of all virtue and learning, you might perhaps be inspired by this external object and recreation of Art—the Imitator of Nature <note>original: "Naturæ Imitatricis." [...which] I have long expected, for which I owe great thanks to Your Highness <note>original: "Celsitudo Tua"</note>, and I vehemently pray that you do not find it burdensome to continue this exchange hereafter. Your last letters were dated December 1st, to which I replied hurriedly at the very moment of the courier's <note>original: "veredarius"</note> departure; on the following 18th, church duties completely occupied me. Now, at the beginning of this year, I find no theme to choose other than the remembrance of my earthly exile and care for the future. 

My sixty-first year of life is passing, in a very delicate and often afflicted temperament. Moreover, my forty-second year of labors and pains spent for the State <note>original: "Respublica"</note> has been completed; of these, nine were devoted to Literary Education <note>original: "Literaria Institutio"</note>, six to the Ministry <note>the pastoral office</note>, nineteen to the Inspection of the Church <note>his role as Superintendent</note>, and eight to advising the Court and Council. 

The Great Climacteric <note>original: "Magnus Climactericus." In early modern medicine, the 63rd year of life was considered a "climacteric" or a dangerous turning point for health.</note> looms, as fatal and mournful for many as it was easy and lively for your Illustrious Lord Father <note>original: "Dn. Pater"</note> three years ago; when I look upon him and his Herculean labors <note>original: "labores Herculeos"</note>, I am entirely ashamed of myself and my own lethargy. But such strength belongs to few, and is a supreme benefit of Heaven, which I am not angry was denied to me, since I have outlived almost infinite companions of my life. 

Nor do I blame my illness for pinching me and warning of pressing and urgent death; I only grieve this: that I cannot reach that harbor after a wearisome voyage, where I might spend the small amount of days that remain in peace, away from the tumult of affairs, and devote the end of my life to myself—having spent all the rest, both before and now, on others. While I strive with all my might for this discharge <note>original: "rudem." Referring to the wooden sword given to a gladiator upon his retirement from service.</note>, and make no or very little progress, I seem to myself—like Saint Augustine <note>original: "D. Augustinus"</note>, though in a different cause—to struggle with myself, and finally to discover that I am hindered by none other than myself. Truly, these spiderwebs must be broken, not untangled, and one must turn a deaf ear to the whispers of others, when you yourself are conscious of a right purpose.

when I look at the brave deeds of others, who voluntarily laid down crowns, rods of office <note>original: "fasces," the Roman symbol of magisterial power</note>, mitres <note>original: "mitras," the headdress of a bishop</note>, priestly ribbons <note>original: "infulas," used here to represent sacred office</note>, pulpits, and treasures, so that they might reach themselves and a state of rest, I am entirely displeased with myself, who hesitates over so little. <page-num>236</page-num>
# LETTERS
<meta>catchword: LETTER</meta>

...joined [together], we might be able to find leisure for the most pleasant exchange of letters. I wish indeed that, just as it is permitted, or even pleasing, for you to have good hope for the obtaining of Peace, it were not necessary for us to be in a most wretched state while delays and one entanglement <note>original: "tricae," meaning perplexities, tricks, or petty obstacles</note> after another are woven together; I wish you might receive more joyful letters from me from time to time. We, however, are exhausted once again by a doubled whirlpool of forced levies <term>exactionum: heavy war taxes or military demands</term>, and oppressed at once by hostile arms clashing against each other, and exposed as prey to everyone. Consequently, we feel and declare the slow progress of Peace quite differently than you do. Truly, just as the hours and nights are longer for the sick and the sleepless than for the healthy and those who sleep; so the delays and postponements of Peace are counted differently by us than by you. And just as time is worn away with difficulty for prisoners, but easily for those who are free: so for us, among so many chains and shackles, it is spent most sadly indeed. Furthermore, just as many perish under the hand of the Physician, so we must fear lest we should not survive such a bloody cure <note>original: "cruentae curae," a play on words where "curae" can mean both medical treatment and anxieties</note>. You will thus forgive this on account of my fatherland’s calamity—that you receive mournful rather than joyful, and harsh rather than sweet letters—since where there is pain, there its sensation and mourning are usually found.

I should think that you have already received Wagner’s <note>Tobias Wagner (1598–1680), a prominent Lutheran theologian and colleague of Andreae</note> complete work, along with my small tokens <note>original: "strenulis," small gifts or New Year tokens</note>, for which I also recently sent the remaining small pages. I await with trepidation what you will pronounce regarding the publication of our letters, although the indulgence of your Most Serene Father <note>Duke August the Elder</note> could give me great confidence; I would hardly think that you, a flourishing youth, could be more difficult than that most wise old man. However, I would not wish to decide anything against your will, and I hold even your mere dissent as a command—provided that your excessive modesty does not blunt my most sincere desire to spread your fame. Meanwhile, grow, flourish, and fare most happily, and continue to show favor.

Stuttgart, Feb-               To your Illustrious Highness,
ruary 5, 1647.               From your most humble client.

# THE YEAR 1647. LETTER CXCVII.
<meta>catchword: LETTER</meta>

->*Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,*<-

I have read your quite extensive letter of January 15th of this beginning year, in which you indicate the number of letters you previously received from me and urge me to continue this exchange with the same passion. You also mention your health—which I heartily wish to be more steady and firm for you—and since you are now in your *sixty-first* year, what you feel is to be expected from the <term>Great Climacteric</term> <note>original: "Climacterico magno." In early modern medicine and astrology, certain years of life—specifically those involving the numbers 7 and 9—were believed to be critical turning points for health. The 63rd year (7 x 9) was considered the most dangerous of all.</note>. For my part, while I have no intention of refuting those things put forth by the learned and proven by experience regarding this matter, I would not hesitate to assert that it is often believed too superstitiously and observed too fearfully by some. I have the example of my Most Illustrious Lord Parent <note>likely referring to Duke Heinrich Julius of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note> before my eyes; just as God, the Best and Greatest, preserves him for us, the fatherland, and the State, and willed that he cross those boundaries, so He is able to add strength to your old age. He can strengthen those powers for the use of the State and the Church, contrary to the decrees of physicians and philosophers and your own expectations. I do not mind repeating this wish often, because your favor is never weary of blessing my own growth. I ask that you read the letters joined to these, and send the sealed ones to Mr. Doctor Wagner. I greatly pray that you testify to him that the little work with which he presented me, and the honorable preface with which he addressed me, are very pleasing.

Farewell. Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelph." abbreviation for Guelphytum/Wolfenbüttel</note>, February 9, 1647.

*Of Your Reverend Dignity,*

->Most devotedly.<-

## LETTER CXCVIII.

-> Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor, <-

Although I know that my ability to write is quite weak (now that <term>Marconnetto</term> <note>Likely Jean Marconnet, a tutor or secretary at the court of Wolfenbüttel who often assisted with Latin correspondence.</note> is absent), nonetheless, lest I fall under suspicion of ingratitude toward you, I could not fail to send you something of my own on this occasion. Truly, I believe everyone must always strive to testify to a grateful heart. Therefore, I considered it my duty this time to give *thanks*; and I give the greatest thanks, and I shall also repay them sometime (God willing), and make my goodwill toward you manifest. Farewell with these few words, and embrace me with your kindness for as long as you find me to be grateful. *Wolfenbüttel, February 16, 1647.*

## LETTER 200.

->*To the Most Reverend and Most Distinguished*<-
->*Lord Doctor,*<-

Having read your letter, I could not help but be moved by a great sorrow along with you. This is partly because your letter indicated that your region is again being violently shaken and miserably destroyed by those horrendous upheavals <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which was entering its final, brutal stages at this time.</note> by which almost the whole world has trembled for many years. It is also because I learned from your words that you are occupied by most heavy cares, which are scarcely explainable to the human mind. But in truth, because it is given to scarcely any mortal—if indeed to any at all—to restrain that untamed lawlessness, it is necessary that we commit these things to the immortal God, since by His direction all our actions are made prosperous. I ask you, *Most Distinguished Man,* not to afflict yourself too much in the meantime, but rather to see to it that the *Peace to be established between the Princes*, for which the greatest hope now shines upon us, may lead your troubled mind back to tranquility and calmer thoughts. I have duly received *Wagner’s* <note>Likely referring to Tobias Wagner (1598–1680), a prominent Lutheran theologian and friend of Andreae.</note> work along with the remaining pages and your New Year's gifts <note>original: "strenas." These were traditional symbolic gifts or tokens of goodwill exchanged at the start of a year.</note>. As all these things greatly pleased me, I give and hold great thanks to you, as is fitting, and I freely profess that I owe you more as a result. Regarding what should be thought about what is to be published next...

## LETTER 202.

-> Most Illustrious and Exalted Prince, <-
-> My Lord, most gracious by far, <-

Lest I should lack any material to write to You, behold, I HAVE BOUGHT A HOUSE. I remember once reading an elegant piece of wit, published in a former age, with the title: *A Poet Has Bought a House* <note>original: "Poëta domum emit." This refers to a satirical work by the German Humanist Helius Eobanus Hessus, poking fun at the typical poverty of poets.</note>. The theme of the booklet is some poet or other who, when he had purchased his own home, was judged harshly by the "Senate of Poets," as if the act were a *new and terrible precedent*. *Eobanus Hessus* <note>Helius Eobanus Hessus (1488–1540), a famous German Latin poet.</note> was appointed President of the Senate, and seated with him were *Celtis, Hutten, Bebel, Brassicanus*, and others <note>Conrad Celtis, Ulrich von Hutten, Heinrich Bebel, and Johannes Alexander Brassicanus were all celebrated German Humanist scholars and poets of the 15th and 16th centuries.</note>. When they delivered their opinions, there was not a single man among them who—whether by the favor of a Patron or the success of his own talent—had progressed so far as to possess his own house, either by inheritance or purchase; all were negligent of family property, and they both confessed and boasted that they had lived in rented lodgings. Therefore, the poet was ordered to sell the house as soon as possible and contribute the money to a banquet <note>original: "symposium"</note>, so that he might wash away this monstrous fault, and learn to live everywhere and without cares, in the poetic fashion. So much for them.

I, however, being no poet, but one of those who just as rarely possess their own homes, have bought a house for the sake of retirement <note>original: "secessûs gratiâ"</note>, so that I might withdraw myself more and more from human crowds in this my ill health and advancing old age. It is joined with a garden that is not unlovely, so that it might almost be called a "Little Villa"; it is not, to be sure, outside the walls of *Stuttgart*, but in a place removed from the commerce and noise of men. I know well enough that unless the mind within itself is tranquil and composed, no solitude and no desert is sufficient for solid rest; and that it is the mark of a weak man to seek from the outside what you can and ought to obtain from Yourself within. But since external objects, and the in-

social <insert>in</insert>cursions <note>The text continues from the previous page's "S-", completing the word "sincursiones," referring to the social interruptions of city life.</note> steal away much time and disturb the meditations of the mind, it has always pleased even Wise Men <note>original: "Cordatis Viris," literally "men of heart," meaning those with prudence or wisdom.</note> to withdraw to their own Country Villas and to "dwell with themselves." # EPISTLE CCIII.

## Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince, 
## My most gracious Lord,

I received your letter dated the 9th of February—rightly so, but only at the very hour when my own letter of the 26th of the same month was being sent out. Thus, the schedule of the **courier’s** <note>original: "veredarii," a post-rider or messenger.</note> journey amidst our current unrest requires that letters arrive and depart with almost no interval between them, so that it is not possible to respond to them except after a week's time; I thought it not irrelevant to mention this in passing. 

Indeed, regarding the fact that you do *not grant too much importance to the **climacteric years** <term>Climacteric years</term> <note>Historical belief held that certain years in a person's life (multiples of 7 or 9) were "turning points" or dangerous periods for health. The most famous was the "Grand Climacteric" at age 63 (7x9).</note>, you certainly feel as I do. For I do not believe that the "Great Climacteric" hanging over me should be superstitiously observed or feared; I have learned that all years—indeed all months, days, and hours—carry their own fates. Yet, having reached the **sixty-third** year or even beyond, it is more certain than certain that one is not far from the finish line of life. If anyone should surpass that age (which is granted to few), I believe it should be attributed to the will and favor of God rather than to the benefit of Nature or even of one's diet. Therefore, we must value all the more the vivid and vigorous old age of your Most Serene Father; because his health is joined with the progress of the Church and the growth and honor of your House, it should be credited to the happiness of this age—a happiness which may **Christ** <note>The catchword "Christus" from the original page footer.</note> wish to be long-lasting for us.*

*Your letter to Dr. Wagner—a man of much learning—will make him truly happy, since you have deemed him worthy of it and approved of his zeal and affection; for he already burns with a love for your virtue and learning, which is quite rare in this order of men. I am laboring to refurbish my **Selenianum** <note>The author's house, named "Seleniani" after the Duke’s pseudonym, "Gustavus Selenus."</note>, into which I have brought your portraits, both as the greatest ornament of the building and the delight of my leisure. Although the house is narrow, it will surely be **August** <note>original: "Augusta." A pun on the Duke’s name, Augustus; the word also means "majestic" or "grand."</note> to me because of your name and your gift.*

<summary>The author discusses the logistics of their correspondence during wartime and reflects on aging, dismissing the superstition of "climacteric years" while acknowledging his own mortality at sixty-three. He also expresses joy in decorating his new home, the Selenianum, with portraits of the Duke’s family.</summary>

### EPISTLE CCIV.

## Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
## My most gracious Lord,

Indeed, I truly find no other gratitude of Yours that I might desire or expect for my very meager **little gifts** <note>original: "munusculis," referring to the books or writings Andreae frequently sent to the Duke.</note>, except for Your **Grace** <note>original: "Gratia." Andreae frequently plays on the double meaning of "Grace" as a theological concept and as the Duke’s formal title.</note> with which You embrace me, or your remarkable favor; unless I value this most highly and prefer it above all other marks of gratitude, I would rightly deserve to be called the most ungrateful of men. On the contrary, this very fact—that You do not disdain those **slight things** <note>original: "levidensia," meaning things of little weight or importance.</note> of mine—binds me to You so much that I can boast not of having given anything, but of having received a great deal, as if I had successfully entrusted a deposit to You, the guardian of noble faith. Indeed, I seem to myself to be resting in the very bosom of Your Grace and Clemency whenever I receive Your **handwritten letter** <note>original: "Cheirographum," a Greek-derived term for a document written in the sender's own hand rather than by a secretary.</note>, than which no other guarantor could be more certain. Allow me, therefore, to remain **in Your debt** <term>in ære Tuo</term> <note>Literally "in your bronze/money," a Latin idiom for owing someone a debt of gratitude or service.</note> for a while, until Christ—whom I earnestly implore—pays it back; may He grant You such grace that, with the increase of Your years and fortunes, You may excel in grace before God and men. Farewell, most noble Prince, and look with favor upon

->Your Illustrious Highness<-

Stuttgart, March 12,
1647.

->Your most humble client.<-

# Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
## My most gracious Lord,

Although I do not wish to overwhelm You with my letters, yet since I have abstained from writing for eight days, I have taken care to devote myself to this task, lest my own service and duty be overtaken by Your own inclination and readiness toward me. I write, therefore, and just as **a craftsman handles his tools** <note>original: "fabrilia fabri," a Latin idiom meaning one should stick to what they know or do best; here, Andreae refers to his ongoing work on his estate.</note>, so while I am entirely occupied in improving my <term>Selenianum</term> <note>The "Selenianum" was Andreae’s study or garden house in Stuttgart, named in honor of Duke Augustus, whose scholarly pseudonym was "Gustavus Selenus."</note>, I have seen fit to share some small account of it with You, from which You may form a judgment of my plan and purpose. Perhaps there will come a time when a freer breeze shall send You forth to survey foreign shores and bring You to us as well, when You shall brighten this retreat of mine with Your presence and see the monuments of my gratitude in person; hardly anything could happen to me that would be more desirable or more honorable.

But to my great sorrow, the not ignoble painter **Iohannes Altermann** <note>Johann Altermann (1591–1647) was a court painter in Stuttgart and a close associate of Andreae.</note> was recently <insert>[ March 9 ]</insert> taken by death. He was my contemporary and a close friend for thirty years; as I had made frequent use of his services, I had intended for him to decorate the <term>Selenianum</term>, because he excelled in the art and judgment which he had refined in Italy for twelve years, and he lived in a house adjacent to the <term>Selenianum</term>. Thus I see myself more and more deserted by the companions of my life; as fewer of them remain to me—and they are indeed very few—their absence makes me more longing, and I am repeatedly warned to **pack my bags** <note>original: "vasa ut colligam," literally "to collect my vessels," a military idiom for breaking camp, used here as a metaphor for preparing for death.</note>, so that I may lay down these human turmoils myself, before and rather than being thrust out and cast out from them. 

But I do not wish to make You sad with these unpleasant matters, for whom a joyful age now promises long years and an abundant harvest of the same. May Christ grant this happily, and may He preserve and keep You, Most High Prince, along with Your renowned brothers. Farewell and look with favor upon

Stuttgart, March 19, 1647. Your Illustrious Highness’s most humble client,

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My most merciful Lord,

*ALTHOUGH I would not wish to weary You with my letters, yet since I have abstained from writing for these past eight days, I have taken care to pursue this task lest, by Your own kindness and readiness toward me, You might anticipate my own service and duty. I write, therefore, and just as "the smith is occupied with his smithing," so while I am entirely devoted to the cultivation of my* Selenianum <note>The name Andreae gave to his study, derived from "Selenus," the scholarly pseudonym of Duke Augustus.</note>*, I have seen fit to share a certain tablet* <note>original: "tabellam." This likely refers to the text of the inscription found on the preceding page.</note> *of that matter with You, from which You may form an idea of my plan and purpose. It will happen, perhaps, when a freer air allows You to travel and survey foreign shores, that it may also bring You to us; then You shall illuminate this retreat of mine with Your presence, and behold the monuments of my gratitude in person. Scarcely anything could happen to me that would be more desirable or more honorable.* 

*Yet, to my great sorrow, I recently lost* [March 9th] *the death of* Johannes Altermann, *a painter of no small reputation. He was my contemporary and a very close friend for thirty years; just as I made frequent use of him in the past, so I had intended him for the decoration of the* Selenianum, *because he possessed great skill and judgment which he had polished in* Italy *over the course of twelve years, and he lived in a house adjacent to the* Selenianum. *Thus, I see myself more and more deserted by the companions of my life. As fewer of them remain for me—and they are very few indeed—their absence makes me long for them all the more, and I am reminded thereafter to pack my bags* <note>original: "vasa ut colligam." A classical military idiom for breaking camp, used here as a metaphor for preparing for death.</note> *so that I might lay aside these human turmoils myself, before and rather than being driven out and cast out from them. But I do not wish to make You sad with these unpleasant things, since Your joyful age promises many long years and a rich harvest of the same. May* Christ *favorably grant this, and may He protect and preserve You, Most High Prince, along with Your* Illustrious *brothers. Farewell, and look kindly upon me.*

Stuttgart, 19 March 1647.
Your Illustrious Highness’s most humble Client,

### EPISTLE 206.

->To the very Reverend and most<-
->Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

I have received the sketch of the Selenianum <note>The private study of Johann Valentin Andreae, named in honor of his patron Duke Augustus, who used the pseudonym "Selenus."</note>, a sight that is not at all unpleasant, together with your letters which breathe the honeyed joy of a solitary life. I readily give you my support <note>original: "calculum meum addo," literally "I add my pebble," a classical expression for casting a vote of agreement.</note> in this matter, and I judge that man to be altogether happy who, far from the waves of tumultuous fortune, lingers and passes away amidst those harmless delights of life. Many more examples of this same sentiment could be produced if I were permitted to unroll the volumes of history.

To offer at least one or two: it is well known that his retreat at Mytilene <note>A city on the island of Lesbos where Marcus Agrippa, the general and friend of Augustus Caesar, withdrew during a period of political tension.</note> was ultimately far more welcome to *Agrippa* than the fickle <note>original: "lubricae," meaning slippery or unstable.</note> cheers of the common people. *Maecenas* <note>Gaius Maecenas, the famous Roman patron of the arts, known for preferring the quiet life of a knight to higher political office.</note> even more deeply loved a "foreign" leisure <note>original: "peregrinum... otium," referring to a lifestyle of quiet seclusion that felt alien to the bustle of the city.</note> within the city itself than the dusty glory of war. Surely, once labors are exhausted, private rest is as safe as it is most pleasant—and a most certain sign of divine grace, if ever there was one. *Annaeus Seneca* <note>The Stoic philosopher and advisor to Emperor Nero.</note> would have held onto the breath of his aged body much longer if he had not displayed to the eyes of envy those palaces whose brilliance dazzled him, but instead had loved his villas and that leisure—which he turned to only late in life—remaining secluded and unaccompanied for the sake of his private studies.

Certainly the poets—who are generally removed from the noise of business <note>original: "negotiorū," referring to public affairs and legal or commercial work.</note>—do not seem to stray from the truth in this: they choose for themselves some pleasant retreat where they can more freely converse with their Gods and Muses, and they love to rise above the common lot of the masses in the quality of their homes. For they are not ignorant that just as an open and free track <note>original: "circus," the arena for horse racing.</note> invites a horse to the race, so it calls the mind to lofty studies and to conversation, and being free <note>original: "vacans," meaning unoccupied or available for a specific purpose.</note> [for the gods]...

...and is driven by a free breeze. According to the Poets, bodily pleasures are brief and cheap, and they merely make a noise within marble buildings; but those pleasures are purer which we are accustomed to call the delights of the soul, and which have a sweet connection with those eternal things that make us blessed. These are accustomed to inhabit the holy library <note>original: "Musæum," referring here not to a public building but a private place of study dedicated to the Muses.</note>, the pious Tusculum <note>A reference to the Roman statesman Cicero's famous villa at Tusculum, a symbol of intellectual retirement and philosophical labor.</note>, and such a retreat as your *Selenianum* represents. ### LETTER CCIX.

### Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
### Most Merciful Lord,

Since *at this time the* Sacred History of the Passion of Christ <note>The account of Jesus's suffering and crucifixion, typically studied intensely during the Lenten season leading up to Easter.</note> *comes to be explained by me as part of my official duty, I, with my whole mind fixed upon it, gladly shut out all other thoughts, so that I may more freely devote myself to a matter of such great importance. ### LETTER CCXI.

#### To the Very Reverend and Most 
#### Renowned Lord Doctor,

I received with a joyful countenance your three letters sent to me not long ago. It will therefore be my duty, this opportunity having been offered, to respond briefly to them. Your *Selenian work* <note>likely referring to a book dedicated to Duke August or produced under his patronage</note>, which you write you are now entirely devoted to refining, is highly approved by me. Indeed, I can gather from it, as if from an oracle <note>original: "tanquam ex tripode" — literally "as if from a tripod," referring to the seat of the Delphic Oracle; meaning a statement of absolute certainty</note>, your singular desire to celebrate our name and commend it to posterity. Furthermore, nothing can be more pleasant than that work, not only in these *miserable and mournful times* <note>A likely reference to the final years of the Thirty Years' War, which devastated Germany</note>, but also in *tranquil and hoped-for ones*. This is especially true for your weary soul, which now seeks rest from great occupations, and for the scholar, who always brings forth something from himself that delights others. 

Truly, if a somewhat more merciful breeze should blow upon me, and one more favorable for traveling through foreign regions—than which nothing more desirable can happen to me—I assure you that I will not pass by you or this "monument" <note>In this context, "monumentum" refers to a lasting literary or scholarly achievement</note> of yours. For I do not know how prone it is for Princes to indulge too much in their own character, by which they are easily led on by the submissive ministers of their will, so that they do not realize how far they stray from the right path. For you may see Princes who, while they wish to be magnificent, are excessively pompous; they exhaust their estates either with insane buildings, or stage plays, or **Apician luxury** <note>original: *luxu Apiciano*; a reference to Marcus Gavius Apicius, a famous Roman gourmet, implying gluttony and wasteful extravagance</note>, being pleasing to craftsmen, actors, builders, and gluttons, but burdensome to their own subjects.

On the other hand, there are those to whom all learning seems base, as if unworthy of their high rank; yet they lower themselves to the most trivial things, or hide away at home to **catch flies** <note>A classical allusion to the Emperor Domitian, who was said to spend his time alone stabbing flies with a sharp pen</note>, or—lest they should have to blush among those skilled in affairs—they converse only with the uncivilized. Next to these are those who, with affected pride, refuse to speak with the best men and the ornaments of their land, [of their...]

*...they despise counsel, disdain outstanding works, belittle incomparable merits, and embezzle the wages due for loyalty and zeal. Meanwhile, among handmaids, camp-followers, mule-drivers, and such dregs of society, these Princes are companions—easygoing, generous, bounteous, pliable, and even submissive; indeed, they are subject to their every nod, to the great groaning and burden of those among their subjects who are wise. Add to this those who are driven by an immoderate passion for hunting, and under its influence take on a wild nature; they are seen more often in the dens of beasts than in the choir or the forum. They are more blessed in the company of a mastiff* <note>original: *cane molosso*; a large, ancient breed of dog used for hunting and guarding</note> *than in that of the most distinguished citizen, the wisest senator, the most devout priest, or the bravest knight. They are happier with a hunting spear than with a code of laws, and more eager for the barking of dogs than for the most exquisite musical harmonies—not without disgrace to their own greatness.*

*I do not wish to bring forward more types of **blemishes*** <note>original: *nævorum*; literally "moles," continuing the metaphor of minor but distracting character flaws from the previous page</note>*, lest I seem to be attacking rather than grieving for the fate of Princes, to which they lower themselves once the rectitude of **Virtue** has been abandoned. Rather, I would wish this to be clear to you, most happy **Prince**, under what a fortunate star you were born—you who see nothing of the sort in your own home, but rather possess all the opposites in the mirror of your father, set forth for your imitation. Namely: **Magnificence** without wastefulness and vanity; **Knowledge** without the investigation of forbidden things; **Affability** without any loss of dignity; **Esteem** for every instance of virtue and duty, with no sacrifice of status; and methods of physical exercise in no way joined with the torment and harassment of the people.*

*O happy are you if you take note of these things! O most excellent and auspicious will you one day be for your people if you keep to this same path of **moderation*** <note>original: *mediocritatis*; referring to the "Golden Mean," the Aristotelian virtue of finding the balance between extremes</note>*, and if you abstain not only from those outrages which everyone rightly abhors, but also from these stains which sometimes tend to pursue even praised men, diminishing the love of their own people and the respect of others. I explain these things the more confidently to you, a Prince of noble mind, because by your character and already...*

Indeed, I promise you that, as far as I can achieve through counsel, diligence, and effort, I will labor so earnestly that—once the veils of *Vices* have been uncovered and cast aside—I may devote myself to solid and true *Virtue*. Furthermore, since we can only truly call that man a "Great Prince" who has acquired *prudence* both from literature and from practical experience, and who neither casts aside the study of the finest *Arts*—as these teach one to rule a people with the most just and equitable authority—nor rejects the counsel of the wisest *Men* (for no mortal mind has ever seen *everything*), I consider this to be my duty. Above all, because in this matter my *Most Serene Lord Father* <note>Duke August the Younger (1579–1666), known for his immense library and scholarship</note> is a total example and source of admiration to me; although he is occupied much of the time with managing the greatest affairs of state, he never departs from his scholarly studies, nor does he push wise men away from him. Instead, he diligently investigates their advice, listens to it eagerly, and follows it carefully. Therefore, I would have you be entirely persuaded that while the opportunity remains and "my knees are still green" <note>original: "virent genua"; a classical idiom meaning "while one is still in the bloom of youth and vigor"</note>, I shall exercise myself especially in those arts by which true glory is obtained; thus, with the Holy Spirit as my guide, I shall preserve a good hope before both God and men for the age to come. With these words, I wish that you may live well and thrive. *Wolfenbüttel*, June 22, 1647.

### Most Illustrious and High Prince,
->Most merciful Lord,<-

I have already sent four letters of mine, which are either in your hands or will be shortly, and I await your responses with confidence in your kindness. Meanwhile, lest I seem an annoying pursuer of them, I thought I should pause until the demands of your studies allow for some reply. Indeed, my subject matter is nothing if not mournful, arising from the sad condition of my homeland, which is a perpetual plaything and spoil of <term>Bellona</term> <note>The Roman goddess of war, often used in this period to personify the Thirty Years' War</note>, so exposed to opposing factions that we are rightly called "Neutral-passives." <note>original: "Neutro-passivi"; a grammatical pun suggesting they are both neutral in the conflict and passive victims of it.</note> That <term>German-French</term> turmoil <note>Refers to the final phase of the Thirty Years' War where France was the primary adversary of the Holy Roman Empire on German soil</note> has not yet ceased its rage; it reaches from the borders into our interior, and unless God prevents it, it will fix the seat of a most deadly plague in our very vitals. Meanwhile, the delays of peace utterly extinguish that hope for better things—which I know not how rashly we conceived—while they add a ferocity more unrestrained than ever to those who occupy our land, so that we almost succumb under a double burden. 

On a private level, these obstacles distress me, for they keep my desired discharge and my retreat to the <term>Selenianum</term> <note>Refers to the court or library of Duke August the Younger, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus." A "Selenic" retreat implies a return to his scholarly service or the safety of the Duke's territory.</note> in suspense, as these things must stand or fall with the coming of Peace. For who does not see what kind of rest we can expect on the very stage of this tragedy? Truly, the weakness of my body (which would otherwise be my one desire) does not allow me to emigrate. Therefore, shut in by these evils, our only refuge remains the help of God. Though He has been called upon so often, He has nonetheless sustained us through the intervals of a Peace—alas, too deceptive—and the stings of renewed fury. Thus we have survived the **Gowned Impiety** <note>original: "Togatae Impietati"; likely referring to corruption among civilian officials or the clergy</note>, the **Armed Pride**, the **Biting Poverty**, the **Neighboring Audacity**, and the **Domestic Madness** by which we are being torn; so that these lashes are not arguments [of His wrath]...

<header>THE YEAR 1647. LETTER 218.</header>

## Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My Most Merciful Lord,

What I took upon myself eight days ago—to respond with a freer mind to Your letter dated the 22nd of last June—I believe must now be fulfilled. I do so with a style and weight of matter that are, however, far inferior to yours. For with what refinements of speech <note>original: "Verborum lenociniis"</note>, what noble purpose of soul, and what pious reverence for the Divine Power have you bound our faith to you! How could my struggling pen ever explain that Racecourse of Virtue <note>original: "Stadium Virtutis"; a classical metaphor comparing a moral life to a race run in a stadium</note> which you have entered, and which you intend to complete with such arduous zeal and great effort? 

You understand, moreover, how great a burden rests upon you. You were not only born a Prince <note>original: <term>Princeps</term>—meaning a first citizen or sovereign ruler</note>, but were born of that Prince who, among all the Great Men of his time, holds the leadership in every kind of Virtue. Since you are not so much his heir as his destined Successor, you know that all of this must be sustained and carried forward by you. 

Yet, how rare is the continuation and growth of fame and virtue through a lineage <note>original: "in traduce"</note>, and how frequent is its fading or decline, is only too well known from History and Genealogies. There, in a long series of descendants, one may often find only a few who are energetic in the foundation of their State, wise in its constitution, prudent in its institutions, fortunate in its growth, and helpful in its preservation. Instead, one finds many more who are idle, inglorious, harmful, and destroyers of the commonwealth <note>original: "publicæ rei"</note> in every rank. Therefore, those good men who happen to us by Divine gift—such as we expect you to be—are to be held in high esteem. 

For this so great and mighty a blessing does not sufficiently depend upon even the best of Parents, nor the most correct education, nor exquisite Instruction, nor suitable tools, nor a perfect Model <note>original: "Archetypo"</note>; rather, it is from the hand of GOD that peace of mind, rectitude of heart, and industry of soul are made.

<sig>M</sig>

<summary>In this letter, the writer encourages a young prince to uphold the high moral and administrative standards set by his father, reflecting on how rarely virtue is maintained across generations. He emphasizes that true leadership qualities are a gift from God rather than a simple result of education or heritage.</summary>

May these make you **Great** one day—but without the burning of lands or the swallowing up of men <note>Andreae writes this during the final years of the Thirty Years' War; he expresses the hope that the Prince will be "Great" through wisdom and peace rather than the destructive conquest associated with figures like Alexander the Great</note>.

You are indifferent to other rewards, which nevertheless seek you out of their own accord, following one who does not crave them and does not even look back for them. May **GOD** preserve you, a leader dear to the lands, dear to the Church, and dear to me—an illustrious star of Germany, indeed of all Europe, and a future ornament of renown. Farewell, and look with favor upon

->Your Illustrious Highness,<-

Stuttgart, July 16, 1647.

# Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
# Most Gracious Lord,

While I was considering what I might best write to Your Highness at this time, so that I might anticipate the most longed-for letters I expect from You, a spontaneous but most sorrowful subject presented itself: the death <insert>[on July 13th]</insert> of the noble and uniquely famous man, Philipp Hainhofer <note>Philipp Hainhofer (1578–1647) was a prominent merchant, diplomat, and art collector in Augsburg, famous for creating elaborate "curiosity cabinets" for European princes</note>. This news is most mournful to all good men, and I was struck by it more than can be expressed in words. Yet, lest I lose heart, I thought it better to speak something in honor of a man who was once so dear a friend to me, rather than indulging in the grief contracted from such a great wound.

Indeed, it is not only the man’s virtue—which was truly exceptional—nor his unusual knowledge of manifold things that deserves mention, but rather his incredible love for me and his tireless devotion to my affairs, which continued constantly for over twenty years. I must never allow his memory to perish within me, and there is no place I might more rightly or safely deposit that memory, Most Generous Prince, than in Your own heart. For I believe that, after the court of Philip, Duke of Pomerania (nicknamed "the Good") <note>Philip II, Duke of Pomerania (1573–1618), was Hainhofer's first major patron; Hainhofer created the famous "Pomeranian Cabinet" for him</note>, there is no other court than Your "August" court <note>A play on the name of the recipient, Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and the Latin word *Augusta* (majestic/imperial)</note>—though he served many—which has more surely experienced the man’s loyalty, more precisely employed his practiced industry, more evidently proven his diligence, or enjoyed his service longer.

Therefore, there is little need for me to explain his talents to You, as they have all long been thoroughly known to You. I will, however, entrust to You the story of how I first came to know this man, and how significant his friendship was to me. *Witnesses to this—besides the vast number that perished in the Fire of Calw in 1634 <note>During the Thirty Years' War, the town of Calw was burned by imperial troops; Andreae lost his home, library, and much of his correspondence</note>—are the more than 350 letters that remain as signs of his burning affection. In these letters, his inexhaustible intellectual power, his uncommon skill in seven languages, his knowledge of all the royal courts, and his extensive interaction with the most famous men from every quarter were revealed. They could not fail to delight me wonderfully, while also educating me on many matters that were both useful and, above all, necessary; I gladly profess myself his debtor. But one favor among all of them stands out as far superior, the estimation and memory of which I shall not lay down except with my life, and I wish and command that its proclamation be immortal and sacred to my descendants.*

### LETTER CCXXIII.

->Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord,<-

Although in this shortage of time <note>original: "temporis angustiâ." ## LETTER CCXXIV.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished*<-
->*Lord Doctor,*<-

Your spirit, so full of devotion toward the piously departed Heinhofer <note>original: "Heinhoferam." Referring to Philipp Hainhofer (1578–1647), a famous merchant, diplomat, and art collector from Augsburg who was a close associate of many European princes.</note>, is something I deeply admire. I see that a man has departed whom we would have wished to remain living, and whose life was beneficial to as many good people as possible. But since it is in vain for even the most pious of men to mourn death too much, I will respond to your letters with a few words—as far as my health permits—and attempt to soothe your grief. 

You should know that the passing of this man was quite bitter for me as well, both because I feel you have been robbed of a great and faithful friend by this event, and because I knew him to be most devoted to our family. Furthermore, it does not escape my notice how much loss the death of such distinguished men, who have served the Commonwealth <note>original: "de Republ. benè meritorum." Andreae uses "Republic" in the classical sense of the state or the public good.</note> so well, brings to the common interest. 

However, because he has not entirely perished, but his better part <note>original: "pars melior," a classical term for the immortal soul.</note> has sought the stars, and the fame of a life well-lived will remain on earth forever, it seems that he has not fared poorly. This is especially true in these times, when such great diminishments of the Empire are happening everywhere, so many regions are being shattered, so many once-flourishing towns are now devastated and torn down, and there is almost nothing in the world that could invite a man—especially an elderly one—to desire to live any longer. 

He, however, having escaped all these turmoils, has reached that eternal home of the blessed. Let us therefore congratulate him on this happiness, quietly submitting to the will of God. I wanted to share these thoughts with you, in case the same things that comforted me might also lessen your grief. As for the rest, I thank you for your kind [regard] toward our...

### LETTER CCXXV.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### Most Merciful Lord,

*Although I believe my utmost respect for Your Highness is already abundantly clear to you, I feel I have done nothing—or certainly not enough for my own satisfaction—unless I occasionally prove my devotion to you. ### LETTER CCXXXI.
->To the Very Reverend and Most<-
->Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

I have duly received your brief but welcome letter of the 3rd of 
this month. I believe you have already learned from my 
previous letters why I was unable to reply to yours 
immediately. Do not suspect that I have grown weary 
of your letters; on the contrary, rest assured—as I 
indicated in my earlier correspondence—that they are 
as much more pleasing to me as they are more frequent. 
They bring me great pleasure, and are always new and 
singular signs of your supreme goodwill toward me. 
I ask, therefore, that you continue this practice of 
writing with me, and I shall respond to you as 
often as I am able. I hope now that your wife’s 
illness has subsided and that she has recovered. 
Your arrival here among us will be all the more 
welcome the sooner it happens. Farewell. *Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelph."; an abbreviation for Guelpherbytum, the Latin name for Wolfenbüttel, the Duke's residence.</note>, September 28, 1647.*

### LETTER CCXXXII.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->My most merciful Lord,<-

*I thought I should report this one thing for now: that I have safely received your letters today, which you sent on September 13. I can easily bear the pause in your correspondence, whether it is for the sake of rest or because this kind of letter-writing exercise ought to be for pleasure and recreation rather than a source of trouble and annoyance. The severity of the disease that seized my wife has left behind a lingering weakness, the recovery from which will still require much time. My "torturer" <note>original: "tortor meus"; Andreae frequently used this term to refer to his chronic physical ailments, likely kidney stones or gout.</note> torments me again, more harshly than before, and I see that I am dealing with death’s broker. The ill-omened Stymphalian birds <note>original: "Stymphalides"; in Greek mythology, man-eating birds that Hercules had to drive away. Here, they represent the return of war or political calamity.</note>, which we thought we had driven away, have returned to nest in our inner chambers and lay their foul eggs. The hope for peace was a dream that entered through the golden gate. We are no longer neutral, but the prey of everyone, the material and the stage for every calamity. May God preserve you, deliver us, and increase you with all good things and gifts. Farewell and favor*

*As I reach my sixty-first year <note>Andreae was born in 1586; in 1647, he was indeed 61 years old.</note>, out of breath and seeking rest with my whole soul, I see that I must decline the judgments of five classes of men. Since they differ greatly from my studies and character, they will never testify in my favor, or if they do, it will be against their will. These are: the healthy, the cheerful, the idle, the ambitious, and the indifferent. I do not envy their way of life or their old age, which are always joined with activity; however, I would greatly ask them to listen to and consider my own reasons, which tend rather toward quiet.*

*And of the first class, I have had many among my companions and peers who, because they were of a* **HEALTHY** *body and were nourished and refreshed by food and drink, brought a ready mind to any duty. Exercised by labors during the day, at night...*

<page-num>286</page-num>
<header>LETTERS</header>

*...revived by sleep; for these people, for whom things were always well, the end of their years is passed without weariness, and they reach old age itself vigorous, full of vitality <note>original: "boni succi"; literally "good juices," referring to healthy bodily humors in Galenic medicine</note>, with easy digestion, senses still intact, and fit for their duties—from which, if you were to drive them away, you would kill them. But for me, even from the cradle, my health was most afflicted, so that not even at two years old was I standing on my feet; from this followed a lingering weakness of digestion, a tenderness of the limbs, and a languor of the whole body. From this came perpetual catarrhs <note>an excessive buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</note>, intestinal cramps, diarrhea, skin irritations <note>original: "scabies"; used here as a general term for itchy skin conditions</note>, and an equal intolerance for both cold and heat. From this also came an ineptitude for childhood games, a quick exhaustion from labors, sleeplessness at night, the terrors of dreams, and frequent fevers. Because of this, a dietary regimen was mandated for me which, having accompanied me for all my life afterward, sustained the constitution <note>original: "crasin"; from the Greek krasis, meaning the mixture of humors that forms a person's temperament</note> of my body as best it could, yet it always made human society more difficult for me. It rendered my life as if doubled by sleeplessness continued through night and day; and since languor, rather than alacrity, followed upon my rest, it brought a burdensome counting of the days, and a weariness and flight from conversation itself. I wish those people could understand this one disparity—which ought to call me away to a simple life—those for whom appetite exists instead of nausea; good digestion instead of indigestion; sweet sleep instead of insomnia; and a firm bodily frame instead of a trembling of the limbs. Surely they would not be unwilling to grant a vacation from thankless labors to one whose soul has been trapped too long in such an unfavorable host <note>meaning the physical body</note>.*

*But I must move on to the second group, whom I called the* CHEERFUL, *namely those of a Sanguine temperament <term>Sanguine: one of the four humors, associated with blood; thought to make a person courageous, hopeful, and amorous</term>, for whom pleasure is born from all things; likewise, they have a great facility for living and for social gatherings. To me fell the Phlegmatic temperament <term>Phlegmatic: one of the four humors, associated with phlegm; thought to make a person calm, stoic, or sluggish</term>; therefore, there has been a rare sweetness in my life even from my boyhood, with bitterness prevailing from time to time. ...excluded me from banquets and social circles, made me unsuited for love affairs, and rendered me more morose on festive and solemn days. Hence, while life is too short for pleasure-seekers, and days and nights are burned up alike, and a forgetfulness of time is brought on by continuous holidays: for me, the nights have been long and the slow days drawn out, separated as I am from companionships. More years have been accumulated than I ever would have wished, since a weariness of life <note>original: "vitæ tædium"; a state of existential boredom or depression</note> has often crept in, and I have very often preferred to live among the dead than among the living. Why should I not think myself, at this time, freed from these things of my own accord? For I feel myself more and more alienated from modern <note>original: "novitiis"; literally "novice" or "new-fashioned"</note> customs, and I have been less able to be present at the jokes and dances of my peers. Since I can least of all endure to have society with the trifles and drunken pleasures of those so far beneath me, I gladly leave to them those noisy joys and costly vanities; I ask for myself only a retreat <note>original: "secessum"</note>, where there is no necessity to be a hindrance, a reproach, or a laughing-stock.

Next come the Third group, whom it pleased me to call **THE IDLE**, not because they are plainly sluggish, but because they do nothing with great effort—they are busy-bodies in their very leisure <note>original: "in ipso otio negotiosi"</note>. They follow the same course of life they first entered upon, with an ordinary and accustomed task; they wear away days with months and years in continual, yet not difficult labor, bringing to it nothing of skill or genius, and nothing of care or anxiety. Devoting themselves to trivial things, and growing gray and dying in them, they rotate their lives and always return in a circle. 

I do not know by what spirit <note>original: "genio"</note>—since I have voluntarily imposed more things on myself to be scrutinized and worked upon than was required by my circumstances—I took on harder tasks and things unequal to my shoulders at an early age, due to my narrow means at home <note>original: "rem domi arctam"; likely referring to his family's financial struggles after his father's death</note>, which have burdened me greatly on the journey of my life.
