...I threw shackles upon myself; so that I might guard my time, I felt it necessary to shut myself in. Meanwhile, having wandered through all **Branches of Knowledge** <term>Disciplinas</term>, even entangled in the subtleties of the Critics, and since I thought the foundations of neither Law nor Medicine should be passed over by me, I later launched my ship into the **sea of Histories**. I made use of six or seven languages and roamed through the most well-stocked **Libraries** <term>Bibliothecas</term>—while I myself possessed three thousand volumes of books—tasting every kind of learning, whether Sacred or Profane. Nor was I unskilled in instrumental **Music**, nor in the more refined **Mechanical arts**. No man of steady and accustomed labor would easily believe what an Economy of Time <note>original: "Temporis Oeconomiam"</note> this requires, how much it demands of the Memory, or how it exhausts the lifeblood <note>original: "succum"; literally the sap or vital moisture</note> of a weak body. 

And when, after a nine-year period <term>Novennium</term> of scholastic labor, I had been employed for a six-year period <term>Sexennium</term> in the **Deaconry of the Church**, I occupied myself as if in profound leisure—though to another it might perhaps have been hard work—and poured out most of my **Writings** <term>Scriptionum</term>. Nor did I give less to private instruction from what remained of my spare, or rather, abundant time. From there, promoted to the **Office of Superintendent** <term>Episcopiam; in the Lutheran context, this refers to his high ecclesiastical rank similar to a bishop</term>, I would never have satisfied myself unless, with greatest zeal over a nineteen-year period <term>Novendecennium</term>, I had formed "kind matter" into an "excellent appearance" <note>This likely refers to his administrative and moral reforms in the district of Calw</note>; and when that work had been destroyed by public disaster <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War, specifically the destruction of Calw in 1634</note>, I restored it again, following an example scarcely seen in our lands, and with truly incredible progress. 

Now even while the **Court** holds me, and the **Council** <term>Curia</term>—which through a nine-year period <term>Novennium</term> has been most full of ungrateful cares and empty labors—forty-two years of **Struggles** <term>Agoniarum</term> have been completed. None have been harder or more unpleasant than these last ones; add to this that they are of less value and praise, let alone grace or honor. If these labors do not reach the number of others' tasks and periods, yet in weight, if anyone should weigh them more rightly, they would easily surpass them; and they might finally obtain a release from judges who are not unfair.

But let us look at those who are **MORE AMBITIOUS**, and for whom life has been more restless; those who long ago set this goal for themselves: that by any daring, and with the greatest mental exertion, they might climb to the summits of affairs. From this point, with arduous effort—whether through right or wrong—by ambition, bribery, servile compliance, friendships, and seeking of votes, they forced their way in. They are never to be satisfied unless they hold the pinnacles of power; and if they should reach them even after a hundred years, they think they will be, or have been, happy. 

But for me, from my youthful years, my mind set no long-range goals for my life, nor for honors, nor for wealth; rather, I set very moderate ones. **Peace of mind** <note>original: "tranquillitate animi"</note> and the knowledge of things were preferred by me over all other things. For this reason, I have been in perpetual flight from the **handling of public affairs** <term>Reipublicae tractatio</term>; nevertheless, these duties occurred from time to time of their own accord and, as it were, to one who was reluctant. Years, offices, fortunes, and friendships came to me beyond hope and contrary to expectation, and they did not allow me to hide at home and live with myself <note>A Stoic ideal of self-possession and privacy</note>, which I wanted most of all. Yet they never, or rarely, affected me, and in no way truly seized me so that I did not always desire more and more in my soul to return to myself. 

Let those, therefore, who gladly **walk on stilts** <note>original: "grallis incedunt"; a metaphor for acting with high-and-mighty pretension</note>, and listen to the Trumpeters of fame, and climb the peaks of the battlements, grant that I may descend of my own accord. Let me lay down my own burdens and strip myself of the superfluous before I am cast headlong into the depths, crushed by the load, or thrown out by the ungrateful. 

I am sated with the observation I made quite diligently through various regions of Europe. I am sated with the explored **vanity and emptiness** <note>original: "vanitatis & inanitatis"</note> that inhabits the Academies, Courts, Halls, Sanctuaries, and the inner rooms of the **Human Comedy** <term>humana fabula; the idea that the world is a stage and human life a play</term>. I am sated with the frauds and wickedness of the World, washing over us through infinite forms. I am sated with the restlessness I have endured among so many **tenth waves** <note>original: "decumanos fluctus"; a Roman expression for the largest and most dangerous wave in a storm</note> and the fierce tempests of a tossed ship. Let those who still find pleasure in traversing the vast Ocean permit me to strive at last for the harbor, while they...

Finally, let us turn also to the **SUPINE** <note>original: "SVPINOS"; referring to the negligent, lazy, or indifferent</note>, who are by no means men of no business, but who, in conducting affairs, are touched by no care for a duty rightly performed, held by no anxiety about giving an account, driven by no pricks of conscience, and hindered by no shame for a poor reputation. These are the most pestilential of all men, especially when placed in high positions. My own conscience, however, was never so made of cork or volcanic stone <note>meaning light or unfeeling</note> that I did not prefer my duties to be established according to the best rules and examples. ...foundation of the ministry <note>original: "ministri Basin"; likely continuing from the previous page's discussion of ecclesiastical roles</note>, which is the legitimate calling and the cornerstone of Orthodoxy <term>Orthodoxia: Correct belief and adherence to the established doctrines of the Church</term>. It remains, therefore, that I deal with **FAIRER JUDGES**. They—taking into account my very delicate constitution (or the temperament of my little body), as well as my premature old age, my meager diet, my exhausted memory, and my considerable labor in the Republic of Letters <term>Res literaria: The international community of scholars and intellectual exchange</term> and the Christian cause—may grant me a Discharge <term>Missionem: A formal release from duty or military-style service</term>. I have, moreover, contracted a nausea from the emptiness of the human stage, and my attempts to help the Church <term>Ecclesia</term>, though arduous, have proven fruitless. Therefore, after my forty-third year of continuous service <note>original: "rationis annum," literally a year of accounting or reckoning</note>, they will perhaps be less likely to deny me this discharge if they understand that I do not seek a sluggish leisure or one hidden away from all human society. Truly, I seek a Release <term>Remissionem: A relaxation or lessening of burden</term> from my duties, not a total cessation or cancellation of them. Nor would I wish to fail the Church in counsel, prayer, or work, if such things are useful to her; nor would I be absent in spirit, body, or fortune if my presence were required. ### LETTER 234.
## Most Illustrious and High Prince,
### Lord most merciful by far,

Your ease in receiving my letters and your diligence in sending yours moves me, even after that wordy letter I recently sent, to dare once again to "smear something on the pages" <note>original: "illinire chartis aliquid"; a self-deprecating expression for writing.</note>. Although this may bring nothing of great importance for you to know, I am by no means reluctant to write to such a kind and noble Prince. For in your last letter, dated September 28, you commanded me to write to you confidently, stating that the more frequent the letters, the more pleasing they would be, and the more they would call forth your goodwill. For who would not gladly enjoy this familiarity and incredible courtesy of yours, especially since you do not so much allow your youth to be gently instructed by me, as you yourself wisely teach my old age? As you grow daily toward the highest virtues, whoever is near to you may more easily raise himself from the ground and strive toward higher things. For you, the offspring of the Great <term>Magnatum Soboles: Referring to the children or descendants of high-ranking nobility.</term>, seem to me...

*...conspicuous and sublime Columns, just like those of Antoninus and Trajan in Rome, or Constantine the Great in Byzantium,* <note>The author refers to the famous triumphal columns of Roman Emperors, which were decorated with reliefs of their victories and topped with statues.</note> *where not only your outstanding deeds might be expressed and displayed for posterity, but also that an ascent might be granted to see those things far and wide—and even from a distance—which, creeping on the ground, lie hidden and fail. Hence the Cross of Christ rightly stands whole and towers over both obelisks and crowns, the royal orbs* <note>original: "pomis" - literally "apples," referring to the *Reichsapfel* or Imperial Orb, a symbol of power.</note> *and scepters of Emperors and Kings—if not now more by custom than by pious feeling. Farewell, and favor your most humble client who ascends through you.*

### LETTER 235.

->To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

Due to my health and other obstacles, it has not been possible to respond to your four letters until now; therefore, I ask you again and again to forgive this slowness. However, your letters delivered to me were by far most dear. Indeed, *Varenbüler’s marriage Jubilee* <note>Thomas Varenbüler (1566–1610) was a prominent jurist and diplomat; the "jubilee" likely refers to a celebration of a long-standing marriage or a commemorative anniversary in his family line.</note> and its festivities, by very clearly explaining to me the happiness of that union, have further confirmed my understanding of it. Moreover, a greater admiration of this matter takes hold of me from time to time, as such examples are rarely to be expected, especially in this old age of the world. <note>The "old age of the world" (*mundi senecta*) was a common 17th-century trope suggesting the world was nearing its end and human virtue was declining.</note> Furthermore, the *Verses* of *Erhard Cellius* <note>Erhard Cellius (1546–1606) was a poet and historian at the University of Tübingen.</note> written on this matter filled my soul with the pleasure of a most delightful reading. Since they taught me more than enough what the expectation of most grave men always was concerning my most Serene *Father*, and how the Outcome always overcame that expectation. And they so captured me that, after the example of *Themistocles*, who was stirred by the trophy of *Miltiades*, <note>This refers to a famous anecdote from Plutarch: the young Greek statesman Themistocles was so inspired by the military success of Miltiades at the Battle of Marathon that he said the "trophy of Miltiades would not let him sleep," driving him to seek his own glory.</note> I think of nothing more day and night than how I might even occasionally seem to follow in the footsteps of my most Serene Father. Since, therefore, the *Virtue of Fathers* is also in their descendants, and "fierce Eagles do not produce a weak dove," <note>A paraphrase of Horace (Odes 4.4): *nec imbellem feroces progenerant aquilae columbam*, meaning that noble ancestry typically produces noble offspring.</note> I would wish you to be certain that, aided by God’s help, I will not fail myself. In the meantime, continue to offer prayers for my happy success. Farewell. Given at *Wolfenbüttel*, <note>original: "Guelpherbytum," the Latin name for Wolfenbüttel, the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> 26 October, in the Year 1647.

->*Most Devoted.*<-

# LETTER 236.

->To the Very Reverend and Most<-
->Distinguished Lord Doctor,<-

Your letters, along with your longing for the end of a most desired age, were duly delivered to me. Because they breathed pure love toward my <term>Most Serene</term> <note>A formal title of address for high-ranking royalty or nobility.</note> Lord Father and me, I wished to respond briefly: both to keep you in this duty of correspondence, and to declare my grateful goodwill toward you from time to time. Indeed, those meditations of yours so captivated me that I was compelled to read and re-read them three or four times.

For although I ought to be deservedly saddened—considering that those countless hardships which surrounded you from the very beginning of your life pertain to me in some way—yet, recognizing the wonderful mercy of *divine favor* and your joyful liberation from dangers, I am also compelled to rejoice. For the shifts of Fortune are not indeed desirable when experienced, yet they are usually pleasant when read about. Moreover, they have also taught me, not without reason, the natures and characters of many men, and have placed before my eyes, as it were, what treachery and vanity there is in life. To know the characters of men, however, and to be able to discern true goods from false ones, is not, I think, something just anyone can do.

Furthermore, I marvel at your great constancy amidst such bodily infirmities, your endurance in labors, and your nobility and spirit in despising dangers and vain opinions. For I entirely believe it is granted only to a few, whom <note>original: "æquus amavit Iupiter" (impartial Jupiter has loved); a classical allusion to Virgil’s *Aeneid*, referring to those favored by heaven or nature with exceptional virtue.</note> impartial Jupiter has loved, to cherish the <term>golden mean</term> <note>original: "Auream mediocritatem"; the classical ideal of moderation and balance between extremes, avoiding both excess and deficiency.</note> and to preserve a steady mind in times of trouble. I cherish your favor, certain that nothing can so weigh down **Your** body or occupy your mind that you would not have something left to bestow upon me out of your extraordinary kindness. You even seek to match and increase the heap of your father’s grace; for this I give immense thanks, and in return for such gratitude—since I shall never be able to pay my debt—I dedicate myself as a servant or even a slave to **Your Highness**. Beyond this, I have little to write to **You** at present, for I would not wish **You** to be rubbed the wrong way by either our public or private misfortunes. Since this **Land** bears nothing but the unhappy <term>darnel</term> <note>original: "lolium"; a common weed that mimics wheat, often associated with corruption or bad luck</note> of <term>Bellona</term> <note>The Roman goddess of war; a reference to the ongoing devastation of the Thirty Years' War</note>, it is as unseemly as it is tedious to always send mournful letters. I will, however, report what happened a few days ago, a significant sign of the uncertainty of human fate:

A certain bridegroom, one of the **Foresters**, while returning home from the **Forest** with a <term>gun</term> <note>original: "sclopeto"; an early modern firearm</note>, stopped to visit his **Bride**. Finding her playing with other girls, he set his gun behind the door and joined in their play. Later, remembering the gun was still loaded and ready to fire, and wishing to prevent any harm, he tried to release the cocked hammer. At the same time, in a playful mood, he aimed at his **Bride**, but his finger slipped. The gun discharged many small lead pellets into the **Bride's** face, and in an instant, he most unwillingly killed the poor girl. Terrified, he looked to his own safety by fleeing; it is uncertain whether he joined the military or where he went, for he has not been seen since. But why do I relate these **Tragic** matters to **You**? I would rather pray that you remain safe from every sinister accident. May GOD grant that while you are stirred up to emulate the **greatest Trophies of your Greatest Father**, which are far more noble than those of <term>Miltiades</term> <note>An Athenian general famous for his victory at Marathon; here used as a symbol of military glory</note> and more memorable, and while you strive with every effort to prove yourself a **chick of the Eagle** or a **cub of the Guelph Lion** <note>original: "Aquilæ pullum, vel Guelphici Leonis catulum"; the Eagle refers to the Holy Roman Empire, while the Lion refers to the House of Welf, the Duke's family</note>, we may follow your happy beginnings with favorable applause. As for me, whether I am a **wren** <note>original: "regulus"; literally "little king," but also the name for a wren or goldcrest, continuing the bird imagery</note> lifted up under **Your** wings, or a little puppy safely playing or hiding under your mane, I shall be entirely **Yours**...

## LETTER 239.

### Most Illustrious and Noble Prince,
### My most merciful Lord,

Nothing is more lovely than your letters, by which I am wonderfully refreshed when I see that you are so far from looking down on my concerns—which I pour out so freely into your most noble bosom—that you are affected by the same sense of labors and pains as I am. As I head toward a harbor of breathing-room and rest, you favor me with all your soul; for this reason, I truly cannot find enough words of praise or thanks to owe you. I am as pleased with myself as I understand my vows and desires to be approved by your judgment, and for that reason, I think I must pursue my plan for a more relaxed life with even more eager dedication. Since the sole foundation—indeed, the crowning achievement <term>coronis</term> <note>original: "coronis"; a Greek term used in Latin to mean the finishing touch or completion of a work</note> and highest peak—of this plan rests in Your House alone, and in its head, your most Serene Father, and in you three, the sacred anchors <term>sacris anchoris</term> <note>A classical metaphor referring to the "sacred anchor" or the last and strongest anchor used in a storm; here referring to the Duke and his family as the author's final hope</note> of my hope, what could happen that is more desirable for me who am broken, sweeter for me who am weary, and more effective for soothing a sick soul, than that my struggles and anxieties be valued from your high station? Others hold these struggles in ridicule, and indeed most hold them in neglect. Truly, how much effort and sweat it takes to finally restrain a fortune that has acted like a hostile stepmother <term>novercantem</term> <note>original: "novercantem"; from "noverca" (stepmother), a common Roman metaphor for fate or fortune acting with cruelty or lack of natural affection</note> for so many years; to evade the hidden tunnels of envy; to break the teeth of slander; to keep a steady mind among so many shifting things; and to keep a straight path through so many windings and <term>labyrinths</term>, as few...

He describes the Duke's family as his "sacred anchors" amid the slander and misfortune of the Thirty Years' War era.</summary>

[...it is for few] to grasp and understand; so it is for far fewer to value a thing by its own price and just weight. The more I admire Your judgment, which is so excellent in this age because it discerns such things more sharply, the more I embrace it with my whole soul. From this right sense and fair estimation, I dare to promise myself firm protection and favor <term>favonium</term> <note>original: "favonium"; literally the West Wind, a classical metaphor for a favorable or helpful influence</note> from You for the future. Posterity will sing the glory of this deed, but I will truly return it with constant commendation of my prayers to God, who shall return You to all good men as the Morning Star <term>Phosphorum</term>, the Lighthouse <term>Pharum</term>, and the Harbor <term>Portum</term> after a stormy voyage. Farewell. I pray for every happiness for your most Illustrious brothers with a devoted heart.

### IT IS ENOUGH.
<note>Andreae’s personal motto was "Satis" or "Sufficit" (It is enough), reflecting his desire to withdraw from the vanities of the world.</note>

Whose living image you see in this small painted tablet,
thunders to all earthly things: "Ho there! It is enough!"

->Birth<-

Having followed the known footsteps of my ancestors
with pious religion, in Spirit, Name, and Fate: it is enough!

->Studies of 43 years<-

To have devoted decent work to letters and sacred things,
with voice, pen, and effort, through eight periods of five years <term>lustra</term>: it is enough!

### Travels for 9 years.
To have followed so many clods of earth <note>original: *glebas*; a poetic way of referring to various lands or soils</note>, people, and customs,
And to have grasped so many of their languages—it is enough!

### Labors.
To have experienced the deep Augean stables <note>A reference to the mythical stables cleaned by Hercules; Andreae uses this as a metaphor for the mess of corruption and bureaucracy</note> of both the Court and the Hall,
Which, by the world’s character, shall never pass away—it is enough!

### Struggles.
With Envy always standing in the way everywhere like a stepmother—
To have combined faith with integrity—it is enough!

### Care for the Fatherland for 9 years.
Then to have proven my faith to the Fatherland and the Father <note>Referring to his patron, Duke August</note> for nine years,
Always and everywhere for Christ and those joined to Him—it is enough!

### Marriage for 34 years.
And being under the constant yoke for nearly seven lustra <note>A *lustrum* is a five-year period; seven lustra is 35 years</note>,
To be a father of nine children and a grandfather of fifteen—it is enough!

### Augustan favor, for 7 years.
Yet to borrow from the Augustan light of Selene <note>Andreae punningly refers to his patron Duke August through the Greek moon goddess Selene; the Duke often used lunar imagery</note>
And to derive sap, motion, and rest from it—
->it is enough!<-

### Old Age, at 62 years.
To have already prolonged my life to sixty-two years,
In a body quite thin, but with the honor of my lineage—it is enough!

### Satiety.
Henceforth, desiring retirement <note>original: *rudis*; referring to the wooden sword given to a gladiator upon his honorable discharge</note>, withered and failing in limb,
Now sated with human affairs—alas! it is enough!
Why should I not depart like a guest full of life? <note>A classical reference to the poet Lucretius, who argued one should leave life like a satisfied dinner guest</note>
What was once pleasing now displeases—alas!
->it is enough!<-

And in my weakness—it is enough!
(a) 2 Corinthians 12, verse 9.
Whatever more You give me is too much (b), being bound by my vow on all sides;
(b) Genesis 32, verse 10.
I am no better than my fathers (c)—alas!
(c) 1 Kings 19, verse 4.
it is enough!

<header>THE YEAR 1647. LETTER 240.</header>

# Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
->My most merciful Lord,<-

You have truly blessed me with Your letter, in which You promised to take care of those who are conspicuous by their **Virtue and merits in the Commonwealth** <note>original: *Rempubl.*, an abbreviation of *Respublica*</note>, but above all those of **Piety**. You do this by the example of Your Ancestors, whom You look upon with great praise, and especially by that most perfect Ideal of Your Great Father [Duke August], than which You could do nothing more fitting. From him you should take that zeal for Piety, which is not a phantom manufactured by "Pseudo-politicians" <note>original: *Pseudopoliticis*; a term Andreae uses for cynical, Machiavellian strategists who use religion only for social control</note> to manipulate and fascinate men, but is a celestial flame lit in the depths of the breast, referring all actions and thoughts back to its Author [God]. It proves its faith to Him by no other price than that of **Conscience**, by whom it is always most amply rewarded in turn. Illustrious examples of this are found everywhere, far surpassing the victories, empires, wealth, and other matters of earthly glory of even the most famous men. If You embrace these things in Your mind—as indeed You are doing—and at the same time assure yourself of their faithfulness by the immense gifts which **GOD** has most liberally bestowed upon Your Most Serene Lord Father, You cannot help but promise Yourself all the greatest and most desired outcomes; if not for the applause of the World, then certainly for that which lasts, and which will one day confer the solid glory of the age to come.

Therefore, **Most Illustrious Prince**, I pray from my heart for this perpetual sentiment and purpose for You: namely, that it should never be contaminated by any allurements of earthly delights, by any students of flattery, nor by any "Secrets of **State**" <note>original: *Status arcanis*; Andreae suggests that what politicians call "state secrets" are often just immoral schemes</note>—or more truly, "wickednesses and shames." May He who gave this purpose to You keep it safe and firm, and may He bless this present year, which has flowed gently by, along with a happier next year, indeed with many August... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword suggests the next page continues with a reference to "Augustan" prosperity or the Duke’s lineage.</note>

**Y**ou have truly blessed me with your letters, in which you promised that you would care for those who are *distinguished by virtue and merits in the State,* <note>original: *Respublica*</note> *but most especially those distinguished by Piety.* You promised to do this following the most praiseworthy example of *your ancestors*, whom you look upon, and especially that most perfect *image of your Great Father,* <note>Referring to Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg, a famous scholar-prince and Andreae’s patron</note> than which you could do nothing more fitting. From him, indeed, you may take up that zeal for *Piety*, which is not some sham <note>original: *simulacrum*</note> crafted by *pseudo-politicians* <note>original: *Pseudopoliticis*; Andreae frequently criticized "Machiavellian" politicians who used religion as a tool of statecraft</note> to manipulate and bewitch men, but a *heavenly flame kindled in the depths of the heart*, referring all thoughts and actions back to its Author, and proving its faith to Him by no other *price than that of Conscience*. By Him, it is always repaid most fully in turn; of this, there are illustrious examples everywhere, far surpassing the victories, empires, wealth, and other materials of earthly glory belonging to even the most famous men. If you embrace these things in your mind, as you are doing, and if you take to heart the great gifts which GOD *has most liberally bestowed* upon your *Most Serene Father*, you cannot fail to promise yourself the greatest and most desired outcomes—if not for the applause of the World, then certainly for that which endures, and which will one day confer the solid glory of the age to come. Therefore, *Most Illustrious Prince*, I pray from my heart that this perpetual sentiment and purpose of rectitude remains with you: namely, that it must be contaminated by *no allurements of earthly delights, no disciples of flattery, and no* Secrets of State <note>original: *Arcana Status*; a technical term for the often-unscrupulous tactics used to maintain political power</note> *as they call them—though they are more truly called wickedness and outrages.* May He who gave this spirit to you keep it safe and firm, and may He grant that this present year, which has flowed by gently, be followed by a next year that is happier, and indeed by many more years.

## LETTER 241.

### *To the Very Reverend and Most*
### *Renowned Mister Doctor,*

For several weeks I have received no letters from you, nor did I wish to be a burden with my own. However, regarding yours of the 19th of last November—which were partly *congratulatory* and partly *announcing news*—your kind and constant goodwill toward us advises and moves me to respond briefly at this time. And for the fact that you *congratulate* me on my health, recovered by the grace of God, I give you great thanks. May God, thrice Best and Greatest, <note>original: *DEVS ter Opt. Max.* (Deus Optimus Maximus), a common honorific for God borrowed from Roman descriptions of Jupiter</note> command weight to be in this your prayer, and for the public good, long and mercifully keep both of us safe.

As for the unexpected event <note>original: *casum*; likely referring to a sudden death or local political upheaval</note> which you mention, it places before our eyes the variety of worldly affairs and shows the inconstancy and deceitfulness of *fortune*. It declares that a man is never sufficiently warned of what he should avoid at any hour. Indeed, it teaches that the path of *death* <note>original: *lethi*</note> must be trodden by all, and that nothing in this world is blessed in every respect. Therefore, having disregarded fortune, I judge that one must rely solely on God, because nothing is more inconstant than fortune, while nothing is more merciful than Him. For the rest, know that since the soldiery is miserably plundering our fields, we are experiencing the cruelty of *Bellona* <note>The Roman goddess of war; a common literary metaphor used here to describe the horrors of the Thirty Years' War</note> more than enough—alas!

Therefore, just as I congratulate the Republic of Letters on this addition, so I have no doubt that all the learned—and those who understand the aim of this labor of yours—will be most grateful that, in a brief and no less accurate little book, you have presented to the eyes of readers at a single glance things which had to be drawn from the most voluminous commentaries of various authors, and that by your tireless care and vigils, [you have eased] the labor of others...

### LETTER 245.
#### To your health! <note>original: *Bene Te!*, a common salutation wishing well to the recipient</note>

Reverend Sir, I have received and gladly read your elegant letter—one written not at all in a hurried manner despite the tumults of war—which, according to the laudably received Christian custom, was sent with the auspicious wish for a most happy year. In it, you hope and pray that I might receive growth of mind and body, along with an abundance of all other favorable blessings from that Supreme Giver. I pray for the same for you in return, and indeed even greater things: that God, the Greatest and Best, might grant that not only this year, but countless others to come, may be peaceful and prosperous for you, and that He may wish for you to survive long for the benefit of the Church.

As for what you add—that it was not only memorable but truly admirable that that distinguished Nuremberg <note>original: *Noricum*</note> painter (whom I deservedly honor here with a capital letter) <note>Refers to Albrecht Dürer, the famous German Renaissance artist</note> was able to reach such perfection and excellence in his art even during that desperate and premature <note>original: *abortivo*; implying a time that cut short potential or growth</note> time—it moves me no less. Furthermore, I recall what was told to me not long ago by our most dear Guide of Studies: that the man had a most terrible Xanthippe <note>A reference to the famously difficult wife of the philosopher Socrates; here used to describe Dürer’s wife, Agnes Frey</note> at home, who harassed his divine

*I am not at all surprised that Dürer is held in such high esteem by you, and from this I measure the keenness of your intellect; for I feel that he has progressed furthest in art who can rightly judge the differences and excellence between artists. For this reason, I have designated for you a vigorous depiction of the Passion of Christ by him as a New Year's gift <note>original: "strenuam," referring to a "strena" or traditional New Year's gift</note> for this year, which you either already possess or will receive shortly. It should be valued not by its price, but by its craftsmanship and the pleasure it brings you, which you will abundantly repay with your own brush, as you promised. Regarding his rather ill-tempered wife <note>original: "morosiore ejus Conjuge," referring to Agnes Frey, who was famously (and perhaps unfairly) rumored by Dürer's friend Willibald Pirckheimer to be a shrew</note>, I had heard nothing before this, but I have learned that artists find something lacking in this regard: that in portraying the Virgin Mother with the infant Jesus, he repeatedly depicted his own wife, who was, however, of less elegant form and features, even though in other matters he was most observant of the symmetry of the human body. I myself, however, possessed the opposite, and to my greatest sorrow lost it in the fire at Calw <note>original: "Calvensi busto." The town of Calw was devastated by fire during the Thirty Years' War in 1634</note>: namely, a face of the Mother of God <note>original: "Deiparae"</note>, painted in lifelike colors and the actual size of a human face, than which nothing more elegant, harmonious, or beautiful could be imagined, and which I would wish to redeem at a great cost of my own money. But other things are also held against this extraordinary man, which Nuremberg <note>original: "Noriberga"</note> constantly denies; among these is what Fioravanti <note>Leonardo Fioravanti (1517–1588), an Italian physician whose writings often mixed fact and folklore</note> reports in his memoirs: that he was such a poor household manager that, despite being the creator of so many works, he had to be buried at public expense when he died. However, it has been shown to me by proven documents that he left behind a far from negligible fortune of money and household goods. If indeed a public funeral was decreed for him, the most prudent Senate and people of Nuremberg <note>original: "Senatus populusque Noribergensis"</note> undoubtedly intended it as a reward for his virtue rather than a mark of infamy. That indeed*

## L E T T E R CCXLVII.

*You do rightly to write, most Distinguished Sir, that you will testify a little later concerning your great grief over the death of the most blessed* Saubertus <note>original: "Sauberti," referring to the Nuremberg theologian Johann Saubert the Elder, who died in 1646</note>, *when the soul has first been thoroughly torn by sorrow, so that tears, a path having been made through the eyes, may flow more abundantly. For just as in a body struck by whips, a bruise does not appear immediately, but after a small delay; so in the soul, struck by some sad news, tears do not fall unless it has been thoroughly bruised and softened by the frequent repetition of pain. Regarding the copper plate of the often-mentioned* Eustachius, *once held in great value by Emperor* RUDOLPH II, *I have no doubt [it is remarkable], since it was not the least of his praises that [he valued] the works of more distinguished artists, clocks* <note>original: "Horologia"</note>...

### THE YEAR 1647.
## LETTER CCXLIX.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord far most merciful,<-

That I spoke with you so briefly regarding the death of my dear Saubert <note>Johannes Saubert the Elder (1592–1646), a prominent Lutheran theologian and librarian in Nuremberg</note> was not due to any lack of endurance for the grief I felt, nor to a particular sensitivity of my soul. Rather, it was because I owed much to the man’s merits—both by right and by our personal agreement—duties which have now been fulfilled according to the meager measure of my talent and submitted to the most refined judgment of your Serene Lord Father. 

Indeed, it is not fitting for us Christians to be so carried away by any grief that we are rendered useless for performing our duty, since duty itself is the most effective medicine for sorrows. Let us truly understand the loss the Church <term>Ecclesia</term> has suffered from the removal of such a great pillar, but let us all the more stoutly repair and support her with whatever strength we have. 

I truly owe you very great thanks, for already at your age you are moved by the successes and setbacks of the Church, and at the same time, you wished to testify how much you valued Saubert for his proven loyalty. May Christ preserve this spirit in you, and grant that soon—after this apprenticeship you are now serving—you may preside over the Church from a more eminent position. May you adorn, help, and protect her, not so much by title and splendor as by piety, counsel, and talent, following the rare example of George, the star of your Ascanian House <note>original: "Gentis Tuæ Ascaniæ sideris Georgi." Likely referring to George III, Prince of Anhalt-Dessau (1507–1553), known for his Reformation piety</note>. This is what I clearly foresee. 

For the many evils we have suffered in this cruel storm <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)</note> must be considered the punishment for our ingratitude and our tyranny against the restored Gospel <note>original: "restitutum Evangelium," referring to the Protestant Reformation</note>. We have turned care for it into luxury, its protection into domination, and its nourishment into a snare. Unless we reform these habits into serious oversight, faithful defense, and generous support, we seek the restoration of Peace and Sacred goods only to our own harm and the loss of the Church.

Looking around at the fortune of all good men, Most Distinguished Sir, we find no one who has not experienced detractors of a good reputation—those who, with a certain headlong license for judging, are accustomed to smear more famous men with things that are not so much shameful as they are false. ## LETTER 255.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My most merciful Lord,

There is no need to repeat the sincere blessings I have offered for you and your elevated dignity, as it is better for my prayers to keep watch before God for your well-being—prayers which, proceeding from a pious soul, can never be in vain. For this reason, I would not wish to appear to you as a *useless servant, worn out by old age and ill health, since the raised hands of Moses fought far more successfully than the sword of Joshua, and brought destruction upon the enemy.* <note>A reference to Exodus 17:11, where the Israelites succeeded in battle only as long as Moses held up his hands in prayer, symbolizing that spiritual support is more powerful than military force.</note> Permit me, therefore, in this "Selenian" <note>original: "Seleniano." This refers to the court or intellectual circle of Duke August of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who used the pen name "Gustavus Selenus."</note> circle of mine, to be counted as one of your own, and to join those who strive with their whole heart for your safety, your reputation, and your every advancement. *For even though you are already preparing yourself with a noble spirit for every excellence and great undertaking, you will nevertheless not despise faithful advisors, lest you ever turn to the right or the left in the slipperiness of human life. In this pious duty, I shall certainly not fail you; for although you are surrounded by the rules and instructions of your governors and tutors, and you see before you the most exact example of virtue, nonetheless—just as things brought from abroad affect us more than those grown at home, and as "mute masters" <term>mute masters: original "muti Magistri," a traditional term for books or letters, which can offer blunt or honest correction without the social pressure of a face-to-face conversation</term> correct us more freely than talkative ones—so I believe that what comes from my heart and my hand, guided by some favorable star, will be neither unwelcome nor useless to you. I pray as a suppliant that Christ may bless these words. May He direct all your affairs for the use of His Church and the honor of your House. Farewell and look with favor upon*

->*Your Illustrious Highness*<-

*Stuttgart,* 16 April,
1647.

->*Your most humble servant.*<-

# Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
## My most merciful Lord,

Since at this time there was no official occasion to congratulate your renowned brothers on their birthdays, I nevertheless did not wish to pass you by, for I am greatly delighted by your most fortunate talent <note>original: "Genio." ### LETTER CCLVII.

->*Greetings and the most happy of prospects!*<-

I am glad, *most illustrious Sir*, that my intention in clearing the reputation of others meets with your approval, the more so because I well know that I wished to come to the aid not of an unworthy man, but of an extraordinary one, who deservedly draws to himself the admiration, fame, and love of all, even after death. However, I began to doubt whether I had satisfied my duty in every respect, or if I had omitted anything that could silence venomous tongues; but now, relying on you, I no longer fear greatly. I would wish that I could have sent a copy of the mentioned *Epitaph* <note>original: "Epitaphii." A funeral oration or inscription for a tomb.</note> now, but I myself have not yet seen it; however, as far as I perceive from the accounts of others, it so clearly proves the man's integrity and diligence in all things—and even in his private affairs—as it truly says that most artistic hands <note>This likely refers to a scholar or an artist known for his technical skill or fine handwriting.</note> are buried beneath that tombstone.

## LETTER CCLVIII.
### *Everlasting happiness!*

Through your letters, you testify in the most generous words how much I am on your mind, and I do not doubt that you always hold me in such regard. Indeed, I shall accept with honest confidence your promise to be not the least among my mentors—you who, having already passed through the darkness of other ages, see with the greatest clarity in the bright midday of wisdom. You see by what good principles of life young and tender minds must yet be cultivated, so that a bountiful reward of virtues may be expected from them.

Our age, however, is on slippery ground, and can easily be pushed here or there, unless the inner impulses are held back by labor, study, and prayer. ## LETTER CCLIX.

->Many greetings!<-

### THE YEAR 1647.

& and of your benevolence. The loss to the Church in the sudden death of your most blessed father-in-law <note>original: "Soceri Tui". This likely refers to Johannes Saubert the Elder, mentioned on the previous page, whose daughter married the recipient.</note> moved you to set his most longed-for *Shadow* <note>original: "Umbram". In this context, it refers to a "shade" or a posthumous portrait/literary memorial that keeps the memory of the deceased alive.</note> before our eyes. But do not labor in grief; there will be gain in that loss. This work of yours will ensure that he, of all people, meets us most frequently in spirit. Others may have a path that they follow with anxious feet even after his death, so that the memory of your bond may be passed down to posterity, and that not only our contemporaries but also future ages may understand that you lived as friends.

Therefore, this devotion of yours will mend whatever damage was inflicted by his sudden passing: and, as I hope, this plan will delight you more every day. In former times, trophies were erected for courageous warriors and defenders of the public safety, made either from tree trunks, or bronze, stone, or the spoils of conquered peoples. Today, however, the permanence of literature and the genius of great men better befit men of great learning and the guardians of Christian piety. Indeed, we can never honor such men with a sufficiently worthy kind of praise. Since you are most prolific in these matters, *praised man*, you have deservedly wished to lend your effort and devotion to our piously departed friend. For that is truly a pleasant praise which proceeds from those who have themselves lived laudably.

Farewell, and accept my greatest thanks for the sharing of the copies <note>original: "Exemplarium". Likely printed copies of the memorial work or poem.</note> and for the dedication of the poem, along with your beloved son.

*Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti". The Latin name for the city in Lower Saxony, famous for its Ducal library.</note>, June 22, 1647.*

# LETTER 262.

->*May you enjoy prosperous happiness!*<-

Since you firmly persist in your purpose of writing, *Most Distinguished Man*, and faithfully keep your promised word, I cannot in turn fail to communicate with you more frequently through this *exchange of letters* <term>commercia literarum: a standard Latin phrase for the "Republic of Letters," the network of scholarly correspondence that linked European intellectuals</term>, even though the quite vast distances between our locations still prevent us from joining in conversation and hearing and returning familiar voices. I believe, however, that you have long since been informed by the evidence of rumor regarding those matters which were pleasant for *You* to hear in my recent letters, and for which you have again congratulated me from your heart. In this, I could not doubt that I stood most beautifully in the estimation of those fit and heroic *Geniuses* <term>Ingeniorum: refers here to both the innate talent and the great men who possess it</term> who so faithfully support my opinion that I see myself most obligated to devote my zeal and effort to the common good.

That *superior and more refined intellects* are transferred from nation to nation, according to the fated and customary *revolution of things* <note>The author is referring to the "translatio studii," the historical theory that the center of learning and culture migrates westward over time.</note>, is not something we should wonder at. Behold for yourself *Protogenes*, *Nicias*, *Parrhasium*, and *Apelles* <note>These were the most celebrated painters of Ancient Greece, famous for their extreme realism.</note>, and others who once reached such excellence and glory in the Eastern regions that—to the wonder of *Nature* itself—their *paintings* <term>pictura</term> deceived horses, dogs, and birds, or expressed the very passions of the soul through colors. Their works were not valued in mere coins but were bought in competition for talents <note>A "talent" was a massive unit of currency in antiquity, implying the works were priceless.</note>. Yet now, people are found there who are so ignorant of these matters that they can hardly distinguish colors and deserve to be called "mess-makers" rather than artists. ### LETTER 264.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**My Lord, by far the most merciful,**<-

From this, I conceive the hope that there will be no lack of more stout-hearted patrons for the Christian cause struggling in Saubert, nor of more fair-minded judges for my lamentation poured out at his funeral—however much the crowd of ill-tempered idlers may snarl and grumble.

For I proposed to commend Saubert—that extraordinary instrument of God—not only for his excellent character, distinguished erudition, singular dexterity, and orderly habits, nor even only for his exceptional wisdom, rare prudence, and devoted piety (within the scope of which three virtues all others are contained). I also intended to explain the struggles that were nearly fatal to him and to expose the stubborn callousness of the World. In doing so, I easily foresaw that Envy was prepared for us both: for him, the deceased, if I were to rub open scars that had somewhat healed; and for myself, the survivor, if I revealed myself as an ally of a hated cause. For since all others of a noble character...

*...more robust* <note>original: *fiores*, likely a continuation of *habitiores* or *fortiores* from the previous page</note> *acts, and the ready applause that follows, the World willingly bears, and it confers rewards upon them; yet it bears most impatiently this one bold act of Reproof and correction, and receives it in unworthy ways. Today,* **Johann Schmidt** <note>original: *Iohannes Schmidius* (1594–1658), a theologian and professor at Strasbourg.</note> *remains, a vigorous Athlete, but sweating and panting under the burden. To each and every one of these, the fame of Virtue and Erudition willingly gave its applause, yet people detracted most from their Fortitude in conducting the Christian cause. This was due to the opposition of their own colleagues of the same Order—men conscious of their own bad faith and dissolute lives; then by the Nobles* <note>original: *Optimates*</note> *most impatient of the Christian or Ecclesiastical rein; and finally by the ill-advised crowd, now more accustomed to a vocal Gospel* <note>A faith based only on preaching and words.</note> *than a moral one, and fallen into every kind of license (which it is a sin to recall) through the vice of the age. ### EPISTOLÆ
<page-num>334</page-num>

...the most depraved license of living among all men holds in contempt such sacred labors, undertaken with the best of intentions. Nevertheless, those whom Christ, when about to depart from the earth, adorned with authority and these gifts, and who desire to deserve well of the **Church** <note>original: *Ecclesia*</note> in a religious and laudable manner, will continue to teach faithfully, warn solemnly, and rebuke freely. In the meantime, let those stubborn **Capitones** <term>original: *Capitones*; literally "big-heads," a term used to describe stubborn or opinionated men</term> keep their ill-will to themselves and live by their own wits; for why should those who have a most abundant reward stored in heaven care about the ingratitude of the world? That is the sole hope and tranquility which can make present troubles and **hardships** <note>original: *ærumnas*</note> much more tolerable, if not erase them entirely.

This was also the primary cause that moved those most famous men mentioned by You to fulfill their duty with a great and eager spirit—a duty to which they were admitted by the swearing of a most holy oath. Would that all others would restore the **loss** <note>original: *orbitatem*; referring here to the void or bereavement left by these men</note> of such figures and follow their **path** <note>original: *orbitam*; a play on words in the Latin with the preceding term for "loss"</note> happily and faithfully; for otherwise, their own wisdom will be nothing, their learning dull, and all their eloquence barbaric. Farewell. Wolfenbüttel <note>original: *Guelpherbyti*</note>, August 4, 1647.

### YEAR 1647. LETTER 265.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord by far most merciful,<-

*It would certainly be better to read your most ingenious and elegant letters than to write my own rude and foolish ones, if I had any way to obtain yours other than through these. Therefore, the more I long for your letters, the more shamelessly I continue to thrust my own upon you, especially since you are most indulgent in pardoning my persistence. Yet I shall be brief, so that I may sin less in this regard and not disturb your studies with my unrefined noise. You rightly lament the departure of noble minds and their labors—a great punishment for an ungrateful people to whom they were granted for a time, and a consequence of their disdain. Truly, I do not doubt that you believe with the same spirit that there is no surer or swifter way to preserve such men than through the favor and generosity of the Great. Generations indeed have their own sunrises and sunsets in these matters, and there are those who attribute this even to the stars—though I pay no heed to them. No happier or greater benefit can befall gifted minds than a favorable Prince who understands such things; nor is anything more sorrowful or harmful than a Prince who is a **foe of the Muses** <term>original: Amuso; a person who is unrefined or hostile toward literature and the arts</term> and recoils from them. For what did that Great **Maximilian I** <note>original: Æmilianus primus; likely referring to Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I, a famed patron of humanists</note> not bestow upon his Germany? Or the Great Francis I upon France; the **Medici** <note>original: Medicæi</note> upon Italy; **Mellerstadt** <note>original: Mellerstadius; referring to Martin Pollich von Mellerstadt, a key figure in the founding of the University of Wittenberg</note> upon Saxony; the **Fuggers** <note>original: Fuggeri</note> upon Augsburg; Baumgartner upon Nuremberg; the Knight **Sturm** <note>original: Sturmius Eques; likely referring to the diplomat and educator Jacob Sturm von Sturmeck</note> upon Strasbourg; and others elsewhere? In almost a single century, they seemed to compete with one another for the glory of adorning and cultivating **Minerva** <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and the arts</note>. Therefore, you must strive all the more so that you yourself may one day uphold the honor of your House—the Juliuses, Henrys, Augustuses, Fredericks, and other **patrons** <note>original: numina; literally "divine powers," here used to describe the protective spirit of the princely line</note> favorable to arts and letters. This you will do all the more easily since in*

## LETTER 266.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### Lord by far most merciful,

*The promise I made eight days ago to write a letter drives me to do so now, even though I am neither at leisure nor at ease in my mind, as many things at home—and especially my wife's very difficult illness—burden me. Yet your most delightful letters cause all the numbness, which arises from such adversity, to be shaken off. For while you, with great spirit, approve of what sharply pricks and publicly accuses those idle **blockheads** <term>original: Capitones; literally 'big-heads,' a term used for stubborn or pedantic critics</term>, the sworn enemies of Christ and his ministers, you prove yourself not only to be a **true descendant** <term>original: Tradux; literally a vine-shoot, indicating biological and spiritual continuity</term> of your excellent Father, who is a perpetual patron of the Christian cause, but you also offer hope that one day, under your foot, the vipers will cease to hiss, and the **roosters will dare to crow** <note>original: cucurrire ausint Galli; this may be a double entendre referring to both the loud boasting of critics and a political jab at the French (Galli) during the final years of the Thirty Years' War</note>. ### LETTER 269.

genius with these frivolous letters of mine. But come, 
Most Noble Prince, let us agree between us that 
one may address the other at intervals; and for the 
other to respond immediately should not be necessary, but the 
freedom to defer to a more convenient time should be left.

of your studies, and some breathing room will be granted to 
me, lest on the same day I receive yours—and that usually 
the busiest day—

### LETTER 270.

->Most Illustrious and Noble Prince,<-
->My most merciful Lord,<-

While I examine our literary correspondence <term>literary correspondence: original "commercium literarium," the network of intellectual and news exchange between scholars and nobles in the 17th century</term>, and compare your diligence with my own persistence, I find it necessary to praise and cherish the former, but to voluntarily accuse the latter of rashness. For within this single passing year, I have assailed <note>original: "impetii"; the author uses a playful military metaphor to describe the frequency of his mail</note> you, most Generous Prince, with thirteen of my letters; and your brothers—the Elder with 23, the Younger with 11, and in shared letters 7—to which you have each replied thirteen-fold. You sent polished letters in response to my rough ones, elegant ones to my common ones, and letters teeming with exquisite matter to my futile and trifling ones. I might add: you sent letters full of good hope and prosperous success in response to my mournful ones, which bring news of continuous calamity <note>The author likely refers to the ongoing hardships of the Thirty Years' War, which was in its final stages in 1647</note>. This, your kindness or perhaps patience, ensures that I do not abstain even now from provoking you, since you yourselves kindly interpret my impudence as duty and my talkativeness as service. By this I so flatter myself that I value the incredible pleasure I take from your letters more than the requirements of your honor and dignity...

## LETTER 271.

Although his Court has been relieved in whatever way, he is nevertheless held at home due to the weakness of his strength. As for me, I spend one half of the day in labors, the other in torments <note>original: "torminibus"; likely referring to colic or sharp intestinal pains common in 17th-century medical accounts</note>, and the night in sleepless watches. These are the "delights" of old men, by which they are reminded of the shortness of this fleeting life, until it is ended by the desired staff <note>original: "caduceo"; the caduceus was the wand of Hermes, but here the author Christianizes the symbol to mean the peace-bringing heraldry of Christ leading the soul to rest</note> of Christ. To me, whatever there is of this suffering would seem light and tolerable, except for the fact that I am excluded from visiting You and Your Court, which was the first and last of my prayers before my fate. But another and better life, and a more splendid and fuller light, will grant this if this present one denies it.

I am greatly glad that you are affected and refreshed by the pictures sent to you; for I intended this: that they might be pleasant interludes between your more serious studies and stimulants for a more refined nature. Among those that are colored, some are true images of buildings and regions captured in Italy; others are fictional works created for the play of the Mind, but such as a learned eye may easily discern. For no painter or sculptor expresses nature more certainly than through the imitation of a present <term>Archetype</term> <note>the original model or the primary form being copied</note>. 

Indeed, I remember reading about Michelangelo Buonarroti, the Prince of Italian artists, that after he had imitated a work of ancient art with the greatest industry, he asked for this one price: that his own copy first be shown as if it were a work produced in the ancient age. Once it was approved, it was then compared with the archetype, so that the degree of excellence between the archetype and his own work might shine forth. 

I experienced something similar myself in Nuremberg <note>original: "Noribergæ"</note> regarding the wing of a Parrot, produced by a certain Gartner <note>Georg Gartner (died 1619), a Nuremberg painter famous for his ability to perfectly mimic the style of Albrecht Dürer</note>, a most successful imitator of Dürer. It was shown to me as if it were a genuine work of Dürer. When I had long admired it as if it were inimitable, the true hand of Dürer was placed alongside and compared; then that copy became so cheapened—like night compared to day, or a shadow to light—that I realized the difference not without stupor, and indeed, even a sense of shame. For besides the most exquisite diligence of the brush, there is that supreme clarity of colors even after a hundred years, and,

### LETTER CCLXXV.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->My Lord by far most merciful,<-

You act most kindly in that you do not shrink from my occasionally mournful letters, in which I unburden a mind weighed down with both public and domestic disasters, when more joyful things, suited to your studies, ought rather to have been brought forward. And indeed, my pen very often halts at these harsh matters; I would rather drive far away that death-bearing Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war</note> who fills every page for us, and have kindly Peace finally dawn as the subject of our writing—to tread cheerful paths with bright papers instead of dark and mournful ones. But what can you do, and what else can you say, when you see and hear nothing else but the roaring of lions and the howling of wolves? We see the desolation of the Church, the ruin of the Lands, the decay <note>original: "situm"; implies the mold and neglect that comes from disuse</note> of the Schools, the squalor of the Fields, the slaughter of men, burdens, hunger <note>original: "famam"; literally "rumor" or "reputation," but likely a common period spelling or error for "famem" (hunger), given the context of war's hardships</note>, desertions, and—what is most saddening of all—the transformation of human nature into a beastly state. For Law itself has turned into steel <note>original: "chalybem"; referring to the sword</note>; worship into the blade; obedience into desperation; discipline into total dissolution; and even the very means of seeking a living has turned into plunder, while those who struggle against it do so in vain...

If the grime could be wiped from my pen <note>original: "calami mei detergi poßet"; likely a metaphor for the author's weariness or the literal soot of war-torn Stuttgart</note>, you would surely receive from me, most charming Prince, letters that are both more pleasant and more elegant. But in every way, as much as winter differs from spring, and the harsh East wind <note>original: "Euro"</note> from the gentle West wind <note>original: "Zephyrus"</note>, so do we differ from one another; yet perhaps my lot is better than yours in this one wish: because I am greatly delighted by your youthful vigor <note>original: "viriditate"; literally "greenness" or "freshness"</note>, you must endure my dry old age.

What do you say, then, in your most pleasant letters sent on December 7th—that you cannot be heard here across such a vast distance, no matter how much you raise your voice? On the contrary, I would assert that you will be heard not only here, but throughout all Germany and the whole of Pindus <note>a mountain in Greece dedicated to the Muses; used here to mean the entire world of literature and learning</note>—that is, the world of letters—and I would gladly take up the role of a Herald to announce that there still remain Princes of the Guelph line <note>the House of Welf, one of the oldest and most powerful European dynasties</note> who have welcomed exiled German piety, literature, and the liberal arts with hospitality, cherish their own people in their embrace, and save these things from destruction for posterity. 

Let this voice and your example resound across Parnassus and Olympus <note>mythological homes of the Muses and the Gods</note> and other peaks of the highest mountains, and let it spread through the trumpet of good fame. For me, it has been a supreme delight to receive and possess your writings from time to time as witnesses and pledges of this miracle. There is no need, therefore, for you to shout or play the part of Stentor <note>a Greek herald in the *Iliad* whose voice was as loud as fifty men</note>; if you only whisper, I will hear you, and I shall be as an Echo <note>a reference to the mythological nymph who repeats what she hears; the author suggests he will reflect and amplify the Prince's ideas</note> for you—the duty you assigned me in your previous letters of September 8th. 

May Christ grant that this honor be unique and perpetual to your renowned House, so that while the affairs of the Church, literature, and the arts are failing in Germany, you may be said to have been a monument, a support, and a pillar for them, along with the eternal glory of the name Augustus <note>likely a reference to the Prince's father, Duke Augustus the Younger, a famous scholar and book collector</note>; and may He lift you above the common fate of Princes. Farewell and be favorable to

### *The Divine Shelter!* <note>original: "Umbraculum Divinum"; a reference to seeking protection under God’s shadow, common in many Psalms</note>

I give and offer you my thanks, *Reverend Sir*, most pious of my friends, for your wish for a most auspicious year. I believe this came not so much from custom as from love—as so many other pledges and signs of your benevolence testify. You love me so much that you place my welfare before all your own business; I certainly understand this, but I cannot provide an equal eloquence in return. Therefore, I now return this *vow* to you in turn, and I pray to God, the Greatest and Best, that He may grant this year (along with many others) to be as happy as possible. May everything flow according to your desire for you, and may your affairs stand firm against all adversities. And since the Most High has again permitted the cruelty of those most fierce soldiers (who today are cursed in every story told) to fall upon you, He will nevertheless soon look back upon your afflicted circumstances as if appearing from a machine <note>original: "ex machinâ"; a theatrical reference to a 'Deus ex machina,' where a god is lowered onto the stage to resolve a seemingly hopeless situation</note>, and He will abundantly provide the means by which you may repair such a magnificent loss. *For the hand of the Almighty, as you know from the Holy Scriptures, is neither maimed nor shortened* <note>A reference to Isaiah 59:1: "Behold, the Lord's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save"</note>, and He can easily bestow what is lacking whenever He wills. Only have confidence; and do not think that your safety is commended to God, the Greatest and Best, by me only now, but rather on each and every day.

Given in the greatest haste on the 11th day of January, 1647.

*Your Reverend Dignity's*

->*Most Respectfully,*<-

->**FERDINAND ALBERT**<-
->**Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg**<-

## LETTER CCLXXX.

->*A prosperous fortune, with the most sincere wish for a most happy Year!*<-

Because you praise me so highly, Distinguished Man, I recognize your kindness and I give you thanks. I wish that I were such a man as your love imagines me, or at least that I could be compared with you in even a very few things; then I would not blush so much at the comparison you have made. In you, signs of learned and varied reading and experience appear everywhere, which I confess are nonexistent in me. To you, a veteran, the springs of the Muses <note>The Nine Muses of Greek mythology, who presided over the arts and sciences</note> lie open; to me, a new man and almost a little recruit <note>original: "Tyrunculo"; a diminutive of 'tiro,' meaning a beginner or soldier in training</note>, even the approach to the small streams is difficult. I ought to have weighed my *limbs* and my *skills* <note>original: "Artus, Artesque"; a play on words in Latin</note> before I descended into this literary wrestling-ground <note>original: "palæstram"; a place for physical training in antiquity, used here as a metaphor for intellectual exchange</note> with you, *most learned Sir*. 

But since, under the guise of praise, you exhort me toward *greater things*, I will follow you, *Greatest of Men*; I will obey you, and supported by your authority, I will dare and attempt to see what my shoulders <note>original: "Humeri"; a classical metaphor for one's intellectual or moral capacity to carry a burden</note> are capable of, or what they might refuse to bear. For I would not wish to be numbered among those *more illustrious men* who have, as it were, declared *war* against Literature, and who fear that their gold and gems might be stained by ink, yet do not fear to have a mind blind and filthy with ignorance—as the words of the most learned Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the Italian poet and scholar often called the "Father of Humanism"</note> describe them. With these things said, fare as well as possible, and as I always ask, may you look with fairness and kindness upon my simplicity and my "whistling." <note>original: "sibilum"; likely a self-deprecating reference to his own writing being a mere weak sound compared to Andreae's eloquence</note>

->To the Distinguished Man,<-

->Your most respectful servant.<-

## LETTER CCLXXXI.

## **Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**
->By far the most merciful Lord,<-

I owe you the greatest thanks for the most sweet breath of your refreshments in this our calamity, which I pray as a suppliant that a merciful God may repay by the continuation of your own happier fortune. The face of our cruel storm is indeed most sad, but while He travels with us in the same ship, who watches even while sleeping <note>A reference to the biblical story of Jesus calming the storm in Matthew 8:23–27, where he was asleep on the boat during a tempest.</note>, let us hope that the winds and waves will at last be commanded to cease their raging, provided that our faith and patience do not fail. But if we are to be completely submerged, either some whale <note>original: "Cetus"; referring to the story of Jonah.</note> will carry us unharmed and vomit us onto some shore after three days; or some basket of reeds <note>original: "fiscella scirpea"; referring to the basket in which the infant Moses was saved from the Nile (Exodus 2:3).</note> will come to rest in the midst of the seaweed for those of us waiting for the hand of salvation. 

You will shortly receive—if you have not seen it already—the very tiny <term>New Year’s gift<note>original: "Strenulam"; a traditional gift given at the beginning of the year as a token of friendship or patronage.</note></term> which I sent to you. It is a representation of the flight of the Christ child into Egypt. Furthermore, you have proved to me with too many clear examples what the leaning of your mind toward me is, which you have taken up following the example of both your parents. You will crown this favor, however, if you would be willing to stand before your Most Serene Mother as the advocate for my devotion, which diligently keeps watch before God for her health and the long-lastingness of her most happy marriage, and if you would convey all my duties of piety. By this your zeal toward me, I myself shall be made happy, and I shall be strongly moved to the proclamation of your virtue and your bloom. Farewell, delight of your parents, flower of an Illustrious House, my expectation, and favor me,

->Your Illustrious Highness’s<-

Stuttgart, 5 February,
1647. ->Most humble client.<-

## LETTER CCLXXXII.

### Good fortune attend you!

I would be a wicked man, *Most Illustrious Sir*, if I did not love you among my most sacred relations. Not long ago, a certain painting, distinguished by the art of <term>Apelles<note>Apelles of Kos (4th century BCE) was the most renowned painter of ancient Greece; his name is used here as a superlative for high-quality art.</note></term>, was brought into our <term>Museum<note>original: "Musæum"; in the 17th century, this referred to a scholar's private study or a room dedicated to the arts and sciences.</note></term> as if it were a gift for me. When I inquired diligently about the *Donor*, I finally understood that it had been sent by you. I was easily led to believe this, not because of any awareness of small services of mine toward you—for there have never been any—but by the memory of your benevolence toward me, who deserved no such thing.

I thought it necessary, therefore, to write these few lines so that you might know as soon as possible that it was delivered to me safe and undamaged, and that the gift was most welcome. But since I can offer nothing else in return to you at this time, I trust that meanwhile my sincere and grateful spirit will be proven to you. Ask for my services and my loyalty; I am both willing and able to provide them, as I am duty-bound, and I promise this with my right hand. I add my devotion and respect, which I shall offer abundantly, and in which I will not allow myself to be surpassed by anyone; whether <term>Hercules<note>The legendary Greek hero of immense strength.</note></term> himself should wish to compete with me, or his descendant <term>Alexander<note>Alexander the Great, who claimed descent from Hercules; the author is using these figures to express a competitive level of loyalty.</note></term>.

May you be entirely persuaded of this, and believe me to be most devoted to you as long as circumstances, age, and the <term>dark threads of the three sisters<note>original: "sororum fila trium... atra"; a classical reference to the Fates (Moirai) of Greek and Roman mythology, who were said to spin, measure, and eventually cut the thread of human life.</note></term> shall permit. Given in haste at <term>Wolfenbüttel<note>original: "Guelpherbyti"; the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in Germany.</note></term> on the 15th of February, 1647.

->Of your Excellence<-
->**The most respectful.**<-

From our <term>Tutor<note>original: "Informatore"; a term for a private educator or mentor to a young noble.</note></term>, we send the warmest greetings to you and yours.

->*Very many greetings!*<-

There is no reason, *Most Illustrious Sir*, for you to give me the greatest thanks for my words of consolation, since it was entirely my duty to lift you up when you were broken by the bitterness of the times, and to <term>pour cold water<note>original: "frigidam affundere"; a classical idiom for reviving someone who is fainting or exhausted, similar to "providing a restorative."</note></term> upon you when you were failing. Nor should the threats of human adversities be recalled so anxiously to your mind; a battle line of these troubles seems to stand against us as well. But we oppose them with a <term>bronze wall<note>original: "murum ahæneum"; a reference to the Roman poet Horace, signifying a clear conscience or a stout, unbreakable spirit.</note></term>: our trust in a better future. You, in the same way, should bid all your cares a long farewell and promise yourself happier things; for who knows whether that tranquility might soon follow which could wipe out all past evils?

As for the <term>New Year’s gift<note>original: "strenam"; a traditional gift given at the start of the year for good luck.</note></term> which you sent, I wrote not long ago that I had received it. It is not so much a representation of the *Flight of the Infant Christ*, as it is a remarkable proof of the trust held by *Joseph*, who, relying on good hope, left his old dwelling and sought a retreat elsewhere with his spouse *Mary* and the little boy *Jesus*. May God grant that you are not only sustained by that same hope, but that the wish you conceived from it becomes altogether established and firm. 

To no one will your arrival be more welcome than to me. I will prepare a guest-room for you, which however will have no ornament other than yourself; we shall spend the most pleasant holidays, and whatever is in my possession that can be of either pleasure or use shall be yours. And although, *Most Illustrious Sir*, you so influence the minds of all that you hardly need the testimony of another, yet as an act of great generosity toward my <term>Exalted Lady Mother<note>original: "Cels. Dn. Matrem," referring to Duchess Elizabeth Sophie of Mecklenburg (1613–1676), a noted composer and scholar.</note></term>, those "good words" which you sought from me have been added. These, in turn, testify most abundantly to her affection for you in every kind of study.

### LETTER CCLXXXIV.

->Most Illustrious and Exalted Prince,<-
->Lord most gracious by far,<-

*Because it most becomes and adorns this tender age of yours, you always mix a certain sweetness into your letters. By this, you prove to your followers how much you are shielded from the <term>smoke of arrogance<note>original: "insolentiæ typho"; 'typhus' is a Greek-derived term used here to mean a delusional pride or "puffing up" of the ego.</note></term>, and how you are becoming accustomed to the courtesy and easy manner of <term>Titus and Trajan<note>Roman emperors often cited as models of "civilitas" (civility) and kindness toward their subjects, in contrast to tyrants.</note></term>, thereby drawing them to you. Furthermore, in showing a love and esteem for <term>literature<note>original: "literarum"; in this period, the term encompassed all classical learning, humanities, and scholarly pursuits.</note></term>—which elsewhere are held in too much contempt—you act most rightly. You give us the greatest hope that one day the practitioners of these arts will find their honor, support, and protection under you, no less than they once did under your most praised Father. If you add to this a zeal for Religion and a care for the Church, these virtues will surely crown you and* **make you a GREAT FERDINAND ALBERT one day,** *to be compared with, or even preferred over, all the famous Ferdinands and Alberts whom fame has raised to the heavens. I shall never cease to advance you toward this goal through my constant prayers to God and my most ready efforts and duties;* **Christ** *indeed shall confirm my vows, He who keeps you safe and unharmed always. Farewell, and look upon me with favor.*

->**To Your Illustrious Highness,**<-
->**Your most humble servant.**<-

*Add my dutiful greetings to your most faithful and skillful Tutor. Stuttgart, February 19, 1647.*
