<header>THE YEAR 1647. LETTER CCLXXXV.</header>

## Most Illustrious and Exalted Prince,
### Lord most gracious by far,

That you hold my <term>trifles<note>original: "quisquilias"; literally "dregs" or "scraps," a modest way for the author to refer to his own writings or letters.</note></term> to be of any importance is truly a mark of your great kindness. I could not be repaid by anything more than that affection you show toward me, which I value most highly, as is my duty. There is no need for you to confirm your loyalty with your right hand [by a formal oath], since the words of a Prince must stand as his word of honor; nor should we believe otherwise. This was testified by the *Great Emperor Charles V*, when he generously declared that if loyalty were exiled from the whole earth, it ought to find a home in the court—or rather, in the heart—of a Prince.

I see it as my duty, then, that while you strive to compete in your love for me with *Hercules* himself or his descendant *Alexander the Great*, I shall emulate the care and concern of <term>Nathan<note>The biblical prophet who acted as an advisor to King David and a mentor to the young King Solomon.</note></term> in cultivating a <term>Solomon<note>The biblical king famous for wisdom; here used as a flattering comparison to the young Prince Ferdinand Albert.</note></term>. Whether from afar or near, I shall support your illustrious progress with my pen, my heart, my prayers, my little gifts, and all that I have, however meager my resources may be, all of which I wish to be dedicated to you.

Truly, you possess in abundance at home everything one could wish for: the example of your parents, the wisdom of your <term>Overseer<note>original: "Ephori"; a high-ranking official or guardian responsible for supervising the Prince’s conduct and education.</note></term>, the learning of your <term>Tutor<note>original: "Informatoris"; the educator responsible for the Prince's academic instruction.</note></term>, the healthy competition of your fellow students, the prayers of the people, and public applause. These combined will pave a smoother path for you to ascend to the very citadel of Virtue. I pray to God that I may one day see you established there in person, or hear of it from afar. Farewell, and look with favor upon

->Your Illustrious Highness's<-

*Stuttgart,* March 12, 1647.

->Most humble servant,<-

<header>EPISTLES</header>

### LETTER CCLXXXVI.

->*Most happy fates!*<-

That you have praised me so much in your most recent letters, and in all those that preceded them, **Most Distinguished Sir**, I owe you as much as I am far from deserving such praise. I wish that you would apply this effort to a more successful subject; then I might read your most sweet letters, when they are brought to me, without a blush—I who <term>measure myself by my own foot<note>original: "meo metior pede"; a classical idiom meaning to judge oneself by one's own standards or to know one's true limits.</note></term>, live with myself, and know how <term>meager my furnishings<note>original: "curta supellex"; a literary reference to having limited intellectual or material resources.</note></term> are. 

But this shall always be a stimulus for me to continue the labor of my studies and to rouse that striving of the soul which, to speak frankly, a <note>original: "Virtutum amor, & gloriae cupiditas"</note> *love of virtues and a desire for glory* has nourished in me from my early youth. You have deserved so much from me, and continue to deserve so daily, that my will should never differ in any matter from your faithful advice; rather, it ought to be most closely joined to yours, and most intent upon this one thing: to do all things according to the <term>plumb-line<note>original: "perpendiculum"; a tool used by masons to ensure a wall is perfectly vertical, here used metaphorically for a standard of rectitude.</note></term> of the Divine will. 

As for the cause of this desire and purpose of mine, I think you will easily guess it; for I am entirely persuaded that this is the only thing that can happen to a man: an honor, a ray, a lamp, spreading its light not just upon one's fame or one's age, but beyond. With these thoughts, fare you most beautifully, and receive in turn many dutiful greetings from our beloved <term>Tutor<note>original: "Informator"; likely referring to the Prince's personal instructor or governor at court.</note></term>. 

Written hurriedly at **Wolfenbüttel**, the 23rd day of March, in the year 1647.

->To your Distinction,<-

->Most respectfully.<-

## LETTER CCLXXXVII.

Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
My Far Most Gracious Lord,

*Regarding the feelings of my soul and my devotion toward your Most Serene Princess Mother, which I recently asked you to interpret for her: it is not that I think I must laboriously win her favor through such a great intercessor—for I have so often felt her to be most inclined and generous toward me of her own accord—but rather so that you yourself might understand what a Mother God has granted you. She has surpassed the typical lot of the female sex and, equaling the praise of both ancient and modern* Women, *captures the admiration and devotion of all* Men. *She deserves a* <term>Philippus of Bergamo<note>original: "Philippum Bergomensem"; referring to Giacomo Filippo Foresti (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk who wrote a famous biographical compendium of notable women.</note></term> *or a* <term>Giovanni Boccaccio<note>original: "Iohannem Bocacium"; the Italian author of "Concerning Famous Women," the first collection of biographies devoted exclusively to women in Western literature.</note></term> *as her* <term>eulogist<note>original: "Encomiasten"; a speaker or writer of formal high praise.</note></term>. *So that this might become better known to you (if indeed it is possible for you to be ignorant of these things) and so that it would be clear to your Most Gracious Mother how much I value these gifts of Heaven, I could use no more suitable messenger than you. Thus, by the same effort, I might suggest to both of you your own happiness and the glory of this age, and most humbly fulfill my duty, which is indebted to you.*

*Furthermore, as for the fact that you offer everything to me in total readiness as I long for you, it cannot fail to greatly lift me up in my weakness. Would that—just as I fly to you in my mind while waking and dreaming (indeed, I often seem to converse and trifle with you through the sight of your portraits)—I were also free to transport this so ill-affected body! You would certainly have someone to applaud your progress and follow your ascent to the highest things with his vows and prayers. How intolerable a desire also holds me to see that most famous* <term>Paternal Library<note>original: "Bibliothecae Paternae"; the Herzog August Library in Wolfenbüttel, which became one of the largest and most significant collections in Europe under the Prince's father.</note></term>, *not to mention the* <term>Librarian<note>original: "Bibliothecario"</note></term> *himself, who is without equal, and who [holds] all my hope and expectation in these lands...*

I have fulfilled my duty in this regard under the title of a certain other person. For a long time, the expectation of your arrival has delighted my soul with pleasant hope; according to your most recent letters, as I was able to see, you had already sent your thoughts ahead to us. But when I truly learned from your last correspondence that you are being held back by a physical ailment, I was affected by such great sorrow that I consider it a primary part of my own misfortune that I have fallen from such great hope. 

May **God, the Thrice Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Deus ter Opt. Max." — a Christian adaptation of the Roman title for Jupiter, *Jupiter Optimus Maximus*, common in Renaissance Latin.</note> grant that, released from this bodily weakness, you may shortly recover your former strength of limb, and that you may shine for us and for the **Christian World** as long as possible. This can be more easily achieved if you sometimes withdraw yourself—as we can easily guess you should—from your tireless studies and the great multitude of your affairs. For that saying of the best advisor on Nature, **Pliny**, is well known: *one must make time for the body, so that the mind may be supported by its pillars.* <note>original: "corpori vacandum esse, ut ejus fulturis animus sustineatur" — a reference to the Roman author Pliny the Younger's view on balancing health and intellectual work.</note> 

If it should ever happen that you survey our **Library**, you will see that it is not only well-furnished with a great multitude of diverse writers and materials, but is also distinguished by your own name. Farewell; and receive greetings from our **Tutor** <note>original: "Informatore" — likely a private teacher or household scholar.</note>, who will reply to your dearest son’s friendly letters as soon as possible. 

Written on the 4th day of May, 1647.
To the Distinguished Man,

# LETTER 295.
## *Prosperous success!* <note>original: "Felicitatem prosperam!" — a standard greeting wishing for the recipient's continued well-being and success</note>

We have read your letters in turn, *O Man never to be sufficiently honored according to your merits, both elegantly writ*ten and imbued with every mark of refinement <note>original: "humanitatis" — in the 17th century, this referred to the "humanities" or the qualities of a cultured, educated, and civil gentleman</note>. We are joyful from our very soul that you hold our friendship in such high regard that you never cease to provoke it from time to time with new gifts; nor can we conclude anything else from this, except that you match us in love and the business of writing, and do so most willingly. Relying on the goodness of this cause, we send our own letters to you more freely and more frequently, for we do not willingly allow your letters to be held by us for too long without a response, nor do we wish our own letters, in making their way to you, to measure out their journey at a tortoise's crawl <note>original: "gradu testudineo" — a classical idiom for moving very slowly</note>. 

Yet here, too, a certain care distresses our mind: the fear that your more serious business might perhaps be hindered by our frequent and ill-timed letters. But we ask that you do only what can be done for your own convenience, and do not allow us to seem an inconvenience to you in any way. We have reason once again to give you our greatest thanks, because you have destined *several books by various Au*thors for our small bookcases <note>original: "forulis" — small cases or pigeonholes used to store books or precious documents</note>; these are indeed such that they almost scorn our praise, and are considered worthy of nothing less than the greatest reward. Concerning me, I would certainly wish you to think thus: that I will diligently embrace in my spirit all those things in turn which seem to pertain to the benefit of you and yours, and to declaring my gratitude by any means possible. My own works have nothing that breathes such a sublime origin; you grant me quite enough if you believe that our <term>Muses</term> <note>In classical mythology, the Muses were the goddesses of inspiration for the arts and sciences; the author uses this to refer to his own literary efforts</note> are still only swimming near the shore. ## LETTER 296.

->Most Illustrious and High-born Prince,<-
->Most deeply merciful Lord,<-

Your ill health easily excused you, and your most loving brother Anton Ulrich <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714) was the son of Duke August the Younger. He later became a famous patron of the arts and a significant novelist and poet.</note> has sufficiently fulfilled your duties. Even though I myself greatly love and desire your letters—which are both cleverly composed and elegantly written <note>original: "eleganter pictas" — literally "elegantly painted." This refers to the fine calligraphy and penmanship practiced by young nobles as part of their education.</note>—I would not want this kind of exercise to become troublesome or tedious for you. Rather, it should be kept as something pleasant. After all, what else should drive you to write letters to me than to display and perfect the flowering of your natural character and the sharpness of your style? This remains true until a more mature age suggests more varied subjects and sends you into the broader field of understanding human affairs. Therefore, I strongly urge you: if continuing this practice of exchanging letters does not displease you, do not undertake anything that burdens your mind, tires your young hand, or disrupts your recreation. You can send me no letters more welcome than those I know have come from a cheerful and festive spirit. Farewell, sweetest Prince, and continue to refresh me with your elegant writings.

->Your Illustrious Highness’s<-

Stuttgart, September 3,
1647.
->Most humble servant,<-

->May good fortune attend you!<-

I have already received three letters from you, **Distinguished Sir**, within the span of a few weeks, to which I have responded nothing until now. It is necessary, therefore, that I awaken my tender and slumbering Muses <note>The writer poetically refers to his creative and intellectual energy as the Muses, the goddesses of the arts.</note>. A bad cough <note>original: *tussis*</note> has troubled me for some time, which rendered me plainly incapable of these and other kinds of duties; indeed, it frequently shook the pen from my hand just as I approached the task of writing. Therefore, let that illness bear all the blame for my negligence and any longer procrastination, if indeed there was any. 

As for what you write—that nothing is more of a concern to you than that those things which were nearly extinct might be brought back into the light, and that all arts and **Studies** might be restored to their former stability and brilliance—we highly praise your spirit. Therefore, because of the affection we hold for you, we congratulate you from the heart on this serious purpose. For how few are there in this day and age whom such a concern touches? Most people are of such modest faith and such short hope that they are easily deterred when moved by difficulty. You act more nobly; you are held by such a love for lost things that you feel no weariness in the labor of restoring them. 

Our most dear **Tutor** <term>Informator: A term used for a private teacher or educational supervisor, often responsible for the moral and academic upbringing of noble children.</term> offers himself as your most humble debtor; he holds you in his eyes, on his lips, and in his heart. He desires that his respect, zeal, and sincerity in every kind of duty be fully proven to you. Indeed, your singular erudition and your knowledge of those matters—which all good men have always valued most highly—deserve nothing less. Farewell. September 6, 1647 <note>original: "8. Iduum Sept." The Roman calendar counted backward from fixed points; the 8th day before the Ides of September is September 6th.</note>.

## LETTER 304.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My far most Gracious Lord,

A most illustrious man, Johann Jacob von Rapp <note>original: "Iohannes Iacobus Rupis." A nobleman from the Sporen region.</note>, lord of Sporen, has returned to us from your lands. This was after he had used the waters of Hornhausen <note>original: "aquas Hornhusanas." Hornhausen was famous in the mid-17th century for its mineral springs, which were believed to have miraculous healing powers.</note> for the restoration of his sight, though in vain. Nevertheless, he has come as a herald of the wonderful cures which he witnessed firsthand in others, or heard praised by those who—destitute of all medical and surgical help—found the restoration of their health here as the fulfillment of their prayers. Indeed, he found the waters to be medicinal, not miraculous (as he had been personally convinced), yet they were useless for his own long-standing ailment. Still, I would not deny that a Divine Power has assisted in the healing of many; though there are those who testify, and indeed detest, that the devotion there has greatly cooled since fortunes have increased. 

But he also magnificently praised this: that during his journey, having passed through several courts, he found among you a far different and more fruitful cultivation of talent and practice of piety than what is seen in these parts. I have both greatly rejoiced at this testimony and given thanks to God, who still prepares latches and barriers from most illustrious families against growing barbarism and atheism, lest Germany lose its eyes and its heart along with its lands and fortunes—that is, the use and fruit of learning and piety together, which were once produced with such great effort and...

## LETTER 308.

### Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,
### Lord of far-reaching mercy,

*I congratulate myself, and I rejoice for You, that at the same moment in time I learned both of Your illness and Your restored health. I would wonder, however, that You are troubled by toothaches at this age, were it not for the fact that I myself suffered that evil harshly in my youth for a whole and continuous decade; from which I was afterward freed by God’s blessing in such a way that, except for the four teeth I lost then, I now make good use of all the rest, which remain intact.*

## LETTER 309.
### Most Illustrious and High Princes,
->My most gracious lords,<-

By the command of your Most Serene Father, my Lord and Master, who is most gracious to all—for how would I have dared such a thing on my own?—I have selected certain <term>mottos</term><note>original: "Symbola." In the 17th century, a "symbolum" or motto was a personal device used by royalty and nobility to express their guiding philosophy.</note> which you might use when signing your names, following the example of other great men, provided they are not foreign to your own feelings. I sent these to you last week, though they were expressed by the unfortunate brush of a painter—or rather, a mud-dauber. I would have preferred indeed that your own <insert>the famous Martin</insert> *Gosky*, that most excellent artist, had performed this service for you; or that your *Buno* and *Freisius* <note>Johannes Buno and likely a scholar or artist named Freisius, who were part of the intellectual circle of the court.</note> might have contributed their more skillful efforts to these more ingenious inventions. However, even if you understand my intentions through your own wisdom, the added verses—though rather clumsy—explain them well enough. Nevertheless, it seemed right to explain them further in this letter and to suggest them more clearly; I ask with all due humility that you do not take offense at this.

I have chosen mottos that align as closely as possible with that world-famous motto of your Most Serene Father: **WEIGH** <note>original: "EXPENDE." This was the famous personal motto of Duke August the Younger of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, meaning "weigh" or "consider" carefully.</note>. Therefore, for your Highness, Most Noble Prince, Lord **RUDOLPH AUGUSTUS**, I have assigned to my mind the motto **ATTEND** <note>original: "ATTENDE." Rudolph Augustus (1627–1704) was the eldest son; his motto "Attend" complements his father's "Weigh."</note>, for since the favor of heaven...

*...so that he, who deserves to be called the base and the pinnacle among the heroes of his own age, may see his legacy in you. Yet to you,* **GOD** *has denied nothing—as the legitimate heir of his blood and talent, but also of his education and righteous upbringing—to prevent you from reaching that same goal of glory and fame through the progress and growth of your Virtue. Dare, therefore, under these happy auspices, to follow after your Father; and promote that most rare weight of gifts granted to you by heaven in the balance of your praised career. By this, you shall equal, in your own weighing, even the greatest weight of your Father's merits toward the Church, the State, and the Republic of Letters <note>The "Republic of Letters" (Respublica literaria) refers to the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note>, or you may even surpass them—a thing which your Father himself would not envy.*

You understand my meaning: though your birthright and the laws and pacts established by your family may grant the first-born their place, your own Virtue shall either prepare a new kingdom for you or amplify the one granted to you. Remember: the greater the effort required by fortune to prepare your path, the greater the honor and the more glorious the work that will follow for you. Truly, Fate will find a way <note>original: "Fata viam invenient." A famous quote from Virgil's Aeneid (Book X).</note> to lead you through the steep windings of the temple of Virtue placed on high, and will finally place you in a glorious seat among your Ancestors. As I* **WEIGHED** *these things in my mind, following the thoughts of your most Serene and happy Lord Father, a great joy and the greatest hope was born...*

It is known that it shall be—and I trust by no unfavorable or empty omen of mine—that these three **Mottos** <term>Symbola: In this context, these are "Devices" or heraldic symbols paired with moral mottos used to guide a noble's conduct.</term> will yield a favorable outcome for you. ### LETTER 310.

## Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,
## Lords far most merciful,

When I set out to write to You, no other matter occurred worthier of You than that which, by its own merit, occupies and exercises us entirely at this time, *namely* the PASSION OF JESUS CHRIST.

<vocab>Virtue, Dido, Augustus, Sirach, Passion of Jesus Christ, Princes, Letter</vocab>

<summary>This page concludes the celebratory poems for the sons of Duke August, using the classical example of Dido to encourage the expansion of their legacy, and begins a formal letter to the Princes regarding the spiritual significance of the Passion of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological reflections addressed to the Princes, moving from the general concept of the Passion into a specific comparative meditation on the "Two Adams" and the "Two Gardens."</meta>

<page-num>389</page-num>
<header>THE YEAR 1648</header>
<sig>R 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: blood-</meta>

**OUR** History <note>The author refers to the history of the Passion of Christ</note>, which, as a wise annual recitation of our ancestors, must be recalled to our memory; so too, through the entire course of our lives, it comes to us as a "Breviary of Theology" to be ruminated upon and repeatedly revisited. There is no study more certain or more effective than this, whether for solidifying our faith or for shaping our lives. And indeed, let the director of this year’s sacred meditation be the **TWIN ADAM**, whom St. Paul describes in his epistle to the Romans, chapter 5, verse 12 and following. We look to him so that we may better understand that as much as the first Adam lost, so much has the second Adam repaired and restored to us. By an exact comparison of the two, weighing our evils and our goods upon this scale of the Passion, let us return what praise and thanks we can to the merits of Christ.

For behold, how (1) that most pestilent serpent offered us the evil of evils—truly an Apple of Discord <note>original: "Eridos pomum," referring to the mythological apple thrown by Eris that sparked the Trojan War; here used to describe the forbidden fruit of Eden</note>—and infected us all with division. Yet, there is prepared from the Tree of Life a <term>remedy against evil</term> <note>original: "Alexicacon," a Greek term for a protective charm or medicine that wards off ill fortune or disease</note>, which has restored Harmony. This occurred while Charity itself descended to us, and—so as not to give from what belonged to another—instituted a way to feed and refresh us with His very Body and His very Blood. Thus, our extreme Ambition was paid for by the deepest Humility and the appearance of a servant; our inexhaustible Greed was satisfied by the most generous Poverty; and our reckless and destructive curiosity was at once corrected and better instructed by a simple example of the true and the good. Oh, how happy are these feasts of the Holy Eucharist and the Paschal lamb, compared to those infernal banquets that had to be expiated by such a precious victim.

Now, (2) let us compare **BOTH GARDENS**, that of Paradise and this one of Olivet <note>The Mount of Olives, specifically the Garden of Gethsemane</note>. For as much as that first garden was a place of delight for the first Adam, so this one was made full of horror and trembling for the second Adam, in view of so dreadful a death and the divine indignation resulting from it. As much as those fruits were sweet and flavorful, so this cup is bitter, filled with all our impurities. As much as that breeze was sweet and joyful, so this heat is torrential...

<summary>The author initiates a comparative meditation on the Passion of Christ, contrasting the fall of the first Adam in Eden with the redemption brought by Christ (the "Second Adam") in the Garden of Gethsemane.</summary>
<keywords>Passion of Christ, Second Adam, Garden of Eden, Gethsemane, Eucharist, Atonement, Romans 5:12, original sin</keywords>

*...sweating bloody clots <note>original: "sanguineas grumas"; a reference to hematidrosis, the sweating of blood during extreme anguish</note>; just as the obedience of animals was once ready for Adam, so now there is a sorrowful solitude and the drowsiness even of those most intimate; just as there was various delight and refreshment from the harmony and elegance of this universe, so now the instruments of the Passion are observed, and the very chaos of introduced evils has become an object of nausea and the fainting of the soul. 3. Let us proceed further to that which is most profane,* **THE SACRED COUNCIL** <note>The Sanhedrin, the supreme religious assembly of the Jewish people</note>, *the mirror of Adam’s piety; was not the Second Adam <note>Christ</note> pronounced a heretic because of Adam's own apostasy? He was accused of blasphemy by hypocrites conscious of their own deception; he was unworthily struck by chatterboxes and peddlers of trifles for his profession of truth; he was held as a fool and a laughingstock by those who think themselves wise yet are delirious with reason. With Caiaphas <note>The Jewish High Priest who presided over the trial of Jesus</note> plotting, Judas betraying, Peter denying, and everyone else deserting, was he not publicly outlawed? 4. Nor was it any better in Adam’s* **FORUM** <note>The public square or court of law</note>, *the tribunal of his own injustice, where tyranny argues for the obedience of a faction; fraud accuses kindness of wrongdoing; the glutton <note>literally "one who worships the belly"</note> blames the excess of sobriety; and noise and shouting convict the tranquility of the crowds, while Pilate <note>The Roman governor of Judea</note> meanwhile plays his theatrical part. 5. And what of the* **PALACE** <note>Referring to the court of King Herod</note>? *It is the true stage of Adam, where there is much pomp against the emptied Christ <note>A reference to the theological concept of "kenosis," or Christ stripping himself of divine status to become human</note>; much curious inquiry against the silent Christ; much insult against the stiffened Christ; much collusion with that ball of mockery (Christ), with Herod acting the lion-like fox, the Scribes appearing as wolves, and the crowd acting like cattle-herding dogs. 6. What other then, but the* **TERRIBLE SENTENCE**, *should we expect—a sentence fitting for Adam’s guilt, not Christ’s innocence. Behold the Man <note>original: "Ecce Homo," the famous words spoken by Pilate when presenting a scourged Christ to the crowd</note>, whom lust and petulance scourge naked; Behold him, whom Ambition crowns with thorns as a masquerade; Behold him, whom Avarice, having stripped him and drained his blood, spits upon and tears apart; Behold him, whom gluttony drenches with filth <note>original: "oleto," implying foulness or the dregs of wine, contrasting with Christ's thirst on the cross</note>, while he is hungry and thirsty!*

*Behold the worm, and not a Man <note>original: "Ecce vermem, non Hominem"; a reference to Psalm 22:6, traditionally interpreted as Christ’s extreme humiliation on the cross</note>, so that he might restore the beast-like Adam back into a Man. — 7. Thus, the very* **PUNISHMENT** *of Christ, as shameful as it was for him, is as glorious for Adam. His departure <note>meaning his death</note> is for the latter a return, a recovery of lost goods, and a restoration to the kingdom from exile. His burden under the cross is for the latter a relief from evils and a refreshment. The piercing of the nails is a joyful liberation from all bonds. The rain of blood is a sacred washing and a cleansing of every kind of filth. Christ’s intercession excuses us; his piety heals us; his example rouses us; his cry helps us; his thirst quenches ours; his completion <note>referring to "Consummatum est" or "It is finished"</note> seals us; his last breath accompanies our salvation. 8. Finally, let us also behold the* **BURIAL** *of Christ, and together let us bury the old Adam. For the death of the old Adam had to be fully expiated by the death of Christ, and the wages of sin had to be paid. Once the ransom <note>term: "Lytro"; from the Greek 'lytron', the price paid to release a captive or debt</note> was paid, he was taken down from the cross so that we might lay aside our Adamic remains. He was wrapped in linens so that a new Righteousness might be credited to us, like shining white robes. He experienced no decay, so that he might drench our nature—which is bound to die—with a vital, eternal essence <note>original: "succo"; literally 'juice' or 'sap', here meaning a life-giving spiritual force</note>. This essence stands by us when we are awakened by the sound of the trumpet, whether we are to be judged for the second death or admitted to a truer life. He himself, the glorious and triumphant* **Head**, *rose again, so that no doubt born from the horror of the grave might ever creep in regarding the joyful succession of his members <note>In Christian theology, Christ is the "Head" and believers are the "members" of his body</note>. These are the things, Most Illustrious Princes, which occurred to my mind during my sacred meditations. It seemed to me not unworthy to share them with you at this time—not because I do not consider you already sufficiently instructed or more elegantly and successfully taught by your own teachers, but because I had to serve the occasion and set aside all other studies for this sacred contemplation. If these thoughts do not seem unwelcome or ill-timed to you, I shall be most grateful. For to be of use to you and to please you at the same time is my goal, and my*

*And my work—from the time I was most mercifully admitted into your service, as it has always been and is my sole purpose—so shall it continue to be carried out by me with the most humble obedience and sincere loyalty, even unto the very grave. ## LETTER 312.

->**Most Illustrious and Highborn Princes,**<-
->**Lords far most merciful,**<-

Because I recently responded to your letters in a somewhat constrained manner, I think I must now repay that with a freer pen, lest I appear either unfair to your diligence or too neglectful of your kindness. The material for this was supplied to me by Juan de Mariana, a Spaniard <note>Juan de Mariana (1536–1624) was a famous Jesuit historian and political philosopher. This reference is likely to his work on kingship and the education of a prince</note>, in an excellent book written in his own mother tongue <note>original: "vernacula sua"; referring to Spanish</note> about the Christian Commonwealth <note>original: "de Republica Christiana"</note> and dedicated to his King, **PHILIP III**, in the year 1615. In this work, after many other things ingeniously devised and wisely expressed, he depicts the **HEAD** of a Good Prince and adorns it with its own senses. Because I have not yet seen this work gifted to Latium <note>original: "Latio donatum"; an idiomatic way of saying "translated into Latin," which was the international language of scholarship</note>, I thought it should be outlined and explained for your use—not indeed with the same length with which he wrote, but as concisely as I can—rather than simply translated. I believe this would be both appropriate for your Dignity and, because of the elegance of the invention, could not be unwelcome.

He thus portrays the **HEAD** of the Prince so that, first of all, he assigns **Wisdom** to the two **EYES**, as if they were the Sun and Moon of this political Microcosm <note>term: "Microcosm"; the philosophical idea that a human being—or in this case, the Prince—is a miniature version of the entire universe or the state</note>.

[The Head] signifies an accurate inspection of all things and actions. It is taught to observe the good and mark the wicked and shameful, but it should attend most especially to the oppressed, lest they suffer any violence; instead, they should be able to use and enjoy their own rights. He asserts that this is the first and highest foundation of a lasting and happy empire.

Next, he adds the **TWIN EARS**, to which he attributes Justice. This is supported by the knowledge of Truth, gathered by listening to everyone, and bolstered by faithful counsel and good-willed listeners who stand in his place. From this, every just and fair exchange proceeds, and distribution can be made according to each person's merits and a worthy estimation: favor is repaid for service, punishment for guilt, and donations are neither too lavish nor too meager, but weighed out exactly <note>original: "ad libellam," referring to a level or plumb-line used by builders to ensure accuracy</note>. This he establishes as the second pillar of a stable and blessed government.

There follows **SMELL**, which he distinguishes with Prudence, divided into sagacity and discretion. This sense notably adorns the head raised so high above others; it renders the prince venerable through greatness and fortitude, and lovable through humanity and courtesy. In this sublime station, nothing is closer to God than these two qualities. Care must be taken, therefore, that he does not allow himself to be easily deceived, nor permit the hearts of the people to be alienated by those who—while their own "nose" (or the search for truth) is missing—act to the ruin of the public.

**TASTE**, however, since it has a double duty—serving both the palate and the voice through the tongue’s articulate speech—is divided between the restraint of desires (which needs a firm rein in the midst of great fortune) and the proclamation and guarding of Truth. The former moderates and restrains pleasures and the recreations of life; the latter teaches that Faith <note>In this context, "Fides" refers to one’s word, promise, or political loyalty</note> must be given and kept, and that silence must be skillfully employed. It cuts off the harmful tongues of flatterers and drives them far away.

There remains **TOUCH**, the lowest of the senses, and

*I believe that a long enough silence has lingered between us in our exchange of letters. ## LETTER 317.

->Much health and peace in Christ.<-
<note>original: "S. P. C.", an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam in Christo*.</note>

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Princes,**<-

*Once again, I must ask for pardon, because since the affairs of the Church are not yet fully settled, I come to writing somewhat unprepared. Yet I felt I had to send some letter, lest I deserve to be called harmful to your exceptional diligence or ungrateful for the incredible inclination of your spirit toward me; although, truly, I am ashamed to wear you down repeatedly with these same trifles* <note>original: "næniis," literally "incantations" or "trifles," here referring to his humble letters.</note> *and to repay your elegance with a hollow noise of words.*

*And now, indeed, I shall not separate you brothers, whom God, blood, and harmony have joined; when there is a bit more leisure, God willing, I shall pay my debt to each of you. To your desires first, most noble Prince,* **ANTHONY ULRICH** <note>Anthony Ulrich (1633–1714), later Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, was a famous patron of the arts and an author himself.</note>, *that you might one day send forth the rays of your illustrious genius into the light and the public, and impart their brilliance and utility to me also in person, and pour out all the silent affection of your soul—as I earnestly favor these things, so I pray with my whole heart to the Supreme Divinity and to the Imperial House that they be made auspicious, and I long to see that day.*

### LETTER CCCXVIII.

->Much health and greetings.<-

->Most Illustrious and Exalted Princes,<-
->Lords most gracious by far,<-

I do not wish to repay your silence with my own, yet it is not fitting for me to demand a response from your pen too insistently. Let it suffice to testify to my duty in these few lines and to suggest some material so that you are not without something to answer. Since I recently happened upon a Fable <note>original: "Apologum"; an allegorical story intended to convey a moral or political truth.</note>, not foreign to the history of these times, it seemed right to share it with you, so that its mysteries—which are still hidden from me—might be revealed through your interpretation, which I have always found to be sharp and most exact. Search it out, gut its meaning <note>original: "exenterate"; literally to disembowel or pull out the guts, used here as a metaphor for deep analysis.</note>, bring forth what is hidden, exercise your wits, and sharpen your pens; you could do nothing more welcome to me. May you flourish most abundantly, and look upon me with favor.

->Your Illustrious Highnesses’<-

Stuttgart, 27 Sept. 1648.
Most humble and devoted servant.

->Greetings to the Overseer and the Tutor.<- <note>original: "Ephorus & Informator"; these were the specific titles for the high-ranking officials and teachers responsible for the Princes' education and supervision.</note>

### A Fable

### *Regarding the Household of the Christian Commonwealth.*

The Christian Commonwealth <note>original: "Res Christiana"; refers to the collective body of the Christian world or "Christendom."</note>, heavily afflicted from without by the stormy violence of raging Bellona <note>Bellona was the Roman goddess of war; here she personifies the Thirty Years’ War, which was reaching its conclusion in 1648.</note>, and further terrified by the all too atrocious threats of Atheism and Barbarism, thought it necessary to look about and explore more deeply what help and strength remained at home for her defense. Therefore, having instituted an inquiry into her own household by the light of grace—for the light of nature had long been clouded—and of conscience, so that she might [examine] all and every one of her domestics most deeply...

...to examine them, he set this task and appointed a day of inspection sacred to the Conception of Saint John the Baptist <note>This refers to a specific feast day in the liturgical calendar used as a deadline for the audit.</note>. The first of all to be examined was the **key-bearer of the house** <note>original: "domus claviger"; the steward or treasurer.</note>, a man of many words but few deeds. When he was ordered to bring forth the keys with which he might access and secure the Mistress’s <note>original: "Heræ"; referring to the personified Christian Commonwealth.</note> treasure, he had the one for opening ready at hand, but confessed that he had lost the one for locking through negligence. He claimed he thought it useless to keep under strict guard and anxious bolt those things which, through the habits of all, have now become public and commonplace.

The second to follow was the **Keeper of the Seal** <note>original: "Sigilli custos"</note>, who was privy to the secret counsel of the Mistress. He was a trifler of great arrogance <note>original: "magni supercilii nugator"; literally "a trifler of big eyebrows."</note>, who happened to be caught signing those papers they call **blanks** <note>original: "blancas"; white or empty documents signed in advance, often used for corrupt purposes.</note> and committing them to be sold at a low price to the clerk named **Dispensation** <note>original: "Dispensationi"; personifying the practice of selling exemptions from church laws or rules.</note>, thus betraying the very secrets of the house; the inquiry found him guilty of a sufficiently great fault.

Then the third was called: **Comus** <note>The Greek god of revelry, representing gluttony and excess.</note>, about whom the entire family had long complained, for he fed them meagerly while lashing them with the harshest words. He appeared pot-bellied and swollen with an immense nose <note>original: "sinaso"; likely a typo or variant for "naso."</note>; by the very mass of his body—a literal whirlpool—he would intercept and swallow down whatever was denied or withdrawn from the service of others. Having confessed, he was ordered to depart to the dining room.

Regarding the fourth, the **Prefect of the house**, there was better hope. He feigned a grave face in public, but otherwise his whole body was jingling <note>original: "tinnulus"; suggesting he was filled with the sound of hidden coins or bribes.</note>. When he was shaken out to see what he carried in his pocket, there were dice, playing cards <note>original: "folia lusoria"</note>, and other such trifles, which would dissolve a family rather than rule or correct it. Furthermore, he seemed to be in league with **the circumcised** <note>original: "recutitis"; a period pejorative for Jewish money-lenders.</note>, as evidenced by tablets of usury with which they corrupted the accounts of lawful revenue.

Almost the same was discovered in the fifth, the **Censor**, who appeared harsh in words and fierce with threats; yet, when it came to the matter at hand, it was clear he was merely acting the part of a stage-player and a buffoon in a play, having nothing less than the settled character required for discipline...

From there, we came eighthly **to the Actuary** <note>original: "actuarium"; a registrar or clerk.</note>, whose duty it is to note the Mistress’s <note>referring to the personified Christian Commonwealth.</note> sayings and deeds, then to prepare accounts of receipts and expenses, and to record them in the annals to be transmitted to posterity. In rendering accounts, he is entirely slippery and futile, as one who knows neither the Mistress’s gains nor her losses, nor distinguishes them, or perhaps hides them through fraud, making small things large and large things small at his own whim. Hence, ninthly, the **Revenue** <note>original: "Census"</note> was indeed collected and shut in cages, but cages so latticed that it either flowed out of its own accord or could be snatched by passersby. Truly, it yielded to no one less than to those to whom it was justly and deservedly owed; it most especially fattened the lazy and those full of fat, and the sustenance was hardly ever cast into the soil for a happy harvest. There remained, tenthly, the **Vernal Law** <note>original: "Lex verna"; likely referring to "domestic law" or a law treated like a household slave (*verna*), lacking authority.</note>, weak and spineless, the laughingstock of the household, who told the fables of the old world without any new example, and as often as he blamed faults committed, he was beaten. This ragged and aged fellow was more to be pitied than feared,

The rest of the household crowd—eleven in total—were nothing but cattle; in a word, they were a lazy *Davus* <note>A common name for a slave in Roman comedy, used here as a trope for a shiftless or deceptive servant.</note>. They were stronger in noise than in worthwhile work, and in voice rather than in labor. From this arose quarrels here, and collusions there; thefts on one side, and denunciations on the other; here sluggishness, there frantic activity; here hunger, there vomiting; here a pact, and there a betrayal. These and similar dissonant things were the result. Since the Cross of Christ, the subjection of reason, the restraint of the flesh, and the bridle of the tongue <note>original: "fræno linguæ"</note> had been cast out of the house, it is nearly a miracle that they have not already destroyed the management <note>original: "œconomiam"; the Greek-derived term for household administration</note> and recently overturned and undermined the very house along with its Mistress <note>original: "Hera"; likely personifying the Church or the Christian State</note>.

When the inspectors <note>original: "inquisitores"</note> had learned of these things and reported them in good faith to the Mistress, she very nearly fainted and breathed her last breath. But when she was revived by aromatic spices and returned a little to herself, dissolving into tears and wailing, and lacking both counsel and resources, she fled to the Wisdom and Mercy of GOD. She laid bare all the insults from without and the distresses from within her house; she entrusted everything to Him, and submitted all to be corrected and transformed. She did this so that she, who because of such a household was the most wretched of all and exposed to certain destruction, might—whether this household be changed or exchanged for another—be rendered the most fortunate and safe on earth: wealthy in resources, firm in defenses, peaceful in harmony, distinguished in morals, happy in character, proven in justice, and holy in religion.

# LETTER 319.
### Everlasting Greetings in Christ.
## Most Illustrious Princes, Lords
### by far most clement,

*The name of PEACE is sweet, after so many—alas—all too deceptive intervals, so many fleeting and winged joys. Now it is proclaimed everywhere, and may he be detestable who does not add his own applause to so great a gift, a gift for which all human thought is inadequate to estimate, and for which every mouth is like a child's and dull in celebrating. For the unique name of* Peace *embraces in a single word whatever is beautiful and desirable in temporal blessings.*

*But how I fear that we may receive* Peace, *as she returns to us, in unworthy ways; that we may manage her with poor reasoning; and that we may hold her by means that are not solid or constant, but rather crash against the old reefs of our previous evils. For 1. if the* cause of Religion <note>original: "Religionis causa"</note> *is at stake (as is indeed publicly boasted), I remember that once, in the height of a deep and long* Peace, *religion was most worn down by partisan zeal, depraved in its meaning, and split into sects. Thereafter, it was turned into a display of cleverness, adapted to veil immoral behavior, and employed to incite disturbances. I know not whether its sparks, lying hidden and smoldering under the ashes until now, will shortly erupt into an internal and deadly paper war* <note>original: "chartaceum bellum"; referring to the intense and often vitriolic pamphlet wars between different religious factions.</note>. *But if 2. the* goods of the Church <note>original: "bona Ecclesiæ"</note> *(as is indeed pretended) are to be claimed for the* nourishment of the Ministry, *the support of youth, and the use of the poor, it is surely to be hoped that we experience more restrained hands hereafter than before. In those days, the* property of Christ <note>original: "Christi peculium"</note>, *snatched from the lust and greed of the* Pope, *passed only to a different set of harpies* <note>In Greek mythology, Harpies were snatched-demons; here used to describe greedy officials who seized church assets for themselves.</note>, *who meagerly fed and spitefully supported those to whom that property was actually owed. Yet 3. we seek a home and nourishment for letters and the liberal arts, upon whom* Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war.</note> *had imposed exile everywhere. Because indeed those...*

<summary>Writing in 1648, the author celebrates the coming of peace but warns the ruling Princes that the end of the war may simply lead back to the religious factionalism and systemic corruption that plagued the Church and academia previously.</summary>

already long ago, it was more unlettered and more ignoble, more profane and more alien to Christ, more deformed, and more stained and contaminated by a monster of the most punishable sort, so that under the weeds <note>original: "loligine"; likely a variation of "lolium" (darnel), referring to the biblical parable of the tares among the wheat.</note> the Christian harvest was nearly choked to death. May a perpetual Peace assist us—a Peace that cultivates holiness and is the mother of a good posterity—and may she restore the cities to beauty, the fields to cultivation, shattered families to integrity, laws to their force, magistrates to authority and holiness, children to piety, servants to faithfulness, and all people to the worship of GOD, whose mercy adds what human weakness cannot provide. Thus we shall again be a benefit to ourselves, a protection to our allies, a terror to our enemies, but a wonder to all; and with GOD appeased, we ourselves shall be at peace among ourselves and be peacemakers, and we shall be called the children of GOD. These thoughts came to my mind, Most Illustrious Prince ANTON ULRICH <note>Anton Ulrich (1633–1714), later Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, a notable patron of the arts and author.</note>, regarding your interests and my own dream, being the ten conjectures written on this matter. *...if it were a clear sign of my affection, this could deter me from all further literary correspondence out of fear of wearying or nauseating You. I sent to* **Your Highness** *thirty-five letters last year—some quite talkative, if I do not admit they were trifles themselves—which You repaid with* **twenty-two** *of Yours, a truly rich yield if I judge by Your dignity. I would also greatly wish the same from the* **Illustrious** *pair of* **Your brothers**, **my most gracious Lords**, *as much as their more serious studies permit.*

*I am most distressed that* **Bellona** <note>The Roman goddess of war; here used as a personification of the Thirty Years' War.</note>, *hateful to us for so many years and the harshest of guests, has now turned toward You as well. For I do not agree with those who find relief in the companionship of misfortunes; rather, I am more afflicted when I see our evils pulled apart and spread through the borders of* **Germany**, *so that there is less room for a remedy. Yet I believe it will be a stimulus for You to enter into the methods of obtaining* **Peace** *with the same affection and effort of mind as we do, and to accept its more difficult conditions with a more composed spirit—but let the more prudent ones, whose concern this is, see to that matter. Indeed,* **History** *will one day testify, and posterity will detest, those through whom it happened that* **Peace** *did not take root for so long a time, and so much innocent blood was shed. Let us persist in prayers, and even if no other peace visits us again, let us embrace that which unites us to God and restores us to the tranquility of conscience.*

### LETTER 322.

-> *Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,* <-

Your letter of 5 January of *this new year* has been safely delivered to me. I give you my greatest thanks for your repeated kind wishes. There is no reason for you to give such great thanks for the letters I sent you last year. I, rather, not only approve and cherish <note>original: "exosculor", literally 'to kiss fondly', used here to show high regard</note> your letters, which always make me wiser, but I greatly desire they come frequently. And I wish—as I ought to wish—for you to understand, and thus to conclude regarding me, that your practice of writing is most pleasing to me, even if I am sometimes unable to respond to yours quickly, whether due to health or other obstacles. Therefore, I ask that you continue in this same duty of showing kindness this year, just as you did last year. The *matter of peace* <note>A reference to the negotiations for the Peace of Westphalia, which would eventually be signed later this year in October 1648</note>, which is being dragged out to the great detriment of our state <note>original: "Reipub.", meaning the public welfare or the Holy Roman Empire</note>, is truly something to be grieved and deplored. If God were favorable to us, and if those who ought to have the safety of Germany at heart and in their care would yield something of their rights (if they think they have any) out of love for their country and for harmony—which is not only useful but sometimes highly necessary—we would not be suffering. If only that single saying of Scipio <note>A famous Roman general; the quote is often attributed to him to emphasize the value of human life over military glory</note> were observed: *that he would prefer to save one citizen than to kill a thousand enemies—*

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
### My Most Merciful Lord,

I have received two of your letters at nearly the same time, for which I owe you double and the greatest thanks; however, time was so constricted that it was by no means possible to reply, owing to the most irrational concerns of Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war; a poetic reference to the chaotic state of affairs during the ongoing Thirty Years' War</note>, which throw into disorder and overturn all regular business. Meanwhile, I have sent to you the explanation of the Emblems <note>original: "Symbolorum"; these were artistic devices combining images and mottos to convey moral truths</note> which I prepared for you at the command of your Most Serene Lord Father, along with my prayer for a more auspicious year. I shall consider myself happy if I have captured your own mind’s sentiments, so that you may hereafter judge them worthy of being accepted as tokens of memory. Truly, I highly praise your noble resolution, by which you take upon yourself the weight and massive burden of your father’s virtues <note>original: "Virtutum Paternarum"</note>; I pray to Christ that He may allow this to be completed successfully and perfectly in every respect. Moreover, your prosperous successes give me confidence—good omens which I gather from the steps and progress you have already made and proven in your attentive imitation [of him]. May **GOD** never allow these steps to be halted or reversed, but always urge them forward.

But regarding your love for me, your judgment of me, and your care for me, what can I say without embarrassment? That you, a Most Illustrious Prince, born in such a station and gifted with these blessings of heaven, should so greatly uplift such a small man? But I shall attribute all this, as I ought, to my Christ, whom you venerate in the least of His little servants; you, in turn, are to be placed by Him among the greatest of His benefactors. For you also have this as an inheritance from your renowned father <note>original: "Incluto Patre"</note>: that you value what the world most despises, take up what it casts away, protect what it persecutes, and deem it your duty to cherish and nourish what it strips of its meager possessions—choosing to stand at the threshold of the court of God <note>original: "atrii Dei"; a reference to Psalm 84:10</note> rather than in the high palaces of the wicked...

## LETTER CCCXXV.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Illustrious*<-
->*Lord Doctor,*<-

ALthough I could understand your intention well enough from the diagrams <note>original: "Schematibus"; likely referring to draft sketches for heraldry or emblems</note> recently sent to me, your letter has taught me your meaning much more precisely. For this reason, your words are all the more welcome to me. I give you my greatest thanks for your most prompt compliance in devising our <term>Symbols</term> <note>These are "impresas" or personal emblems—symbolic images combined with a motto that were highly fashionable in the Baroque era to express a person's character or goals</note>. Indeed, they please me greatly both for their ingenious invention and their fitting consistency. For what, I ask, is more honorable than to come as close as possible to the most celebrated virtues of one's parents? What is more necessary than to seek counsel for our own and future affairs from the present actions of wise men, while paying attention to all things? Since *it is no less a virtue,* to speak with the Poet <note>original: "Poëtâ"; referring to the Roman poet Ovid in his work *The Art of Love*</note>, *to protect what has been acquired than it is to seek it out?* What is more worthy, or more useful, than to extend one's fame by diligently cultivating the fruits of one's genius? Finally, what is more praiseworthy than to extend the ancestral name through brave deeds? To this is added the fact that you seem to point quite clearly toward the mutual bond of **CONCORD**, and to remind us of it—and truly, what could be more greatly desired than this? Especially since, according to that saying of Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian often quoted in political contexts</note>, *through concord small things grow, but through discord even the greatest things fall apart.* As for the rest, from the innermost chamber of my heart I humbly pray **GOD** that He might deign to grant weight to your wish, and to direct all our actions to the glory of His name, the safety of many, and the stability of our Illustrious House. Farewell. Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherb."</note>, 15 February 1648.

*Your Reverend Dignity’s*
->*Most Devoted [Servant].*<-

### LETTER CCCXXVI.
## Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,
## Lord by far most merciful,

I see that *You have equipped Yourself with a most noble spirit for this year’s literary exercise <note>original: "literarium exercitium"; likely referring to a formal academic or courtly debate or a published exchange of intellectual essays common among the nobility</note> as well, a fact which I cannot explain how greatly it pleases me. For even if it could be observed by my mind how much I am inferior to You both in the brilliance of Style and the elegance of subject matter, nevertheless, provided it adds to Your glory and the advancement of Your studies, I gladly suffer this loss of my own reputation—a loss which You abundantly repay with the value of Your favor. But how much, according to the feelings of my own soul, you deplore in Your recent letters the postponement of that most longed-for Peace, the unjust delays after delays, the obstacles and the perplexities; and how You are incensed at those who seek their own glory through the destruction of so many provinces; wealth through the slaughter <note>original: "internecione"; a total or murderous destruction</note> of so many souls; the extension of borders through such great injury to neighbors; the price of benefit through such great shedding of innocent blood; the specter of liberty through the imposition of so harsh a yoke upon others; and the cause of Religion through such great loss and ruin of true religion—rendering themselves cursed to posterity.*

*But it must be believed that these things are permitted entirely by the indignation of God, who turns away from us and our affairs; for we, amidst our accumulated and heavy evils, grow harder and harder. We are so far from having softened hearts to return to Him from whom we have wandered, and from making Him favorable to us through true repentance and a solemn reformation of our conduct. I rejoice from my soul that You are in any way relieved and exempted from greater danger, and I pray with my whole heart that this safety may be long-lasting and perpetual. But above all, I pray that Your renowned House may be safe, that You Yourself may be safe, Most Illustrious Prince, and as You were born and given for the good of the Christian world, so may You survive for as long as possible. Farewell, and cherish Your Illustrious Highness's*

*Stuttgart, February 16, 1648.*
->*Most humble servant.*<-

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord by far most merciful,<-

That the emblem <note>In the 17th century, an "emblem" was a symbolic illustration accompanied by a motto and a short poem, used to convey a moral or philosophical lesson.</note> which I recently sent to You was to Your liking, and found the approval of *Your Serene Father* <note>original: "Serenissimi Dn. Patris Tui"</note>, is something for which I congratulate myself greatly and regard as a significant part of my good fortune. For neither could You have given, nor I have earned, a greater reward for my slight effort than that You graciously accepted this token of my Symbol <note>original: "Symboli"; likely referring to the specific allegorical theme or device chosen for the emblem.</note>, which witnesses in the *Temple of Memory* that I have held some place in Your esteem.

Truly, because You fashion Your whole self in imitation of Your best and greatest Father, I value You highly; and I pray from my heart that You may do and perfect this under the guidance of *CHRIST*, for You must consider how much weight lies upon You—as much as the difference between the precepts of virtue and the acts themselves—*so that You might express the actions of Your most praised Father, not so much by the attempt as by the work itself, and (that which even the Father himself would not envy) that You might surpass him; which, except by divine gift, You would never achieve.*

Therefore, following the example of Your Father himself, You will first need *Piety* <note>original: "Pietate"; here referring to the classical and Christian sense of duty toward God, family, and country.</note>, which is the primary virtue in him, so that by a favorable Divinity You may obtain all the rest which lead to the highest praise. This I shall procure for You through perpetual prayers, which I have never found to be in vain when used for the sake of His *Church* and the public welfare.

As for me, I shall consider it a glorious thing to have distinguished You with some mark of character, no less than once did that most famous *Knight Pierre Terrail, Lord of Bayard* <note>original: "Eques Petrus Terrailius Bajardus"; a legendary French knight known as "le chevalier sans peur et sans reproche" (the knight without fear and beyond reproach).</note>, *whom alone FRANCIS I, King of the French* <note>original: "FRANCISCVS I. Rex Galliarum"</note>, judged worthy to receive from him the ornaments and insignia of the *Order of Knighthood* <note>This refers to the historical event of 1515 where King Francis I insisted on being knighted by Bayard on the battlefield of Marignano.</note>. I shall be happy if one day I behold You not only as a fortunate *imitator of another's example, but as a perfect example for posterity itself.*

### LETTER CCCXXVIII.
### To the Very Reverend and Most 
### Renowned Sir Doctor,

I am glad that my letters, sent not long ago, were pleasing to you; for I have always considered it to be no small praise to have pleased learned men. Therefore, the more delightful your most recent letters were to me, the more prompt I have been in responding to them. First, however, I believe I can leave the opening section of your letter in silence, because my previous letters—which have doubtless already been delivered—were able to show you more than enough with what great joy the Symbols <note>original: "Symbola"; in this context, these are likely the intellectual concepts or mottos for an emblem book.</note> devised by you have overwhelmed me. As for my goodwill toward you, there is no reason for you to give thanks so extensively. Since I have learned both from my *Most Serene Father* and from the writings of wise men that those who have served the public good <term>public good: (original: "bono publico") the general welfare or common interest of society</term> are to be admired and honored. ### LETTER CCCXXIX.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->My Lord, by far most merciful,<-

How much I owe to Your Highness for the ease with which you accepted the suggestion of a certain Symbol <note>original: "Symboli"; in this context, a motto or intellectual concept for an emblem book</note> and its explanation, I have already frankly testified eight days ago. I do not think it needs to be repeated, lest I seem either to flatter You or to flatter myself. May Christ be present with favor under Your auspices and fulfill my prayers for You. Regarding the fact that You sent letters to the grandson of the once Great <term>Matthias Hafenreffer: (1561–1619) a prominent Lutheran theologian and professor at Tübingen, known for his work "Loci Theologici"</term>, who is of sacred memory to me, I have correctly seen to it. I wish that he might represent his grandfather as much in reality as he does in name; however, since he is known to me only by sight, it is not my place to pronounce judgment on him. In that man, however, all things were of the highest order: piety, learning, sincerity, moderation, and every excellent ornament found in a Theologian. I have often congratulated myself on having seen these qualities in person and having fixed them in my mind through household intimacy. On the other hand, it pained me to experience very different qualities in others of the same order <note>The author is likely contrasting the elder Hafenreffer's virtue with the behavior of other contemporary clergy or theologians.</note>. Therefore, I freely profess myself beholden to the family of a man who deserved so well of me; as he was once my father’s colleague and closest friend, he richly repaid me for whatever he acknowledged having received. To him I already owed much before this, because I was washed in the <term>baptismal font: (original: "lustrico fonte") the vessel used for the Christian rite of baptism</term> through his ministry. But it is necessary that the Grandson be worthy and fit for Your affairs; it is not for me to promise this, much less to guarantee it. Regarding what hope we have for peace...

### LETTER CCCXXXI.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Lord, by far most merciful,<-

I see that we are repeatedly doing the same: I, for my part, promising myself all the greatest and best things concerning You; You, on your part, confirming their trust to me with distinguished proofs and generous pledges. But now, held as if in a prison by the expectation and longing for peace <note>The Peace of Westphalia was being negotiated in 1648 to end the Thirty Years' War</note>, let us prepare for ourselves—as if in leisure and under cover—those instruments which, when brought into the light of men and into action, may serve not so much for utility as for praise and ornament among all people. 

Undoubtedly, the incredible prudence of your Most Serene Lord Father aims toward this; having detained you longer with him, he instructs you at home in those arts by which you might one day excel the rest of your peers abroad, and be an object of admiration to all (which is characteristic of your family). You will therefore bear any further delay more patiently, since with greater interest <note>original: "foenore"; used metaphorically for the "interest" or "profit" gained from time spent in study</note>, having been released a little later—and would that you were granted to us in these parts—you will bless the world of learning <term>res literaria: literally "the literary thing," referring to the international community of scholars and the pursuit of knowledge</term>.

May Christ grant this, He who [leads] you...

## LETTER CCCXXXIV.

### To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,

Your pious [reflections] <note>The Latin "Piæ Tuæ" likely refers to a gift of devotional writings or meditations.</note> concerning the passion of our Savior Jesus Christ have delighted us greatly. Indeed, we agree with you that nothing is more certain or more effective—whether for solidifying our faith or for shaping our lives—than the remembrance and constant pondering of that passion. 

I rejoice that your expectations of me are being more and more confirmed; I shall work diligently so as not to disappoint them. And although I cannot express my Illustrious **Lord Father** <note>original: "Dn. Parentem," referring to a high-ranking nobleman, likely a Duke of the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> to the life, nor represent him in every feature, I shall nevertheless strive with all my strength to sketch at least some image of him. It would be shameful indeed not to imitate such a great Father, and not to satisfy the expectations of so many good men. 

I therefore congratulate myself and declare it a happy thing to have been born to such a Father and to have been royally educated. To look upon him daily as a living example of virtue to be imitated is a blessing. Whatever he wishes to be decided regarding my future, I rightly commit to His Highness’s <note>original: "Cels." for "Celsitudo," a title of honor for princes.</note> wisdom and fatherly disposition, and I submissively subject myself to him. 

In the meantime, I earnestly pray to God, the Thrice Best and Greatest, that He may wish my Illustrious **Lord Father** to survive and remain safe for a very long time, and that He may bless your own prayers. Farewell. Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelph.", the Latinized name for Wolfenbüttel, the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick.</note>, 18 April, in the Year 1648.

->To Your Reverence,<-

->Most Devotedly.<-

## LETTER 335.

->*To the Very Reverend and Most Distinguished*<-
->*Lord Doctor,*<-

Your letters were very pleasing to me. Indeed, I saw in them your constant benevolence toward us, which you furthermore testified in your letters to my Most Serene Lord Father, while you are concerned for my safety because of my journey to the **Elector of Brandenburg** <term>one of the high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire entitled to elect the Emperor</term>, who is currently staying in **Belgium** <note>original: "Belgio"; at this time, the term often referred generally to the Netherlands or the Low Countries</note>, and truly not without reason. For, especially in this turbulent state of the **Republic** <term>original: "Reipub." for Respublica; here referring to the state or the general public welfare</term>, almost all travel is dangerous; and because of contemporary manners and the current custom of traveling, it ought to be forbidden by a most heavy edict, following the example of the **Chinese** <note>A reference to the isolationist policies of China during this era, which restricted foreign travel and influence.</note>. 

But truly, let the *Abuse* be removed, and let the *use* remain. Indeed, to examine the wonders of various nations, to soften rougher manners with the "file" of travel, to steep domestic rusticism in the "salt" of foreign civility and culture; finally, to strive to flee those **vices** one might have heard of or seen elsewhere; and on the contrary, to convert what one has noticed as **praiseworthy** into one's very lifeblood <note>original: "succum & sanguinem," literally "juice and blood," meaning to internalize something deeply</note>, so that, when the opportunity arises later, one can adapt these things to the affairs of one's own State with profit and grace—this I consider not only pleasant, but publicly and privately useful, indeed necessary, often yielding the greatest interest in glory and reputation. I shall not mention how much utility it brings for Leading Men to nourish and foster familiarity with their *equals and superiors*. 

Since, therefore, my Most Serene Lord Father has taken care that I be imbued with every kind of discipline from an early age, and especially that the **articles of faith** <term>the fundamental doctrines of the Church</term> and those things which concern eternal salvation be taught to me at home as diligently and exactly as possible...

# Letter CCCXXXIX.
## Very Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor,

I have well understood from your own letter dated August 30 that my letters are always welcome to you, and therefore I could not help but persevere in this duty toward you, always giving thanks for that affection with which you never fail to embrace me and my affairs. I hear with pleasure that our friend **Lentius** <note>Cyriacus Lentulus (1620–1678), a scholar and tutor mentioned on the previous page</note> was not "slow" <note>original: *lentum*; the author is making a play on words between the name *Lentius* and the Latin word for slow, *lentus*</note> in praising me; I hear this gladly because it is a sign of his extraordinary love toward me. However, I fear that since he has taken on the name of "Father," he has also put on a father's affection in such a way that he has indulged a father’s blind love more than the truth of the matter. Perhaps he has conceived greater things of me in his mind than I have actually performed in spirit and body. Therefore, I praise his love, and if he has exceeded the mark a little, I believe it is my duty to behave in the future in such a way that he may have something that he truly loves. Just as all elderly men who lead an upright life are to be held in the place of a Father, so he—who is great in my eyes both for his stainless years and his kindnesses—is easily worthy of that name. If, furthermore, the spirit I have brought to this **journey** <term>peregrinationem: a "peregrination" or educational tour through foreign countries, a common rite of passage for young nobles and scholars</term> is approved by you, I beg you to continue to commend it to GOD, so that it never [strays] from the right path...

## LETTER CCCXLV.

### Most Illustrious and Exalted Prince,
### Lord by far most Merciful,

I am very glad and congratulate you from my heart that you have been relieved of your illness; had I been certain of it—for no such thing had entered my mind—I would indeed have been consumed by the greatest sorrow. And while I believe your youthful vigor easily overcame it, and that medical aids were not lacking to you, nevertheless I have learned from sad examples that even over you [of high birth], unexpected death looms. 

As for me, since the feast of Christmas <note>original: "Natalis Christi".</note>, my own illness—after three years of affliction—treats me more mildly. If it continues to strike a truce with me, it would give hope of finally fulfilling my vow of traveling to you, unless the madness of Bellona <note>original: "Bellonæ rabies"; Bellona was the Roman goddess of war. This refers to the ongoing violence of the Thirty Years' War, which was in its final months in early 1648.</note> intervenes. 

For many years, two doctors have attended to my delicate constitution: one is *Abstinence*, the other is *Patience*. They are served by *recreation of the mind* and the *exclusion of cares and noise*. By their service, I support and sustain the weak frame of my body, until the collector of Nature’s debt <note>A common early modern metaphor for Death, who eventually "collects" the life that nature "loaned" to a person.</note> summons me to court—and the later he does so, the more fiercely he will demand it. 

May a merciful Christ long preserve you for your House and for the affairs of Germany; may He allow both this present year and the many to follow to flow happily, and lead you to the highest peaks of Virtue. With this wish proceeding from a heart devoted to you, since I am by no means able to repay you otherwise, I return thanks for your singular affection toward me, ready to perform whatever duty lies within me, however small—

## LETTER CCCXLVII.
->*Prosperous fortune!*<-

Your pleasing testimony of affection through your letters, <term>Most Distinguished Sir</term> <note>original: "Vir Cl." / "Vir Clarissimus," a standard honorific for a scholar</note>, contained this one unpleasant thing: that it came from one who was unwell. But I am uniquely consoled by the longed-for remission of that illness, which is no small sign of full recovery; just as I pray for this from my heart, so I wish it to be permanent. You say most truly that even a vigorous age, such as we currently enjoy, is never immune to these evils and ailments—indeed, never free from the danger of life itself. For just as every sky has its clouds and its changes, so too does our life, and every stage within that life; this cycle of evils, returning to every age, will continue as long as the world <note>original: "orbis"; the author uses a play on words, comparing the "circle" or cycle of recurring illness to the "orb" of the earth</note> itself endures. Thrice happy and more are those who know remedies and other ready aids for these sicknesses...

...to be honored by me at some time with some service or not unwelcome gift. Moreover, I am pleased by a clever saying in the *Travels of Illustrious Youth* <note>original: "Peregrinatione illustris Juventutis"</note> by the most famous Justus Lipsius <note>A renowned Flemish humanist and philosopher (1547–1606) whose works on Stoicism and politics were widely influential</note>, which I am not reluctant to write down here: Just as farmers who have nurseries are accustomed to transplant young stocks, and to move them from their native soil into another, so that they may grow more broadly and freely; so it is not right for children to grow sterile while fixed to their birth soil, but having been moved from one place to another, they should take on strength and increase, and grow up in virtue. Yet I do not advise that this absence be too long: but just as those who seek fire in the neighborhood do not sit down there, but having received it, return home and kindle it there; so I believe they should seek sparks and kindling among foreigners, then light them at home, and shine for themselves and others. Meanwhile, my letter has grown, by which I have gone about expiating the fault of my long silence as best I could, unless perhaps I have contracted another fault of talkativeness. Farewell, most Illustrious Prince, and may you one day illuminate even foreign shores with your light; may Christ increase that immeasurably.
