### LETTERS OF THE YEAR 1648. LETTER 355.

->Very hearty greetings!<-

I do not know by what intuition of the soul you so greatly desire my presence at your **Illustrious University of Tübingen** <note>original: "Illustri Vestra Tubingensi," referring to the university in Württemberg where Andreae was educated and which remained a center of Lutheran scholarship</note>, since everything that could perhaps be argued in favor of this is completely unknown to me. In this current age, nothing is better or more useful than to assist the development of minds and diligently provide everything that can lead to their well-being. For as I have lived, I have seen the "dregs" of this era <note>likely a reference to the social and moral exhaustion at the end of the Thirty Years' War in 1648</note>; yet that initial rawness of nature must be purged so that it may shine with pure colors. Whether this can be achieved more safely and easily through external remedies is a matter for those "curators of intellects" <note>referring to tutors or educational reformers</note> who have learned these things through use and experience; I commit the whole matter to their judgment and estimation. 

I see that you are greatly delighted by the frequency of my letters. I would write them more often, were it not for the respect I have for your person and your high office <note>original: "provinciae," referring to the recipient's administrative or territorial responsibilities</note>. I do not wish to constantly disturb you or interrupt when you are distracted by business pressing in from all sides. However, we would not want to measure our mutual affection by such common duties; we have sunk that affection deeper into our souls than to require such light supports for its stability. 

Our beloved brother ***Rudolph Augustus*** <note>Rudolf August, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1627–1704)</note>, as we have learned, still enjoys good health. I commend him, as I do all of us, to divine protection with most fervent prayers. 

**Wolfenbüttel** <note>original: "Guelpherbyti"</note>, July 16, 1648.

To Your Excellence,

->Most devoted.<-

## EPISTLE 357.

->Greatest greetings!<-

I wish, **Most Distinguished Man**, that I had fulfilled the duty for my brothers and myself as well as you write that I have diligently upheld it. For I, a minor writer, know my own insignificance, and I have never believed myself suitable enough to take up the tasks of others. However, since I understand that this light and humble exchange of letters is not unwelcome to you, I will continue now to perform my part. I believe that this kind of writing serves as the bricks or mortar <note>original: "laterculorum aut calcis"</note> in stabilizing the supports of my studies, rather than merely being a gesture of friendship.

I will remind my beloved brother, **Rudolph Augustus** <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704), who later became the Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note>, through letters to send both you and me more frequent correspondence in the future, although I suspect he has been somewhat hindered by the usual courtly commotions. I hear that not long ago, the infant son of the **Elector of Brandenburg** <note>Frederick William, the "Great Elector"</note> was initiated there into the most holy Christian rite <note>baptism</note>, where the words of **Psalm 132, verses 11 and 12** <note>These verses concern God’s promise to David to place his descendants upon his throne, a common theme for royal baptisms</note> were explained in the sermon. What other noteworthy events have occurred, I shall be able to write to you on the next occasion, God willing.

**Lord von Lent** will deliver my greetings and respects to you in person. He set out from here for **Strasbourg** <note>original: "Argentoratum"</note> about two weeks ago to take up an inheritance, I believe, which came to him upon the death of his father-in-law. He will visit you, **Most Distinguished Man**, on his return, as he has other business to attend to at your court. Farewell, and continue to love him who loves you. **Wolfenbüttel** <note>original: "Guelp."</note>, **August 8, 1648.**

->To the **Most Distinguished Man**,<-
->Most Devotedly.<-

### YEAR 1648. LETTER 358.

### ->Wishing you every success!<-

Your recent letters have shown me clearly how diligently you still maintain your old habit of supporting and advancing my studies, and how much you still desire my presence, which we have both so often hoped for. Indeed, I must take no small care to prove myself worthy of such great affection and to remain mindful and grateful for your friendship. Would that a late evening might finally come when I could show you my affection in person—an affection I currently keep, as it were, in secret—and bring it into the clear light of day, so that your long-held wishes might at last be fulfilled. 

I have no doubt of the readiness and zeal you have always shown toward me. Why should I fear that one who has never denied his goodwill to anyone, and who has judged even those without formal learning <note>original: "illiteratos"</note> to be worthy of his friendship, would reject me? On the contrary, it is usually the case that those who excel most in intellectual gifts <note>original: "ingenii dotibus," referring to natural talent or scholarly merit</note> feel a deep bond with those who admire and love those same qualities. 

In the meantime, I have received no letters from our brother **Rudolph Augustus** <note>Rudolf August (1627–1704), the eldest son of Duke Augustus the Younger, who would eventually become the Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note> to inform me of the situation in that place. It is not clear to me what might be preventing him from writing. Meanwhile, I wish you the very best of health. **Wolfenbüttel** <note>Latin: "Guelpherbyti," the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg</note>, August 22, 1648.

To your Distinguished Self,
->Most devoted.<-

### LETTER CCCLIX.
->Many greetings and well-wishes!<-

**Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,**
->Lord most gracious by far,<-

Although I have not yet received any letters from You, I am mindful that I am in your debt <note>original: "in ære Tuo," literally "in your copper," a Latin idiom for being in someone's debt</note> and owe you a letter. I have poured out these lines to testify how much I long for yours, and perhaps to lure them out with my own untimely words rather than by bringing anything of great weight. I shall write, therefore, what I saw in a dream—whether because my imagination was burdened and filled with our daily thoughts of PEACE, or perhaps informed by that Drama of yours, performed four years ago in the ancestral Hall, and now finally printed and skillfully rendered with copper-plate engravings. This is how I seemed to see it:

After a sad and horrid silence and thick clouds, **Expectation** stepped forward, her eyes raised upward and her hands folded in prayer, a herald of good news. Following closely behind her was **Penance** <note>original: "Pœnitentia"</note>, dressed in black <note>original: "pulla," the color of mourning</note>, her face cast down toward the earth and her fist beating her breast. At her side was her sister **Amendment** <note>original: "Emendatio," or Improvement</note>, wearing a white robe and a more upright countenance. 

Next followed **Concord** and **Acquiescence**, entwined in each other's arms, repeatedly confirming a treaty between them with joined hands. And then appeared, with a face more majestic than a human's, the **Reconciliation of GOD**, showing in his hand a diploma <note>a formal charter or decree</note> granting remission of both guilt and punishment. Joined with him was the **Blessing of GOD**, pouring out abundance from a horn of plenty.

Afterward walked **Religion** in a purple garment, holding out the face of Truth and explaining the written Word. With her was her companion **Discipline**, the bearer of the cross, restrained by a bridle; to these were joined **Faith** and **Charity**, with the handmaidens **Work** and **Duty** added to the procession. 

Then indeed **Germany** <note>represented as a personified woman, a common motif during the Thirty Years' War</note> raised herself up; she was pale indeed and bloodless, not adorned according to her high dignity, but she whose eyes until now...

### LETTER 360.

I say that this <term>Ecclesiastical Ordinance</term> <note>original: "Institutum Ecclesiasticum"; these were legal frameworks used by German states to reorganize church life and education after the chaos of the Thirty Years' War</note> in your diocese is as highly necessary as it is useful for establishing the sincerity of ministers and the holiness of life. ## LETTER 361.
-> Sending many greetings. <-

If there were nothing else for me to do today, Most Illustrious and Most High Prince, most clement Lord—indeed, whatever other business there might be—I would make this my primary task: to congratulate you on your 16th birthday, and to offer prayers to God the Best and Greatest that it may dawn happily for you. *This is for you a stepped year <note>original: "annus scalaris"; a metaphorical "ladder year" representing a significant transitional point in growth</note>; I pray that just as it is a year of youthful age, so may it be one of progress in every kind of virtue and discipline. It is, in an arithmetic series, the beginning of the sixth <note>The author is likely counting the years of the Prince's second decade (10+6)</note> following fifteen revolutions of the Sun <note>original: "Solis revolutiones"; a common 17th-century way to describe years based on the solar cycle</note>, and to be finished at your 21st, along with six other happy and auspicious years. It is the fourth in a double proportion <note>A geometric progression of 2 (2, 4, 8, 16). The author uses the mathematical properties of the number 16 to wish the Prince a long life by doubling the numbers</note>, to which may a merciful GOD add a fifth, the 32nd year of your age—indeed, a fifth of 64 and a sixth of 128, beyond which I would dare to pray...*

->Very many greetings!<-

There is no doubt, **Most Distinguished Man**, <note>original: "Vir Cl." for *Vir Clarissime*, a standard respectful address for scholars and officials</note> that you have dreamed of heavy matters. To explain these properly, I should not be summoned, but rather someone else from *Parnassus* <note>Mount Parnassus was the mythological home of the Muses; the author implies the dream requires a poet or a divinely inspired interpreter</note>, one well-drunk from the *Castalian* waters <note>The Castalian Spring provided inspiration to those who drank from it</note>, who might know how to interpret these things more clearly and with words worthy enough. However, to show what my own feeling is regarding this, I think I will not differ much from your own view if I say that all these things concern the state of our fatherland—partly the past, and partly also the present and the future—how it has been prepared, and how it must yet be prepared. There are some who say that dreams otherwise ought not to be cared for, since they often deceive many and are accustomed to stir the mind with false visions. But I would dare to gather from this that peace is the last thing to be expected by us now <note>original: "nihil minus jam quàm pacem," implying that peace is currently far out of reach</note>, even though that merciful **GOD**, in His immense kindness, can grant us even more than we have deserved. For what and how great is the series of those things that ought to precede peace? Amendment of life, Harmony, Faith, Truth, Sincerity, and others of this kind; we can hardly boast that even a shadow of these has been seen among us for a long time. Therefore, unless these things present themselves to us first (just as they did previously to your mind) and open the path like heralds with a more certain footstep, that nourishing **Peace** we have so often longed to embrace is unlikely to follow. How gladly we would wish that monster of <term>Bellona</term> <note>Bellona was the Roman goddess of war; here she represents the devastation of the Thirty Years' War</note> bound to those furthest columns <note>A reference to the Pillars of Hercules, the perceived end of the known world</note>, and if anything lies further still, so that our land—shaken and almost overturned by her horrendous tumults—might be restored for a little while and enjoy a certain tranquility

### LETTER CCCLXIII.

->*Many greetings.*<-

I embrace you in turn with an even more passionate affection, **Distinguished Man**, the more religiously you fulfill your vows <note>In this context, "vows" refers to prayers or well-wishes offered on a specific occasion.</note> for my birthday. How long the Supreme Ruler of all things <note>God</note> wishes to extend my life is all the same to me; although there are others to whom this light and the breath of this sky seem so pleasant (especially at this age) that they would rather have their days prolonged beyond the limits of human knowledge than circumscribed by such a short course. I am glad to hear that **Lucas Cranach** <note>Lucas Cranach the Elder (1472–1553), a celebrated German Renaissance painter and printmaker.</note>, that most celebrated painter of all time, was born at the same time of year as I was many years ago. I possess several of his engravings <note>original: "cælaturas," referring to woodcuts or copperplate engravings.</note>, though of different types, and I am still anxiously searching for more. He was, unless I am mistaken, the very same man whom **Philip Melanchthon** <note>A key leader of the Protestant Reformation and collaborator of Luther.</note>—a man who deserved the very best from our Germany—writes was present at the wedding of the **Blessed Luther** <note>Martin Luther's marriage to Katharina von Bora in 1525; Cranach was a close friend of Luther and served as a witness.</note>. Melanchthon cites him in testimony of this matter in a Greek letter to **Camerarius** <note>Joachim Camerarius, a noted classical scholar and friend of Melanchthon.</note> (on page 33 and page 114).

Dr. Müller <note>Likely Johannes Müller (1598–1672), a prominent Lutheran theologian and pastor in Hamburg.</note>, a preacher in Hamburg, in his little book which he published not long ago, wrote against our adversaries, who were severely criticizing the doctrine, life, and character of *Luther*. Farewell; and since I was somewhat busy yesterday, I send only a greeting for now, but soon you will also have a response from my Master brother. Written in haste on the last day of October, 1648.
Yours, Cl.

I owe very much to you, who have acted in the stead of [others], and I ask in a greater way that no weariness from the writing creeps over you, so that one may more leisurely supply the business of the other.

We join you in making common vows for the fruits of the Peace so long desired—fruits more flavorful than those we are tasting at present <note>The Peace of Westphalia had been signed in October 1648, but its practical benefits were not yet felt by a war-weary population.</note>. It is in vain for us to expect a "Golden Age" while the Colossus of Monarchies <note>original: "Monarchiarum Colosso." This is a biblical allusion to the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar in the Book of Daniel, describing an empire with feet of iron and clay, destined to collapse.</note> is already nodding with its feet mixed of iron and clay, and threatening a ruin which we should fearlessly await as a sign of the approaching eternal Peace. Those who dream otherwise seem to me to do the same as those who, in decrepit old age, promise themselves the strength of rejuvenation, health, eagerness, and cheerfulness. Let us rather believe that our affairs are fragile, even now falling, and soon to collapse along with this very Universe; and with heads lifted high, let us await the coming of our Lord the Liberator.

I pray from my heart that this passing year may flow out happily for you, your Brothers, and your Most Serene House, and that another year follows, far more happy and abounding in all good things; and I bid you farewell.

->To Your Illustrious Highnesses<-
Stuttgart, 20 December 1648.

### V.
## With Prince
## FERDINAND ALBERT.
### LETTER CCCLXVIII.

->*A most happy omen for the new year.*<-

It was out of the sorrow of my heart, Distinguished Sir <note>original: "Vir Cl." abbreviating "Vir Clarissime," a standard respectful address for a scholar or person of high standing.</note>, that I have sent no letters to you for some time, and otherwise did not see what was of great importance to be written. For that reason, I deferred this small task until a moment of slightly more relaxed leisure; and I did so with all the more confidence because I was frequently sitting by my beloved brother and recalling his poor health to my grieving mind. Now, however, setting aside all excuses <note>original: "seclusis ambagibus"; literally "with circumlocutions set aside."</note>, I am discharging my debt and responding briefly to your three letters. I have seen and read all that you promised to do for my sake. These are certainly exceptional proofs of your love and goodwill toward me, which shall make me most ready for every kind of service in return. Indeed, it is the true characteristic of the great not to be born so much for themselves as for others, and to consult the utility of their own people rather than their private interests; just like a tree heavy with fruit, which lowers its branches and invites others to pluck from them. I pray to GOD, in whom and from whom all health and safety <term>salus</term> <note>The Latin "salus" encompasses both physical health and spiritual salvation.</note> proceeds, that He may keep you safe and sound for a long time for the public good and the benefit of others, for whom you were born. Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti."</note>, 11 January 1648 <note>original: "III. Idus Ianuarii"; using the Roman calendar, the 3rd day before the Ides of January.</note>.

### LETTER 369.

-> *May fortune be favorable!* <-

I could hardly say that a day has passed, Distinguished Sir <note>original: "Vir Cl." abbreviating "Vir Clarissime," a traditional honorific for a renowned scholar or person of high status.</note>, in which you have not most frequently come to mind, you who hold me so bound to you by so many and various types of study. Nevertheless, my respect for you was so great that I did not wish to stubbornly interrupt your very heavy occupations on my own, or to cause you delay with my interruptions. But at last, my affection has conquered, so that I now add my own letter to that of my most beloved brother and, as it were, accompany it. For I burn with the desire to practice my skills and to most abundantly compensate for whatever has been neglected by me until now in the way of love and respect; although I am not unaware that the love of both of us is hardly so weak that it needs to be fostered by more frequent conversations through letters. Therefore, Distinguished Sir, I hope you will interpret this ardor of mine in the best light, and if you find any spare time <note>original: "subcisivi temporis," literally "time cut off" or "stolen time," referring to moments of leisure between official duties.</note>, you might kindly grant it to me in the future as well. Farewell. *Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti," the Latin name for the ducal residence of the House of Brunswick.</note>, on the Kalends of February [February 1st], 1648. *If you prefer this, I certainly praise you. ### LETTER 376.

#### To the most longed-for good fortune!

Indeed, you strive excellently for my well-being and benefit, Distinguished Sir, you who let no suitable time pass without shaping my youth toward Virtue and all the best things with your most faithful precepts and warnings. But what do I do? The same as the bees: I gather and store the liquid honey of your teaching, which I go to harvest through the pleasant meadows of your most elegant letters—hardly a slight delight for my studies, which draws me toward higher things more powerfully than a **Magnet** draws iron! For it can hardly be otherwise than that, by ingratiating myself into the familiarity of the most learned, I receive their gifts into myself by a silent and gentle flow, as it were, or depart from them increased in some way—just as those who walk through the Sun either change their color or at the very least feel its burning heat. Farewell, and love me in turn as I love you. From our beloved <term>Instructor</term> <note>original: "Informatore." As on the previous page, this refers to a private tutor or governor.</note> I add many greetings to you—

### LETTER 377.

->Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,<-
->Most Merciful Lord,<-

*If my eloquence in teaching were as great as your readiness to learn, I would surely write to you both more frequently and more fully, because I understand that you are not only bearing with my letters, but are even moved by them. For although you abound at home with both the precepts and the examples of Virtue, and you lack neither mute <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for books.</note> nor speaking Teachers for every preparation of Learning, you nevertheless love my instructions, such as they are—certain, if I am not mistaken, that they proceed from one who, if less than learned, is surely most respectful of you and most dedicated to your interests. I write, therefore, not so much driven by your command as enticed by the inclination of your most noble mind toward me. I gently soothe your character <note>original: "ingenium," referring to his natural disposition or talent.</note>—from which I expect no mediocre light, but a truly great one—with precepts of piety and modesty; for those things which are most excellent by nature stand in the greatest need of instruction. We see this in the example of the most noble [animals], who, although they are high-spirited and sharp, become most useful and excellent if they are tamed from an early age; but if they are left untamed, they become most headstrong and wicked. For even if Virtue takes certain impulses from nature, Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> says it must nevertheless be perfected by instruction. And Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> says: Fiery and burning spirits grasp nothing slight or meager, but that vigor is imperfect, just as in all things which, without art, [proceed from] their own [nature]...*

*The more informal letter I promised, most flourishing Prince, I now deliver. It is not born of more elegant material, nor is it groomed with a sharper style, but it is the sort of familiar and extemporaneous letter you yourself requested. For so it is: we are not doing anything serious when we exchange nearly the same things—namely, You expressing affection for me, and I expressing the highest respect of mind.*

### Excerpts
# OF THE
## Royal French Catechism.

->I.<-

1. Just as nursing women provide guidance and protection for tender limbs to form and strengthen their steps and prevent them from falling, so do Guardians <note>original: "Ephori"</note> provide this for youthful minds; with vigilant care, they ensure that they do not go astray or stumble too often.
2. Beasts are driven by blows, restrained by jagged bits <note>original: "lupatis": a type of horse bit with sharp, tooth-like edges used for breaking stubborn horses</note>, and terrified by shouting. Noble characters, however, are to be ruled by words, invited by examples, and enticed by kindness.
3. Those who are in a more eminent rank should know themselves to be men, and Christians, and Princes.

...humans, so that they know nothing human is foreign to them and learn to endure the common lot. Christians, so that they never forget paternal charity in Christ and the common fellowship and inheritance in heaven. Princes, so that they know themselves to be God's vicars <note>The Latin "vicarios" implies those acting in the place of God to maintain order and justice.</note> on earth and guardians of His law, whose image it is a sacrilege to stain with vices.

4. God Himself clearly expressed the necessity of fraternal harmony in the structure of the human body, whenever He entrusted the operation of a single sense to twin organs. For neither do eyes see correctly unless they aim at the same object, nor do ears hear distinctly unless both attend to one sound, nor does one hand perform its duty correctly and conveniently without the help of the other, and if one foot moves back while the other moves forward, the body would undoubtedly come to a standstill.

5. The holy ethereal Spirit is not a savage and fierce hawk, nor a foul raven gasping over rotting corpses, but a dove, conspicuous for its whiteness, gentleness, and temperance; from this, it must be discerned by what spirit a person is ruled.

6. It is an unworthy thing that those who, coming from the class of cobblers <note>original: "Cerdonum": specifically low-born manual laborers or shoemakers, used here to denote those of low social birth.</note>, and who for some time associated with camp-followers <note>original: "lixas": servants or sutlers in a Roman army camp.</note> and soldiers' servants <note>original: "calones": low-ranking servants or drudges.</note> and became known for cruel examples, are freely received and recognized when inserted into the knightly order. Yet it is not so for those who have shone with the praise of Wisdom and Prudence and for their public utility in the Republic; instead, they are clearly allowed to wither in neglect.

7. Beware, Prince, of being carried away by <term>Philautia: Excessive self-love or conceit; a Greek term frequently used in moral philosophy.</term>, for whoever praises you to your face unseasonably and more than is fair, is laying a trap or seeking a gift he does not deserve; it is unseemly to be ensnared by such a one.

8. Let sudden anger <note>original: "excandescentia": a quick-burning or flaring passion.</note> be far from Princes,

## Agapetus the Deacon
### On the Duty of the Prince to 
### Justinian the Emperor.

1. Under GOD, rule yourself and your people.
2. Be a watchful pilot of the ship. <note>A common metaphor comparing the state to a ship and the ruler to its captain or "nauclerus".</note>
3. To know yourself is to know GOD.
4. The birth of every person is but mud. <note>A reminder of the shared, humble physical origins of all humans, regardless of rank.</note>
5. As an image of GOD, be grateful.
6. Since you can do all things, wish for nothing but what is right.

33. Neither be puffed up by your high position <note>original: "apice," literally the summit or the tip of a crown</note>, nor be crushed by the weight of your burdens.
34. Gold is the same in every shape. So should be the soul of a Prince. <note>This implies that a ruler's character should remain consistent and pure regardless of the circumstances.</note>
35. To rule over those who follow willingly is a secure empire.
36. Let reason be just as angry with your own faults as it is with the faults of others.
37. An emulator of God is closest to Him in mercy.
38. Doing good <note>original: "Beneficentia"</note> is the best and most lasting treasure.
39. To treat the worthy and the unworthy in the same manner is an unworthy thing.
40. Humanity brings one close to God; inhumanity is closest and most similar to wild beasts.
41. Let the scale of Justice <note>original: "Iustitiæ lanx"</note> neither tip in favor of friends nor be used to deceive enemies.
42. The truth of a matter must be unearthed with great care.
43. Just as you will never leap over the shadow that walks before you, so you will never fully grasp the works of God.
44. Wealth is truly gathered by giving it away rightly; wealth that is badly hoarded melts away.
45. Being full of good things, you should do good for many people.
46. As the eye is to the body, so the Prince is given as a provider for his world.
47. If you harm no one, you are safe; if you are a benefactor to many, you are by far the safest.
48. Be formidable in power but lovable in goodness; let your love not make you lowly, nor your judgment make you terrifying.
49. Let your deeds harmonize with your words, and you will obtain whatever you command.
50. The pious who offer holy prayers for you return your gifts to them in great abundance.

51. Just as the Sun revives the earth, so a Prince refreshes and warms the unfortunate with his light.
52. A kingdom brings honor to some, but happy is he who himself brings honor to the kingdom.
53. It is of little value to excel in power unless one also surpasses others in Virtue.
54. Consider first, then command; for there is no greater danger than a hasty tongue.
55. It is fitting for a Prince to be ready for everything, yet slow to anger.
56. Pay close attention to those you keep near you, whether they are faithful or deceitful.
57. Either learn for yourself, or learn from others and then put it into practice.
58. Mercy and generosity are the walls of the Empire, surrounded by the towers of the people's prayers.
59. He who is a Father through love and a Prince through authority holds a stable empire.
60. There is no finer royal purple than the garment <note>original: "stola"</note> of fatherly love toward the poor.
61. The more you have received from God, the greater a debtor you are to Him.
62. All people need God's protection, but a Prince has the greatest need of all.
63. Since you yourself are in need of God’s grace, learn to bestow it upon others.
64. Since you are a sinner yourself, forgive those who do wrong.

66. For a private citizen, the disgrace is to commit evil; for a Prince, the disgrace is to fail to do good.

71. A Prince comes from the earth, and from the Prince, earth will come again. <note>A reminder of mortality: the ruler is made of dust and will return to dust.</note>
72. Let the ladder of life and honors find its end in heaven.

## LETTER 385.

->Greatest greetings!<-

You do everything for my sake with such effort and ease, **Distinguished Sir** <note>original: "Vir Cl." / Vir Clarissimus, a standard honorific for a scholar or person of high standing</note>, that I do not see how I can ever repay the debt. You write to me often—is there anything else to say?—most kindly and elegantly. You recently sent those items which, if I recognize them correctly, though they may have been written for *Kings* or others, I say apply perfectly to me as well. They will be like precepts to me, according to which I shall study to shape and conform my life's path; or they will provide material for translating into the German language and from there back into Latin; or whatever utility can be drawn from them, I shall convert into my very sap and blood. 

You previously included a portrait of a certain *Baron Jörger* <note>likely Johann Septimius Jörger von Tollet, a nobleman known for his artistic interests</note>, by whose skillful hand, if I remember correctly, I saw something inserted into our Tutor's *album* <note>original: "albo," referring to an "Album Amicorum" or book of friends, common among 17th-century students and scholars for collecting signatures and art</note>. In the middle were the coat of arms of that family, which Pallas <note>the goddess Athena</note> with her spear held from the left, while on the right was Jörger himself sitting upon a horse. Everything was most skillfully engraved in copper, and others with us could not admire it enough. Nature has indeed equipped some with such excellent gifts of this kind, while on the contrary one finds many so crude and unskilled that even when trained for a long time by the work of instructors, they cannot achieve even the slightest thing. We would like to know whether he drew this likeness with his own hand or used the work of another. 

Farewell, and continue to love the one you once judged worthy of your kindness and zeal.
At Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti"</note>, October 10, 1648.

->To Your Reverence<-

->Most Devotedly.<-

### LETTER 386.

*Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir,*

What I recently promised, I now fulfill in good faith; would that it were with some pleasing interest <note>original: "fœnore," a financial metaphor for paying back a debt with interest</note> that might lighten the obligation I owe you, and cheer you, who are perhaps weary of this long delay. You so little dread death that you write of it without any disturbance of mind—and, I believe, without even a change in your expression—plainly showing that you count it as a gain <note>The author alludes to the biblical sentiment in Philippians 1:21, "to die is gain"</note>. I confess that it is the mark of a Christian to thus steady one's soul against that final goal. Indeed, those who have reached it can boast that they have at last completed the stormy journey of this life; freed from all the miseries that usually accompany us in this world, they attain a far greater happiness—one bounded by no limits, which they may enjoy in eternal and untiring joy. 

Yet, while many can be found for whom the passage to this state is easy, there are also many who tremble at this manner of passing with every fiber of their being and their innermost senses. This is true especially for those whose blood still boils <note>original: "ebullit sanguis," a common 17th-century medical and philosophical idiom for the vitality and heat of youth</note> and who suffer more harshly under the rule of Nature, which recoils from its own destruction. We, however, separate ourselves from such people, and with a tempered longing, we always await the divine will. 

Written at Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti," the Latin name for this prominent German ducal residence and center of learning</note>, November 14, 1648.

->To Your Distinguished Self,<-

Most devotedly.

# Most Illustrious and High Prince
## My most merciful Lord,

*You say that you are paying a debt to me when you actually owe me nothing; I, however, am a great debtor and quite slow to pay. Yet now, through your elegantly and sincerely written letters, I find satisfaction for my own soul. I shall do what is currently possible, if not as much as I might wish, and I give you great thanks for that kindness with which you have repeatedly shown me favor. I ask you most earnestly not to weary yourself on my account in the future. As for the presence of mind you seem to attribute to me as I gaze more closely at Death—although it is only right that my advanced age should be prepared for it by both lessons and examples—nonetheless, I would not wish to claim even a tiny bit of credit for myself if the Divine hand were absent. Only under His guidance is it possible to pass through the dark and shadowy valley* <note>The author is alluding to the famous imagery of Psalm 23:4, "the valley of the shadow of death."</note> *to the longed-for light of heaven and to look upon the joyful face of our Savior Jesus. It is indeed a cause for shame to us that the pagans of old, though they were spiritually blind, often met death with such constancy of mind—even though they either did not know where they were going or what good they could expect, or at the very least were in great doubt. Yet we, who are certain of the good things to come, still tremble and shrink from such a desirable change. But since it is safest to depend on Christ alone, the conqueror and creator of death, let the glory of that happy calling and peaceful departure* <note>original: "placidae resolutionis," a common 17th-century term for a calm death</note> *remain entirely His; for us, the duty of persistent prayer and a ready mind remains.* But these things are perhaps too somber for one of your age. Nevertheless, the Wisest of Kings <note>The author refers to King Solomon, traditionally considered the author of the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note> nudges us thus: *Revere God himself and observe his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man* <note>original: "DEVM ipsum reverere, & præcepta ipsius observa, quia hoc est totum hominis," quoting Ecclesiastes 12:13.</note>; for every work God [will bring into judgment...]

### LETTER CCCLXXXVI.

*Reverend and most Distinguished Sir,*

What I recently promised, I now discharge in good faith—would that it were with some pleasing interest, which might relieve me of my obligation and cheer you, who are perhaps weary of the long delay. You so little dread death that you write of it without any disturbance of mind, or even, I believe, of expression; you clearly show that you count it as gain <note>original: "eam à Te in lucro poni." This is an allusion to the Apostle Paul’s words in Philippians 1:21: "To die is gain."</note>. I confess that this is the mark of a Christian: to so steady one's soul against that final goal. For those who have reached it can boast that they have at last traversed the turbulent journey of this life. Freed from all the miseries that usually accompany us in this world, they attain a happiness bounded by no limits, which they may enjoy in eternal and untiring joy. While one may find many for whom the transition to this state is easy, there are also very many who tremble at this manner of passing with every fiber of their being and their innermost senses—especially those in whom the blood still boils <note>The author uses the "boiling blood" as a metaphor for the vitality of youth, which finds the prospect of death more unnatural than the elderly do.</note> and who suffer under the heavy command of nature, which recoils from its own destruction. We, however, separate ourselves from such people and, with a tempered longing, always await the divine will.

Given at Wolfenbüttel <note>original: "Guelpherbyti." Wolfenbüttel was an important residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg and a major cultural center in the 17th century.</note>, November 14, 1648.

Your Illustriousness’s

Most devoted servant.

### VI.
# With Princess SIBYLLA URSULA. <note>Sibylla Ursula (1629–1671) was the daughter of August the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. She was highly educated and a noted writer and translator.</note>

->Honored Friend,<-

You receive a letter, written to you not by some learned man, but thinly exarated <note>meaning: "composed" or "scratched out."</note> by the hand of a girl. Your celebrated *Virtue* and distinguished Piety work in such a way for you that you are loved everywhere, but among us most notably. You sent to me *The Twelve Months* <note>likely a reference to a devotional book or a spiritual calendar</note>, and at the same time you recalled to memory the consideration of time. The world itself is now worn out by its old age. And Time groans in the disease of Vanities. Men, blinded by their neglect of Time, are unmindful of time within Time; they are certainly curious about the present and briefly passing Time, but *indifferent* to the times—if one may speak thus—of the future. I give you thanks for your declared affection; you may certainly promise yourself that my mind is always mindful of the benefit and is devoted to you in turn with a gracious affection. Farewell for a long time yet, for the public...

### LETTER 390.

->Most Illustrious and High-born Princess,<-
->Most Gracious Lady,<-

I received with incredible pleasure of mind your Latin *Letter*, written by a most illustrious hand of the female sex. This is an example as rare among the Germans today as it is laudable and memorable for posterity. I have now learned for the first time that your August House and Court is a proper seat and a literary workshop for both the male and the female sex, before which all the learned rise and offer their applause and worthy praises. I remember indeed, when I was once in Durlach <note>The residence of the Margraves of Baden-Durlach.</note>, seeing a book in the Illustrious Library there, which the most illustrious Maiden of Baden <insert>Lady CATHARINE URSULA, married to OTTO, Landgrave of Hesse</insert> had brought in. It contained an inscription written with a wonderful brilliance of style and the most elegant calligraphy, by which she testified that the Muses <note>The ancient Greek goddesses of inspiration in literature, science, and the arts.</note> had also found a place with her, and had brought delights beyond what can be believed or said, to be held in preference to all treasures and maidenly finery <note>original: "mundo Virgineo." This refers to the traditional jewelry, clothing, and ornaments associated with high-born women.</note>. But that remained the sole example for us in these lands, and was an object of admiration rather than imitation. I have indeed seen others who dared the same, but because they embraced too much—wishing to master the Italian and French languages at the same time as Latin, and wanting the theory of Music alongside its practice—they grasped less firmly and established a knowledge [that was...]

...pardon, I promise myself an easy forgiveness from your most generous Kindness, which, since it is hereditary and natural to you, could by no means be more harsh or stubborn toward me than that of your Most Serene Father. This is the same sentiment of all those to whom I have been permitted to show your writing; they have counted having seen it as a great part of their happiness, and they long to see it more often, as it is so rare and unusual in these lands. To refuse this would be consistent neither with Maidenly gentleness, nor with Welf <term>Guelphica|Referring to the House of Welf (Guelph), the ancient European dynasty to which the Princess belonged.</term> humanity, nor with your Most Illustrious clemency.

Moreover, I think they will be stirred by the immense joy that approaches your House (on the 10th of April), from the **Seventieth Birthday** of your Most Serene Lord Father. Though this age was once called the boundary of human life <note>A reference to the biblical "threescore years and ten" from Psalm 90:10.</note>, given his current vigor and the freshness of his old age, we should consider it a step toward his hundredth year rather than a Limit; he is to be crowned and dedicated to God by our collective prayers. This joy, which is yours by right and ours to enjoy the fruits of, will supply you with enough material to adorn with your eloquent pen, even if the stars should be missing from the sky, the birds from the air, or the fish from the water. But I shall stop, lest I seem to have wrung something from you by my persistence, rather than you having conferred a benefit voluntarily with a ready hand.

### LETTER CCCXCII.

->Very Reverend Lord Doctor,<-
->My friend to be honored in a singular way,<-

You have not only honored me once again with the favor of your address, but moreover, you have stirred my affection with a beautiful little gift of beautiful meditation. You will not doubt that as often as I look upon and read these images and rhythms <note>original: "Rythmos," likely referring to poems or devotional verses</note> of our soul—filled with lovely invention and rich meaning—so often do I kindly heap up expressions of gratitude toward you in my silent mind. I do not deny that I am held and satisfied by nothing so much, whatever it may be, as by the sweetness of pious and sacred thought. All things perish and pass away; piety alone is that which will enjoy temporal and eternal joy. I wished to gladly send back this brief response of mine, since you so desire it. To the Fate and Vow <note>original: "Fato & Voto," likely referring to a formal motto or a prayer for her father's health</note>, which you undoubtedly wish from the heart for my most loving and merciful Lord Father, may God, thrice Greatest and Best, add strength and stability; this I also pray for from my heart, as we all do. May God [keep] you happily...

### Most Illustrious and High-Born Princess,
### My most merciful Lady,

*I confess that I am held by a longing for your letters, and that I seek out ways of obtaining them. For who would not love them, having come from such a talent, written with such elegance, expressed in such courteous speech, and from that sex, and in such great fortune, that they are so far from having anything in common with others that they make the prize* <note>original: "palmam," the palm branch of victory</note> *doubtful even for* Men *born to literature. Lest, however, I should appear as one who brings no contribution* <term>asymbolus (a Greek-derived term for a guest who pays no share of the bill at a banquet)</term>, *behold, I bring a Device* <term>Symbolum (an emblematic motto or intellectual gift)</term>, *not unlike those which I sketched not long ago for your* Renowned Brothers, *in which I wished to express your remarkable gifts granted from heaven above your sex. Indeed, it is:* STRIVE <note>original: "CONTENDE"</note>. *Specifically, since it is the duty of your elder brother—so that he may one day fulfill the role of his* Most August Father <note>Referring to Duke August the Younger of Braunschweig-Lüneburg</note>—*to* PAY ATTENTION <note>original: "ATTENDAT"</note> *to that perfect archetype, and reflect him through virtue rather than by mere chance. Let the younger brother seek fame through letters and the care of religion, following the most praised example of your* George of Anhalt <note>A 16th-century German prince who became a Lutheran reformer and was noted for his holy life</note>, *and* REACH FORWARD <note>original: "PROTENDAT"</note> *in that same balance of comparison. Let the youngest brother, whatever he may have later in time of birth, anticipate with the wings of a swifter talent; and as the craftsman of his own fortune,* EXPAND <note>original: "EXTENDAT"</note> *it by his deeds.*

*It remains that you, O Princess of most lofty talent, should* STRIVE <note>original: "CONTENDAS"</note> *not so much with your brothers as with nature itself; and that you prove—though examples may be fewer—that by these more distinguished ones,* Nothing *is denied to your sex, if the mind pays attention to masculine and outstanding deeds through a noble competition of* Virtue *with* Men; *if it reaches forward through the common lot with arduous effort; and if it expands its fame and glory even beyond the duties of its station by the greatness of its works. There are women set before us in the Sacred Scriptures who were full of the* Divine Spirit <note>original: "Numine"</note>,

by name, *Deborah, Huldah, Hannah;* with masculine courage *Jael and Judith;* in wisdom the *Queen of Sheba* <note>original: "Nicaula Sabea," a traditional name for the Queen of Sheba used by humanists</note>, in obedience *Sarah,* in prudence *Abigail,* in charity *Michal,* in chastity *Susanna,* and in humility the *Mother of the Lord herself.* I will not extend my reach into pagan <note>original: "gentiles"</note> histories, for I do not know if they are as well known to you as the Sacred ones are, nor shall I repeat those things which *Juan Luis Vives* <note>A Spanish humanist and pioneer in women's education</note> encompassed in the first book of his elegant little work *On the Christian Woman* <note>original: "de Christiana foemina"</note>, a book entirely worthy of your reading.

## LETTER 395.

->Very Reverend and Most Renowned Lord Doctor,<-

I have duly received your first and then your second letter, together with the depiction of the *Emblem* <note>original: "Symboli," referring to a symbolic image or device often used in moral or religious instruction</note>, which expresses a certain singular gift of the female sex. # LETTERS OF THE YEAR
# 1649.

## I.

### With Prince RUDOLPH AUGUSTUS.

### LETTER 397.

->Heartiest greetings.<- <note>original: "S. P. C.," an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam Cicit* or *Commendo*, a standard Latin greeting wishing "much health."</note>
->*And a most happy beginning of the New Year.*<-

->*Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,*<-
->*Most gracious Lord,*<-

*The longing for your letters and my concern for your health and safety* make me think that I should take the initiative to reach out to you; perhaps unseasonably on your part, but certainly on mine with the utmost devotion. *For it is not enough for me to learn that nothing is amiss regarding you from the letters of your noble brothers,* <note>The "noble brothers" refers to Rudolph Augustus's younger siblings, Anthony Ulrich and Ferdinand Albert, who were also students and correspondents of Andreae.</note> *unless I also hear all things joyful and favorable from you yourself,* which I humbly pray to God may happen at the earliest opportunity. *And since at this beginning of the year I altogether owe you vows of happiness and consider them rightly due to be paid,* I believe you will more easily tolerate these letters of mine, *which carry nothing other than warm prayers, with which I might entreat the propitious Divinity for the growth and success of your virtues, studies, and undertakings, together with the safety of your soul and body;* *all my other efforts, of whatever kind they may be that might proceed from me,* I dedicate them all, and in their entirety, to you. *I shall be happy if you—as the future heir of your father’s realm and glory, and the successor to his clemency and favor toward me—* make those things endure for me *which are the sum of my earthly wishes and the security of my old age—* <note>The sentence continues onto the next page. ### LETTER 398.

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince,<-
->Most gracious Lord,<-

There is no need for haste, since it is done "soon enough if well enough" <note>original: "sat citò, si sat benè," a Latin proverb suggesting that quality is more important than speed.</note>, provided our letters present themselves to each other and happily reach the goal they seek. For since your letters give me assurance of your constant kindness—which is to be continued even after your Serene Father’s time—and my letters bear witness to the duty of my perpetual intercession before **God** for your health and safety and my most humble obedience, whatever intervals of time or place may divide us, they will always, and quite opportunely, join us together in the relationship between a Most Gracious Lord and a most faithful Minister. We are never to be separated in this world except by death, and are to be truly and eternally joined again in heaven.

I could indeed seek shorter routes to you from here, and approach you more quickly and frequently; but I prefer to act under the gaze of your Serene Father, my most indulgent Master. Since it was by his counsel and will that this **exchange of letters** <term>commercium literarum</term> <note>A formal network of intellectual and personal correspondence common among scholars and nobility in the 17th century.</note> between us was established and has flourished until now, I prefer that it also be subject to his judgment and decision, and be laid open before him, our common Sun. Your recent letters excellently testify how very respectful you yourself are of him; in them, you securely deposit all your desires and prayers into your father's breast, certain that while he is safe, all your...

## LETTER 399.
### Very Reverend and Most Renowned
->Master Doctor,<-

I would be ungrateful if I did not acknowledge your concern for my safety, nor would I be worthy of your prayers which you send for it, if I did not also testify by letter how much I value them. For just as the raised arms of **Moses** sustained his people <note>A biblical reference to Exodus 17:11, where the Israelites prevailed in battle as long as Moses held up his hands.</note>, just as the burnt offerings of **David’s** lips prevailed, and just as the prayers of the pious have achieved great things, I trust that you also can obtain the same from **God** through your prayers. If therefore you persist in them, and I, as much as is in me, [perform my] duty...

### 44. Jotham.

*By the mutual duties of the sword and the plowshare,* <note>original: "Mutuis gladii & ligonis officiis." This refers to Jotham’s balanced focus on both military defense and the cultivation of the land.</note>
*He willed that those who are nourished be protected, and those who protect be nourished,*
*Yet he performed brave deeds more easily than he spoke of them.*

### 45. Ahaz.

*This man, malicious despite receiving favors,*
*Despoils himself, so that he might not be despoiled,* <note>Refers to Ahaz stripping the gold from the Temple to pay tribute to the Assyrian king, Tiglath-Pileser III, to buy protection.</note>
*With God shut out and stripped,*
*Being lost, he destroys himself.*

### 46. Hezekiah.

*Alas, what is solid in human affairs?*
*If age is a sundial, a year a line, and life a shadow,* <note>A reference to the "Shadow of Ahaz," the miraculous sign where God moved the shadow backward on the sundial as a promise of Hezekiah’s healing (2 Kings 20:11).</note>
*A lethal shadow, which kills as many lines as it touches.* <note>The Latin text here splits the word "attingit" (touches) across the line break with "(tingit."</note>

### 47. Manasseh.

->*The evening star of the Eastern world,*<- <note>original: "Orbis Eoi vesper." Likely a poetic way of describing the decline of the kingdom toward its "sunset" or end.</note>

*Those he corrupted by his example, he corrected by his example,* <note>Manasseh was notoriously wicked but eventually repented after being taken captive to Babylon.</note>
*So that he might grieve longer, no one reigned longer.* <note>Manasseh had the longest reign of any King of Judah—55 years.</note>

### 48. Amon.

*Dividing his life between vices and virtues,*
*So that he might grow old uprightly, he grew up wickedly,* <note>Amon followed his father’s early wickedness but was assassinated before he could follow the path of repentance.</note>
*He lies among flowers, but they are fruit-destroying.* <note>original: "frugiperdas." Suggests a life that had the appearance of youth and beauty but produced no spiritual "fruit."</note>

### 49. Josiah.

*He alone neither committed crimes, nor promised them,*
*He gave light to the unearthed Law,* <note>Referring to the discovery of the "Book of the Law" during the renovation of the Temple, which sparked Josiah's reforms.</note>
*Whether he conquered by dying, or died by conquering, is uncertain.* <note>original: "incertu." Josiah died in battle at Megiddo; the author weighs the glory of his righteous life against his tragic end.</note>

### 50. Eliakim & Jehoahaz.

*This one was first from the second, and last from the first,* <note>A reference to the chaotic succession of Josiah’s sons and the interference of Egypt and Babylon in the Judean throne.</note>
*He overturned the kingdom because he bypassed it,*
*That one lay in a tomb while alive, and lived outside the tomb while dead.* <note>original: "tumulum." Likely referring to the exile of the kings; to be in exile was seen as a living death or "living outside the tomb."</note>

### Zedekiah.

*This man, amid deaths, did not find death,*
*Bereft of eyes and children,* <note>Zedekiah was forced to watch the execution of his sons before his own eyes were put out by the Babylonians.</note>
*He did not see the City within the City.* <note>Refers to his blindness and the destruction of Jerusalem.</note>

### Susanna.

*The queen of flowers, and the flower of queens,* <note>The name "Susanna" is derived from the Hebrew word for "Lily."</note>
*In the crisis between life and virtue,*
*Truth shone forth and broke the cloud.* <note>Refers to the story from the Book of Daniel (Apocrypha) where Susanna chose to face a death sentence for a false accusation of adultery rather than compromise her virtue with two corrupt elders.</note>

# LETTERS

At the dawn of the year [16]49, *to You and Your illustrious Brothers*, Lord Rudolph Augustus and Lord Ferdinand Albert, *my most merciful Lords, I speak good words and vows*, and from my heart I *pray that God may be favorable to you. If only this number of years, which was once sacred to the People of God and constituted a Jubilee—during which everyone returned to their possessions, slaves were manumitted, debts were forgiven, and all returned to their families.* <note>The author is referencing the Biblical "Year of Jubilee" described in Leviticus, where social and financial inequities were reset every fifty years.</note>

<margin>[Leviticus 25.]</margin> *So to us, who have suffered such hard servitude under Bellona* <note>The Roman goddess of war; here used as a personification of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which had just concluded with the Peace of Westphalia.</note> *for so many years, may this Jubilee year shine forth as peaceful, in which a forgetfulness of our evils is brought about, and a harvest of every kind of honor may restore our ancestral seats. For you, most Illustrious Princes, may the year* CROWN *you with vigor of mind, health of body, growth of virtues, progress in studies, success in your undertakings, increase of fortune, and the distinction of your exercises—happy, auspicious, easy, and visible—and everything intended for the glory of God, the honor of Your House, and the welfare of the Republic. Live flourishingly, farewell, and look upon me with favor.*

->To Your Most Illustrious and Clement Highnesses.<- <note>original: "Ill. C. C. C. V. V. V.," a standard abbreviation for highly formal addresses to nobility.</note>
Stuttgart, January 3, 1649. ->*From your most humble servant.*<-

# LETTER 304.

->*Prosperous happiness!*<-

# THE YEAR 1649.

...[I would have time for] holidays, yet still be free from busy distractions of the mind and the loss of time. For we are no longer occupied in cleaning out beehives <note>The writer continues the metaphor from the previous page, where "beehives" represented smaller, perhaps more pleasant, intellectual projects.</note>, but in the very Augean stable <term>Augean stable: In Greek mythology, the fifth labor of Hercules was to clean stables that had not been washed for thirty years; it represents a task that is seemingly impossible or disgusting due to long neglect.</term> itself, which not drones, but oxen have filled with their dung. To clean this, one Hercules is not enough; for its rebuilding, there is need of some second Alexander. Indeed, we experience how easy it was for Herostratus <note>Herostratus was an arsonist who destroyed the Temple of Artemis in Ephesus (one of the Seven Wonders) solely to ensure his name would be remembered.</note> to destroy the Temple of Ephesus by fire, even though all of Asia contributed incalculable labor and expense over two hundred and twenty years to build it. Not only has that which was sumptuously prepared through many years of labor, vigilance, and study by the most skilled architects and workers in the Church and State suddenly, through the violence of destroyers, turned into wilderness, barbarism, and dissolution; but minds, alongside bodies, have become so brutalized <note>original: "efferatis," meaning made wild or like a beast.</note> that much labor and time is required to tame and restrain them. 

Nor are there lacking among us meanwhile those like Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem <note>These are the biblical figures who opposed Nehemiah’s efforts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 2:19).</note>, who with every effort hinder the restoration of Jerusalem and the building of the Temple of the Lord. Instead, we have need of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who might call us back from private studies to the public work of God, and of Nehemiah the governor, who might seriously and sincerely handle the business of Christ and turn aside the various obstacles that occur. 

But O, blessed are those by whom all other things are ruled in order and decency by one "first mover" <note>original: "primo mobili," a term from Aristotelian astronomy referring to the outermost sphere that moves all others; here it refers to a strong central leader or God.</note>, and are fashioned according to the standard of the Divine Word and the example of the most praised restorers of their Fatherland. Every age has produced only a few such men, yet all posterity proclaims them. How much more is your Guelphic House <note>The House of Welf (Guelph), the ruling dynasty of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> to be congratulated, which has so often had **AUGUSTI** <note>A pun on the name of the prince’s father, Duke August the Younger, while also invoking the title of "Augustus" used by Roman Emperors to signify majesty and venerability.</note>, and now truly possesses your Father—the most noble teacher and author of the Religion and the Region entrusted to him, whose praise—

## LETTER 307.

### Much health!

**I**t is certainly true, *Distinguished Sir*, that you are carrying out a heavy work indeed, since you write that there is such an overturning of all things among you, and everything is filled with such a heap of filth <note>The writer refers to the literal and metaphorical "rubbish" left behind by the Thirty Years' War, which was ending as this was written.</note> that even men of the greatest labor are not sufficient to cleanse them. Nor do I doubt that you are capable of fulfilling whatever and however much anyone might wish to demand of you. For you so abound in every kind of learning and varied experience that you may boast of having reached a rich old age <note>original: "copiosam senectam"</note> and can far surpass everyone else. You will likely reply, as you often do elsewhere, that this is a small matter. But you know that the wealthier a person is, the more he humbles himself beneath the station of the lowliest. As for the points you discuss at length regarding the condition of *our life*, there is no reason they should frighten one of my age; for my life, just as much as that of more mature men, is exposed to various changes at the whim of the **Supreme Director** <note>A common 17th-century reference to God as the providential ruler or "stage director" of human life.</note>. Nor is there anything that can more easily turn us away from the vanities of this world than frequent reflections upon them; these show us more clearly what we once were, what we are now, and what we must ultimately hope for. 

It was possible to see this with our own eyes not long ago in the case of our **Master of the Horse** <note>original: "Stabulario"; a high-ranking court official, in this case likely the Equerry or Stallmeister.</note>, *Lord von Lentz*, who, after being confined to his bed for eight days, departed this life nearly four weeks ago. While we leave his soul in the dwelling of the blessed, we in turn—should it please God at this beginning of a *new year*—sincerely pray for a most happy and long life for one another. I penned these lines at **Wolfenbüttel** <note>The residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in Lower Saxony.</note>, on the 15th of January, in the year 1649.

Of Your Illustriousness,

->the most devoted<-

->Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg<-

## LETTER 410.

->*Greetings and prosperous happiness!*<-

I now have two letters from you, *Distinguished Sir* <note>original: "Vir Cl." (Vir Clarissimus); a formal honorific for a scholar or person of high standing</note>, which move me with a grateful urging as I return sluggishly to our mutual duty of writing, lest you think this has happened through negligence or that I have forgotten that old friendship between us. You portray and place before the eyes a most elegant and pleasant writer, possessed of a polished and brisk style—yet perhaps that example was not taken from me, but from yourself. For I know how far I fall short of such a likeness, and how slightly I have moved my feet from the dense shadows of ignorance; I have progressed almost not at all, so that upon a more accurate examination I must confess myself to be lowly, narrow, and thin. Therefore, while I am still surrounded by those shadows and remain stuck, as if suppressed, I wonder how those things I have sent out until now could ever see the light of the public. In them, one can find nothing cultivated by genius, polished by art, or labored over by industry that could be brought forth and proposed as a model for others—unless a diligent correction <note>original: "litura"; literally an erasure or smearing of wax on a tablet to wipe it clean for rewriting</note> is applied, which either removes everything or frees what can be healed from its faults. 

As for what we have long conceived among ourselves in hope and prayers concerning the public tranquility, we see that it is gradually coming to pass, and indeed as desired. For it is certain that all the transactions <note>A reference to the treaties of the Peace of Westphalia, signed in late 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War.</note> are now ratified and firm, nor will it be permitted to doubt the discharge of the soldiers <note>original: "exauctoratione militum"; the demobilization of the massive mercenary armies that had devastated Germany for decades</note> which will shortly follow. We are attending with all zeal and effort to ensure they are sent elsewhere as quickly as possible. Farewell. Given at **Wolfenbüttel** <note>The residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note>, the 27th day of February, in the year 1649.

->*Your Most Distinguished [Friend],*<-

->Most Devoted.<-

## LETTER 411.

### Most Illustrious and Most High Prince, my far most merciful Lord,

**E**ven if you respond only once to every three or four of my letters, that is more than enough for me, given the immense pleasure I take in your affection for me and your progress in letters. For however much you might hide it—and perhaps you do not even notice it yourself—I perceive through these intervals how much you progress daily, and how you come ever closer to the model of your most praised Father. For those most brilliant flowers of talent and virtue that he produced at your age, to the admiration and applause of onlookers, I see those same qualities now emerging and pressing forward openly from you, and I rejoice that they will be displayed in public at the proper time. Meanwhile, I will not cease to encourage you, so that you may put forth more and more from the garden of your illustrious Genius in this springtime of your life; may they mature with age, and bring forth a harvest of fruit, seeds of good reputation, and public usefulness. Regarding the Peace, we are all full of hope alongside you, though we hardly see it yet; we shall truly possess it when the dislocated members of the Church and the State <note>original: "Ecclesiæ & Politiæ"; here referring to the fractured religious and political institutions of the Holy Roman Empire</note> are once again properly restored to one another on all sides. Then indeed we shall truly rejoice and congratulate one another. I respectfully greet your most illustrious Brothers, and from my heart I pray for all happy and bright things for you all. Farewell along with them; flourish and favor me.

->Your Illustrious Highness’s<-

Stuttgart, March 21, 
1649.

## LETTER 412.

->*Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir,*<-

You write that you are awaiting my letters with eagerness, though I know not what desire drives you, for you will find nothing from me to suit your particular taste <note>original: "palatum," literally "palate," suggesting the recipient has high intellectual or literary standards</note>. However, since I can easily believe that you are sometimes satisfied with small and humble things, here are these few brief lines; may you find as much delight in them as you would in a more lavish presentation. I am grateful for your concern for my health <note>original: "valetudo," referring to one's physical state or wellbeing</note>, and I pray for your own continued prosperity, so that you may always be well-disposed to undertake your labors. I can easily imagine that these tasks are very great; yet, if we consider the fruit that we may hope to harvest from them, we judge that they will be neither unpleasant to you nor of little benefit to the common welfare of your people. For you yourself know what rewards are stored up for those whose work is most earnest and who have kept watch most diligently. May God grant that we too, as we hope, may eventually receive something of those promises for the eternal salvation of our souls. I shall write more when I am at leisure; I write these things suddenly and, as you see, with a swift pen <note>original: "celeriori calamo," a common Latin idiom for writing in a hurry</note>.

Wolfenbüttel, 3 April 1649.
Your most devoted servant.

Our educators <term>Efformatores: tutors or mentors responsible for the moral and intellectual "forming" of students</term>, having first sent their respectful greetings to you and yours, likewise pray for your every happiness.

### LETTER 413.

->*Greetings and prosperous happiness!*<-

If any flowers are to be found in my little garden <note>original: "hortulo meo," a common literary metaphor for one's collection of writings or intellectual exercises</note>, as you write, Reverend Sir, I freely confess that I am ignorant of either their elegance or their growth. And perhaps that happens in the manner of the unskilled, who—because they can scarcely perceive with their eyes the growth of plants and whatever has its own natural progressions—are also unable to conceive of it in their minds. But it is far different for the more learned and those well-skilled in natural matters, for whom it is established and certain that all these things have both their motion and their growth. Since you are counted among their number, I gladly place my trust in you. 

You will consider, however, that these things of ours are not born of gold—as the New India <note>original: "nova India," referring to the Americas, which were famous in the 17th century for the gold and riches sent back to Europe</note> boasts of itself—but from an intellect that is still impure and unfruitful in judgment. Therefore, in my name and that of my brothers, I still wish to ask you that if there is anything "monstrous" in them <note>original: "monstrosi," meaning deformed, unnatural, or simply erroneous in a scholarly sense</note>—which we easily believe and know to be the case—you correct it through your own industry before you present it to others. For since others are usually more refined and can easily perceive where an error has been made, they might otherwise develop a sense of nausea or disgust toward the work. We hope that you will care for all these things diligently, and in turn, we promise you our own readiness and zeal.

Wolfenbüttel, April 17, 1649.

->*To Your Reverend Dignity,*<-
->**Most Respectfully.**<-

Our educators <term>Efformatores: literally "those who form," referring here to the tutors or governors responsible for the moral and intellectual shaping of the young princes</term> likewise ask that their respectful greetings be announced to you.

# LETTER 414.
## Sends many greetings.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**By far the most merciful Lord,**<-

While your letters are always most welcome to me, I receive them even more eagerly at this time, as the printer <note>original: "Typographo." In the 17th century, authors often lived in a state of anxiety as the "press" or "printer" hurried to finish a job.</note> is hurrying toward the finish line. I desire to present many specimens of your elegant wit and to let our little book—a child of noble ventures—emerge into public view. For although, out of your modesty, you direct all its praise toward others, I nevertheless assert that a great part of it is owed entirely to you. For who would not grant to you an alacrity in undertaking this labor of writing, a sagacity in imitation, a striving in completion, a diligence in expression, a patience in continuing, and the seasoning of all these things with the highest grace and humanity? I consider these qualities, both individually and gathered together in you, to be certain omens of the greatest future progress, worthy of both esteem and praise. Do not, therefore, accuse your little field <note>original: "agelli Tui," continuing the "hortulo" or garden metaphor from the previous letter to describe the Prince's intellectual output</note> of sterility, or believe the seeds to be unfruitful, or even now find the form and elegance of the flowers to be lacking. Rather, be raised up in certain hope that those things which are now tender will acquire strength; those which are hidden will show themselves; and those which are raw will proceed toward maturity and a bountiful harvest itself. For the beauty of Spring—which is now properly yours—and the yields of Summer and Autumn are each distinct; they are pleasing in their variety, lovely to look upon, convenient for use, and finally, each is specifically suited by its own power to the health and pleasure of mankind. Therefore, we shall now take delight in your flowers. That you may produce them happily and display them vividly, we shall pray to GOD, the author and preserver of the grass, the flower, and the grain, that after these great beginnings there may be even greater progress, and finally...

**Lady by far most merciful,**

I acknowledge it is my duty, at this solemn turning of the season <note>original: "temporis reflexu," referring to the start of the New Year</note>, to bring my wishes to you, illustrious Virgin: humble, pious, and religious; learned and literary; ingenious and elaborate. Model yourself after this example, most Illustrious Princess, and strive without envy; the prize is offered equally and—saving the respect due to Royal Majesty—is denied to no one where the contest is not of rank, but of intellect. Since your Most Serene Lord Father has surpassed all the Princes of his time by universal consensus <note>original: "communibus calculis," literally "by common pebbles," referring to the ancient method of voting</note>, what forbids you from testing the strength of your own extraordinary talent in a praiseworthy rivalry with that most learned Queen, and awaiting the judgment of the literary Senate? I have received and read your reply, and in it your many congratulations for a prosperous Christmas <note>original: "Natalis die," referring to the Feast of the Nativity</note>; with a grateful heart, I recognized your devoted mind. ## THE FOLLOWING ARE
# SEVERAL LETTERS
### FROM WURTTEMBERG.

#### LETTER I.

->Fondest Greetings.<- <note>original: "S. P.", an abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam*, a standard Latin greeting wishing the recipient "the greatest health" or "much health."</note>

The letters from Your Reverend Dignity were a favorable omen for the start of the New Year. In them, we foretell a prosperous success of all happiness and a praiseworthy following of your Ancestors; they were the most delightful and most welcome of all. We heartily pray that every kind of prosperity may rejoice through its presence and continuation in the most pious sanctuary of your heart. Furthermore, because Your Reverend Dignity has offered us the sincerity of your soul and your love for us with this ardent vow, we not only recognize your sincere mind and singular affection, but in turn, we place our own love, favor, and a token of remembrance <note>original: "mnemosynon," a Greek-derived word for a memorial or a gift given to preserve a memory</note> of you at the altar of faithfulness and clemency. We wish that we also had the ability to express in reality those things included in our prayers, so that our deeds might thus prove our intent; but where strength is lacking, good intention supplies the defect. Therefore, the strongest favorable breeze <note>original: "favonius," referring to the West Wind, often used metaphorically in Latin to symbolize a gentle, productive, or helpful influence</note> of a sincere mind and affection compels us to pray together that everything flows according to the desire of your heart for Your Reverend Dignity. May the Triune **GOD** keep you and yours safe <note>The text ends mid-word with "incolu-"; the catchword "mes" indicates the word is *incolumes*, meaning "safe," "unharmed," or "healthy."</note>

<header>OF WÜRTTEMBERG.</header>

### LETTER II.

->MUCH GREETINGS.<-
<note>original: "S. P.," an abbreviation for "Salutem Plurimam," a standard formal greeting meaning "much health" or "many greetings."</note>

Very Reverend Sir. Your Dignity’s most kindly written letters urge us not to delay, but rather to press forward with a response; both due reverence and gratitude persuade us to do so. Your venerable white hair <note>original: "canities," a poetic reference to the wisdom and status of old age</note> invites and attracts our youth above all else, especially because you have once again set aside your own affairs to bless us with such great praise <note>original: "Adoreâ," an ancient Roman term for a reward of grain, used here metaphorically to mean honor or glory</note> worthy of our ancestors, and because you wish for us to become such as you hope for in your prayers. Furthermore, you wished to hold us certain and assured of your constant faithfulness and most dutiful mind, and to offer us a most welcome New Year’s gift <note>original: "strenam," a traditional gift or token given at the start of the year</note> as a testament to your sincerity of spirit. In this way, you have bound us to you entirely by your good affection and readiness. 

If our circumstances matched our will and desires, you would certainly soon experience for yourself the loyalty and spirit of friends who are not ungrateful. But truly, although the present time keeps us deprived of all benefits, the passage of time and the smallness of our resources will not wrap in the mists of oblivion the God who blesses us and who confirms our rightful intentions. Therefore, let your gentle heart, Reverend Dignity, rejoice for now despite the delay, while we ourselves endure being nourished by the hope of a better lot. 

As for the rest, we owe and pay you mindful thanks, venerable sir, for the most desired New Year's gift and your respectful mind. See to it that in the future your good affection remains ours, and we shall continually embrace Your Reverend Dignity with our customary love, honor, and favor. 

Given at Brackenheim <note>A town in the district of Heilbronn, Baden-Württemberg</note>, the 13th of January, 1641.

### LETTER III.

*To the Very Reverend and most Distinguished Lord Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Counselor and Court Preacher at Stuttgart, health and prosperity from Jehovah.*

Very Reverend and most Distinguished, much beloved Lord Court Preacher! What we established for ourselves some time ago by the command of our beloved Lady Mother—namely, to write certain letters to you—is now made urgent, as it were, by your own hand. For our part, we congratulate ourselves not a little on the dedication made to us, being grateful for your singular affection toward us and our studies, and for your most ready spirit in supporting them.
