## LETTER IV.
### *To the Princes of Württemberg,*
### For Silvius Nimrod.
<note>Silvius Nimrod (1622–1664) was a prince of the House of Württemberg who later became the first Duke of Württemberg-Oels.</note>

*Not from any itch of ambition, but solely from the high esteem for your excellent character, I long for your letters. Although I would have preferred to prompt them with my own, I modestly invite you, wondering if the confidence of a noble spirit toward you might come first. That is to say, while in the common calamity of our Fatherland <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which hit Württemberg particularly hard</note>, you have both a sad leisure and solace from literature; unless I am unworthy of your favor, I ask that you seek from me those things which, along with honorable business, might perhaps refresh the pleasantness of your mind. As much as is in my power, I shall do this as dutifully as I profess myself indebted to your Virtue and Integrity in every way. Farewell, Illustrious Prince, with your most distinguished Mother and Sister; and may Christ keep you peaceful and without harm amidst these most turbulent affairs.* February 12, 1643.

### To Lord Julius Peregrinatus, &
### To Lord Sueno Martialis Edelnolphus, etc.
### Sons of Prince Julius of Württemberg.

*To pray for an auspicious year for you, Princes of Youth <note>original: "Principes Iuventutis," a classical title for noble heirs</note>, both your most illustrious piety invites me, and my own devotion; that devotion by which I venerate your renowned House and its most celebrated merits in both sacred and public affairs. This piety of yours shows us now not merely the seeds, but the blade and the flower of all the Württemberg virtues, and thus promises us a magnificent crop and harvest of happiness. These blessings we expect all the more confidently—indeed, we demand them of you—because under the image of that Most Illustrious Hero, your Father <note>Julius Frederick, Duke of Württemberg-Weiltingen (1588–1635)</note>, of most praised memory, and under the watchful care of your most pious Mother <note>Anna Sabine of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg (1593–1659)</note>, and by the guidance of the Noble Helmstetter <note>Johann Georg von Helmstatt, the princes' governor</note> and the instruction of the famous Betsius <note>Johann Jakob Bechius, a scholar and tutor</note>, your ascent to every summit of virtue is made more ready, so that you may crown the glory of your family. Therefore, I pray that those benefits of Fortune and Nature which you have already received from the Supreme Deity beyond the common lot, you may so adorn and increase—through the worship of God, the imitation of your Father, reverence for your Mother, respect for your Cousin Eberhard <note>Eberhard III, Duke of Württemberg (1614–1674)</note>, elegance of manners, the practice of honorable arts, obedience to your guides <note>original: "manuductorum," literally "hand-leaders" or tutors</note>, innocence of life, and the applause of your subjects—that you may fulfill the circle of the best princes, not only of Württemberg, but of all Germany. May **GOD** confirm these vows, to whom I commend you, along with your most praised Mother and your most flourishing sister Floriana Ernesta, with earnest prayers.*

...founded by two Eberhards, more firmly established by Ulrich and Christopher, loved by Ludwig, adorned by Friedrich, and expanded by Johann Friedrich—namely, your ancestors, the Dukes of Württemberg—which, though cast down by the calamity of this age <note>A reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which hit the Duchy of Württemberg and its educational institutions particularly hard.</note>, your renowned Father **EBERHARD III** now moves to restore. Although I know you are already equipped with a protective retinue through the wisdom of your Father and the care of your Mother, so that you need fear no obstacle on the path to Virtue and may expect every advantage for the best progress—for you have indeed a Governor <term>Ephorus: a high-ranking supervisor or guardian of a prince's education</term>, Ludwig Berchtold, a man of long-proven loyalty and experienced in affairs; you have an Instructor <term>Informator: a private tutor responsible for direct academic instruction</term>, the Great Hæfenthaler, conspicuous for his singular industry and diligence; nor is there lacking the noble attendant Georg Heinrich Reischach, a youth of skillful wit, a companion of your studies, and a servant of good repute—surrounded by whom you could not possibly be led astray. 

Yet, what forbids me, out of my devotion to you and my desire for the continued growth of your House, from adding a guard of my own? Your parents would not refuse such a guard, nor would those guardians I have mentioned, and you, no doubt, out of the generosity of your spirit, will gladly admit, embrace, and wish to keep it with you forever. 

Therefore, most flourishing Prince, I appoint for you the Governor **PIETY**, so that you may think rightly concerning **GOD**, worship Him correctly, obey Him reverently and constantly, and establish Him as the judge and rule of all your thoughts and actions. To this one, I join the Instructor **ATTENTION**, so that you may fix the things you hear and the precepts you are taught deeply in your heart, hold them in memory, and express them through imitation—especially those which pertain to the example of **GOD**, whose image you must one day reflect, and the mirror of your ancestors...

*whom good fortune designates as your heir, and may the prayers and expectations of your People shape you. That King Solomon, who by the consensus of all peoples and indeed by the testimony of GOD himself was the wisest of kings, having surveyed the course of his whole life and thoroughly inspected everything that might seem great to anyone in this world, and having perceived the vanity of all those things which are admired by the greater part of men—as is vividly depicted in his book *Ecclesiastes*—finally, at the end of the book, intending to show what ought to be the supreme goal of all our actions, breaks out into these words: *Fear GOD, and observe his commandments, for this is the duty of all men. <meta>This page continues the dedication of Johann Valentin Andreae to the young Prince Johann Friedrich of Württemberg. It transitions from the formal closing of the preface into a theological exhortation based on King Solomon’s Ecclesiastes, focusing on the "Fear of God" as the primary duty of a Christian ruler.</meta>

<page-num>554</page-num>
<header>LETTERS</header>

This aphorism <note>Referring to the conclusion of Ecclesiastes: "Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man."</note> should be seen reading on the frontispiece of the book. For by this single aphorism, he indicates the goal toward which all the actions of all men in every life ought to be directed. However, although Solomon commands this to all men: let those know that it is said especially to themselves who, with Solomon—God willing and granting—will in their own time take up the administration of the Republic <term>Republic: Used here in the classical sense of "the state" or "the commonwealth" (Res publica).</term> upon their own shoulders. Since God wishes you also to be among their number, O Prince, in the name of your most Illustrious Father (whose name in our vernacular <note>original: "vernaculâ" - German. The name Friedrich is derived from the German words for "peace" and "ruler," mirroring the Hebrew name Solomon, which is derived from *Shalom* (peace).</note> exactly expresses Solomon’s name), I exhort you:

1. That you should fear **GOD**. The fear of **GOD** presupposes knowledge of Him. Therefore, before all things, see that you know Him, the Triune true **GOD**—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to be adored forever. To this end, the King of Kings and Lord of Lords gave commands to the future king in Deuteronomy 17:18: *After the King has sat upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a scroll, receiving the exemplar from the priests of the Levite tribe; and he shall have it with him and read it all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the Lord his **GOD**, and to keep His words and ceremonies which are commanded in the law.* King David, his father, had impressed this upon Solomon, saying while he was already drawing his final breath <note>original: "animam agendo"</note> in 1 Chronicles 28:9: *You, Solomon my son, know the **GOD** of your father,* who indeed has revealed himself to us in the writings of Moses, the Prophets, the Evangelists, and the Apostles. Not only do the aforementioned books testify concerning His essence and will: but the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed, and the Athanasian Creed also encompass it; and most recently, the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church (1530).</note> and the Formula of Concord <note>A definitive Lutheran doctrinal statement (1577) intended to resolve theological disputes.</note> have declared it abundantly.

> To know this one true **GOD**, and Jesus Christ whom He has sent, is eternal life. John 17:3.

As Christ Himself bears witness. On the other hand, even if someone were to be perfect among the children of men, if Your Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientia Tua" — referring to the personified Divine Wisdom.</note> is absent from him,

> he shall be reckoned as nothing,

as the Book of Wisdom says in chapter 9, verse 6.

2. To simply know **GOD** is not enough. The servant who knew his Lord’s will, yet did not prepare himself and did not act according to His will, shall be beaten with many blows. <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 12:47.</note> Therefore, *fear this **GOD**, and keep His commandments.* What are those commandments? Their summary is found in Deuteronomy 6:4–5 and Leviticus 19:18:

> *Hear, O Israel: The LORD our **GOD**, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your **GOD** with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself.*

Know that this is spoken to you above all others. But hear also David himself speaking to his son in 1 Chronicles 28:9: <note>original: "1. Par. 28. v. 9." — Paralipomenon is the Latin name for the Books of Chronicles.</note>

> *You, my son, know the **GOD** of your father, and serve Him with a perfect heart and a willing mind. For the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek Him, you will find Him; but if you forsake Him, He will cast you off forever.*

Hear Solomon in Proverbs 4:5:

> *Get wisdom, get understanding.*

In order to acquire this, follow with honor and obedience first your most Illustrious and Dearest Parents—who are to be cherished with perpetual reverence—and then the Governors <term>Governors: (Latin: "Ephoros") Tutors or officials appointed to oversee a young prince's education and moral conduct.</term> appointed to you by their will.

> *Indeed, every man has the mind of a king within himself, so that he wishes power over others to be given to him, but does not wish it to be used upon himself,*

as Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher whose writings on ethics and leadership were highly influential in Renaissance education.</note> testifies. But you should remember that:

> *no one knows how to rule, unless they have also been ruled.*

And certainly:

> *He does not know how to command, who has not learned to obey.*

Rule over your own passions: <note>original: "Affectibus Tuis dominare" — A core Stoic and Christian virtue for a leader.</note>

> *For just as he ought to be judged unfit to rule others who cannot rule his own passions:*

so to the people...

<center>

### LETTERS

</center>

One does not deserve to rule over Christians who is not himself endowed with the knowledge, reverence, and love of **GOD**. What is a mere speck in another's eye will be a plank in yours; what is a minor defect in another's body will be a glaring blemish <note>original: "vitiligo" — a skin condition causing patches of lost pigment, here used to mean a visible moral stain.</note> in yours. Mistakes that are called "pardonable errors" in others will be judged as crimes in you. Do not imagine that your high rank diminishes your faults, and certainly do not think that your position gives you a license to sin. Rather, consider this: the height of your honor only increases the gravity of your sins. For whatever wrong you commit is not the fall of just one man; you do more harm by your example than by the sin itself, as you will make countless mortals guilty by their imitation of you. The Best Prince teaches his citizens to act rightly most effectively by *doing* so himself; though he is Greatest in Power, he is even greater as an example.

These things apply to everyone, but especially to the high-ranking. For **GOD** will also bring this to judgment, judging them for both hidden and manifest deeds, whether they be good or evil. Frightening indeed are the words read in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 6, verse 7 <note>In modern Bibles, this passage is typically found in Wisdom of Solomon 6:5-8.</note>:

> *He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because a most severe judgment shall be dealt to those who rule. For to the lowly, mercy is granted; but the powerful shall suffer torments powerfully. For **GOD**, who is the Ruler of all, will not exempt any person, nor will He stand in awe of any greatness.*

To strive for this and to reach it, *he who plants is nothing, and he who waters is nothing, but it is **GOD** who gives the growth.* <note>original: "nil erit qui plantat..." — a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:7.</note> Therefore, like Solomon, pray to Him for this, from Wisdom chapter 9, verses 1–5:

> ***GOD** of my fathers, and Lord of mercy, who made all things by Your word, and by Your wisdom established man, that he might rule the creation made by You, and that he might govern the world in equity and justice, and render judgment with an upright heart: give me Wisdom, the attendant of Your throne, and do not reject me from among Your children.*

Pray with that same man: 3 Kings— <note>original: "3. Re-" — This is the catchword "gum" referring to "Regum." In the Latin Vulgate, 1 Kings is titled 3 Kings.</note>

From the third book of Kings <note>original: "gum 3." — in the Vulgate Bible used at the time, 1 Kings was often called 3 Kings. This refers to 1 Kings 3:9.</note>, verse 9:
> Give to your servant a teachable heart, so that I may one day be able to judge your people and discern between good and evil.

But you shall not pray alone; I also join my prayers to yours, seeking the same thing with my mouth and heart that David sought for his son in Psalm 71 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 72:1-3.</note>, verses 1 and 2:
> **GOD**, give your judgment to the King, and your justice to the King’s son, to judge your people in justice and your poor in judgment: let the mountains bring peace to the people, and the hills justice.

Indeed, all the people pray with you, repeating that phrase from Psalm 118:
> O Lord, grant prosperity; O Lord, give successful outcomes, so that the glory of Your Holy Name, and the prosperity of the Church and the Commonwealth <note>original: "Reip." or "Respublica" — referring to the state or organized community.</note> may be advanced:

The safety of our Princes, and the well-being of our entire Homeland may be extended, increased, and preserved, so that it may be said of you what the Son of Sirach <note>original: "Syracides" — referring to the Book of Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Sirach from the Apocrypha.</note> writes of Solomon in chapter 47, verse 16:
> He was learned in his youth, and filled with wisdom like a river, and his soul covered the earth.

By diligently carrying these things out, you fulfill the will of **GOD**, who will abundantly add glory and riches to the Spirit of Wisdom. In this way, you will satisfy the pious prayers of your most Illustrious Parents and the expectations of all the people.

> May you graciously grant our prayers, O Most Holy Trinity, blessed forever, Amen.

### LETTER XII.

->To the Reverend and Most Renowned<-
->Lord Doctor,<-

I have understood with great pleasure from the latter of your letters with how much love you embrace mine. That honor which you offer, I count among the testimonies of your affection, yet I scarcely dare to receive it now, because I do not deserve it. For I still use a substitute hand <term>vicariâ manu</term> <note>original: "vicariâ manu" — indicating that the Duke is dictating to a secretary or scribe rather than writing with his own hand.</note>; but if indeed I am able to use my own, and it should then please you to decide something concerning our little letters—as they are now yours—it will scarcely be right for me to forbid it. However, you have achieved much by this very offering, since you have inflamed me with a vehement passion, which will not cease until I become worthy of some part of that praise, of which I desire you to be appointed judge hereafter. Farewell now, and ensure that my person always experiences the same spirit in you,

->Your Dignity’s<-
Tübingen, January 26,
In the year 1649.              Most devoted

## JOHANN FRIEDRICH
->*Duke of Württemberg and Teck*<-

### LETTER XV.

->**Most Illustrious and Most High Prince,**<-
->**Lord by far most merciful,**<-

You do rightly, you who *prefer to be learned rather than to seem so, and to deserve praise for it from within yourself,* for which you request a due delay; I freely grant it. I pray to God that your individual months, weeks, and indeed your days may bestow upon you growth in Virtue and Study; such progress as I already seem to perceive from this short interval. But it is no small thing that you are already doing by imitating *your instructor* <note>original: "Informatoris Tui," referring to his private tutor</note>; for in this way you prove both your diligence and your teachability, and you delight me greatly by your elegant penmanship <note>original: "pingendis eleganter literis," literally "painting letters elegantly"</note>, which will itself one day adorn your scholarship. Continue, therefore, flourishing Prince, to deem me worthy of your correspondence—I who keep watch diligently and ardently before God for your health, and that of your Cousin, and for your perpetual happiness. Farewell. March 12, in the year 1649.

->Your Most Illustrious Highness’s<-
->Most humble client.<-

## LETTER XVI.

->Reverend and Most Illustrious Lord Doctor,<-

I indeed thought that I had already replied to your last letter; now I regret that the response has been so far delayed, and I ask that you be willing to grant me your pardon, as I confess my fault. I should have been the very last to remain silent for so long regarding those letters, since they contained things that were very pleasing to me. Undoubtedly, you grant a delay for my letters, that they not be published until I myself can be their author <note>original: "scriptor"</note> rather than merely their transcriber <note>original: "descriptor"</note>. Furthermore, I give great thanks that my desires have been heard. For your part, continue to promote my studies with your advice and your pen, and commend them to God with your prayers and your voice; and farewell.

**EBERHARD**, the son of Louis the Elder, Count of Württemberg, and Mechthild of the Palatinate—nicknamed the **Bearded**, the **Elder**, the **Wise**, and the **Honest**—was a Prince of great spirit and virtue. He demonstrated his wisdom not only at home through peaceful governance, but also abroad in the common affairs of the Empire. He first saw the light <note>i.e., was born</note> on December 11, in the year 1445, at Urach. In the year 1468, he set out in the month of May for Palestine, and in November of the same year he arrived safely back home; this journey was documented by Joachim Münfinger of Frundeck, a Doctor of Medicine. In the year 1474, he married Barbara, the daughter of Ludovico Gonzaga, Marquess of Mantua. The wedding was celebrated magnificently at Urach, where 14,000 <note>original: "XIVM"</note> people were provided with food. In the year 1477, since he was a great supporter and patron of scholars and wisdom, he established the University <note>original: "Academia"</note> at Tübingen, which he endowed with generous and royal liberality. 

In the year 1480, having traveled to Rome, he was gifted the Golden Rose by Pope Sixtus IV <note>original: "P. M." for Pontifex Maximus</note>. He obtained permission for founding a monastery of Hermits <note>these were the Canons of the Common Life</note> at the "Beautiful Beeches," commonly known as the **Schönbuch**. Here he established twelve Canons Regular of Saint Peter, over whom he placed a Provost; all of these men were of the Knightly Order. To them, he joined twelve laymen, or converts from among his subjects. 

On account of the praise of his virtues, wisdom, and eloquence, he was admitted into the Order <note>original: "Collegium"</note> of the Golden Fleece by Emperor Maximilian I. By the same Emperor, at the Diet of Worms in the year 1495, he was inaugurated by solemn rite as the FIRST DUKE OF WÜRTTEMBERG AND TECK. He did not survive this honor for more than thirty weeks and a few days. For, as he suffered daily from fever, dysentery, and the stone <note>likely kidney or bladder stones, a common ailment of the era</note>, the disease...

**EBERHARD**, the son of Ulrich "the Well-Beloved," Count of Württemberg, and Elizabeth of the Palatinate-Bavaria, was the **SECOND DUKE OF WÜRTTEMBERG**. A confirmer <note>meaning he formally renewed the privileges</note> of the University of Tübingen, he succeeded Duke Eberhard I, who had died without children. However, on account of his poor administration, he was replaced in his position by Emperor Maximilian I with Ulrich, the son of his brother Henry. His wife was Elizabeth, the daughter of Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg.

**ULRICH**, the son of Count Henry of Württemberg and Elizabeth, Countess of Zweibrücken and Bitsch <note>original: "Bipotinæ & Bitschenfis"</note>, was the **THIRD DUKE OF WÜRTTEMBERG**. He was born on February 8, in the year 1487, at Riquewihr <note>original: "Richovillæ," a town in Alsace</note>. He was named Itel Friedrich at his baptism, but received the name Ulrich at his confirmation. While he was still lying in his cradle, Eberhard the Bearded saw to it that he was brought to Stuttgart and raised with the greatest care. In the year 1504, he fought for Emperor Maximilian I against Philip of the Palatinate in the Bavarian War <note>referring to the Landshut War of Succession</note>, and by right of war he seized several towns from him, following the example of other Princes who, each for himself, pounced upon the property of the outlawed Prince. Truly, after a fifteen-year exile, restored by the armed hand of **Philip, Landgrave of Hesse**, he recovered his ancestral lands; and having abolished the idol-mania of the Pope's superstition, he brought the light of the Orthodox faith <note>original Latin: "Orthodoxæ fidei," here referring to the reformed Lutheran faith, which the author considers the correct or "orthodox" version of Christianity</note> into his entire Principality. Thus brought back, he finally reached an agreement with **Archduke Ferdinand**, such that the beneficial ownership <term>utile Dominium: the right to possess and profit from the land</term> of the Duchy of **Württemberg** remained with him, while the direct ownership <term>directum: the legal title and superior lordship</term> remained with **Ferdinand**.

In the year 1546, having followed the side of **John Frederick, Elector of Saxony**, and **Philip of Hesse** <note>these were the leaders of the Schmalkaldic League, a Protestant military alliance</note>, he was forced by the unfairness of fortune—of which he was like a plaything <note>original: "pila," literally a ball or sphere tossed about</note>—to excuse his actions and plead for mercy before the Emperor. Thus having experienced varied fortune, and long troubled by gnarled arthritis, the Prince yielded to the fates on November 6, in the year 1550, when he had ruled the Principality for 52 years and 5 months. 

Following the customs of his ancestors, he brought distinction to the praiseworthy school of the **University of Tübingen** with learned professors and fair salaries; he administered the state with no common prudence and quite successfully, holding the rudder of government bravely until his very last breath, despite the most serious schemes of his adversaries. I cannot restrain myself from adding the Eulogy of this Excellent Duke from a manuscript by **Trithemius** <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous Benedictine abbot, historian, and polymath</note>, which the Harpies of War <note>original: "Martiales Harpyiæ," a poetic reference to the looting or destruction of libraries during conflict</note> have kept from us:

> *This is,* he says, *that magnificent Prince **Ulrich**, who today* (for Trithemius was living then) *at twenty-six years of age, vigorously governs the Duchy of **Württemberg**, preserves the peace, administers justice to all, second to none in wealth, glory, virtue, and power, no less prepared for war, should it be necessary, than for peace. Nature gave him a body conspicuous in its build and character, and well-suited to his spirit...*

### 4.

**CHRISTOPHER**, son of Duke Ulrich of Württemberg and Sabina of Bavaria, **FOURTH DUKE OF WÜRTTEMBERG and TECK**, called the *Peaceable* and the *Wise*, born at **Urach** on May 12, at 2 o’clock in the morning. He was held at the font during his baptism not by John (as **Crusius** <note>Martin Crusius (1526–1607) was a famous humanist historian who wrote the "Swabian Annals"</note> wrongly writes), but by Peter, the Provost of **Denkendorf**, on Cantate Sunday in the year 1515. As a four-year-old boy <term>quadrimus: four years old</term>, he was besieged along with his sister **Anna** in the castle of **Tübingen** by the members of the **Swabian League** [as is clear from the letter of **Ulrich von Hutten** to **Lukas von Ehrenberg**], who had 26,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry in their army. After his father was expelled and Tübingen was captured, he was taken away to **Bavaria** to his maternal uncle, **William, Duke of Bavaria**, under whose education he remained for some time. From there he was sent to **Innsbruck** <note>original: "Oenipontem," the Latin name for the city of Innsbruck</note> in the year 1522, and placed in the household of a certain doctor of medicine to be educated in letters alongside the doctor’s two sons, without any of the status due to a prince. From there...

Having been moved to Austria by King Ferdinand, he had as his Governor of Morals <term>morum praefectum: a supervisor of conduct and character</term> **William of Reichenbach**, a nobleman and Doctor of Law. His instructor in letters was **Michael Tifernus**, an Illyrian and Professor of Philosophy at the University of Vienna. Trained by Tifernus's faithful work, he successfully mastered the primary languages then in use, Greek and Latin.

After some time, he was transferred to the court of **Emperor Charles V**, and having been admitted into the Chamber among the honorary pages <term>ephebos honorarios: young noblemen serving as pages at court</term>, he traveled through **Austria** and neighboring provinces, as well as **Belgium** and **Italy**. He became acquainted with the customs of many peoples and cities, and was especially dear and well-received by the Emperor. 

However, when he learned from his relatives that a plan was underway whereby *the sole heir to the Principality of Württemberg was to be taken away to Spain and forced into the ecclesiastical order* <note>The Emperor and King Ferdinand likely intended to force Christopher into the priesthood or a monastery to ensure he could not inherit his father's lands, effectively ending the Württemberg dynasty's claim.</note>, he successfully escaped in secret from the Emperor's retinue with the help and assistance of his most faithful **Tifernus**. He fled to **Bavaria** to his uncle **Louis**, where he remained in hiding for six months. 

From there he went to **France** in the year 1532, where he lived for eight years at the court of King **Francis I**. At the age of twenty-two, he was appointed a Commander of Soldiers and led twenty-four cohorts into **Italy**, with which he laid siege to **Alexandria**. 

Following a subsequent truce, when **Emperor Charles V** and King **Francis I** met at **Aigues-Mortes** <note>original: "Aquis Mortuis," a port town in southern France</note> to discuss peace with **Paul III** (of pious memory) acting as arbiter, it happened that the Pope and Francis I met in the city of **Nice** in Provence. There, when King Francis kissed the Pope’s right foot, and all the other Princes and Magnates followed his example, **Christopher**—whether led by a heroic instinct of true piety, or exercising his German frankness, sincerity, and liberty—openly refused, even though he had been warned by the Master of the Horse,

...that he would [rather] kiss the sandals of a Priest. <note>original: *se Sacerdotis crepidas basiaturum*. This refers to his rejection of a forced religious career; he mockingly suggests that to do so would be to become a servant of the church hierarchy.</note> By his example, he persuaded others, and especially the **Count of Fürstenberg**, to refuse this shameful and slavish obedience. In the year 1542, having returned from **France** to **Germany**, he was preparing an expedition against the **Turks** in **Hungary** <note>original: *Pannoniam*</note>, but he changed his plan at the wish of his father, who was now aged and infirm. When his father returned to the favor of the **Emperor**, Christopher steadfastly rejected the "tragic buskin" of religion <note>original: *Cothurnum Religionis*</note>, which they called the **Interim** <term>Augsburg Interim: a 1548 imperial decree that attempted to force Protestants back toward Catholic practices while allowing some concessions, which many staunch Lutherans like Christopher resisted</term>.

After the death of his father in the year 1550, he took up the government of the Duchy, which he administered most justly, prudently, and peacefully. In the year 1555, he was the first to promulgate the **Provincial Law** <note>original: *Ius Provinciale*</note>, having the year before established both orders of delegates, which they even now call the **Small and Large Committees** <note>original: *den Kleinen und Grossen Ausschuß*</note>. He brought to order **Wolfgang, Master of the Teutonic Order**, who had occupied the city of **Ellwangen**. He also compelled **Claude Francis, Lord of Rye**, who had seized the castle and town of **Héricourt** by force, to restore them. He magnificently built and completed ten castles. 

In the year 1568, on the 28th of December, having passed away in a blessed death, he paid his debt to nature. He was a Prince tossed by various misfortunes from his boyhood, and treated as if he were a "stepchild of fortune." <note>original: *fortunæ velut alter privignus*</note>. Nevertheless, he was highly cultivated in letters, skilled in languages, renowned for his experience, incomparable in his prudence, and unbroken by dangers.

# WÜRTTEMBERG HISTORY

[...declaring] that he would sooner kiss the sandals of a priest <note>original: "se Sacerdotis crepidas basiaturum"</note>. By his own example, he persuaded others, and especially the **Count of Fürstenberg**, to refuse this shameful and servile obedience. In the year 1542, having returned from **France** to **Germany**, he was preparing an expedition against the **Turks** in **Pannonia** <note>A region covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>, but at the wish of his father, who was now elderly and in poor health, he changed his plan and went to the court of **Duke William of Bavaria**. Two years later, he took as his wife **Anna Maria**, the daughter of **George the Pious, Margrave of Brandenburg**, with whom he celebrated his wedding in **Ansbach** <note>Latin: "Onoldini"</note> in the year 1544. He brought her to **Montbéliard** <note>Latin: "Mompelgartum," a Württemberg territory in present-day France</note>, where, as his father wished, he had established his residence.

When his father returned to the Emperor’s favor, Christopher steadfastly rejected the "buskin of religion" <note>original: "Cothurnum Religionis"; a theatrical metaphor for the religious compromise forced upon the Protestants</note>, which they called the **Interim** <note>The Augsburg Interim (1548), a decree ordering Protestants to re-adopt Catholic practices while a general council was pending.</note>.

In the year 1555, he was the first to promulgate **Provincial Law**, having established the year before both orders of the Elect, which they still call the **Small and Large Committees** <note>German: "den Kleinen und Grossen Ausschuß"</note>. 

He brought **Wolfgang**, Grand Master of the **Teutonic Order**, who had occupied the city of **Ellwangen**, back into order. He compelled **Claude-François of Neuchâtel, Lord of Rye**, who had captured the citadel and town of **Héricourt** by force, to return them through military action. He magnificently built and completed ten castles. 

On the 28th of December in the year 1568, having died a blessed death, he paid his debt to Nature—a Prince who from boyhood had been tossed about by various misfortunes, and treated by fortune as if he were a stepchild. Nevertheless, he was highly educated in literature, skilled in languages, renowned for his experience, incomparable in prudence, and unbroken by dangers.

# LOUIS, FIFTH DUKE OF WÜRTTEMBERG AND TECK,

Born to his father Duke Christopher of Württemberg and Anna Maria, Margravine of Brandenburg, in **Stuttgart** on the first of January after six in the evening, in the year 1554. His godparents were the delegates of the Provincial Estates <note>The representative body of the region's nobility, clergy, and towns.</note>, who presented him with a gilded bowl worth 250 florins, inside of which were placed 1,000 <note>The Latin text uses "clɔ," an archaic Roman numeral for 1,000.</note> Rhenish gold coins. As a boy, he was placed under the guardianship of **Wolfgang, Count Palatine**; **George Frederick of Brandenburg**; and **Charles of Baden**. He had as his tutor **Andreas Laubmayer** of Stuttgart, who instructed him in the liberal arts. Meanwhile, until he reached adulthood, **Henry, Count of Castell**, served as Pro-Duke <note>A regent or acting governor.</note>. He took up the reins of the state's government in the year 1571, having previously been appointed the Supreme Head of the **Swabian Circle** <note>One of the administrative districts of the Holy Roman Empire, of which the Duke of Württemberg was a primary leader.</note>. In the year 1577, he joined himself in marriage to **Dorothea**, daughter of Charles, Margrave of Hachberg and Baden; the wedding was celebrated on the seventh day of November. In the same year, 1577, amidst great applause, he celebrated the jubilee <note>The 100th anniversary of the university's founding in 1477.</note> of the **University of Tübingen**, where he prepared a solemn banquet for the professors. In the year 1583, he lost his wife, taken by a fatal stroke <note>original: "fatali ictu"</note>, in **Nuremberg** on the very feast of Pentecost. On May 10, 1585, he celebrated his second marriage to **Ursula**, daughter of George John, Count Palatine of Lützelstein—

<header>LETTERS</header>

He was born <note>Referring to Frederick I, Duke of Württemberg.</note> not on July 11, as **Crusius** <note>Martin Crusius (1526–1607), a renowned humanist and historian at the University of Tübingen.</note> holds, but on August 19 in the year 1557 at **Montbéliard** <note>original: "Mompelgarti"; a county in eastern France held by the House of Württemberg.</note>. He was first raised by his mother at **Riquewihr** <note>original: "Richovillæ"; a town in Alsace.</note>, and soon after by his paternal relative **Duke Christopher**. In the year 1568, he was summoned to **Stuttgart** and educated together with **Duke Louis**. In the year 1573, he served as the Rector of the **University of Tübingen**. In the year 1578, he came into mortal danger through treachery. In the year 1580, having traveled through **Swabia, Bavaria, Bohemia**, and both **Saxonies**, he penetrated into **Denmark, Silesia, and Moravia**, as well as both **Pannonias** <note>Upper and Lower Hungary.</note>.

In the year 1586, as an ambassador of the German Princes, he went to **France** with **Wolfgang, Count of Isenburg**; and in the same year, he established the **Colloquy of Montbéliard** <note>A significant theological debate between Lutheran and Reformed (Calvinist) theologians, notably Jakob Andreae and Theodore Beza.</note> between the adherents of the **Augsburg Confession** and the ministers of the Swiss and Genevan Churches. Two years later, the **Marquis of Pont-à-Mousson** <note>Charles of Lorraine.</note> and the **Duke of Guise** <note>Henry I, Duke of Guise, a leader of the Catholic League.</note>, along with their allies, poured their soldiery into the **County of Montbéliard**, where they raged with every kind of lust, cruelty, and greed; approximately 300 villages were consumed by fire, an injustice about which **Frederick** complained to the **Emperor** <note>original: "Cæsari." Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>. One may consult **Meteren** and **Thuanus** <note>Emanuel van Meteren and Jacques Auguste de Thou, prominent contemporary historians.</note> regarding this year. Likewise, he was present at the **Baden Colloquy** in the month of November, 1599. He published the **Formula of Concord** <note>The authoritative doctrinal statement of the Lutheran Church.</note> anew, with his own preface attached.

Having become Duke in the year 1593, he set out the following year with a splendid retinue for the **Diet of Regensburg** <note>original: "Comitia Ratisbonensia."</note> and entered the city on the 20th day of June. He afterwards confirmed the privileges of the **University of Tübingen** and of the provincial estates. He constructed fortresses and princely houses at **Heidenheim, Backnang, Calw, Neuenbürg, Neustadt**, and **Tübingen**. He founded the town of **Freudenstadt** in the **Black Forest** <note>original: "Martianâ sylvâ."</note>, establishing there a church of remarkable structure. He also built a sacred building and a college at **Montbéliard**. WÜRTTEMBERG LETTERS

## LETTER XVIII.

->*Reverend and Most Illustrious Lord Doctor,*<-

I never learn the contents of your letters without a certain sense of shame and modesty. For in them, you always attribute something to me—and indeed with a generous hand <note>original: "longa manu"; a Latin idiom suggesting both a reach from afar and a lavishness in praise or giving.</note>—which I can hardly find within myself. Nevertheless, you achieve this: that the goal at which I ought to aim is placed more frequently before my eyes, to be reached at last. But you do not follow my progress with letters alone; you also add gifts most welcome by far. Indeed, I have duly received the little book <note>original: "Libellum"; common terminology for a small scholarly or devotional treatise.</note> recently published by you, and from its very title, which puts forward the **Friendship of God** <note>original: "amicitiam Dei"; likely a reference to a specific contemporary theological work on divine grace or mysticism.</note>, I have judged its excellence. I confess myself bound to you for many reasons, both by this gift itself and by your affection, which is so pious and so constant. Therefore, count firmly on my reciprocation of these feelings, and fare most excellently.

->Yours, devoted to Your Reverend Dignity.<-

Tübingen, May 9,
1649.

->Your devoted servant,<-
->**JOHN FREDERICK**<-
->*Duke of Württemberg and Teck.*<-

## LETTER XIX.

->Reverend and Most Distinguished Lord Doctor.<-

You have chosen most illustrious couriers for your letters, and splendid ones beyond my expectation. Namely, three Princes of our Germany, and especially the pre-eminent jewels of the House of Guelph <note>The House of Guelph (Welf) was one of the oldest and most powerful European dynasties; the "jewels" likely refer to portraits or engravings of specific princes sent by the recipient.</note>. They will be guests most welcome by far to me, and wherever they may reside in person, the memory of them will always remain with me. Truly I give you fresh thanks, because you urge me toward Virtue <term>Virtue: in this context, "Virtus" implies not just moral goodness but the excellence, courage, and duty expected of a high-ranking nobleman.</term> not only with words but also with images. I shall see to it that your concern for my growth is never in vain. To this end, I shall entreat God in pious prayers that He may keep us safe for a long time. May you help me with your support, and fare well.

To Your Reverence.
Tübingen, May 23, 1649.

->With Respect:<-
->JOHN FREDERICK<-
->Duke of Württemberg.<-

## Letter 418.

### To Prince Anton Ulrich, many greetings.

->Most Illustrious and High-Born Prince, my most merciful Lord,<-

I have seen nothing from you since the third of April <note>original: "tertio Non. Aprilis."</note>, a delay that feels far too long for me given my longing for your letters, which never fail to bring something of great substance and wit. And what shall I say of your brother, Lord Rudolph August, from whom I have received nothing since the seventeenth of February? <note>original: "13. Cal. Martii."</note> Indeed, I count that silence as almost a full year. 

Lest you should abandon this literary exchange, I have decided to lead you back to the path with this message of mine. Along with it, I have sent a small gift: a depiction of Michelangelo Buonarroti’s *Last Judgment* <note>original: "Judicium extremum."</note>. It is in a larger format than is commonly found, created in imitation of that work which is viewed with such admiration in the Pope’s Chapel <note>The Sistine Chapel in Rome.</note> in Rome; I have no doubt it has reached you. 

I was also delighted to hear that the musical organ, which I dedicated at the altar of gratitude in the Great Temple <note>original: "Augusto Templo."</note>, has been well-received. Regarding this, I wish to comment further for your benefit and in memory of the craftsman. The inventor of this machine was Conrad Schott of Stuttgart, that famous <term>Organ-builder: "Organopœus," a specialist craftsman who designs and constructs pipe organs.</term> who, though he completely lost his sight to smallpox <note>original: "Variolorum morbo."</note> as a young boy, so compensated for it with his natural genius that he was more capable than any Argus <note>A reference to Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek mythology; Andreae is saying the blind craftsman "saw" better with his mind than those with many eyes.</note>...

*...but more sharp-eyed <note>original: "oculatior." Referring to the spiritual or intellectual vision of the blind man mentioned on the previous page.</note>. Indeed, he worked not so much with his intellect as with his hands, more by night than by day, because with his weak eyes he could easily endure neither the light of the sun nor of a torch. However, he had as the chief craftsman of his inventions one Jacob Ganser <note>original: "Iacobum Ganserum"</note>, born in the village of Laubach <note>A small village in the Oberkirchen district.</note>, which belongs to the lordship of Oberkirchen. He was born to a peasant father and laborer in humble circumstances, but possessed an equally incomparable and plainly noble talent, so that in generous emulation he did not so much follow his blind master as he might have been said to surpass him, had he himself not possessed sight; certainly, whatever the former devised, the latter expressed even more successfully and perfectly, so that you might doubt whether to wonder more at the blind speculations of the one or the skillfully finished works of the other. Having first been taught to make windows, he moved on to cabinet-making, and finally emerged as an organ builder <term>Organopæus: a specialist in the construction of pipe organs</term>. I knew both men as friends; the latter even lived in my home for half a year when he was repairing the public organ at Calw in 1628. There, in the sacred building itself, he almost perished when he was lightly struck by lightning. He was a man whose face and body suggested nothing great; he was no boaster or seeker of self-esteem, sparing in food and drink, most greedy of his time, and a most fair seller of his labor, which he was uniquely anxious to prove in good faith. Moreover, just as his intellect encompassed and flitted through everything, so was his hand skilled in various crafts. And although he was admired by all, he was never satisfied with himself—to such an extent that, had he fallen into the world of letters, he might perhaps have become the founder of some sect. However, since his circumstances at home were rather narrow, he lacked an Augustus or a Maecenas <note>The Roman statesman Maecenas was the famous patron of Horace and Virgil; Andreae uses the name here to mean any wealthy sponsor of the arts.</note>. Likely referring to the devastating outbreaks during the Thirty Years' War.</note> along with his entire family on August 26, 1635. This was a great loss to the citizens of Cannstatt <note>original: "Canstadiæ," a district of modern Stuttgart.</note>, where he had settled, because of his modest and easy character and his growing fame in his art. He left me with the greatest sense of loss, for I was entirely intent on transferring the man to Calw,*

I humbly congratulate him on this, I rejoice from my heart, and I pray from my soul that this journey has contributed to his growth in Virtue and Science, and that he may achieve even greater things hereafter. I judge Theophilus <note>Likely referring to Andreae's own work, *Theophilus*, or a personification of a "God-lover."</note> happy to have been admitted by you; he will be happier still if you take him into your protection and your embrace; and if you should even approve of him, he will be the happiest of all. The *Selenianae Augustalia* <note>A work by Andreae dedicated to Duke August the Younger, whose pseudonym was "Selene."</note> are even now in port after a long voyage; soon, with God’s grace, they will revisit you, their authors, so that you may look upon yourselves in that splendid mirror of Illustrious elegance and humanity. Farewell, most Illustrious and most United brothers, and look with favor [upon me].*

->To your Illustrious Highnesses,<-
->Your most humble client,<-
->Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor of Theology.<-

*To those of your household who greet me and wish me well, I return the same with interest.*
*Stuttgart, June 13, 1649.*

->To the most Reverend and<-
->most Distinguished Sir,<-

We have seen those things which your diligent hand has culled for us from the most pleasant gardens of the "Treasure" <note>original: "Thesauri." A reference to the rhetorician Emanuele Tesauro, punning on his name meaning "treasure."</note> for our use and delight; from these, one may conjecture what else is displayed in them, or what still lies hidden within. Truly, they possess a most sweet spirit, though for one to scent it correctly, he must be of a more refined nose <note>original: "emunctioris naris." A Latin idiom meaning one must have sharp discernment or sophisticated taste.</note>. We, meanwhile, admire not so much the buds as the soil itself; indeed, we consider that these were produced not by the effort of a single man, but by the mutual and untiring labor of many. But if indeed God has granted such great powers to one man, we acknowledge His kindness and celebrate it with a grateful proclamation of praise. We would like to know—since it has not yet been permitted to look deeply into the flowerbeds—whether exotic things are contained there, and those which might perhaps disturb with a heavy odor. Even if this be the case, we do not doubt that they could at least provide a pleasing spectacle for the eyes. If you wish to attach any of those things to our own, it will be welcomed; we too shall labor to add something from time to time to what has been successfully begun, so far as our meager ability <note>A conventional expression of humility common in 17th-century aristocratic correspondence.</note> permits us. We see that our household also burns with love for your *Theophilus* <note>Referring to Andreae's work *Theophilus*, a dialogue on Christian education and piety.</note>; he will find us, in turn, favorable and admirers of his hidden learning as soon as he appears. Meanwhile, we offer you whatever services are in our power and bid you to be in the very best of health. At Wolfenbüttel, the 22nd day of May, 1649.

### I.

# Johann Valentin Andreae, Doctor 
# of Sacred Theology, etc.

->Through an anagram, with an added breathing mark <note>original: "per ἀναγραμμα addit. aspir." The "aspiration" refers to the letter 'h' added to the letters of his name to make the following wordplay work.</note><-
->When he had reached his seventh Climacteric <note>The "climacteric" was a concept in early modern medicine and astrology where every seventh year of life (7, 14, 21, etc.) was seen as a critical turning point. The 49th year (7 x 7) was considered especially significant.</note>,<-
->God granting.<-

->Ah! Is not this leader <note>original: "hierarcha," referring to his high ecclesiastical rank.</note> and<-
->theologian of ours to be called immortal <note>original: "atanatos," from the Greek "athanatos" (deathless).</note><-
->after death?<-

That there is something divine, and not fully fathomable,
In numbers, the vast machinery of the world persuades us—
A world driven by numbers, and held together by numbers.
It is no wonder, then, that throughout all ages,
Some years are healthy while others are more dangerous than the rest.
Above all are those we might call "sacred,"
By which we climb as if by specific stairs and steps <note>A play on the word "climacteric," which comes from the Greek "klimax," meaning a ladder.</note>,
And are carried forward ever closer to death.
These we also call the "Ladder-years," forerunners of death
And old age; in them, a certain change
And significant shifts always occur in our bodies,
And our strength, weakened by time, creeps away.
Thus, we grow teeth in the first <note>Age 7.</note>, we reach puberty in the second <note>Age 14.</note>,
The third <note>Age 21.</note> covers our cheeks with an unfamiliar downy beard,
And something new always approaches, until having progressed
To our peak <note>original: "ἀκμην" (akme), meaning the prime or highest point of life.</note>, we ourselves gradually decline again
Toward the final span of life and the late grave,
While meanwhile, diseases and deaths draw near in a thousand ways:

It is asked whether Andreae—who is also Johann Valentin—has

## VII.

## Johann Valentin Andreae,
### Doctor of Sacred Theology.

->*Anagram.*<-
->Do you not hold it? In the Theology of Jesus<-
->you shine greatly.<- <note>original Latin anagram: "Johannes Valentinus Andree" rearranged to "Nonne tenes? in Theologia Jhesu valde radias." Anagrams were a popular 17th-century intellectual game used to reveal a person's "true" nature.</note>

**HE** who deserved to live the years of ancient Nestor <note>Nestor was a legendary Greek king known for his wisdom and great age.</note>
*And to see the ages of old Methuselah,* <note>The biblical figure said to have lived 969 years.</note>
Today Andreae happily approaches
*Sixty-three years: Glory to God alone.*
He must certainly be congratulated with prayers, just as once
*The law-giving Augustus of the Empire did for himself,* <note>The Roman Emperor Augustus famously celebrated surviving his 63rd year, which was considered the most dangerous "climacteric" or turning point in a man's life.</note>
When he had overcome the fatal force of the "climbing year,"
*And had prayed for more time to be given to him,*

<summary>This page contains poetic tributes to Johann Valentin Andreae, marking his 62nd and 63rd birthdays with references to his endurance of worldly suffering and his survival of the "grand climacteric" year.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Valentin Andreae, Johann Heinrich Faber, Marcus Dolmetsch, Augsburg, St. Ulrich, 63rd birthday, grand climacteric, Augustus, Nestor, Methuselah, anagram</keywords>

*Now, since this same longed-for time has come,*
*We weave this prayer for him from the heart.*
*Just as the beginning of the climbing year shone with light,* <note>original: "scansilis Anni." This refers to the progression of the year or the "ascending" milestone of a birthday.</note>
*May the end likewise pass joyfully and without clouds.*
*Live long, venerable Old Man; may your lively life*
*Breathe honorably on the earth: breathe honorably in the Heavens.* <note>original: "Polo," literally the celestial pole, used poetically to mean the sky or the dwelling of God.</note>

->Out of favor, honor, and love,<-
->And also<-
->As a good omen,<-
->from<-
->Master Johann Joachim Schüele,<-
->Colleague and Godfather.<-
->Master Christopher Zeller,<-
->Colleague, Relative, and Godfather.<-
->Master Johann Schmidt,<-
->Pastor at St. Leonard’s.<-

### VIII.

**IN** vain, Sculptor, do you paint the white hair and serene brow,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;though using a tool however skillful.
In vain you carve the radiant eyes and the closed chest:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In vain does Art, nature's rival, attempt the work.
A mind whiter than snow lies hidden within, and the brow is open:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And who could ever paint that lynx-like vision? <note>original: "Lyncejamque aciem." In mythology, the lynx was famed for sight so sharp it could see through solid objects; here it refers to Andreae's intellectual or spiritual insight.</note>
Who [could paint] a more sincere heart, open and without deceit? <note>original: "sine fuco," literally "without dye/makeup," meaning genuine or without pretension.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Even Momus <note>The Greek god of satire and mockery, known for finding fault in everything.</note> has nothing he might easily criticize.
A bright mind, and a gentle character within the man:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;These things alone have the power to truly adorn the Man.

->Added out of<-
->owed honor and love by<-
->Peter Meuderlin,<-
->Superintendent of the St. Anne Gymnasium<- <note>A prestigious school in Augsburg founded during the Reformation.</note>
->at Augsburg.<-

# ON THE SELENIANUM,

->Stay a while, Guest, and Read!<-

**WHOSOEVER** has entered this **SELENIANUM**, <note>original: "Selenianum." A name given to a building or room in honor of Duke August the Younger of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who used the pseudonym "Gustavus Selenus" (the "Moon" prince).</note>
Consider the Name from which it is attached to this place:
That **SELENUS**, the Glory of the Princes of the Earth,
The Eye of Brunswick, **AUGUSTUS** most August, <note>original: "Augustus Augustissimus." A play on the Duke's name, August, and the Latin title for an emperor, "Augustus," meaning venerable or majestic.</note>
Indulged his dear **VALENTIN ANDREAE** so much,
Out of his most excellent Generosity,
That he claimed these splendid buildings for himself;
Which **HE** <note>Referring to Andreae.</note> decorates with all kinds of paintings,
And adorns with whatever Elegancies he can;
Among which is the Gift of **AUGUSTUS** Himself—
**AUGUSTUS** Himself, depicted in this Image, <note>original: "Agalmate." Derived from the Greek word for a statue or a cult image dedicated to a god.</note>
Stands out upon the threshold of this Dining Hall, <note>original: "TriclinI." Traditionally a Roman dining room, used here to denote a formal reception room or hall.</note>
Receiving visitors along with a Trio of Princes. <note>original: "Ternione." This refers to Duke August's three sons: Rudolph Augustus, Anton Ulrich, and Ferdinand Albert.</note>
To the glory of the Illustrious House of Brunswick, <note>original: "Brunoniæ." The Latinized name for the territory of Brunswick.</note>
So that you might rightly call it the Sanctuary of **AUGUSTUS**,
Which is consecrated to his own nourishing Name.
Pray, therefore, for the best of lives for him,
Together with that great Trio of Sons;
And likewise, perpetual Happiness for the Host, <note>The host being Johann Valentin Andreae.</note>
Whosoever looks upon this **SELENIANUM**:
Thus enter joyful, and depart with good peace!

<vocab>Selenianum (The Moon-House/Hall), Selenus (The Moon-Prince/Duke August), Brunsvvigi (of Brunswick), Augustus (Venerable/August), Valenti Andreio (to Valentin Andreae), Agalmate (Image/Statue), TriclinI (Dining Hall/Reception Room), Ternione (Trio/Group of Three), Brunonia (Brunswick)</vocab>

### LETTER I.

->*Most Reverend and Most Distinguished Sir,*<-

Time slips away so gradually and unexpectedly that its path can scarcely be noticed. You do well, however, to rouse me from this lethargy and call me toward the proposed goal. It would have been more fitting to prick me with spurs than to soothe me with a small gift; thus, with shame, I now see how careless and thoughtless a procrastinator I have been. 

That sharply drawn page concerning the resurrection of the dead <note>original: "resurrectione mortuorum"</note>, which you mention, I received not long ago from our most Gracious Lady Mother <note>original: "Clem: Dn. Matre nostra." This likely refers to a royal or noble patroness, possibly the Duchess Mother of Württemberg.</note>. I do not know where it originated. I have long possessed the same in a smaller format and of the most perfect craftsmanship; indeed, unless the Author <term>Author</term><note>The word "Auctor" here refers to the artist or engraver of the print.</note> himself were to sign his name, it could rightly be substituted for another. 

Diligence produced it. The imitation is so elegantly deceptive that it brings before the eyes the blessed living here in eternal delights, while the damned truly endure the most exquisite tortures of hell. As for the works of great art, as they say, of your blind Organ-maker <term>Organ-maker</term><note>original: "Organarii." This could refer to either a builder of pipe organs or a musician. In this period, blind organists were often renowned for their exceptional memory and hearing.</note>, I have not yet had the opportunity to see them. However, I easily place my trust in you and in those things which we have heard from public report—that is, the talk of the common people. I marvel at the dispensation and compensation of Nature, which has abundantly returned to this man in other areas what she took from his eyes...

<vocab>resurrection of the dead, Organ-makers, Nature, imitation</vocab>

<summary>In this opening letter, the author apologizes for his procrastination and discusses artistic works, specifically a detailed engraving of the Resurrection and the reputed skill of a blind organ-maker.</summary>
<keywords>correspondence, Resurrection of the Dead, engraving, art criticism, organ builder, Nature’s compensation</keywords>
